etymologies: From the surname of George Babbitt, the title character of the novel Babbitt (1922) by the American author Sinclair Lewis (1885–1951). The word was also popularized by the George (1898–1937) and Ira Gershwin (1896–1983) song “The Babbitt and the Bromide”, first featured in the 1927 musical Funny Face and later in the film Ziegfeld Follies (1945).
See babbitt.

definitions.text: A surname.
A city in Saint Louis County, Minnesota, United States.
A person who subscribes complacently to materialistic middle-class ideals.

examples: Running while low on oil had galled the babbitt.
definitions.text: Ellipsis of babbitt metal or Babbitt metal (“a soft white alloy of variable composition used in bearings to diminish friction”).

examples: The main bearings were babbitted and line-bored.
definitions.text: To line (something) with babbitt metal to reduce friction.

quotations.passage: One speaks of a babbitt habit, a babbitt era. Nothing is more true. America recognized itself in Babbitt, it demurred, but it also admired.

quotations.author: James Truslow Adams
quotations.passage: The top and bottom are spiritually and intellectually nearer together in America than in most countries, but there are plenty of Babbitts everywhere.
If there's one thing I can't stand, it's a Babbitt. Say, there's nothing more wonderful than defying middle-class conventions.

quotations.author: Saul Bellow
quotations.passage: I myself think that Doc overdid the Yankee Doodle stuff. Being a Babbitt inspired him almost the way Swinburne did me. He was dying to say goodbye to Jewry, or to feudalism.

quotations.author: William Hyland
quotations.passage: Ira relished telling the story that Fred Astaire took him aside and said he knew what a babbitt was, but what was a bromide?

quotations.author: Phillip G. Payne
quotations.passage: In this sense Harding was a Babbitt. Intellectuals and journalists rejected Harding as being as empty as the Sinclair Lewis character.
quotations.work: Dead last: the public memory of Warren G. Harding's scandalous legacy

quotations.author: John Underwood
quotations.passage: Figure 2 represents a top plan of the "Babbitting" jig, placed in or upon a cast-iron frame, preparatory to the pouring or casting of the "Babbitt" or other soft metal on to or around its journals, to form journal bearings in said cast-iron frame.

quotations.author: June
quotations.passage: The cross-head is cast of crucible steel and faced with Babbitt. […] The rod is secured to the crank pin by body bound bolts, this bearing being provided with Babbitt shells which are prevented from turning by paper liners extending to the pin.

quotations.author: Robert C. Juvinall
quotations.passage: The most common bearing materials are Babbitts, both tin-base (as 89% Sn, 8% Pb, 3% Cu) and lead-base (as 75% Pb, 15% Sb, 10% Sn), and copper alloys, primarily copper lead, leaded bronze, tin bronze, and aluminium bronze. […] The Babbitts are unexcelled in conformability and embeddability, but they have relatively low compressive and fatigue strength, particularly above about 77°C (170°F). Babbitts can seldom be used above about 121°C (250°F).

Babbitt.title: Babbitt

etymologies: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Χάρυβδις (Khárubdis).

definitions.text: A dangerous whirlpool on the coast of Sicily opposite Scylla on the Italian coast.
A personification of the above whirlpool as a female monster.
Any dangerous whirlpool.
A dangerous whirlpool on the coast of Sicily opposite Scylla on the Italian coast.
A personification of the above whirlpool as a female monster.
Any dangerous whirlpool.

quotations.author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon
quotations.passage: I have never yet been able to steer my lovers through the Scylla of presence, or the Charybdis of absence.
quotations.work: Ethel Churchill: Or, The Two Brides.

quotations.author: Sir Thomas Herbert
quotations.passage: …that night, wee sailed merrily by the Mascarenas, a Charybdis in 21 degrees, var.13 and 17 minutes…
quotations.work: Some yeares travels into divers parts of Asia and Afrique

quotations.author: James Bell
quotations.passage: The tide here sets in alternately from N. to S. and from S. to N., which causes the whirlpool of Galofaro, the Charybdis of the ancients.
quotations.work: A system of geography, popular and scientific

Charybdis.title: Charybdis

etymologies: Borrowed from Latin Corybās, from Ancient Greek Κορύβᾱς (Korúbās).

definitions.text: Alternative spelling of Korybant.

Corybant.title: Corybant

etymologies: From Latin Daedalus, from Ancient Greek Δαίδαλος (Daídalos).

definitions.text: Greek mythological figure who crafted the waxen wings of Icarus.
Project Daedalus: A scheme for an interstellar probe that would use fusion rockets.

Daedalus.title: Daedalus

etymologies: From Latin, from Ancient Greek Ἠλῠ́σῐον (Πεδῐ́ον) (Ēlŭ́sĭon (Pedĭ́on)).

definitions.text: The home of the blessed after death.
A place or state of ideal happiness; paradise.
A region in the northern hemisphere of Mars.

quotations.author: Emily Brontë
quotations.passage: Joseph seemed sitting in a sort of elysium alone, beside a roaring fire; a quart of ale on the table near him, bristling with large pieces of toasted oat-cake; and his black, short pipe in his mouth.

quotations.author: Jeffrey Goldberg
quotations.passage: Not since a journalist morphed into Al Pacino in The Devil’s Advocate has a metamorphosis been so jarring. Of course, there were clues: Michael kicked a puppy in the very second episode, and no self-respecting Elysium so closely resembles a chichi outdoor mall in Pasadena.

Elysium.title: Elysium

etymologies: From Hobson + -’s + choice, widely claimed to have been named after Thomas Hobson (c. 1544–1631) of Cambridge, England, who rented horses and had an extensive stable, but is said to have required each customer to take the horse in the stall closest to the door, to prevent the best horses from always being chosen and becoming overused.

The Oxford English Dictionary also suggests an alternative etymology based on a 1607 work, The Pleasant Conceites of Old Hobson, which refers to one William Hobson (died 1581), a haberdasher from London, who is said to have been unable to recognize his own horse, and so had the habit of waiting at stables until other people had claimed their horses as the one remaining had to be his. This story is most likely fictional as it is identical to one entitled “Of the Two Yong Men that Rode to Walsingham” in Mery Tales and Quick Answeres (1530).

definitions.text: A situation where a person is presented with the illusion of a free choice, but in reality there is only one option available: accepting the offer or having nothing at all.
A choice between several undesirable options; Sophie's choice.
The voice.

quotations.author: John Ray
quotations.passage: A man is said to have Hobsons choice given him, vvhen he must either take vvhat is left him, or choose vvhether he vvill have any part or no.

quotations.author: James Fenimore Cooper
quotations.passage: Several other marriages took place, the scarcity of subjects making it somewhat hazardous to delay: when Hobson's choice is placed before one, deliberation is of no great use.
quotations.work: The Crater; or, Vulcan’s Peak. A Tale of the Pacific.

quotations.author: George Bernard Shaw
quotations.passage: In other words, they might go to the devil and starve—Hobson's choice!—for all the other factories were owned by men who offered no better terms.

quotations.author: Stephen King
quotations.passage: This Hobson’s choice is the beating heart of "Raymond Carver: A Writer's Life." Any writer might wonder what he'd do in such a case.
quotations.work: The New York Times Book Review

quotations.author: Lawrence Wright
quotations.passage: Such Hobson's choices are the stuff of high drama, but unfortunately for poor, lovely Lebanon it is a tragedy that never seems to end.

quotations.author: Stephen King
quotations.passage: "Hobson's Choice." He was still stroking Radar, long glides of his hand from nape to tail. "In the end, it seems to me that one or two good months are better than six bad ones. If it works at all, that is."

quotations.author: Ray Galton
quotations.passage: He's claiming copyright on his hobson's. / I beg your pardon. / His hobson's choice—his voice.

Hobson’s_choice.title: Hobson's choice

definitions.text: Alternative spelling of casbah.

etymologies: From Biblical Hebrew מְתוּשֶׁלַח (Məṯûšelaḥ), also spelled מְתוּשָׁלַח (Məṯûšālaḥ). The planet's name stems from the fact that, at the time of its discovery in 2003, it was the oldest known planet.

definitions.text: The oldest person whose age is recorded in the Hebrew Bible, having reportedly lived 969 years.

A planet in the PSR B1620-26 star system, Messier 4 globular cluster, Milky Way Galaxy, Scorpius constellation; a circumbinary planet, officially named PSR B1620-26 b, orbiting a pulsar (“PSR B1620-26 A”) and white dwarf (“WD B1620-26 B”).
Any person or thing that has lived to a very old age.
A large wine bottle with the capacity of about 6 liters, equivalent to 8 standard bottles.
A small pattern that takes many generations to stabilize.

quotations.passage: And Methuselah lived an hundred eighty and seven years, and begat Lamech: And Methuselah lived after he begat Lamech seven hundred eighty and two years, and begat sons and daughters:

quotations.author: Paul Callahan
quotations.passage: The first known methuselah was the r pentomino, but even longer lasting ones have been found by enumerating and testing small patterns. The following, called "rabbits," takes over 10000 generations to stabilize.

quotations.author: Michael Hedera
quotations.passage: Is there somewhere a list of n-cell methuselah patterns in Conway's Life? (assuming some reasonable limits on the bounding box)

quotations.author: Andrzej Megier
quotations.passage: The pattern below seems to take about 30000 generations to stabilize. The initial population is 20. Is this methuselah a known one?

Methuselah.title: Methuselah

etymologies: From modern + -ism.

definitions.text: Modern or contemporary ideas, thought, practices, etc.
Anything that is characteristic of modernity.
Any of several styles of art, architecture, literature, philosophy, etc., that flourished in the 20th century.
A religious movement in the early 20th century, condemned as heretical by Pope Pius X, which tried to reconcile Roman Catholic dogma with modern science and philosophy.

quotations.author: Cullen Murphy
quotations.passage: Penrod is so referential as to be almost a work of postmodernism—assuming Tarkington could have imagined such a thing with modernism itself just beginning to steamroll over him.

Modernism.title: modernism

etymologies: Named after the English Franciscan theologist William of Occam, an advocate of the law of parsimony, and the idea of a razor as a tool that trims or shaves.

definitions.text: The principle of preferring the simplest of competing theories.

quotations.author: Burning Beard
quotations.passage: Bugger, bugger, bugger dumb the last of academe / Occam's razor makes the cutting clean / Shaven like a banker, Lilac Vegeta

Occam’s_razor.title: Occam's razor

etymologies: From post- + modernism.

definitions.text: Any style in art, architecture, literature, philosophy, etc., that reacts against an earlier modernist movement.
An attitude of skepticism or irony toward modernist ideologies, often questioning the assumptions of Enlightenment rationality and rejecting the idea of objective truth.

quotations.author: Daniel Gordon
quotations.passage: The most famous definition of postmodernism is Lyotard's: “I define postmodern as incredulity towards metanarratives.” […] To accept Lyotard's definition of postmodernism is to accept the premise that postmodernism is the first movement since the Enlightenment to think critically about such narratives.

Postmodernism.title: postmodernism

definitions.text: Synonym of Rube Goldberg machine.

etymologies: From Latin Scylla, from Ancient Greek Σκύλλα (Skúlla).

definitions.text: A taxonomic genus within the family Portunidae – mud crab, mangrove crab.

A dangerous rock on the Italian coast opposite the whirlpool Charybdis on the coast of Sicily. The passage between Scylla and Charybdis was formerly considered perilous; hence, the saying between Scylla and Charybdis signifies a great peril on either hand.
A personification of said rock as a ravenous monster.
A princess, daughter of King Nisos of Megara, who fell in love with King Minos and betrayed her city to him.
The main belt asteroid 155 Scylla.

quotations.author: Alexander Pope
quotations.passage: Ah cease rash Youth! desist e'er 'tis too late, / Fear the just Gods, and think of Scylla′s Fate!

quotations.author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon
quotations.passage: I have never yet been able to steer my lovers through the Scylla of presence, or the Charybdis of absence.
quotations.work: Ethel Churchill: Or, The Two Brides.

Scylla.title: Scylla

etymologies: From New Latin, from Old Norse Valhǫll (from valr (“dead warriors”) +‎ hǫll (“hall”)).

definitions.text: The home of half of all warriors who died gloriously in battle as well as many of the Æsir.
A hamlet and census-designated place in the town of Mount Pleasant, Westchester County, New York, United States.
An abode of the gods or afterlife in general.

quotations.author: Moore's Inquiry into the Subject of Suicide
quotations.passage: [S]uch souls as were detruded from the body by any violent method went strait to Valhalla. (Latin original: Nostratibus sane hoc erat infallibiliter persuasum, animas, non vulgares, neque senio morbove, sec cruenta morte & vi corporibus exeuntes, recta ad Vahlallam ferri)

quotations.author: Carolyne Larrington
quotations.passage: In some poems they are envisaged as divine figures, women who serve mead to the dead warriors in Valhall, and who fulfil the will of Odin in overseeing battle and making sure that victory is awarded to the right man.

quotations.author: Shannon Liao
quotations.passage: So it’s hardly a surprise that the “Call of Duty” and “Assassin’s Creed” franchises put out new releases this week. “Assassin’s Creed Valhalla,” about Vikings and Norse mythology, debuted on November 10, the same day as the Xbox Series X. Three days later, “Call of Duty: Black Ops Cold War,” set in the 1980s, was released.

quotations.author: Ray Sanchez and Ben Brumfield
quotations.passage: Investigators are not sure why the woman’s Mercedes SUV stopped on the tracks Tuesday night in Valhalla, about 30 miles north of New York City, National Transportation Safety Board Member Robert Sumwalt said Wednesday.

quotations.author: Lord Dunsany
quotations.passage: “The swans are singing again,” said to one another the gods. And looking downwards, for my dreams had taken me to some fair and far Valhalla, I saw below me an iridescent bubble not greatly larger than a star shine beautifully but faintly, and up and up from it looking larger and larger came a flock of white, innumerable swans, singing and singing and singing, till it seemed as though even the gods were wild ships swimming in music.

quotations.author: Ernest Bramah
quotations.passage: That we possessed no Westminster Abbey must have touched his native pride somewhere, and he has set out to remove the slur by building and endowing a lordly private Valhalla on one of his seventeen estates for the last sleep of the great.

quotations.author: Tom Lehrer
quotations.passage: You will all go directly to your respective Valhallas / Go directly, do not pass 'GO', do not collect two hundred dollars

quotations.author: Jan Morris
quotations.passage: Like Philip's, Franco's autarchy was shrouded in religiosity—not Christianity alone, but also a sort of dim Wagnerian vision of hero-gods and Valhallas, a gloomy level of devotion on which paganism, Catholicism and the apotheosis of the State could conveniently be mingled.

Valhalla.title: Valhalla

etymologies: Unadapted borrowing from German Zeitgeist (literally “spirit of the age”).

definitions.text: The spirit of the age; the taste, outlook, and spirit characteristic of a period.

quotations.author: Martin Luther King Jr.
quotations.passage: She was anchored to that seat by the accumulated indignities of days gone by and the boundless aspirations of generations yet unborn. She was a victim of both the forces of history and the forces of destiny. She had been tracked down by the Zeitgeist—the spirit of the time.

quotations.author: Michael Vanden Heuvel
quotations.passage: After quickly summarizing the zeitgeisten of the Greek, Elizabethan, and early modern periods and their effects on the theatre, Rice turns to the contemporary world.
quotations.work: Elmer Rice: A Research and Production Sourcebook

quotations.author: Scott Timberg
quotations.passage: [Robert] Heinlein’s gift was to catch the zeitgeist. “That’s what made him so successful, but it makes his work seem dated.”

quotations.author: Anthony Faiola
quotations.passage: The vote also stoked fears that Swiss citizens were reflecting the zeitgeist across Europe, where right-wing populists increasingly are seizing the spotlight with an anti-immigration political agenda.

Zeitgeist.title: zeitgeist

etymologies: Unadapted borrowing from Latin ab initiō (“from the beginning”), from ab (“from”) + initiō, ablative singular of initium (“beginning”).

examples: As the Act was passed without the required quorum, the constitutional court struck down the Act and declared it to be void ab initio
definitions.text: From the time when a law, legal right or decree, contract, ownership interest, partnership (etc.) comes into force.
Calculated from first principles, i.e. from basic laws without any further additional assumptions.
Taken with no prior qualifications.

quotations.author: Parliament of India
quotations.passage: Any child marriage solemnised in contravention of an injunction order issued under section 13, whether interim or final, shall be void ab initio.

ab_initio.title: ab initio

etymologies: Learned borrowing from Latin ab ōvō (literally “from the egg”).

definitions.text: From the beginning.

quotations.author: Ludwig Büchner
quotations.passage: We should be led too far, nor would it possess sufficient interest for our readers, were we, in this place specially, to discuss this important and complicated question, and to show ab ovo why this notion has been rejected.
quotations.work: Force and Matter: Empirico-Philosophical Studies, Intelligibly Rendered

ab_ovo.title: ab ovo

etymologies: Attested from 1303, as Middle English abaisen, abaishen, abashen (“lose one's composure, be upset”), from the later 14th-century also transitive "to make ashamed, to perplex or embarrass"; from Anglo-Norman abaïss, from Middle French abair, abaisser (“lose one's composure, be startled, be stunned”), from Old French esbaïr, (French ébahir), from es- (“utterly”) + baïr (“to astonish”), from Medieval Latin *exbadō, from ex- (“out of”) + bado (“to gape, yawn”), an onomatopoeic word imitating a yawn, see also French badaud (“rubbernecker”).

definitions.text: To make ashamed; to embarrass; to destroy the self-possession of, as by exciting suddenly a consciousness of guilt, mistake, or inferiority; to disconcert; to discomfit.
To lose self-possession; to become ashamed.

quotations.author: Thomas Babington Macaulay
quotations.passage: He was a man whom no check could abash
quotations.work: The History of England from the Accession of James the Second

quotations.author: Agatha Christie
quotations.passage: The stare seemed to abash Poirot.

quotations.author: Sir Thomas Malory
quotations.passage: [...] as King Uther lay by his queen, he asked her, by the faith she owed to him, whose was the body; then she sore abashed to give answer.

abash.title: abash

etymologies: From Middle English abaten, from Anglo-Norman abatre, from Late Latin abbattere, from Latin battere.
The noun is derived from the verb.

From Anglo-Norman abatre, probably an alteration of Anglo-Norman and Middle French embatre, enbatre (“to drive or rush into; to enter into a tenement without permission”) (compare Late Latin abatare), from Middle French, Old French em-, en- (prefix meaning ‘in, into’) + Middle French, Old French batre (“to beat, hit, strike”) (from Latin battere, battuere, the present active infinitive of battuō (“to beat, hit; to beat up; to fight”); see further at etymology 1). The English word was probably also influenced by the verb abate.

Borrowed from Italian abate (“abbot”), from Latin abbātem, the accusative singular of abbās (“abbot”), from Ancient Greek ἀββᾶς (abbâs), a variant of ἀββᾱ (abbā, “father; title of respect for an abbot”), from Aramaic אַבָּא (’abbā, “father; ancestor; teacher; chief, leader; author, originator”), from Proto-Semitic *ʔabw- (“father”), ultimately imitative of a child’s word for “father”. The English word is a doublet of abbot.
Unknown

definitions.text: To lessen (something) in force or intensity; to moderate.
To reduce (something) in amount or size.
To cut away or hammer down (material from metalwork, a sculpture, etc.) in such a way as to leave a figure in relief.
To lower (something) in price or value.
To demolish or level to the ground (a building or other structure).
To give no consideration to (something); to treat as an exception.
To dull (an edge, point, etc.); to blunt.

examples: to abate a writ
definitions.text: To make (a writ or other legal document) void; to nullify.

examples: She was ordered by the court to abate the nuisance.
definitions.text: To put an end to (a nuisance).
To dismiss or otherwise bring to an end (legal proceedings) before they are completed, especially on procedural grounds rather than on the merits.

examples: to order restrictions to abate an emergency
definitions.text: To curtail or end (something); to cause to cease.
To give (someone) a discount or rebate; also, to relieve (someone) of a debt.
To bring down (someone) mentally or physically; to lower (someone) in status.

examples: We will abate this price from the total.
definitions.text: Chiefly followed by from, of, etc.: to omit or remove (a part from a whole); to deduct, to subtract.
Chiefly followed by of: to deprive (someone or something of another thing).
To decrease in force or intensity; to subside.
To decrease in amount or size.

examples: Bequests and legacies are liable to be abated entirely or in proportion, upon a deficiency of assets.
definitions.text: To lower in price or value; specifically, of a bequest in a will: to lower in value because the testator's estate is insufficient to satisfy all the bequests in full.
Of an edge, point, etc.: to become blunt or dull.

examples: The writ has abated.
definitions.text: Of a writ or other legal document: to become null and void; to cease to have effect.
Of legal proceedings: to be dismissed or otherwise brought to an end before they are completed, especially on procedural grounds rather than on the merits.
To give a discount or rebate; to discount, to rebate.
To bow down; hence, to be abased or humbled.
Chiefly followed by of: to deduct or subtract from.
Abatement; reduction; an instance of this.
Deduction; subtraction; an instance of this.
To enter upon and unlawfully seize (land) after the owner has died, thus preventing an heir from taking possession of it.
An Italian abbot or other member of the clergy.
In the habit of.
A surname from Italian.

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: Abate throw at Nouum, and the whole world againe, / Cannot picke out fiue such, take each one in his vaine.

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: Abate the edge of traitors gracious Lord, / That vvould reduce these bloudy daies againe, / And make poore England vveepe in streames of bloud, […]
quotations.work: The Tragedy of King Richard the Third.

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: She hath abated me of halfe my traine, / Lookt blacke vpon me, strooke mee with her tongue / Most Serpent-like vpon the very heart, […]

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: My fury shall abate, / And I the Crownes will take.
quotations.work: The Cronicle History of Henry the Fift

quotations.author: Edmund Spenser
quotations.passage: [folio 8, verso] For Winters wrath beginnes to quell, / And pleasant spryng appeareth. […] [folio 10, recto] Gloss. […] To quell) to abate.

quotations.author: Daniel Defoe
quotations.passage: The third Day in the Morning, the Wind having abated over Night, the Sea was calm, and I ventur'd; but I am a warning Piece again to all rash and ignorant Pilots; for no sooner was I come to the Point, when even I was not my Boat's Length from the Shore, but I found my self in a great Depth of Water, and a Current like the Sluice of a Mill: […]
quotations.work: The Life and Strange Surprizing Adventures of Robinson Crusoe

quotations.author: Walter Scott
quotations.passage: […] Lance, after having made some shew of helping him to his horse, ran back to tell his master the joyful intelligence, that a lucky accident had abated Chiffinch's party to their own number.

quotations.author: Walter Scott
quotations.passage: So toilsome was the road to trace, / The guide, abating of his pace, / Led slowly through the pass's jaws, […]

quotations.author: Herman Melville
quotations.passage: Whether fagged by the three days' running chase, and the resistance to his swimming in the knotted hamper he bore; or whether it was some latent deceitfulness and malice in him: whichever was true, the White Whale's way now began to abate, as it seemed, from the boat so rapidly nearing him once more; though indeed the whale's last start had not been so long a one as before.

quotations.author: Herman Melville
quotations.passage: So then, weighing all things well, and myself severely, I resolved to follow my Mentor's wise counsel; neither arrogating aught, nor abating of just dues; but circulating freely, sociably, and frankly, among the gods, heroes, high-priests, kings, and gentlemen, that made up the principalities of Mardi.

quotations.author: Mark Twain
quotations.passage: Three shillings and eightpence, your worship—I could not abate a penny and set forth the value honestly.
quotations.work: The Prince and the Pauper: A Tale for Young People of All Ages

quotations.author: Francis Bacon
quotations.passage: Wherefore you shall obserue that the more deepe, and sober sort of Politique persons, in their Greatnesse, are euer bemoaning themselues, what a Life they lead; Chanting a Quanta patimur. Not that they feele it so, but onely to abate the Edge of Enuy.

quotations.author: Francis Bacon
quotations.passage: […] the same greatness of wealth is for the most part not collected and obtained without sucking it from many, according to the received similitude of the spleen, which never swelleth but when the rest of the body pineth and abateth.

quotations.author: John Stuart Mill
quotations.passage: To abate the force of these considerations, an enemy of free discussion may be supposed to say, that there is no necessity for mankind in general to know and understand all that can be said against or for the opinions by philosophers and theologians.

quotations.author: Thomas Browne
quotations.passage: That men weigh heavier dead than alive, if experiment hath not failed us, we cannot reasonably grant. For though the triall hereof cannot so well be made on the body of Man, nor will the difference be sensible in the abate of scruples or dragmes, yet can we not confirm the same in lesser animalls from whence the inference is good; […]

quotations.author: Gerard Legh
quotations.passage: [Jupiter] whiche by his goodnes as Marcianus saieth, abateth the malice of Saturne. Therfore the Poets faine, that he did put his father out of his kingdome, Isidore writeth as he abateth the malice of the euill Planets, […]

quotations.author: John Evelyn
quotations.passage: By the oft removal of a Wild-stock, cutting the ends of the Roots, and dis-branching somewhat of the Head at every change of place, it will greatly abate of its natural wildness, and in time bring forth more civil and ingenuous Fruit: […]
quotations.work: Sylva, or A Discourse of Forest-trees and the Propagation of Timber in His Majesties Dominions.

quotations.author: Izaak Walton
quotations.passage: And it is to be noted that in the sharpest of his extreme fits he [George Herbert] would often say, 'Lord, abate my great affliction, or increase my patience; but, Lord, I repine not; I am dumb, Lord, before Thee, because Thou doest it.'
quotations.work: The Complete Works in Verse and Prose of George Herbert.

quotations.author: William Robertson
quotations.passage: In the one period, an hundred and fifty years of peace between the two nations, the habit of being subjected to the same King, and governed by the same maxims, had considerably abated old animosities, and prepared both people for incorporating.
quotations.work: The History of Scotland, during the Reigns of Queen Mary and of King James VI, till His Accession to the Crown of England.

quotations.author: J. C. Murray
quotations.passage: O, Blessed Bean! How often have I ate / Whole plates of Thee, my hunger to abate! / And thou abatedst it, Thou didst indeed, / Thou ever over-satisfying feed!
quotations.work: Rhymes of the Miner: An Anthology of Canadian Mining Verse

abject.title: abject

etymologies: From Late Middle English abjuren (“to give up (something); to recant or renounce (something) under oath”), from Anglo-Norman abjurer, Middle French abiurer, abjurer, and Old French abjurer (“to reject or renounce (something) on oath”) (modern French abjurer), and from their etymon Latin abiūrāre, the present active infinitive of abiūrō (“to deny on oath, recant, renounce, repudiate, abjure”), from ab- (prefix meaning ‘away from, from’) + iūro (“to take an oath, swear, vow”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yew- (“(adjective) right; straight; upright; (noun) justice; law; right”).

examples: to abjure errors
definitions.text: To solemnly reject (someone or something); to abandon (someone or something) forever; to disavow, to disclaim, to repudiate.

examples: to abjure allegiance to a prince
definitions.text: To renounce (something) upon oath; to forswear; specifically, to recant or retract (a heresy or some other opinion); to withdraw.
To cause (someone) to recant or retract (a heresy or some other opinion).
Especially in abjure the realm: to swear an oath to leave (a place) forever.
To cause or compel (someone) to leave a place forever; to banish.
To solemnly reject; to abandon forever.
To recant or retract a heresy on oath.
To swear an oath to leave a place forever.

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: Her[mia]. […] But I beseech your Grace, that I may knovve / The vvorst that may befall mee in this case, / If I refuse to vved Demetrius. / The[seus]. Either to dy the death, or to abiure, / For euer, the society of men.

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: Graues at my command, / Haue vvak'd their sleepers, op'd, and let 'em forth / By my so potent Art. But this rough Magicke / I heere abiure: […]
quotations.work: Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies

quotations.author: John Milton
quotations.passage: She disappeerd, and left me dark, I vvak'd / To find her, or for ever to deplore / Her loss, and other pleasures all abjure: […]

quotations.author: John Milton
quotations.passage: Easily canst thou find one miserable, / And not inforc'd oft-times to part from truth; / If it may stand him more in stead to lye, / Say and unsay, feign, flatter, or abjure?
quotations.work: Paradise Regain’d. A Poem. In IV Books. To which is Added, Samson Agonistes

quotations.author: Thomas More
quotations.passage: [T]he man ye write of, was of many thinges borne wrõge [wrong] in hande, & therin so sore handeled that he was forced to for swere and abiure certaine heresyes, & openly to penance therfore, where he neuer held any such.
quotations.work: The Workes of Sir Thomas More Knyght

quotations.author: Thomas More
quotations.passage: Nor neuer yet found I ani. j. [any one] but he would once abiure, though he neuer intended to kepe his othe.
quotations.work: The Workes of Sir Thomas More Knyght

quotations.author: Thomas Hobbes
quotations.passage: When a clerk heretofore was convicted of felony, he might have saved his life by abjuring the realm; that is, by departing the realm within a certain time appointed, and taking an oath never to return. But at this day all statutes for abjuration are repealed.
quotations.work: The English Works of Thomas Hobbes of Malmesbury;

quotations.author: Edmund Burke
quotations.passage: [T]he concession vvas far short of satisfying the principle vvhich Lord Hillsborough had abjured; or even the pretence on vvhich the repeal of the other taxes vvas announced: […]
quotations.work: Speech of Edmund Burke, Esq. on American Taxation, April 19, 1774

quotations.author: Thomas Babington Macaulay
quotations.passage: [B]oth Charles [I] himself and his creature [William] Laud, while they abjured the innocent badges of Popery, retained all its worst vices, […]
quotations.work: Critical and Historical Essays, Contributed to the Edinburgh Review .

quotations.author: Thomas Lake Harris
quotations.passage: Only as thou abjurest self, / Lovest thy Brother more than pelf, / And drivest out the impish elf, // Sectarian pride, from all thy heart, / Canst thou have place, or lot, or part / Within the Heaven-created mart […]
quotations.work: An Epic of the Starry Heaven

quotations.author: Robert Marshall
quotations.passage: [S]he is an ardent golfer. Except during the season in town, she spends her year in golfing, either at St. Magnus or Pau, for, like all good Americans, she has long since abjured her native soil.

quotations.author: William Beckford
quotations.passage: VVouldest thou devote thyself to me? Adore then the terrestrial influences; and abjure Mahomet.
quotations.work: An Arabian Tale, from an Unpublished Manuscript

quotations.author: Adelaide O’Keeffe
quotations.passage: [W]hen, guided by learned rabbis, invincible generals, and sublime and enlightened heathens, thou in evil hour abjuredst the gospel, in outward act if not in heart, and ungratefully dismissed thy faithful adviser, thou didst seal the fate of thy country and thyself.
quotations.work: Zenobia, Queen of Palmyra; a Narrative, Founded on History.

quotations.author: Robert Southey
quotations.passage: I wrote to him, saying, 'all these things, Lord, he hath abjured before me; admit him, therefore, if it pleaseth thee.' But he hath written back, 'unless he abjureth all this in writing, and in his own hand, I will not admit him.'
quotations.work: All for Love; and The Pilgrim to Compostela

quotations.author: Thomas Fuller
quotations.passage: [T]hey vvere betrayed, and then many of them to the number of six or seven score vvere abjured, and three or four of them burnt. Novv although vve knevv not hovv to call these Martyrs vvho so suffered, their Names no doubt are vvritten in the Book of Life.
quotations.work: The History of the Worthies of England

quotations.author: William Blackstone
quotations.passage: [A]s a feme-covert recusant may be imprisoned, so all others must, vvithin three months after conviction, either submit and renounce their errors, or, if required so to do by four justices, must abjure and renounce the realm: and if they do not depart, or if they return vvithout the king's licence, they shall be guilty of felony, and suffer death as felons.
quotations.work: Commentaries on the Laws of England

quotations.author: Michaell i.e., Michael Drayton
quotations.passage: The strong effect of theyr conceiued ire, / Vrging the vveake King vvith a violent hand, / T' abiure those false Lords from the troubled land.
quotations.work: The Barrons Wars in the Raigne of Edward the Second .

quotations.author: Thomas Fuller
quotations.passage: About this time a subject brought in a Bull of Excommunication against another subject of this Realm, and published it to the Lord Treasurer of England, and this vvas by the ancient Common-Law of England adjudged Treason against the King, his Crovvn and dignity, for the vvhich, the offender should have been dravvn and hanged, but at the great instance of the chancelour and Treasurer, he vvas onely abjured the Realm for ever.

quotations.author: John Strype
quotations.passage: In the Time of King Edward III. one should have been hanged, dravvn and quartered, for publishing an Excommunication, directed from the Bishop of Rome against one of the King's Subjects. But at the Entreaty of the Lord Chancellor and Lord Treasurer, his Life vvas pardoned; notvvithstanding he vvas abjured the Realm.
quotations.work: Annals of the Reformation and Establishment of Religion, and Other Various Occurrences in the Church of England;

quotations.author: Umberto Eco
quotations.passage: And going toward the Justice Gate, many said to him, "Recant! Recant! Don't insist on dying," and he said, "Christ died for us." […] At the Field of Justice, one said to him he should do as a certain monk, his superior, had done, abjuring: but Michael answered that he would not abjure, and I saw many in the crowd agree and urge Michael to be strong: so I and many others realized those were his followers, and we moved away from them.

quotations.author: John Palsgrave
quotations.passage: I Abiowre⸝ I forsake myne errours as an heretyke dothe⸝ or forswere the kynges landes⸝ ie abiure, prime coniugationis.

quotations.author: John Foxe
quotations.passage: Well to bee short, what for the causes before recited, as also for that they had once alreadie abiured, and yet (as they terme it) fell againe into relapse, they were both (as you haue heard) in the end burned together in Smithfield: […]
quotations.work: The Second Volume of the Ecclesiasticall Historie, Containing the Acts and Monuments of Martyrs

quotations.author: John Kelynge
quotations.passage: One abjureth and is after taken in England, and demanded what he could say, why Execution should not be awarded, he stands mute, he shall be hanged, and not put to penance or pressed; because he was attainted of the Felony before by his Confession: For he cannot have the Benefit of the Sanctuary to abjure, unless he confess the Felony which is entered on Record by the Coroner; […]
quotations.work: A Report of Divers Cases in Pleas of the Crown, Adjudged and Determined in the Reign of the Late King Charles II .

abjure.title: abjure

etymologies: From Middle English ablucioun (“cleansing of impurities”), from Old French ablution, and its source, Late Latin ablūtiō (“a washing away”), from abluō (“wash away”), from ab- (“away”) +‎ lavō (“wash”).

definitions.text: Originally, the purifying of oils and other substances by emulsification with hot water; now more generally, a thorough cleansing of a precipitate or other non-dissolved substance.
The act of washing or cleansing the body, or some part of it, as a religious rite.
Washing oneself; bathing, cleaning oneself up.
The rinsing of the priest's hand and the sacred vessel following the Communion with, depending on rite, water or a mix of it and wine, which may then be drunk by the priest.
wudu, ritual washing of the limbs and head performed immediately before prayer or holding the Quran
The liquid used in the cleansing or ablution.
The ritual consumption by the deacon or priest of leftover sacred wine of host after the Communion.
The location or building where the showers and basins are located.

quotations.author: Herman Melville
quotations.passage: At that time in the morning any Christian would have washed his face; but Queequeg, to my amazement, contented himself with restricting his ablutions to his chest, arms, and hands. He then donned his waistcoat, and taking up a piece of hard soap on the wash-stand centre table, dipped it into water and commenced lathering his face.

quotations.author: William Beckford
quotations.passage: Let water be brought to perform my ablutions, and let the pious Fakreddin be called to offer up his prayers with mine.

quotations.author: William Gilmore Simms
quotations.passage: He followed the steps of Bella, who soon conducted him to his chamber, and left him to those ablutions which a long ride along a sandy road had rendered particularly necessary.

quotations.author: J. M. Coetzee
quotations.passage: She treats him not as a doddering old fool but as a man hampered in his movements by injury. Patiently, without baby-talk, she helps him through his ablutions.

quotations.author: Maria Cramer
quotations.passage: There are now indications that it has caused some Americans to become more spartan when it comes to ablutions.

quotations.author: Homer
quotations.passage: Cast the ablutions in the main

ablution.title: ablution

etymologies: First attested in 1657.

definitions.text: To deny (oneself something); to renounce or give up (a right, a power, a claim, a privilege, a convenience).
To relinquish; to surrender; to abjure.

quotations.author: Asbell v. State
quotations.passage: To compel a state, upon theories of doubtful statutory interpretation, to appear as defendant suitor in its own courts, and to litigate with private parties as to whether it had abnegated its sovereignty of exemption, would be intolerable.

quotations.author: January
quotations.passage: All ancient and modern histories of nations abnegate God.

abnegate.title: abnegate

etymologies: First attested in 1644. Perhaps a back-formation from abomination. Alternatively, perhaps from Late Latin abōminātus, past participle of abōminarī (“to deprecate as an ill omen”), from ab + ominari (“to forebode, presage”), from omen.

definitions.text: Abominable; detested.
To feel disgust towards; to loathe or detest thoroughly; to hate in the highest degree, as if with religious dread.

examples: I absolutely abominate waking up early on weekends.
definitions.text: To dislike strongly.

quotations.author: Jane Austen
quotations.passage: "Much as I abominate writing, I would not give up Mr. Collins's correspondence for any consideration."

abominate.title: abominate

etymologies: From a- (“in the act of”) +‎ born + -ing.

definitions.text: That is in the process of being born; coming into existence; before coming to completion.

examples: This festival is an excellent chance to see new talent aborning.
definitions.text: While being born or produced.

quotations.author: Mousie Mousie Wildflower
quotations.passage: What a shock this morning / A terror without warning / Turned out a blank / What heavens thank / The "frie" died a borning.

quotations.author: James McPherson
quotations.passage: No fewer than five planned “uprisings” died a-borning.

aborning.title: aborning

etymologies: From Latin abrādō (“scrape off”), from ab (“from, away from”) + rādō (“scrape”). First attested in 1677.
From Middle English abraiden. See abraid.

definitions.text: To rub or wear off; erode.
To wear down or exhaust, as a person; irritate.
To irritate by rubbing; chafe.
To cause the surface to become more rough.
To undergo abrasion.
Obsolete spelling of abraid.

quotations.author: NASA’s Perseverance Rover Investigates Geologically Rich Mars Terrain
quotations.passage: “Wildcat Ridge” is the name given to a rock about 3 feet (1 meter) wide that likely formed billions of years ago as mud and fine sand settled in an evaporating saltwater lake. On July 20, the rover abraded some of the surface of Wildcat Ridge so it could analyze the area with the instrument called Scanning Habitable Environments with Raman & Luminescence for Organics & Chemicals, or SHERLOC.

abrade.title: abrade

etymologies: First attested in 1526, from Middle English abrogat (“abolished”), from Latin abrogātus, perfect passive participle of abrogō (“repeal”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), formed from ab (“away”) + rogō (“ask, inquire, propose”). See rogation.

definitions.text: To annul (as a law, decree, ordinance, etc.) by an authoritative act; to abolish by the authority of the maker or their successor; to repeal.
To put an end to; to do away with.
To block a process or function.
Abrogated; abolished.

quotations.author: Edmund Burke
quotations.passage: Whose laws, like those of the Medes and Persian, they cannot alter or abrogate.
quotations.work: Letter I. On the Overtures of Peace.

quotations.author: Robert South
quotations.passage: But let us look a little further, and see whether the New Testament abrogates what we see so frequently used in the Old.

quotations.author: Parliament of the United Kingdom
quotations.passage: The rule of law whereby it is a crime for a person to commit suicide is hereby abrogated.

quotations.author: Legislative Council of Hong Kong
quotations.passage: The rule known as the “year and a day rule” […] is abrogated for all purposes.
quotations.work: Government of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region Gazette

quotations.author: Cormac McCarthy
quotations.passage: Where hunters and woodcutters once slept in their boots by the dying light of their thousand fires and went on, old teutonic forebears with eyes incandesced by the visionary light of a massive rapacity, wave on wave of the violent and insane, their brains stoked with spoorless analogues of all that was, lean aryans with their abrogate semitic chapbook reenacting the dramas and parables therein and mindless and pale with a longing that nothing save dark's total restitution could appease.

abrogate.title: abrogate

etymologies: Either borrowed from Middle French abscondre or directly from Latin abscondō (“hide”); formed from abs, ab (“away”) + condō (“put together, store”), from con- (“together”) + *dʰeh₁- (“to put, place, set”).

examples: The thieves absconded with our property.
definitions.text: To flee, often secretly; to steal away.
To hide, conceal, or absent oneself clandestinely, with the intent to avoid legal process
To abandon a hive.
To hide, to be in hiding or concealment.

examples: The captain absconded his responsibility.
definitions.text: To evade, to hide or flee from.
To conceal; to take away.

quotations.author: Thomas Babington Macaulay
quotations.passage: […] that very homesickness which, in regular armies, drives so many recruits to abscond at the risk of stripes and of death.

quotations.author: Ambrose Bierce
quotations.passage: Spring beckons! All things to the call respond; / The trees are leaving and cashiers abscond.

quotations.author: January
quotations.passage: The driver had absconded, but both railway and county police were searching for him. Mitchell was arrested in Carlisle on June 9, 1863.

quotations.author: Julius J. Epstein
quotations.passage: I've often speculated why you don't return to America. Did you abscond with the church funds? Run off with a senator's wife? I like to think you killed a man. It's the Romantic in me.

quotations.author: John Niven
quotations.passage: Andy did break his bargain, lurked in the neighborhood a few days, and then, being pursued by the sheriff, absconded to parts unknown.
quotations.work: Years of Turmoil: Civil War and Reconstruction

quotations.author: Amiya K. Samanta
quotations.passage: A printed leaflet of the Anushilan was dropped here, and at another place a manuscript of swadeshi songs, which has been proved to belong to Lal Mohan De, another member of the Samiti, who lived in Pulin's akhara and is now absconding.
quotations.work: Terrorism in Bengal: Origin, growth and activities of the organizations like

quotations.author: N. Lokendra
quotations.passage: Moirangthem Kalachand Singh, City Inspector, Imphal P.W. 14 searched the house of one Chaoba Singh in village Khagempali in the hope of arresting Boro Singh and Mohendra Singh accused, who were absconding in […]
quotations.work: The Unquiet Valley: Society, Economy, and Politics of Manipur (1891-1050)

quotations.author: Richard Rojcewicz
quotations.passage: Modern technology accompanies the absconding of the original attitude.
quotations.work: The Gods And Technology: A Reading Of Heidegger

quotations.author: Sonia Brill
quotations.passage: You cannot abscond from the responsibility both you and your partner owe to this event, and that includes dealing with anger issues and any other emotional issues that come with it.

quotations.author: Randy Carl Lynn
quotations.passage: [European honey bees] raise large colonies, hoard large quantities of honey, are more gentle than other species and almost never abscond.

quotations.author: John Ray
quotations.passage: the Marmotto, […] which absconds all Winter doth […] live upon its own Fat.
quotations.work: The Wisdom of God Manifested in the Works of the Creation

quotations.author: Aldo E. Chircop
quotations.passage: If the distress situation is solved successfully, the anonymous shipowner will reap the commercial benefit, if the situation ends in disaster, the shipowner will hide behind an anonymous post box in a foreign country and will abscond responsibility.

quotations.author: Somar
quotations.passage: The driver snatched a packet of cigarettes out of the glove compartment and absconded the driver's seat without a word

quotations.author: Vendela Vida
quotations.passage: Those who evidently did not get invited back to their top choices have already absconded the scene, tripping in their high heels as they ran.
quotations.work: Girls on the Verge: Debutante Dips, Drive-bys, and Other Initiations

quotations.author: James Morton
quotations.passage: In 1939 she absconded her bail in Melbourne and went to New Zealand, where she also absconded on a charge of stealing diamonds.

quotations.author: William Porterfield
quotations.passage: for having applied to the Side of the Head any thin black Body, such as the Brim of a Hat, so as it may abscond the Objects that are upon that Side
quotations.work: treatise on the eye, the manner and phaenomena of vision

quotations.author: John Esquemeling
quotations.passage: They examined every prisoner by himself (who were in all about two hundred and fifty persons) where they had absconded the rest of their goods

abscond.title: abscond

etymologies: Both from Middle French absinthe, from Latin absinthium, from Ancient Greek ἀψίνθιον (apsínthion, “wormwood”). Doublet of absinthium.

definitions.text: The herb absinthium Artemisia absinthium (grande wormwood); essence of wormwood.
Bitterness; sorrow.
A distilled, highly alcoholic, anise-flavored liquor originally made from grande wormwood, anise, and other herbs.
A moderate yellow green. absinthe green:
Sagebrush.

quotations.author: Edgar Rice Burroughs
quotations.passage: Let us go out and drink to the very good health of Monsieur Tarzan in some of old Plancon’s unparalleled absinth; not forgetting that the Count de Coude is one of the best swordsmen in Paris, and by far the best shot in all France.

quotations.author: Paul Owens
quotations.passage: Absinthe ads like to trade on artists like Van Gogh and Toulouse-Lautrec, as if the history of the green fairy began in the Pigalle neighborhood of 1870s Paris, but wormwood-infused drinks have been around for thousands of years.
quotations.work: The Little Green Book of Absinthe

absinthe.title: absinthe

etymologies: Learned borrowing from Latin abstrūsus (“concealed, hidden; having been concealed”), an adjective use of the perfect passive participle of abstrūdō (“to conceal, hide; to push or thrust away”), from abs- (from ab- (prefix meaning ‘away; from; away from’)) + trūdō (“to push, shove; to thrust”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *trewd- (“to push; to thrust”)).

definitions.text: Difficult to comprehend or understand; obscure.
Concealed or hidden; secret.

quotations.author: John Milton
quotations.passage: Be less abstruse, my riddling days are past.
quotations.work: Paradise Regain’d. A Poem. In IV Books. To which is Added, Samson Agonistes

quotations.author: Alexander Hamilton
quotations.passage: The objects of geometrical enquiry are so intirely absracted from those pursuits vvhich stir up and put in motion the unruly passions of the human heart, that mankind vvithout difficulty adopt not only the more simple theorems of the science, but even those abstruse paradoxes, vvhich hovvever they may appear susceptible of demonstration, are at variance vvith the natural conceptions vvhich the mind, vvithout the aid of philosophy, vvould be led to entertain upon the subject.
quotations.work: The Federalist: A Collection of Essays, Written in Favour of the New Constitution

quotations.author: John Milton
quotations.passage: Mean while th’ Eternal eye, whose sight discernes / Abstrusest thoughts, from forth his holy Mount / And from within the golden Lamps that burne / Nightly before him, saw without their light / Rebellion rising, saw in whom, how spred / Among the sons of Morn, what multitudes / Were banded to oppose his high Decree; […]

quotations.author: Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley
quotations.passage: In a thousand ways he smoothed for me the path of knowledge, and made the most abstruse inquiries clear and facile to my apprehension.

quotations.author: David Hume
quotations.passage: 'Tis certain, that the easy and obvious Philosophy vvill always, vvith the Generality of Mankind, have the Preference to the accurate and abstruse; and by many vvill be recommended, not only as more agreeable, but more useful than the other.

quotations.author: John Hooper
quotations.passage: Some time the good makithe an ile end⸝ ãd the ile a godd. In this opiniõ⸝ and in scrutable misterie be werithe all his wittes⸝ and at the end of his cogitacions⸝ fyndithe more abstruse⸝ and doutfull obiections thẽ at the beginning⸝ […]
quotations.work: A Declaration of the Ten Holy Cõmaundementes of Allmygthye God

quotations.author: John Machin
quotations.passage: Those propositions relating to the Moon's motion, which are demonstrated in the Principia [by Isaac Newton], do generally depend on calculations very intricate and abstruse, the truth of which is not easily examined, even by those that are most skilful; […]
quotations.work: The Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy.

quotations.author: Isaac Watts
quotations.passage: The best VVay to learn any Science, is to begin vvith a regular System, or a short and plain Scheme of that Science, vvell dravvn up into a narrovv Compass, omitting the deeper and more abstruse Parts of it, and that also under the Conduct and Instruction of some skilful Teacher.
quotations.work: The Improvement of the Mind: Or, A Supplement to the Art of Logick

quotations.author: Henry Hart Milman
quotations.passage: A second rescript followed, commanding all bishops not merely to subscribe the dominant opinions on these profound and abstruse topics, but to condemn their authors, Pelagius and Cœlestius, as irreclaimable heretics, and this under pain of deprivation and banishment.

quotations.author: Walter Lionel George
quotations.passage: After the subject (victim, if you like) had read say thirty of the best solid novels of the twentieth century, I think I should draw him to the more abstruse modern novels and stories.

quotations.author: Miguel de Cervantes
quotations.passage: O vvho is he that could carrie nevves to our olde father, that thou vvert but aliue, although thou vvert hidden in the most abstruse dungeons of Barbarie; for his riches, my brothers and mine vvould fetch thee from thence.
quotations.work: The History of the Valorous and Wittie Knight-errant Don-Quixote of the Mancha.

quotations.author: Joseph Beaumont
quotations.passage: [T]he abstrusest Things / VVhich in the Mindes dark Temper nestling ly, / By you exposed are to every Eye.

abstruse.title: abstruse

etymologies: From New Latin abūlia, from Ancient Greek ἀβουλία (aboulía, “irresolution”), from ἀ- (a-, “without”) + βουλή (boulḗ, “will”).

definitions.text: Absence of willpower or decisiveness, especially as a symptom of mental illness.

quotations.author: John Fowles
quotations.passage: He felt without volition, plunged into a state of aboulia.

quotations.author: Camille Paglia
quotations.passage: His virginal modesty is a modern abulia.

abulia.title: abulia

etymologies: First attested in the early 15th century. From Middle English acceden, from Latin accēdō (“approach, accede”), formed from ad (“to, toward, at”) + cēdō (“move, yield”) (English cede). Compare French accéder. Unrelated to ascend, aside from the common ad prefix.

examples: to accede to a request
definitions.text: To agree or assent [with to ‘a proposal, a request’]; to give way.

examples: the house of Hanover acceded to the English throne
definitions.text: To come to an office, state or dignity; to attain, assume (a position) [with to].

examples: to accede to the European Union
definitions.text: To become a party to an agreement or a treaty [with to].
To approach; to arrive, to come forward.
To give one's adhesion; to join up with (a group, etc.); to become part of.

quotations.author: E. H. Nolan
quotations.passage: It was added that if he acceded to these proposals, his fortresses and sea-ports should be garrisoned by French and Spanish troops to protect him from England’s vengeance, but that if he refused—and the answer was to be given within four days—he must take the consequences of such a line of policy.

quotations.author: John Wesley Powell
quotations.passage: But in 1874 the editors of Scribner’s Monthly requested me to publish a popular account of the Colorado exploration in that journal. To this I acceded and prepared four short articles, which were elaborately illustrated from photographs in my possession.

quotations.author: May
quotations.passage: Referring to the "hero of the day," No. 92220, Mr. Hanks acceded that she was not of the Great Western breed, but they had done their best to make up for that by "dollying her up in good old Western colours and conferring upon her the finest honour we can—the halo or crown of Swindon, the copper top to her chimney."

quotations.author: Leslie Feinberg
quotations.passage: Some of the countries of Eastern Europe had already acceded to all the privatization and austerity measures drawn up by imperialist bankers. The Socialist Federation of Yugoslavia was the last of the Eastern European workers' states trying to hold on to what was left of its planned, socialized framework of production and its collective ownership.

quotations.author: Dario Amodei
quotations.passage: The Department of War has stated they will only contract with AI companies who accede to “any lawful use” and remove safeguards in the cases mentioned above. […] Regardless, these threats do not change our position: we cannot in good conscience accede to their request.

quotations.author: Colin Jones
quotations.passage: Maintenon had been governess to the children in the late 1670s before acceding to the king's favours.

accede.title: accede

etymologies: From Middle French accoster, acoster, from Old French acoster (“to stand beside”) (whence Medieval Latin accostare), from Old French a- + coste (“side, flank”).

examples: A beggar accosted me as soon as I stepped outside.
definitions.text: To approach and speak to boldly or aggressively, as with a demand or request.
To join side to side; to border.
To sail along the coast or side of.
To approach; to come up to.
To speak to first; to address; to greet.
To adjoin; to lie alongside.
To assault.
To solicit sexually.
Address; greeting.
An attack.

quotations.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
quotations.passage: At last, when I was already within reach of her, I stopped. Words were denied me; if I advanced I could but clasp her to my heart in silence; and all that was sane in me, all that was still unconquered, revolted against the thought of such an accost.

etymologies: Learned borrowing from Latin accrētiō (“increase, increment”) + English -ion (suffix forming nouns denoting actions or processes, or their results). Accrētiō is derived from accrēscō (“to grow, increase”) +‎ -tiō (suffix forming nouns denoting actions or processes, or their results); and accrēscō is from ac- (a variant of ad-, prefix meaning ‘to’, or having an intensifying effect) +‎ crēscō (“to grow; to increase”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱer- (“to cause to grow; to grow; to nourish”)).
Doublet of accrue, crescent, and increase.

definitions.text: Increase by natural growth, especially the gradual increase of organic bodies by the internal addition of matter; organic growth; also, the amount of such growth.

examples: A mineral augments not by growth, but by accretion.
definitions.text: (Gradual) increase by an external addition of matter; an instance of this.
The process by which material is added to a geological feature; specifically, to a tectonic plate at a subduction zone.
Followed by of: external addition of matter to a thing which causes it to grow, especially in amount or size.

examples: The accretion of particles forms a solid mass.
definitions.text: The process of separate particles aggregating or coalescing together; concretion; a thing formed in this manner.
The formation of planets, stars, and other celestial bodies by the aggregating of matter drawn together by gravity; also, the growth of a celestial body through this process.

examples: accretion of ice
Accretions of dirt on clothing are often left in place by conservators because they can provide additional details about the artefact’s importance or history.
definitions.text: Something gradually added to or growing on a thing externally.

examples: Accretions of dirt on clothing are often left in place by conservators because they can provide additional details about the artefact’s importance or history.
definitions.text: A substance which has built up on the surface of an object, rather than become embedded in it.

Increase in property by the addition of other property to it (for example, gain of land by alluvion (“the deposition of sediment by a river or sea”) or dereliction (“recession of water from the usual watermark”), or entitlement to the products of the property such as interest on money); or by the property owner acquiring another person’s ownership rights; accession; an instance of this.
Increase of an inheritance to an heir or legatee due to the share of a co-heir or co-legatee being added to it, because the latter person is legally unable to inherit the share.

quotations.author: Thomas Hardy
quotations.passage: She had no fear of the shadows; her sole idea seemed to be to shun mankind—or rather that cold accretion called the world, which, so terrible in the mass, is so unformidable, even pitiable, in its units.

quotations.author: Edith Wharton
quotations.passage: The immense accretion of flesh which had descended on her in middle life like a flood of lava on a doomed city had changed her from a plump active little woman with a neatly-turned foot and ankle into something as vast and august as a natural phenomenon.

quotations.author: Francis Bacon

quotations.work: Sylua Syluarum: Or A Naturall Historie. In Ten Centuries.

quotations.author: Thomas Hobbes
quotations.passage: God hath from the beginning made all the Kindes of Hard, and Heavie, and Diaphanous Bodies that are, and of such Figure and magnitude as he thought fit; but hovv small soever, they may by accretion become greater in the Mine, or perhaps by generation, though vve knovv not hovv.

quotations.author: Charles Waddell Chesnutt
quotations.passage: Warwick was unable to perceive much change in the market-house. […] There might have been a slight accretion of the moss and lichen on the shingled roof.

quotations.author: Rufus Wilmot Griswold
quotations.passage: Suddenly starting from a proposition, exactly and sharply defined, in terms of utmost simplicity and clearness, he rejected the forms of customary logic, and by a crystalline process of accretion, built up his ocular demonstrations in forms of gloomiest and ghastliest grandeur, or in those of the most airy and delicious beauty—so minutely and distinctly, yet so rapidly, that the attention which was yielded to him was chained till it stood among his wonderful creations—till he himself dissolved the spell, and brought his hearers back to common and base existence, by vulgar fancies or exhibitions of the ignoblest passion.
quotations.work: Hurry-graphs; or, Sketches of Scenery, Celebrities and Society, Taken from Life

quotations.author: Amelia Gere Mason
quotations.passage: Our social life is largely a form, a whirl, a commercial relation, a display, a duty, the result of external accretion, not of internal growth. It is not in any sense a unity, nor an expression of the best intellectual life, which seeks other channels.

quotations.author: Jack London

quotations.passage: If therefore it is admitted that a large part of the narrative of Dionysius [of Halicarnassus] is false, what good ground have we for believing the rest? Ācrimōnia is derived from Latin ācer (“sharp; bitter, sour”) (from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱrós (“sharp”), from *h₂eḱ- (“sharp”) + *-rós (suffix forming adjectives from Caland system roots)) + Latin -mōnia (the feminine form of -mōnium (suffix forming collective nouns and nouns designating legal status or obligation), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *-mō (suffix forming agent nouns from verbs)).
