quotations.author: Daniel Taylor
quotations.passage: The Southampton striker, who also struck a post late on, was being serenaded by the Wembley crowd before the end and should probably brace himself for some Lambert-mania over the coming days but, amid the eulogies, it should not overlook the deficiencies that were evident in another stodgy England performance.

eulogy.title: eulogy

etymologies: From eu- +‎ peptic.

definitions.text: Having or relating to good digestion.
Cheerful, optimistic, contented, or of good spirits.
A person characterized by good digestion.
A person of a cheerful or optimistic disposition.

quotations.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
quotations.passage: As to the self-sufficiency of this world, a successful Professor with a eupeptic body might take such a view, but if one found oneself with cancer of the stomach in a London garret, one might question the doctrine that there was no need to yearn for any state of being save that in which we found ourselves.

quotations.author: John Buchan
quotations.passage: I envied Blenkiron his now eupeptic slumbers.

eupeptic.title: eupeptic

etymologies: Recorded since 1656; from Ancient Greek εὐφημισμός (euphēmismós), from εὐφημίζω (euphēmízō), from εὔφημος (eúphēmos, “uttering sound of good omen, abstaining from inauspicious words”), from εὖ (eû, “well”) + φήμη (phḗmē, “a voice, a prophetic voice, rumor, talk”), from φημί (phēmí, “to speak, say”).

definitions.text: The use of a word or phrase to replace another one that is more offensive, blunt or vulgar.
A word or phrase that replaces another in this way.

quotations.author: James Beattie
quotations.passage: Akin to it [litotes] is euphemism, which may be applied to the same purpose.

quotations.author: David J. Ulin
quotations.passage: In 1946, George Orwell addressed the relationship of language to reality and suggested that euphemism, not imperfect analogy, was the real danger. If we don’t use shocking language to describe a shocking circumstance, can we truly recognize what is happening?

quotations.author: James Beattie
quotations.passage: When it is said of the martyr St. Stephen, that “he fell asleep,” instead of—he died, the euphemism partakes of the nature of metaphor, intimating a resemblance between sleep and the death of such a person.

quotations.author: George Carlin
quotations.passage: Euphemistic language turns up in many areas of American life in a variety of situations. Not all euphemisms are alike, but they have one thing in common: They obscure meaning rather than enhance it; they shade the truth.

euphemism.title: euphemism

etymologies: From euphonical +‎ -ous (suffix forming adjectives denoting possession or presence of a quality, commonly in abundance). Euphonical is derived from euphonic +‎ -al (suffix forming adjectives with the sense ‘of or pertaining to’); with euphonic from euphony +‎ -ic (suffix forming adjectives with the sense ‘of or pertaining to’), and euphony borrowed from French euphonie, from Ancient Greek εὐφωνία (euphōnía), from εὐ- (eu-, prefix meaning ‘good, well’) + φωνή (phōnḗ, “sound; (human) voice; discourse, speech”) (from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂- (“to say, speak”)) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā, suffix forming feminine abstract nouns).

definitions.text: Of sounds, especially speech: demonstrating or possessing euphony; agreeable to the ear; pleasant-sounding.

quotations.author: Charles Dickens
quotations.passage: After casting about for some time for a name which should be worthy of her, he decided in favour of Sophronia Sphynx, as being euphonious and genteel, and furthermore indicative of mystery.

quotations.author: Joel Collier
quotations.passage: Before I set forward on my travels, I chose to change my name from Collier to Coglioni or Collioni, as more euphonious; […]

quotations.author: December
quotations.passage: We think it difficult to copy more successfully a model so curiously polished as the Botanic Garden; to assemble ideas more luxuriously elegant; to annex epithets more unexpectedly apposite: or to harmonize couplets more imitative and euphonious.

quotations.author: March
quotations.passage: I know our theatrical managers, major and minor, are very particular in selecting euphonious titles for their melodramas, especially if on a domestic subject, such as "Bennet, the Butcher," "Davidge, the Dustman," "Harley, the Harper," "Vining, the Vintner." quotations.author: Davis Wasgatt Clark
quotations.passage: Many persons, hoping to appear polite, deprive their words of the letter "r," which gives a forcible and euphonious ending to many English words and syllables. […] Yet, quite by chance, the ill-chosen words are euphonious: l's, m's and n's predominate, there are only a few plosives or fricatives, and the vowel sounds fit together in a melodious way. euphonious.title: euphonious

definitions.text: To think over something carefully; to consider fully; cogitate.

examples: After many years of study, he excogitated a solution.
definitions.text: To reach as a conclusion through reason or careful thought.

quotations.author: William Hamilton
quotations.passage: The first organs which Gall excogitated, he placed in the region of the sinus; and it is manifest he was then in happy unacquaintance with everything connected with that obnoxious cavity.

quotations.author: William Whewell
quotations.passage: This evidence […] thus excogitated out of the general theory.

excogitate.title: excogitate

etymologies: First attested in the first part of the 15th century, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English *excoriaten (only attested in its past participle), borrowed from Late Latin excoriātus perfect passive participle of excoriō (“to take the skin or hide off, flay, skin”), from ex- (“out off, from”) + corium (“hide, skin”) + -ō. Regular participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English, later archaic.

definitions.text: To remove the skin and/or fur of, to flay, to skin.
To wear off the skin of; to chafe.

examples: The teacher continued to excoriate the student after his academic issues.
definitions.text: To strongly condemn or criticize.
Excoriated.

quotations.author: China Miéville
quotations.passage: Madeleina di Farja had described Ori, and Cutter had envisaged an angry, frantic, pugnacious boy eager to fight, excoriating his comrades for supposed quiescence.

quotations.author: Patrick Healy
quotations.passage: Mr. Green, a former city public advocate and candidate for mayor in 2001, ran ads excoriating Mr. Cuomo’s ethics.

quotations.author: Radhika Jones
quotations.passage: The tabloids branded him forevermore as the “love rat,” and Pasternak was excoriated for peddling mawkish fantasy.

quotations.author: Katharine Viner
quotations.passage: Police are under pressure to accelerate the criminal investigation into the Grenfell Tower fire after an excoriating report found that companies operated with “systematic dishonesty” and that all 72 deaths were avoidable.

quotations.author: Thomas Phaer
quotations.passage: If the bowelles be excoriate, ye shall gyue thys peculier remedy.
quotations.work: translation of Jean Goëvrot's Regiment of Lyfe

excoriate.title: excoriate

etymologies: Borrowed from Latin excrēmentum, from excernō (“to excrete”).
Borrowed from Latin excrēmentum, from excrēscō (“to grow out”).

definitions.text: Human and non-human animal solid waste excreted from the bowels; feces.
Any waste matter excreted from the human or non-human animal body, or discharged by bodily organs.
Something which grows out of the body; hair, nails, etc.

quotations.author: Harry E. Wedeck
quotations.passage: The Roman poet Horace states that the excrement of the crocodile has aphrodisiac virtues.

excrement.title: excrement

etymologies: From Middle English, early 15th century, in sense “(action of) growing out (of something else)”. Borrowed from Latin excrescentia (“abnormal growths”), from excrescentem, from excrēscere, from ex- (“out”) (English ex-) + crēscere (“to grow”) (English crescent). Sense of “abnormal growth” from 1570s, from earlier excrescency (1540s in this sense).

definitions.text: Something, usually abnormal, which grows out of something else.
A disfiguring or unwanted mark or adjunct.
The epenthesis of a consonant, e.g., warmth as [ˈwɔrmpθ] (adding a [p] between [m] and [θ]), or -t (Etymology 2).

quotations.author: Charlotte Brontë
quotations.passage: I have again and again intimated that I desire the hair to be arranged closely, modestly, plainly. Miss Temple, that girl’s hair must be cut off entirely; I will send a barber to-morrow: and I see others who have far too much of the excrescence—that tall girl, tell her to turn round.

quotations.author: George Orwell
quotations.passage: It is taken for granted that a beggar does not 'earn' his living, as a bricklayer or a literary critic 'earns' his. He is a mere social excrescence, tolerated because we live in a humane age, but essentially despicable.
quotations.work: Down and Out in Paris and London

quotations.author: Jack London
quotations.passage: The squirrels were in hiding. One only he saw,—a sleek gray fellow, flattened against a gray dead limb so that he seemed a part of it, a woody excrescence upon the wood itself.

quotations.author: Edward Morgan Forster
quotations.passage: Perhaps he meant that towns are after all excrescences, grey fluxions, where men, hurrying to find one another, have lost themselves.

quotations.author: Andrea Loewenstein
quotations.passage: Being bussum buddies, the two friends often communicated with mere exchange of psychic forces, verbal communication having been rendered unnecessary excrescence.

excrescence.title: excrescence

etymologies: From Medieval Latin exculpātus, perfect passive participle of exculpō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ex- (“out, from”) + culpa (“fault; blame”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix).

definitions.text: To clear of or to free from guilt; exonerate.

quotations.author: Harold Bindloss
quotations.passage: The inquest on keeper Davidson was duly held, and at the commencement seemed likely to cause Tony Palliser less anxiety than he had expected. Northrop knew all about Tony's flirtation with Lucy Davidson, but it also knew a good deal more about that lady than Tony did, and exculpated him.

quotations.author: Douglas Husak
quotations.passage: Only a handful of defendants who are ignorant of the law succeed in exculpating themselves on either of the grounds discussed in Part B. […] In the examples to which I will refer, defendants who make mistakes of law are exculpated by denying mens rea—the mechanism I described in Part C through which all defendants are exculpated when they plead ignorance of fact.

exculpate.title: exculpate

etymologies: Learned borrowing from Latin excursus (“excursion; raid, sally, sortie”), a verbal noun from excurrō (“to run out; to sally forth”) +‎ -sus (suffix forming verbal nouns), with the verb derived from ex- (prefix meaning ‘away; out’) + currō (“to run; to move, proceed, travel; etc.”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱers- (“to run”)). Doublet of excurse.

definitions.text: A fuller discussion (usually in a separate section at the end of a chapter or book) of a particular part of the text of a work, especially a bible commentary or classical Greek or Latin text.
An act of departing from the main narrative in speech or writing to discuss an incidental issue; a digression.
A brief journey or trip, especially one out of the usual way; an excursion.
A brief instance of trying out a new activity, etc.

quotations.author: Kyril Bonfiglioli
quotations.passage: Here is what us scholars call an excursus. If you are an honest man the following page or two can be of no possible interest to you.

quotations.author: Glen Bowersock
quotations.passage: In his excursus on the Jewish people at the opening of the fifth book of his Histories […], Tacitus was at a loss to uncover any deep cause for the war that broke out in 66.

quotations.author: Sabine Fiedler
quotations.passage: Part III (Chapters 12 to 16) includes an excursus which leads us to the use of Esperanto outside the community of its speakers.
quotations.work: Esperanto – Lingua Franca and Language Community

quotations.author: Massimo Introvigne
quotations.passage: The authors devote a fascinating excursus to the Western imagination’s preoccupation with serpents—from Eden to esoterica—and how this primed the ground for Kuṇḍalinī’s reception.

excursus.title: excursus

etymologies: From Old French execrable, from Latin execrabilis.

definitions.text: Of the poorest quality.
Hateful, disgusting.

quotations.author: David Langford
quotations.passage: The arcanely evil words of that despicable, loathsome, suppressed, vile, pululating [sic], odious, nictating, repellent, repugnant, noxious, abhorrent, abominable, tory, execrable, nauseous work, Ye Boke of Guts, moved as if on a conveyor belt before his eyes.

execrable.title: execrable

etymologies: Learned borrowing from Late Latin exēgēsĭs (“exposition”), or from its etymon Ancient Greek ἐξήγησῐς (exḗgēsĭs, “explanation, interpretation; narration”), from ἐξηγέομαι (exēgéomai, “to guide, lead; to expound, interpret; to explain, relate”) + -σῐς (-sĭs, suffix forming abstract nouns or nouns of action, process, or result). Ἐξηγέομαι (Exēgéomai) is derived from ἐξ- (ex-) (a variant of ἐκ- (ek-, prefix meaning ‘away; off; out’)) + ἡγέομαι (hēgéomai, “to guide, lead”) (possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eǵ- (“to drive”) or *seh₂g- (“to follow; to seek out, trace”)).
The plural form is a learned borrowing from Late Latin exēgēsēs or its etymon Ancient Greek ἐξηγήσεις (exēgḗseis).

definitions.text: Critical commentary or discussion; an instance of this.

Chiefly of scripture: the action of using a phrase, sentence, etc., to interpret or paraphrase another phrase, sentence, etc.; a phrase, sentence, etc., used for this purpose; an explanatory note, a gloss.
In full numeral exegesis: a procedure formerly used to solve algebraic equations.

quotations.author: Moses Stuart
quotations.passage: [Y]ou have told us, that we are not to adopt rules of interpretation for the purpose of saving the consistency of inspired writers; that if by the fair rules of exegeses apparent contradictions cannot be reconciled, the credit of the writer must go down.

quotations.author: William Ewart Gladstone
quotations.passage: The amount of licence in the interpretation of Scripture which is involved in the first five propositions above stated is absolutely indispensable, in order to sustain the Christian character of the Divorce Bill. […] [W]e think it will appear that they are such as go far towards that most wretched consummation, which reduces all exegesis to a profane and deluding art; with no other business than to frame contrivances, under which we may hug the supposition that we are obeying God, when in truth we are denying His laws.

quotations.author: Matthew Arnold
quotations.passage: The good faith of the Bible writers is above all question; it speaks for itself; and the very same criticism, which shows us the defects of their exegesis and of their demonstrations from miracles, establishes their good faith.
quotations.work: Literature & Dogma: An Essay towards a Better Apprehension of the Bible

quotations.author: Archibald Robertson
quotations.passage: Accordingly Athanasius [of Alexandria] complains loudly of their exegesis (Ep. Æg. 3–4, cf. Orat. i. 8, 52), and insists (id. i. 54, cf. already de Decr. 14) on the primary necessity of always conscientiously studying the circumstances of time and place, the person addressed, the subject matter, and purpose of the writer, in order not to miss the true sense.
quotations.work: Select Writings and Letters of Athanasius, Bishop of Alexandria.

quotations.author: Francis Aveling
quotations.passage: As with Deism and Materialism, the German Rationalism invaded the department of Biblical exegesis. Here a destructive criticism, very similar to that of the Deists, was levelled against the miracles recorded in, and the authenticity of the Holy Scriptures.

quotations.author: Mortimer Jerome Adler
quotations.passage: Historical scholarship bears exclusively on interpretive reading; when it is properly subordinated as a means, its end is exegesis; all of its techniques are of service to the grammatical art. But exegesis is not the end; nor is grammar the highest art. Exegesis is for the sake of a fair critical judgment, grammar for the sake of logic and rhetoric.
quotations.work: Reforming Education: The Schooling of a People and Their Education beyond Schooling

quotations.author: Mitch Therieau
quotations.passage: Sometime on Saturday, Oct. 4, 12 orange doors were installed in 12 cities around the world. […] Affixed to each door was a QR code that, when scanned, called up a YouTube Shorts video loosely themed around Taylor Swift's new album "The Life of a Showgirl." […] It is a fitting device for an artist who has long seen herself as the creator of a parallel world: one where fans can go "down a rabbit hole," as she has put it, hunting for clues to the star’s next move and subjecting her every word to endless exegesis.

quotations.author: Christine Emba
quotations.passage: Influencers on TikTok, Instagram, YouTube and streaming sites […] dispense warnings about bops (those with many sexual partners), exegesis on the importance of body count (the number of people someone has slept with) and the dangers of simping (being excessively attentive or submissive to an uninterested love object), constructing entirely new categories by which to sort and judge potential mates.

quotations.author: George Abbot
quotations.passage: The manner of Scripture is sometimes to propose an action, at the first in grosse, and then aftervvard to particularize the circumstances of it. So here it is, and the next verse as an Exegesis to the former, doth explane the difficultie.
quotations.work: An Exposition vpon the Prophet Ionah .

quotations.author: Edward Leigh
quotations.passage: The reason of the germination, is not barely by vvay of exegesis; but to shevv that not onely the Jevves, but the Syrians, the Greeks, and Latines, should call God Father.
quotations.work: Annotations upon All the New Testament Philologicall and Theologicall

quotations.author: Satan
quotations.passage: The scope and design of the writer compel us to understand the latter part of the verse of angels, as well as the former; and thus interpreted, these heavenly beings are "flames of fire" as well as "spirits." And one part of this passage cannot be taken as an exegesis of the other. Spirit is not fire, or, if it be, it is not immaterial; and fire is not spirit, unless it can be shown that fire is not material.
quotations.work: The Methodist Magazine and Quarterly Review

quotations.author: Involution and Evolution
quotations.passage: [John] Wallis, in his Algebra (1684), gives the method of the ‘numerose exegesis’, as he calls it (Vieta [François Viète] had called it potestatum adfectarum ad exegesin Resolutio) with an example of the fourth degree worked to seventeen places of the root. He makes use of the method of contracting the figures towards the end. In this same Algebra appeared, for the first time, [Isaac] Newton’s method of approximation, which soon superseded the exegesis, into which however it had been virtually incorporated by [Henry] Briggs. Newton’s approximation, at least in the general form which it took in the hands of [Brook] Taylor, is as follows. If a be a near value of x in ϕx=0, then, except when there are two nearly equal roots, a nearer value is a−ϕaϕ′a or a+−ϕaϕ′a The old exegesis, and especially Briggs’s form of it, employs this principle; −ϕa is calculated, and either ϕ′a or ϕ(a+1)−ϕa.
quotations.work: The Supplement to the Penny Cyclopædia of the Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge

exegesis.title: exegesis

etymologies: From Ancient Greek ἐξηγητής (exēgētḗs, “expounder, interpreter”).

definitions.text: A person skilled in exegesis; an interpreter of texts, difficult passages, law, oracles, and similar obscure or esoteric sources.
To interpret; to perform an exegesis on.

quotations.author: Karen Armstrong
quotations.passage: A text that could not speak to the present was dead, and the exegete had a duty to revive it.

quotations.author: Glenn R. Morrow
quotations.passage: In Plato's state all three exegetes will be selected by Apollo. This is contrary to the practice of Hellenistic times, according to the evidence so ably marshaled by Oliver, when only two of the exegetes were named by the oracle.
quotations.work: Plato's Cretan City: A Historical Interpretation of the Laws

quotations.passage: Theophrastus' "superstitious man" finds that a mouse has gnawed a hole in his meal sack and, obviously thinking it a portent, consults the exegete as to what he shall do... The exegete tells him, according to Theophrastus, to take the sack to a leather shop and have it mended. If this is drawn from life, it indicates that the exegetes discharged their functions with humour and common sense.

quotations.author: Borden P. Bowne
quotations.passage: History, not the dictionary, must exegete this doctrine. When thus exegeted, the secularity of our Government, as shown by the intentions of its founders, the customs of the people, and the continuous decisions of the courts, means simply the separation of church and state.

exegete.title: exegete

etymologies: From Middle English exempler, from Middle French exemplair, and its source, Latin exemplar, from Latin exemplum (“example”).
From Middle English exempler, from Middle French exemplaire, and its source, Latin exemplāris. By surface analysis, example +‎ -ar. Doublet of exemplary.

examples: Michelangelo's "David" is an exemplar of Renaissance sculpture.
definitions.text: Something fit to be imitated; an ideal, a worthy model or role model: a desirable example.
Something typical or representative; an example that typifies its class.
A pattern after which others should be made; an archetype.
A well-known use of a scientific theory.
A manuscript used by a scribe to make a handwritten copy; the original document to be reproduced in a copy machine.
A copy of a book or piece of writing.
Exemplary.

quotations.author: Michel de Montaigne
quotations.passage: In our age we have no patterne of motherly affection more exemplare, than yours.

quotations.author: Nigel Harris
quotations.passage: A ray of light amid all this nonsense was Gwyn Topham's piece in the Guardian, which was timely, measured, accurate and of appropriate tone. That this single report stood out so clearly as an exemplar is a scathing comment in itself on the volumes of drivel surrounding it.

quotations.author: Richard Taverner
quotations.passage: To amend the same [default] according to the true exemplars.

exemplar.title: exemplar

etymologies: From Middle English exorten, from Old French exhorter, from Latin exhortārī (“to encourage”), from ex- (“out of, from”) +‎ hortārī (“to incite, spur”).

definitions.text: To urge; to advise earnestly.

quotations.author: James Joyce
quotations.passage: Asked if he had any message for the living he exhorted all who were still at the wrong side of Maya to acknowledge the true path for it was reported in devanic circles that Mars and Jupiter were out for mischief on the eastern angle where the ram has power.
And with many other words did hee testifie and exhort, saying, Saue your selues from this vntoward generation.

quotations.author: John Campbell Shairp
quotations.passage: And now, my dear sir, let me exhort you to take care of yourself.

quotations.author: February
quotations.passage: Finally, I would again exhort all railway photographers to concentrate on the older and disappearing types of engines, many of which will not be with us much longer.

quotations.author: J. K. Rowling
quotations.passage: Perhaps because he was determined to make up for having walked out on them, perhaps because Harry’s descent into listlessness galvanized his dormant leadership qualities, Ron was the one now encouraging and exhorting the other two into action.
quotations.work: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows

quotations.author: Alex McLevy
quotations.passage: Jon, watching the chaos unfold, is in shock. A Stark in spirit if not blood, he comes to the aid of a woman before she’s raped by a fellow soldier, but mostly, he’s struck dumb by the needless violence playing out around him, eventually able to do little more than exhort everyone to fall back and flee the city.

exhort.title: exhort

etymologies: From Middle French exigence, from Late Latin exigentia (“urgency”) (from exigēns + -ia), from exigere (“to demand”).

definitions.text: The demands or requirements of a situation which often demand immediate action.
An urgent situation, one requiring extreme effort or attention.
↑ Douglas Harper (2001–2026), “exigency”, in Online Etymology Dictionary.

quotations.author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon
quotations.passage: My business is with you, and you only. You should not have undertaken your office, unless prepared for its various exigencies.

quotations.author: Edgar Rice Burroughs
quotations.passage: No ordinary man could have escaped those frightful claws when Numa sprang from so short a distance, but Tarzan was no ordinary man. From earliest childhood his muscles had been trained by the fierce exigencies of his existence to act with the rapidity of thought.

quotations.author: July
quotations.passage: [...] but these details I am compelled by exigencies of space to hold over until next month.

exigency.title: exigency

etymologies: From Latin exigēns, present active participle of exigō (“demand, require”). Doublet of exigeant.

definitions.text: Urgent; pressing; needing immediate action.
Demanding; requiring great effort.
Extremity; end; limit; pressing urgency.
The amount that is required.
A writ in proceedings before outlawry.

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: These Eyes, like Lampes, whose wasting Oyle is spent, / Waxe dimme, as drawing to their Exigent.
quotations.work: Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies

quotations.author: Robert Browning
quotations.passage: [H]is enterprise / Marked out anew, its exigent of wit / Apportioned, she at liberty to sit / And scheme against the next emergence, […]

quotations.author: Miles Smith
quotations.passage: Therefore as one complaineth, that always in the Senate of Rome [Cicero 5° de finibus.], there was one or other that called for an interpreter: so lest the Church be driuen to the like exigent, it is necessary to haue translations in a readinesse.

quotations.author: John Cowell
quotations.passage: They also make forthe writs of executions, and of seifin, writs of super seders, for appearance to exigents

exigent.title: exigent

etymologies: From Latin exiguus (“strict, exact”), from exigere (“to measure against a standard”).

definitions.text: Scanty; meager.

quotations.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
quotations.passage: The herdboy in the broom, already musical in the days of Father Chaucer, startles (and perhaps pains) the lark with this exiguous pipe.

quotations.author: G. K. Chesterton
quotations.passage: The path on which I then planted my feet was quite unprecedentedly narrow. I had never had to walk along a thoroughfare so exiguous.

quotations.author: Michael Ignatieff
quotations.passage: They are entering the market, setting up stalls on snowy streets, moonlighting to supplement exiguous incomes.

quotations.author: Terence Brown
quotations.passage: Among the pressures provoking these distresses were a father's financial inadequacy and a growing awareness that, by finding employment himself, he could ameliorate the family's exiguous circumstances.
quotations.work: The Life of W. B. Yeats: A Critical Biography

exiguous.title: exiguous

etymologies: From Middle English exoneraten (attested in past participle exonerated), from Latin exonerātus, past perfect participle of exonerō (“to discharge, unload; to exonerate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Exonerō is from ex- (“out, from”) +‎ onerō (“to burden, lade; to load”) further from onus (oner-) (“a burden, load”) +‎ -ō (first conjugation verb-forming suffix), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃énh₂os (“burden, load”), from *h₃enh₂- (“to charge, onerate”). Compare French exonérer.
Learned borrowing from Latin exonerātus (more at etymology 1), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

definitions.text: To relieve (someone or something) of a load; to unburden (a load).
Of a body of water: to discharge or empty (itself).
To free (someone) from an obligation, responsibility or task.
To free (someone) from accusation or blame.
Freed from an obligation; freed from accusation or blame; acquitted, exonerated.

quotations.author: Robert Burton
quotations.passage: I would examine the Caspian Sea, and see where and how it exonerates it selfe, after it hath taken in Volga, Iaxares, Oxus, and those great rivers; at the mouth of Oby, or where?

exonerate.title: exonerate

etymologies: From Middle English exorcisen, exorzisen, from Medieval Latin exorcizō, from Ancient Greek ἐξορκίζω (exorkízō, “to banish an evil spirit; bind by oath”), from ἐξ (ex) + ὅρκος (hórkos). Compare Old French exorciser.

examples: The priest attempted to exorcise the evil spirit from the house.
The ritual was performed to exorcise the demons from the village.
definitions.text: To drive out (an evil spirit) from a person, place or thing, especially by an incantation or prayer.

examples: They hired a specialist to exorcise the haunted object.
definitions.text: To rid (a person, place or thing) of an evil spirit.

exorcise.title: exorcise

etymologies: From the participle stem of Latin expatior, from ex- + spatior (“walk about”).

definitions.text: To write or speak at length; to be copious in argument or discussion.
To range at large, or without restraint.
To expand; to spread; to extend; to diffuse; to broaden.

quotations.author: Alexander Pope
quotations.passage: [L]ooks on heav'n with more than mortal eyes, / Bids his free soul expatiate in the skies, / Amidst her kindred stars familiar roam, / Survey the region, and confess her home! Such was the life great Scipio once admir'd, / Thus Atticus, and Trumball thus retir'd.

quotations.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
quotations.passage: Governor Bellingham, in a loose gown and easy cap,—such as elderly gentlemen loved to indue themselves with, in their domestic privacy,—walked foremost, and appeared to be showing off his estate, and expatiating on his projected improvements.

quotations.author: Herman Melville
quotations.passage: Now, as the business of standing mast-heads, ashore or afloat, is a very ancient and interesting one, let us in some measure expatiate here.

quotations.author: Joseph Addison
quotations.passage: [H]e expatiated on the inconveniences of trade, that carried from us the commodities of our country, and made a parcel of upstarts as rich as men of the most ancient families of England.
quotations.work: The Works of the Right Honourable Joseph Addison, Esq;

quotations.author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon
quotations.passage: To the pure mind of Isabella thought of no other had arisen; and it was far better that the generous romance of her young heart should expatiate on the rival in heaven, than for a moment dread a rival on earth, and therefore become subject to jealousy...
quotations.work: Lady Anne Granard; or, Keeping up Appearances.

quotations.author: Clive Exton
quotations.passage: Wooster: If you ask me, art is responsible for most of the trouble in the world. / Jeeves: An interesting theory, sir. Would you care to expatiate upon it? / Wooster: As a matter of fact, no, Jeeves. The thought just occurred to me, as thoughts do. / Jeeves: Very good, sir.

quotations.author: Clive James
quotations.passage: “It can't fly,” he expatiated. “It can move forward only by hopping.”

expatiate.title: expatiate

etymologies: From Middle English expedient, from Old French expedient, from Latin expediens (stem expedient-), present participle of expedire (“to bring forward, to dispatch, to expedite; impers. to be profitable, serviceable, advantageous, expedient”), from ex (“out”) + pēs (“foot, hoof”).

examples: Most people, faced with a decision, will choose the most expedient option.
definitions.text: Suitable to effect some desired end or the purpose intended.
Affording short-term benefit, often at the expense of the long-term.
Governed by self-interest, often short-term self-interest.
Expeditious, quick, rapid.
A method or means for achieving a particular result, especially when direct or efficient; a resource.

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: the adverse winds / Whose leisure I have stay'd, have given him time / To land his legions all as soon as I; / His marches are expedient to this town / His forces strong, his soldiers confident.
quotations.work: Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies

quotations.author: Alexander Hamilton
quotations.passage: To secure such a market, there is no other expedient, than to promote manufacturing establishments.
Nevertheless I tell you the truth; It is expedient for you that I go away; for if I go not away, the Comforter willnot come unto you; but if I depart, I will send him unto you.

quotations.author: Richard Whately
quotations.passage: Nothing but the right can ever be the expedient, since that can never be true expediency which would sacrifice a greater good to a less.

quotations.author: Thomas Babington Macaulay
quotations.passage: [T]he judges were unanimously of opinion that [...] by the common law of England, no man, not authorised by the crown, had a right to publish political news. While the Whig party was still formidable, the government thought it expedient occasionally to connive at the violation of this rule.
quotations.work: The History of England from the Accession of James II

quotations.passage: That's because the debate pits textbook economics — which argues that bailouts beget bad behavior begets more bailouts — against practical politics. And politics, or the taking of expedient steps to keep people happy, will almost always win.

quotations.author: Jesse Ventura
quotations.passage: Government has slowly but positively moved from an active course of following plans and policies to the easier and more expedient course of the counterpuncher.
quotations.work: The Secret Team: The CIA and Its Allies in Control of the United States and the World

quotations.author: Douglas B. Klusmeyer
quotations.passage: Its policies toward foreign lab or across these eras reflect these sharp differences in context, but also reflect a common pattern to treat the recruitment and deployment of foreign nationals as an expedient measure to serve immediate economic objectives
quotations.work: Immigration Policy in the Federal Republic of Germany

quotations.author: October–December

extempore.title: extempore

etymologies: From Middle English extenuat (“(medicine) made thin, emaciated”), from Latin extenuātus (“diminished, reduced, thinned”), perfect passive participle of extenuō (“to diminish, reduce, thin”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from ex- (“out-, thoroughly”) +‎ tenuō (“to enfeeble, weaken, wear down; to lessen, reduce; to make thin”), from tenuis (“fine, slender, thin; feeble, weak”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tenh₂- (“to extend, stretch; thin”)) + -ō (first conjugation-verb forming suffix). Compare attenuate.
From Latin extenuātus (“diminished, reduced, thinned”) (more at etymology 1), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

definitions.text: Of a person: emaciated, wasted, weakened; of the body or part of it: atrophied, shrunken, withered.
Of a quality or thing: lessened, weakened.
Reduced to poverty; impoverished.
To make (something) less dense, or thinner; also, to lower the viscosity of (something).
To make (someone or something) slender or thin; to emaciate, to waste.

examples: to extenuate his faults to extenuate their crimes
definitions.text: To diminish or seek to diminish the extent or severity of (a crime, guilt, a mistake, or something else negative) by making apologies or excuses; to palliate.
To beat or draw (a metal object, etc.) out so as to lessen the thickness.
To reduce the quality or quantity of (something); to lessen or weaken the force of (something).
To degrade (someone); to detract from (someone's qualities, reputation, etc.); to depreciate, to disparage.

definitions.text: A quarter of any monetary unit or measure.
Former British unit of currency worth one-quarter of an old penny; or a coin representing this.
A very small quantity or value; the least possible amount.
A division of land.
A surname.

quotations.author: Howard Pyle
quotations.passage: "Nay, Heaven forbid, indeed," quoth Robin, "that I should take from such as thee, jolly fellow! Not so much as one farthing would I take from thee, for I love a fair Saxon face like thine right well—more especially when it cometh from Locksley Town, and most especially when the man that owneth it is to marry a bonny lass on Thursday next. But come, tell me for what price thou wilt sell me all of thy meat and thy horse and cart."
quotations.work: The Merry Adventures of Robin Hood

quotations.author: William Blair Morton Ferguson
quotations.passage: I had never defrauded a man of a farthing, nor called him knave behind his back. But now the last rag that covered my nakedness had been torn from me. I was branded a blackleg, card-sharper, and murderer.

farthing.title: farthing

etymologies: Borrowed from Latin fastīdiōsus (“passive: that feels disgust, disdainful, scornful, fastidious; active: that causes disgust, disgusting, loathsome”), from fastīdium (“a loathing, aversion, disgust, niceness of taste, daintiness, etc.”), perhaps for *fastutidium, from fastus (“disdain, haughtiness, arrogance, disgust”) + taedium (“disgust”). Cf. French fastidieux.

definitions.text: Excessively particular, demanding, or fussy about details, especially about tidiness and cleanliness.
Overly concerned about tidiness and cleanliness.
Difficult to please; quick to find fault.

examples: fastidious organism
fastidious species
definitions.text: Having precise requirements for nutrition and environment (chemical and physical); especially, being difficult to culture because of those requirements.

quotations.author: Henry James
quotations.passage: You're too fastidious, and too indolent, and too rich.

quotations.author: Lynsay Sands
quotations.passage: He had at first tried to clean up as they ate, his fastidious nature kicking in, but Chris had told him to just stop, he was blocking the TV.

quotations.author: Maria Osborne Perr
quotations.passage: As she cleaned the room daily, she knew it was against his fastidious nature to bring or have food in his room.

quotations.author: Robert Fisher
quotations.passage: His fastidious nature had been evident in his careful snipping of a customer's hair and now he guided his pencil with the same adroitness.

quotations.author: Debra Lee Baldwin
quotations.passage: "If you are fastidious, clean previously used pots inside and out; if not, merely clean the outside (unless you are battling a pest infestation; then the inside will need scrubbing as well)."
quotations.work: Succulent Container Gardens: Design Eye-Catching Displays with 350 Easy-Care ...

quotations.author: Kate Chopin
quotations.passage: "It's burn[t], M'sieur," said Marie Louise, politely, but decidedly, to the utter confusion of Mr. Billy, who was as mortified as could be at the failure of his dinner to please his fastidious little visitor.

fastidious.title: fastidious

definitions.text: Alternative letter-case form of Fata Morgana.

quotations.author: Michael Chabon
quotations.passage: On the other side of the electric fence, the fata morgana shimmers.

etymologies: From Latin fātidicus, from fātum (“fate”) + dico (“to speak”). Via Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂- cognate with the synonymous English prophetic.

definitions.text: Of or pertaining to prophecy; prophetic.

quotations.author: Vladimir Nabokov
quotations.passage: At that moment he felt quite proud of his stratagem. He was to recall it with a fatidic shiver seventeen years later [...].

quotations.author: David Brin
quotations.passage: Auntie Kapur tapped a steady beat on a miniature ceremonial drum — which some called a zzxjoanw — while making fatidic statements about amorous goddesses and other superstitious nonsense.

fatidic.title: fatidic

etymologies: From Latin fatuus (“foolish, silly, simple”).

definitions.text: Inanely stupid; vacantly silly; content in one's foolishness.

quotations.author: Joel Coen
quotations.passage: Maude Lebowski: Lord. You can imagine where it goes from here. / The Dude: He fixes the cable? / Maude: Don't be fatuous, Jeffrey.

quotations.author: Frank Tallis
quotations.passage: A fatuous love affair can easily result in a fatuous marriage. A couple who hardly know each other and, indeed, may not even really like each other, make a commitment that has little chance of being honoured.
quotations.work: Love Sick: Love as a Mental Illness

quotations.author: Christian Wolmar
quotations.passage: While much publicity is given to fatuous 'reversing Beeching' ideas, the reality is that the real investment is focused on expanding the road network - [...].

fatuous.title: fatuous

audio.accent: Standard Southern British, Australia, New Zealand

etymologies: Borrowed from New Latin fauna, from Latin Fauna, sister of Faunus (“god of forests and herdsmen”); akin to Ancient Greek θαῦνον (thaûnon, “wild animal, beast”), θώς (thṓs, “jackal, wild dog; panther”), Phrygian δάος (dáos, “wolf”).

examples: the flora and fauna
definitions.text: Animals considered as a group; especially those of a particular country, region, time, biological group, etc.
A particular group of animals as distinguished from another.
A book cataloguing the animals of a country.
The goddess of animals, nature, spring and fertility; she is also the consort of Faunus.
A female given name from Latin.

pronunciations.accent: Standard Southern British, Australia, New Zealand

quotations.author: Richard Ellis
quotations.passage: Japanese waters also support a rich and diverse shark fauna, including the smallest known shark Squaliolus laticaudus, and the bizarre goblin shark, Mitsukurina owstoni.

quotations.author: Alfred Russel Wallace
quotations.passage: More than this, at least twenty genera, which are common to New Guinea and Aru, do not extend into Ceram, indicating with a force which every naturalist will appreciate, that the two latter countries have received their faunas in a radically different manner.

fauna.title: fauna

etymologies: Borrowed from Latin favōniānus, from Favōnius (“the West Wind”), which heralded the beginning of spring.

definitions.text: Pertaining to the west wind.
Mild, gentle.

quotations.author: Vladimir Nabokov
quotations.passage: Sunday. Heat ripple still with us; a most favonian week. This time I took up a strategic position, with obese newspaper and new pipe, in the piazza rocker before L. arrived.

favonian.title: favonian

etymologies: Inherited from Middle English feaute, feute, from Anglo-Norman fëauté, fëuté, from Latin fidēlitās (“faithfulness”; “homage, fealty” in Medieval Latin), from fidēlis (“faithful”) +‎ -tās (noun suffix); the modern form (for expected *feauty /ˈfjuːti/) is due to learned influence. Equivalent to obsolete feal +‎ -ty. Doublet of fidelity.

definitions.text: Fidelity to one's lord or master; the feudal obligation by which the tenant or vassal was bound to be faithful to his lord.

quotations.author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon
quotations.passage: I doubt whether the most devoted fidelity would bear strict examination as to the short reposes even the most entire fealty permits itself.

quotations.author: Relic Entertainment
quotations.passage: Ordo Malleus Inquisitor: In fealty to the God-Emperor, our Undying Lord, and by the grace of the Golden Throne, I declare exterminatus upon the Imperial world of Typhon Primaris.
quotations.work: Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War II – Retribution

quotations.author: Richard Fausset
quotations.passage: And yet the war has come, full of double-crossing, internecine accusations of lying and incompetence, and a bitter cleavage into factions over the question of how much fealty should be shown to President Trump — and the extent to which Republicans should amplify his false argument that the election in this fast-changing Southern state was stolen from him.

quotations.author: Paul Sonne
quotations.passage: In one recent video, he said the problem posed by a Russian military led by people who demand nothing but blind fealty would need to be dealt with — “or one day the Russian people will solve it themselves.”

quotations.author: Cameron Joseph
quotations.passage: I think the central characteristic Trump seems to be looking for in all of the appointees we’ve seen so far is fealty to him.

quotations.author: Howard LaFranchi
quotations.passage: But [Max Bergmann, director of the Europe, Russia, and Eurasia Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington] says there’s a growing sense that what Mr. Trump really wants is unquestioned fealty – and that, he says, is not going to happen.

fealty.title: fealty

etymologies: Borrowed from Medieval Latin febrīlis, from Latin febris (“fever”). By surface analysis, Latin febr- +‎ -ile.

definitions.text: Feverish, or having a high temperature.
Involving fever as a symptom or cause.
Full of nervous energy.

quotations.author: Isaac Asimov
quotations.passage: Aurora's orange sun (Baley scarcely noted the orange tinge now) was mildly warm on his back, lacking the febrile heat that Earth's sun had in summer (but, then, what was the climate and season on this portion of Aurora right now?).

quotations.author: Tom Fordyce
quotations.passage: An already febrile atmosphere within the ground before the start had been stoked still further when France's players formed an arrow formation to face down the haka, and then advanced slowly over halfway as the capacity crowd roared.

quotations.author: Marina Hyde
quotations.passage: Out in the ground, meanwhile, it was particularly disappointing to hear former England captain Andrew Strauss put the febrile atmosphere down to “people who don’t normally come to Lord’s”.

quotations.author: Katharine Viner
quotations.passage: Harry Potter has become such a febrile battleground that the pattern has already become well worn.

febrile.title: febrile

etymologies: From Scots feckless, variant of Scots fectless (“ineffectual”) (an aphetic variant of effectless), equivalent to effect +‎ -less.

definitions.text: Lacking purpose.
Without skill, ineffective, incompetent.
Lacking the courage to act in any meaningful way.
Lacking vitality.

quotations.passage: It is the beauty of great games when they are played at their highest level and the extraordinary thing now is that we do not have to trawl back through all the years of your inexorable progress from feckless beach boy to master sportsman.

quotations.author: March
quotations.passage: This was the West Lancashire Railway, an ambitious but feckless little concern which, in a life lasting a quarter of a century, never earned a dividend, failed to keep up its debenture payments (despite a dangerous attempt to do so by issuing more debentures) and ended up in the hands of a receiver.

quotations.author: Adam Reed
quotations.passage: “Lana, when I want you to talk, I will tell you. And until then, zip it.” “Wha-- what did I do?” “Nothing.” “Yeah, Lana.” “Which is why these feckless idiots lost 200 kilos of cocaine.” “Yeah, Lan-- oh. OK. Technically. But then we stole a plane loaded with, like, twice as much cocaine.” “Is this the part where you tell me to look under my seat?”

quotations.author: Cameron Joseph
quotations.passage: Across the country, Democratic voters who have been reeling from Mr. Trump’s sweeping and possibly illegal cuts to government, his head-spinning policy moves, and his politicization of federal law enforcement are growing more and more incensed at their own party’s seemingly feckless response.

quotations.author: Nicholas Burns
quotations.passage: China is “proving to be a feckless friend for its authoritarian allies,” Nicholas Burns, the U.S. ambassador to China under President Joe Biden, wrote on X.

feckless.title: feckless

etymologies: From Middle French fécond, from Latin fēcundus (“fertile”), which is related to fētus and fēmina (“woman”).

definitions.text: Highly fertile; able to produce offspring.
Leading to new ideas or innovation.

quotations.author: Massimo Livi Bacci
quotations.passage: The number of children per woman depends, as has been said, on biological and social factors which determine: (1) the frequency of births during a woman's fecund period, and (2) the portion of the fecund period--between puberty and menopause--effectively utilized for reproduction.
quotations.work: A Concise History of World Population

quotations.author: Olivia Judson
quotations.passage: The druids […] believed that mistletoe could make barren animals fecund, and that it was an antidote to all poisons.

quotations.author: Charles Sanders Peirce
quotations.passage: This idea of Aristotle's has proved marvellously fecund; and in truth it is the only idea covering quite the whole area of cenoscopy that has shown any marked uberosity.
quotations.work: The Essential Peirce: Selected Philosophical Writings

fecund.title: fecund

etymologies: From Middle English feynen, feinen, borrowed from Old French feindre (“to pretend”), from Latin fingere (“to form, shape, invent”). Compare French feignant (present participle of feindre, literally “feigning”). Also compare feint, figment and fiction.

examples: The pupil feigned sickness on the day of his exam.
They feigned her signature on the cheque.
feign ignorance, feign illness, feign indifference, feign injury, feign innocence, feign interest
definitions.text: To make a false show or pretence of; to counterfeit or simulate.

examples: He feigned that he had gone home at the appointed time.
definitions.text: To imagine; to invent; to pretend to do something.
To make an action as if doing one thing, but actually doing another, for example to trick an opponent; to feint.

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: [T]he truest poetry is the most / feigning, and lovers are given to poetry, and what / they swear in poetry may be said as lovers they do / feign.

quotations.author: William Makepeace Thackeray
quotations.passage: She had not been much of a dissembler, until now her loneliness taught her to feign.

quotations.author: Daniel Taylor
quotations.passage: Cahill was beaten far too easily for Miller's goal, although the striker deserves the credit for the way he controlled Alan Hutton's right-wing delivery, with his back to goal, feigned to his left then went the other way and pinged a splendid left-foot shot into Hart's bottom right-hand corner.

feign.title: feign

etymologies: From Latin fēlicitātus, perfect passive participle of fēlīcitō (“to felicitate”) (from fēlīx (“happy”)), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Compare French féliciter.
From Latin fēlicitātus, see Etymology 1 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more.

definitions.text: To congratulate.
Made very happy.

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: I am alone felicitate / In your dear highness' love.
quotations.work: Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies

quotations.author: George Orwell
quotations.passage: […] he waddled to the platform, bowed as low as his belly would permit, and was duly decorated and felicitated […]

quotations.author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon
quotations.passage: […] we contemplate death under quite a different aspect;—creating in us such sweet influences of joy, that our beloved brethren, under one common Father, have attained what we ought all to be in search of, the heavenly goal, that rather than repine at this their advancement, we sincerely felicitate them.

quotations.author: Norman Lindsay
quotations.passage: Still, he tucked in handsomely to bacon and tomato on fried bread, felicitating himself on the considered wisdom of his arrival in the character of guest to Bradly.

felicitate.title: felicitate

etymologies: From felicity +‎ -ous.

definitions.text: Characterized by felicity.
Appropriate, apt, fitting.
Auspicious, fortunate, lucky.
Causing happiness or pleasure.

examples: This sentence is grammatical; it is just not felicitous.
definitions.text: Of a sentence or utterance: semantically and pragmatically coherent; fitting in the context.

quotations.author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon
quotations.passage: Walter again pursued his way, lost in a very mixed reverie; sometimes writhing under an idea of degradation, in thus making a trade of his talents; and then, again, somewhat consoled by the pride of art; for how many felicitous and stinging epigrams arose in his mind!
quotations.work: Ethel Churchill: Or, The Two Brides.

quotations.author: George Augustus Sala
quotations.passage: As a post-prandial speaker, however, Thackeray was undeniably the reverse of felicitous.
quotations.work: Things I Have Seen and People I Have Known

quotations.author: Pertrella
quotations.passage: The recommendations of the experts, however, have not proved very felicitous. […] [S]cant regard has been paid to Albania's much stronger claims, both on ethnographical and on strategical grounds, in the North, […]
quotations.work: The Near East: A Weekly Review of the Politics and Commerce of the Balkan Peninsula, Egypt and the Sudan, Morocco, Asia Minor, Arabia, Mesopotamia, Persia, and India

quotations.author: Daniel Lerner
quotations.passage: […] Sykewar was not conceived, in [P. M. A.] Linebarger's felicitous phrase, as "warfare psychologically waged."
quotations.work: Sykewar: Psychological Warfare against Germany, D-Day to VE-Day

quotations.author: John Robert Morrison
quotations.passage: There are a variety of charms, of various kinds, for which there are no names and no particular uses; but they are considered felicitous, and are therefore worn by the poorer classes, who cannot buy the more valuable charms.
quotations.work: Transactions of the Royal Asiatic Society of Great Britain and Ireland

quotations.author: William
quotations.passage: The same chronicler [John Capgrave] makes Henry of Agincourt die a day earlier than he really did, apparently only for the purpose of manufacturing a sort of coincidence. 'His end fell well on the feast of Saint Felix, for he was felicitous in all things—felicitous in endowing the church, felicitous in ordering more clearly the divine offices, felicitous in the administration of justice, and in fine, felicitous in all his life.[']
quotations.work: Chambers’s Journal of Popular Literature, Science and Art

quotations.author: Rabindranath Tagore
quotations.passage: He is looking the very picture of health, and on the whole his dreams are felicitous. For instance, last night he dreamt that he had been buying strawberries as large as gourds. It proves the magnificent vitality of his dreams.

quotations.author: Laurence Danlos
quotations.passage: The aim of this paper is to compare rst [rhetorical structure theory], sdrt [segmented discourse representation theory] and discourse dependency dags [directed acyclic graphs] with respect to the following question: do these formalisms allow the representation of all the discourse structures which correspond to felicitous discourses and exclude those which correspond to infelicitous discourses?

felicitous.title: felicitous

etymologies: From Middle English felicite (“bliss, happiness, joy; delight, pleasure; a source of happiness; good fortune; prosperity; well-being; of a planet: in an influential position”) [and other forms], borrowed from Old French felicité (modern French félicité (“bliss, happiness; felicity”)), from Latin fēlīcitātem, the accusative singular of fēlīcitās (“fertility, fruitfulness; happiness, felicity; good fortune; success”), from fēlīx (“happy; blessed, fortunate, lucky; fertile, fruitful; prosperous; auspicious, favourable”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to nurse, suckle”)) + -itās (a variant of -tās (suffix forming nouns indicating a state of being)).

definitions.text: Intense happiness.
An instance of intense happiness.
An apt and pleasing style in speech, writing, etc.; an apt and pleasing choice of words.
Good luck; success; An instance of unexpected good luck; a stroke of luck; also, a lucky characteristic.

examples: The quotation was rendered with felicity.
definitions.text: Reproduction of a sign with fidelity.
Something that is either a source of happiness or particularly apt.
Period (as opposed to lifetime) utility.
A female given name from English.

quotations.author: Christopher Marlowe
quotations.passage: […] to weare our selues & neuer rest, / Untill we reach the ripest fruites of all, / That perfect blisse and sole felicitie, / The sweet fruition of an earthly crowne.
quotations.work: Tamburlaine the Great. The First Part

quotations.author: Daniel Defoe
quotations.passage: [T]he wise Man gave his Testimony to this, as the just Standard of true Felicity, when he prayed to have neither Poverty nor Riches.
quotations.work: The Life and Strange Surprizing Adventures of Robinson Crusoe

quotations.author: Jane Austen
quotations.passage: […] Mr. and Mrs. Norris began their career of conjugal felicity with very little less than a thousand a year.

quotations.author: Marcus Aurelius
quotations.passage: For two reasons then it is right to be content with that which happens to thee; the one, because it was done for thee and prescribed for thee, and in a manner had reference to thee, originally from the most ancient causes spun with thy destiny; and the other, because even that which comes severally to every man is to the power which administers the universe a cause of felicity and perfection, nay even of its very continuance.
quotations.work: The Thoughts of the Emperor M. Aurelius Antoninus

quotations.author: Leszek Kołakowski
quotations.passage: Although he shows traces of the Romantic belief in the felicity of the savage, these are not numerous or important and there is no suggestion in his work that mankind could or should revert to a primitive life-style.

quotations.author: Henry Bradshaw
quotations.passage: Whan this sayd monument discouered was / Suche a suauite and fragrant odoure / Ascended from the corps by singular grace / Passyng all worldly swetnes and sauour / That all there present that day and hour / Supposed they had ben / in the felicite / Of erthely paradise / without ambiguite.
quotations.work: The Holy Lyfe and History of Saynt Werburge: Very Frutefull for All Christen People to Rede

quotations.author: Joshua Ferris
quotations.passage: The season’s main attraction, the felicities of the sun, dimmed in the light of our competition and our growing friendliness.

quotations.author: Ben J. Heidra
quotations.passage: In equation (19.24) UC(⋅) is the marginal felicity of consumption[.]

felicity.title: felicity

etymologies: From Latin fera (“wild beast”, noun) +‎ -al or Latin ferus (“wild; savage; cruel”, adjective) +‎ -al. Alternatively, borrowed from Middle French féral or Late Latin ferālis.
From Latin fērālis (“funereal”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰéh₁s (“god, sacred place”).
Homophone.

examples: In this region, the wild boars can be dangerous, but (perhaps counterintuitively) the feral hogs can be even worse.
definitions.text: Wild; untamed.

examples: In this region, the wild boars can be dangerous, but (perhaps counterintuitively) the feral hogs can be even worse.
definitions.text: Of an animal, wild but descended from domestic or captive ancestors; thus, in the wild, although not necessarily of the wild type.
Having the characteristics of an animal; animal-like.
Of a person, contemptible; unruly; misbehaved.
Behaving in an out-of-control way due to enthrallment with a certain thought, behavior, person, etc.
That is a feral character; zoomorphic.
A domesticated (non-human) animal that has returned to the wild; an animal, particularly a domesticated animal, living independently of humans.
A contemptible young person, a lout, a person who behaves wildly.
A person who has isolated themselves from the outside world; one living an alternative lifestyle.

examples: The story is about a group of ferals which have to explore the ruins of society after the humans die out.
definitions.text: A furry character in art or literature which has the appearance of a regular animal (typically quadrupedal), that may or may not be able to communicate with humans or "anthros".
Deadly, fatal.
Of or pertaining to the dead, funereal.
Misspelling of ferrule.

quotations.author: Jesse Green
quotations.passage: Among the ensemble’s strange, outmoded, “original” instruments — the feral horns, sour violins, wooden flutes, cellos without endpins — she seemed right at home, despite her Broadway provenance.

quotations.author: Charles Darwin

quotations.author: Harvey Randall
quotations.passage: It owes its existence to a feral culture of internet goblins who sentence-mixed the same few janky cutscenes for years.

quotations.author: Ian Fleming
quotations.passage: There were about fifty tables and the customers were packed in like black olives in a jar. It was hot and the air was thick with smoke and the sweet, feral smell of two hundred negro bodies.

quotations.author: Stephanie Hoyt
quotations.passage: Miners fans have been going absolutely feral over you, [and] you're also disgustingly talented. People want you to play for them! You had Canadians bitching about you being American born the first time you played for Team USA.

quotations.author: Notes and Comments: No homes for the pigeons
quotations.passage: Although it is not difficult to induce domestic pigeons to nest in boxes fixed to trees, London′s ferals are not yet acclimatized to arboreal holes.

quotations.author: Alexandra Powe Allred
quotations.passage: Traffic, abuse, inhumane traps, and accidental poisoning are other hazards ferals must face. […] In England one gamekeeper claimed to have killed over three hundred ferals, while another brought home pelts to his wife so that she could design rugs from cat skins as a source of secondary income.
quotations.work: Cats' Most Wanted: The Top 10 Book of Mysterious Mousers, Talented Tabbies, and Feline Oddities

quotations.author: Clea Simon
quotations.passage: You trap ferals, neuter them, and give them their rabies shot. Maybe distemper.

quotations.author: Gina Spadafori
quotations.passage: If you′ve ever put a saucer of milk out for a hard-luck kitty, or if you′re spending your lunch hour sharing sandwiches with the ferals near your office, this is the chapter for you.

quotations.author: Bill Metcalf
quotations.passage: The intolerance which was directed towards us during the early years has now shifted to ‘the ferals’ who embrace a new version of nonconformist behaviour that even some of us in their parent′s generation — the Aquarian settlers — don′t like. The ferals are the scapegoats for the drug problems here, and are highly visible since many of them have nowhere to live.
quotations.work: From Utopian Dreaming to Communal Reality: Cooperative Lifestyles in Australia

quotations.author: Shane Maloney
quotations.passage: A pod of ferals was moving towards the exit, a half-dozen soap-shy, low-tech, bush-dwelling hippies.

quotations.author: Anna Krien
quotations.passage: It′s the rootlessness of the ferals that people don′t seem to trust; their claims of connectedness to all wild places touches a nerve. Even residents of Maydena who want to see the Florentine protected dislike the ratbags′ itinerancy.
quotations.work: Into The Woods: The Battle For Tasmania's Forests

feral.title: feral

etymologies: From Middle English furet, ferret, from Old French furet, from Vulgar Latin *furittum (“weasel, ferret”), diminutive of Latin fūr (“thief”).
Borrowed from Italian fioretto.

definitions.text: A long-bodied domesticated mammal of the species Mustela furo, descended from the European polecat and often trained to hunt burrowing animals.
A black-footed ferret (Mustela nigripes).
A diligent searcher.
To hunt game with ferrets.
To uncover and bring to light by searching; usually to ferret out.
A tape of silk, cotton, or ribbon, used to tie documents, clothing, etc. or along the edge of fabric.

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: Master Fer! I'll fer him, and firk him, and ferret him.
quotations.work: Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies

quotations.author: Charles Dickens
quotations.passage: I confess that we were so unpopular with the outrageous mob, that I only got away from England at the risk of being ducked to death, and that Cly was so ferreted up and down, that he never would have got away at all but for that sham.

quotations.author: Charles Dickens
quotations.passage: red tape and green ferret

quotations.author: Virginia Woolf
quotations.passage: She ferreted in her bag; then held it up mouth downwards; then fumbled in her lap, all so vigorously that Charles Steele in the Panama hat suspended his paint-brush.

quotations.author: Charles Nicholl
quotations.passage: The most challenging documentary discoveries were made by a tenacious archival ferret, Dr Antonio Bertoletti. In 1879 he published his findings in a slim, refreshingly dry volume, Francesco Cenci e la sua Famiglia.

quotations.author: Edgar Alan Poe
quotations.passage: He had been piqued by the failure of all his endeavors to ferret out the assassins.

ferret.title: ferret

etymologies: Borrowed from Latin ferrūgineus, from ferrūgo (“rust”).

definitions.text: Synonym of ferrous, of or related to iron.

examples: ferruginous:
definitions.text: Synonym of rusty, of or related to rust, rust-colored.

quotations.passage: A few miles north of Coquimbo, I met with the ferruginous, balaniferous mass (E) with many silicified bones; I was informed that these silicified bones occur also at Tonguay, south of Coquimbo […]

etymologies: From Middle English feye (“fated to die”), from Old English fǣġe (“doomed to die, timid”), from Proto-West Germanic *faigī, from Proto-Germanic *faigijaz (“cowardly, wicked”), from Proto-Indo-European *peyk- (“ill-meaning, bad”).

Akin to Old Saxon fēgi, whence Dutch veeg (“doomed, near death”), Old High German feigi (“appointed for death, ungodly”) whence German feige (“cowardly”), Old Norse feigr (“doomed”) whence the Icelandic feigur (“doomed to die”), Old English fāh (“outlawed, hostile”). More at foe.
From Middle English faie, fei (“a place or person possessed with magical properties”), from Middle French feie, fee (“fairy", "fae”), from Old French fae, from Medieval Latin fāda. More at fairy.

Cognate with Swedish feja (“to sweep”), Danish feje (“to sweep”), German fegen (“to cleanse, scour, sweep”), Dutch vegen (“to sweep, strike”). More at feague, fake, fair.

etymologies: From Middle English firmament, furmament (“heaven; sky”), from Old French firmament (“firmament”), or from its etymon Latin firmāmentum (“support; sky”), from firmāre (“to strengthen”) + -mentum (suffix indicating an instrument or medium, or the result of an action). Firmāre is the present active infinitive of firmō (“to make firm, strengthen”), from firmus (“firm, strong, stable”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰer- (“to hold; to support”).

The Latin word was used in the Vulgate version of the Bible to translate the Ancient Greek στερέωμα (steréōma, “foundation, framework; firmament”) in the Septuagint (Greek Old Testament), which in turn was used to translate the Hebrew רָקִיעַ (rāqī́aʿ, “celestial dome, vault of heaven”), from the root ר־ק־ע (r-q-`); in Classical Syriac the similar root ܪ ܩ ܥ (related to compacting) gave rise to ܪܩܝܥܐ (rəqīʿā, “compact; firm; firmament, heavens, sky; celestial sphere”).
