definitions.text: A noisy disorderly quarrel, fight, brawl, disturbance or scrap.

quotations.author: Jane Austen
quotations.passage: Fanny read to herself that “it was with infinite concern the newspaper had to announce to the world, a matrimonial fracas in the family of Mr. R. of Wimpole Street; the beautiful Mrs. R. whose name had not long been enrolled in the lists of hymen, and who had promised to become so brilliant a leader in the fashionable world, having quitted her husband’s roof in company with the well known and captivating Mr. C. the intimate friend and associate of Mr. R. and it was not known, even to the editor of the newspaper, whither they were gone.”

quotations.author: Philip K. Dick
quotations.passage: The Oregon-Northern California region had lost much of its population during the fracas of 1980; it had been heavily hit by Red Chinese guided missiles, and of course the clouds of fallout had blanketed it in the subsequent decade.

quotations.author: Kazuo Ishiguro
quotations.passage: And I recall also some years ago, Mr Rayne, who travelled to America as valet to Sir Reginals Mauvis, remarking that a taxi driver in New York regularly addressed his fare in a manner which if repeated in London would end in some sort of fracas, if not in the fellow being frogmarched to the nearest police station.

quotations.author: David Gelles
quotations.passage: To the ranks of wonky risk management professionals who have toiled over the minutia of E.S.G. reports for decades now, the political fracas is perplexing.

quotations.author: Jeffrey Goldberg
quotations.passage: But as a matter of corporate drama, the OpenAI fracas is above all a great example of why the incredibly boring-sounding term corporate governance is actually extremely important.

fracas.title: fracas

etymologies: From fraction (“discord”) (now obsolete) +‎ -ous.

definitions.text: Given to troublemaking.
Irritable; argumentative; quarrelsome.

quotations.author: Charlotte Brontë
quotations.passage: […] to him, in his present fractious mood, she dared whisper no observations, nor ask of him any information.

quotations.author: Matt Bai
quotations.passage: That brief moment after the election four years ago, when many Americans thought Mr. Obama’s election would presage a new, less fractious political era, now seems very much a thing of the past.

quotations.author: Stephen Halliday
quotations.passage: Flair and invention were very much at a premium, suffocated by the relentless pace and often fractious nature of proceedings. The absence of James Morrison from the centre of Scotland’s midfield, the West Brom man ruled out on the morning of the game by illness, had already diminished the creative capacity of the home side in that department.

quotations.author: Katharine Viner
quotations.passage: COP stands for conference of the parties under the UNFCCC, and the annual meetings have swung between fractious and soporific, interspersed with moments of high drama and the occasional triumph (the Paris agreement in 2015) and disaster (Copenhagen in 2009).

quotations.author: Ryan Mac
quotations.passage: With his twin notes, Mr. Musk waded directly into a fractious debate over the right way for corporations to bring workers back to the office during the coronavirus pandemic.

quotations.author: Katharine Viner
quotations.passage: After a fractious party conference and dire opinion polls for the Tories, the prime minister attempted to speak directly to the public, saying: “I want what you want.”

quotations.author: Katharine Viner
quotations.passage: German chancellor Olaf Scholz’s fractious centre-left coalition has received a sharp rebuke from voters in the key states of Bavaria and Hesse, with economic woes and immigration fears boosting the opposition conservatives and the far right.

quotations.author: Ben Jones
quotations.passage: Up to 250 trains will be needed to modernise all these lines, though the current government's fractious relationship with London Mayor Sadiq Khan makes that massive investment difficult to envisage in the short term.

quotations.author: Katharine Viner
quotations.passage: But beyond the fractious rhetoric, the US president brought a deeper message on Wednesday that sought to unify the west rather than divide it. It was his most dark, insidious and sinister project of all.

quotations.author: Mark Sappenfield
quotations.passage: While [US president Donald Trump] has been able to centralize significant power, allowing him wide scope for decisive action, Europe remains a comparatively fractious collection of nations more comfortable with incremental steps.

fractious.title: fractious

etymologies: From Late Middle English frangible, frangibil, from Middle French frangible, or from Medieval Latin frangibilis, from Latin frangere (from frangō (“to break, shatter”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreg- (“to break”)) + -ibilis (suffix forming adjectives indicating a capacity or worth of being acted upon).

definitions.text: Able to be broken; breakable, fragile.
Something that is breakable or fragile; especially something that is intentionally made so, such as a bullet.

quotations.author: GLASS
quotations.passage: A certain learned and curious Author gives us the following Characters or Properties of Glass, whereby it is distinguish'd from all other Bodies, viz. […] That it is frangible when thin, without annealing.
quotations.work: The Builder’s Dictionary: Or, Gentlemen and Architect’s Companion. Explaining not only the Term of Art in All the Several Parts of Architecture, but also Containing the Theory and Practice of the Various Branches thereof, [...] In Two Volumes

quotations.author: William Williams Mather
quotations.passage: Another object still [of roasting iron ore], is to make the ore more frangible, that it may be easily broken into fragments of a suitable size for smelting.
quotations.work: First Annual Report on the Geological Survey of the State of Ohio

quotations.author: Charles Panati
quotations.passage: Folklorists claim that the superstitious belief that opening an umbrella indoors augurs misfortune has a more recent and utilitarian origin. In eighteenth-century London, when metal-spoked waterproof umbrellas began to become a common rainy-day sight, their stiff, clumsy spring mechanism made them veritable hazards to open indoors. A rigidly spoked umbrella, opening suddely in a small room, could seriously injure an adult or a child, or shatter a frangible object.
quotations.work: Panati’s Extraordinary Origins of Everyday Things

quotations.author: Richard Marcinko
quotations.passage: So, to make sure that I stay both current and deadly, I built the range, where the guys can sharpen their lethal talents, and—careful always to use only approved military weapons—I can sharpen mine. Shooting, after all, is a frangible skill. At SEAL Team Six we shot daily.

quotations.author: Robert K. Campbell
quotations.passage: For extreme close range training, frangible bullets – those that disintegrate on hitting a hard target – are available. I have found the Winchester frangible loads especially suitable to high-volume training with the 9mm pistol. Frangibles are intended to give peace officers real safety when training at close range with steel reaction targets and vehicles used as range props.
quotations.work: The Gun Digest Book of Personal Protection & Home Defense

quotations.author: G. Paul Chambers
quotations.passage: Is there some law of nature that states that an assassin can only use one kind of ammunition? Couldn't he just as easily load a frangible bullet and a nonfrangible one into his magazine as two frangibles or two regular, hardened rounds?
quotations.work: Head Shot: The Science behind the JFK Assassination

quotations.author: Robert E. Walker
quotations.passage: Like other lethal-use frangibles, it is designed exclusively for use against soft targets. The "projectile" is composed of tungsten powder encapsulated by a traditional copper jacket. The powdered medium itself does not comprise a solid-mass projectile, per se, but it is tightly packed and contained within the jacket, which acts as the container. Like all frangible projectiles, these projectiles return to powder when impacting an object.

frangible.title: frangible

etymologies: From Middle English frenetik (also frentik, frentyk, frantike > modern English frantic), from Old French frenetike, from Latin phreneticus, from Ancient Greek φρενητικός (phrenētikós, “delirious”), from φρενῖτις (phrenîtis, “delirium”), from φρήν (phrḗn, “mind”). Doublet of frantic and phrenitic.

Etymologically, initial stress would be expected (compare the syncopic form phrentic); the modern pronunciation with stress on the second syllable is due to the influence of other words ending in -etic such as phonetic and sympathetic.

examples: After a week of working at a frenetic pace, she was ready for Saturday.
definitions.text: Frenzied and frantic, harried; having extreme enthusiasm or energy.
Mentally deranged, insane.
Characterised by manifestations of delirium or madness.
One who is frenetic.

frenetic.title: frenetic

etymologies: Borrowed from French friable, from Latin friābilis (“friable”), from friō (“to crumble”).

definitions.text: Easily broken into small fragments, crumbled, or reduced to powder.

examples: Sand has been incorporated to make the soil more friable.
definitions.text: Of soil, loose and large-grained in consistency.
Of a poison, likely to crumble and become airborne, thus becoming a health risk.
Of a number: smooth, that factors completely into small prime numbers.

quotations.author: Vladimir Nabokov
quotations.passage: […] I cautiously increased the magic friction that was doing away, in an illusional, if not factual, sense, with the physically irremovable, but psychologically very friable texture of the material divide (pajamas and robe) between the weight of two sunburnt legs, resting athwart my lap, and the hidden tumor of an unspeakable passion.

quotations.author: Angela Carter
quotations.passage: Spiders had woven their vague trapezes between the friable heads of dead peonies in enormous glass jars streaked with tide marks where the water had evaporated long ago.

quotations.author: Lawrence Durrell
quotations.passage: This light, friable type of material offered excellent insulation against both desert heat and also the cold of darkness during the winter.

quotations.author: James George Frazer
quotations.passage: So while two men under his directions were digging the grave with sticks in the friable granitic soil, he superintended the costume of the other actors in the drama.

quotations.author: Dan Olson
quotations.passage: The Glen Rose Formation, an expanse of rock 20 feet deep with alternating layers of solid limestone and softer, friable clay.
quotations.work: Mantracks: A True Story of Fake Fossils

quotations.author: April
quotations.passage: It is when asbestos-containing products are friable that hazardous asbestos fibers are likely to be released and sent airborne.

friable.title: friable

etymologies: From Latin frīgorificus, from frigus (“cold”) + facere (“to make”): compare French frigorifique.

definitions.text: Causing to chill or cool.

quotations.author: Robert Boyle
quotations.passage: [W]hen vve have, as vve very frequently have, put mixtures of snovv and salt into vials, and left them in the open Air, vve generally observ'd, that the outside of the Glass vvas cas'd vvith ice, or covered vvith hoar frost, directly over against that part of the inside of the Glass, vvherein the frigorifick mixture vvas.
quotations.work: New Experiments and Observations Touching Cold, or, An Experimental History of Cold, Begun.

quotations.author: Richard Walker
quotations.passage: "Pr. LOWITZ has discovered a single frigorific mixture, by which quicksilver may be frozen..."
quotations.work: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society

quotations.author: C.A. Hidalgo et al.
quotations.passage: "They would certainly have the soil, climate, packing technologies, and frigorific trucks."

frigorific.title: frigorific

etymologies: Borrowed from French frisson.

examples: I felt a frisson just as they were about to announce the winner in my category.
definitions.text: A sudden surge of excitement.

examples: Whenever the villain's theme played in the movie I felt a sudden frisson down my back.
definitions.text: A shiver; a thrill.

quotations.author: Greil Marcus
quotations.passage: As a perversion of freedom it was, like any perversion, erotic; as alienation it carried the frisson of having just missed the brass ring, a sensation that always brought one back for more.

quotations.author: Charles McGrath
quotations.passage: All the Crichton books depend to a certain extent on a little frisson of fear and suspense: that’s what kept you turning the pages.

frisson.title: frisson

etymologies: From Middle English froward, fraward, equivalent to fro +‎ -ward. Compare Old English fromweard, framweard (“turned away, having the back turned”).

definitions.text: Disobedient, contrary, unmanageable; difficult to deal with; with an evil disposition.
Away from.

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: Her onely fault, and that is faults enough, / Is, that she is intollerable curst, / And shrow’d, and froward, so beyond all measure, / That were my state farre worser then it is, / I would not wed her for a mine of Gold.
quotations.work: Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies

quotations.author: Walter Scott
quotations.passage: The old man […] began to suffer in the body as well as the mind. He had formed the determination of setting out in person for Dumfriesshire, when, after having been dogged, peevish, and snappish to his clerks and domestics, to an unusual and almost intolerable degree, the acrimonious humours settled in a hissing-hot fit of the gout, which is a well-known tamer of the most froward spirits, […]

quotations.author: Francis Bacon
quotations.passage: All this is true, if Time stood still; which contrariwise moueth so round, that a Froward Retention of Custome, is as turbulent a Thing, as an Innouation: […]

quotations.author: Myles Coverdale
quotations.passage: The wayes of the frowarde are straunge, but yͤ workes of him yͭ is cleane, are right.

quotations.author: George Crabb
quotations.passage: A froward child becomes an untoward youth, who turns a deaf ear to all the admonitions of an afflicted parent.

quotations.author: Richard Francis Burton
quotations.passage: So I took a great dry gourd and, cutting open the head, scooped out the inside and cleaned it; after which I gathered grapes from a vine which grew hard by and squeezed them into the gourd, till it was full of the juice. Then I stopped up the mouth and set in the sun, where I left it for some days, until it became strong wine; and every day I used to drink of it, to comfort and sustain me under my fatigues with that from froward and obstinate fiend; and as often as I drank myself drunk, I forgot my troubles and took new heart.
quotations.work: A Plain and Literal Translation of the Arabian Nights’ Entertainments, now Entituled The Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night

quotations.author: John Ronald Reuel Tolkien
quotations.passage: ‘I owe much to Éomer,’ said Théoden. ‘Faithful heart may have froward tongue.’
quotations.work: The Two Towers : Being the Second Part of The Lord of the Rings

quotations.author: Jan Morris
quotations.passage: […] most of its mansions, now sadly dingy, were built with American gold, and it was to this cold and froward city [Cuenca] […] that the last of the Aztec royal princes, Don Pedro, was brought to die.

quotations.author: Peter Marshall
quotations.passage: […] which so incensed this old hag that she grew as froward and sullen as the doctor, […]
quotations.work: Mother Leakey and the Bishop: A Ghost Story

quotations.author: Thomas Malory
quotations.passage: Whan Sir Galahad herde hir sey so, he was adrad to be knowyn; and therewith he smote hys horse with his sporys and rode a grete pace froward them.

froward.title: froward

etymologies: From Latin fructuōsus.

definitions.text: fruitful

quotations.author: Owen Felltham
quotations.passage: As fruits of hotter countries, transearthed in colder climates, have vigour enough in themselves to be fructuous according to their nature: but, that they are hindered by the chilling nips of the air, and the soil, wherein they are planted.

fructuous.title: fructuous

etymologies: From Latin fruitiō (“enjoyment”). By surface analysis, fruit +‎ -ion.
Erroneously from fruit (though now standard usage)

examples: After six years of hard work, the engineers had brought the project to fruition.
definitions.text: The fulfillment of something worked for.
The enjoyment derived from a possession.
The condition of bearing fruit.

quotations.author: Christopher Marlowe
quotations.passage: […] to weare our selues & neuer rest, / Untill we reach the ripest fruites of all, / That perfect blisse and sole felicitie, / The sweet fruition of an earthly crowne.
quotations.work: Tamburlaine the Great. The First Part

quotations.author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon
quotations.passage: Perhaps,—for the Divine purpose runs through every aim of our being,—the disappointment and the endurance are but sent to raise those hopes above, which else might cling too fondly to their fruition below.
quotations.work: Ethel Churchill: Or, The Two Brides.

quotations.author: John Jay Chapman
quotations.passage: The myths possess us: through our agony / They work to new fruition.
quotations.work: Homeric Scenes: Hector’s Farewell and The Wrath of Achilles

quotations.author: September and October
quotations.passage: Largely by reason of the persistence of John Crevallier Cobbold, a leading townsman and a member of a respected Suffolk family, the scheme was brought to fruition and by an Act dated July 19, 1844, the Eastern Union Railway came into existence.

quotations.author: Richard Foster
quotations.passage: That progress has taken over ten years and £20 million to bring to fruition. But, as Mands explains, the journey has been one that HSG has been almost obligated to undertake. "First and foremost, this is an environmental project," she says.

fruition.title: fruition

etymologies: Borrowed from Latin fugācius (whence -acious), comparative of fugāciter (“evasively, fleetingly”), from fugāx (“transitory, fleeting”), from fugiō (“to flee”).

definitions.text: Fleeting, fading quickly, transient.

quotations.author: O. Henry
quotations.passage: Restless, shifting, fugacious as time itself is a certain vast bulk of the population of the red brick district of the lower West Side. Homeless, they have a hundred homes.

quotations.author: George Edmund De Schweinitz
quotations.passage: Watering of the eye, conjunctival congestion, distinct catarrhal conjunctivitis, and deep-seated scleral congestions, sometimes fugacious, and often accompanied by intense headache […]

quotations.author: James Branch Cabell
quotations.passage: " […] The years slip away fugacious, and Time that brings forth her children only to devour them grins most hellishly, for Time changes all things and cultivates even in herself an appreciation of irony,—and, therefore, why shouldn't I have changed a trifle? You wouldn't have me put on exhibition as a lusus naturae?"

quotations.author: Michael Feeney Callan
quotations.passage: It may be that Redford's fugacious nature is not so mysterious, that it is studded in the artwork of the labs and the very stones of Sundance.

fugacious.title: fugacious

etymologies: From Middle English fulgent, from Latin fulgēns. By surface analysis, Latin fulg(ere) +‎ -ent.

definitions.text: Shining brilliantly; radiant.

quotations.author: Charlotte Brontë
quotations.passage: Shirley takes life easily: is not that fact written in her eye? In her good-tempered moments, is it not as full of lazy softness as in her brief fits of anger it is fulgent with quick-flashing fire?

quotations.author: Isaac Newton
quotations.passage: And universally, the greatest and most fulgent tails always arise from Comets, immediately after their passing by the neighbourhood of the Sun.
quotations.work: The Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy.

fulgent.title: fulgent

etymologies: From Latin fūlīginōsus, from fūlīgō (“soot”).

definitions.text: Pertaining to or resembling soot in such features as colour, texture or taste; sooty, dusky.

quotations.author: Thomas Carlyle
quotations.passage: To that dingy fuliginous Operative, emerging from his soot-mill, what is the first duty I will prescribe, and offer help towards? That he clean the skin of him.

quotations.author: Henry Miller
quotations.passage: On the beach, masts and chimneys interlaced, and like a fuliginous shadow the figure of Albertine gliding through the surf, fusing into the mysterious quick and prism of a protoplasmic realm, uniting her shadow to the dream and harbinger of death.

quotations.author: John Gardner
quotations.passage: I toy with shouting some tidbit more – some terrifying, unthinkable threat, some blackly fuliginous riddling hex – but my heart's not in it.

quotations.author: Thomas Pynchon
quotations.passage: With its own fuliginous Weather, at once public and private, created of smoke billowing from Pipes, Hearths, and Stoves, the Room would provide an extraordinary sight, were any able to see […]

fuliginous.title: fuliginous

etymologies: Inherited from Middle English fulminaten, borrowed from Latin fulminātus, perfect passive participle of fulminō (“to lighten, hurl or strike with lightning”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from fulmen (“lightning which strikes and sets on fire, thunderbolt”), from earlier *fulgmen, *fulgimen, from fulgeō, fulgō (“flash, lighten”). Doublet of fulmine. More at fulgent.
From fulminic acid +‎ -ate (“salt or ester”). By surface analysis, fulmine +‎ -ate.

definitions.text: To make a verbal attack.
To issue as a denunciation.
To thunder or make a loud noise.
To strike with lightning; to cause to explode.
(Can we verify this sense?) to act as lightning, appearing quickly and destructively
Any salt or ester of fulminic acid, mostly explosive.

quotations.author: William Neilson
quotations.passage: In short, the criticism which the great lexicographer fulminated against an unfortunate author, seems to have been adopted by the profession as applicable to everything under the sun […]
quotations.work: Mesmerism in its relation to health and disease

quotations.author: Jeffrey Goldberg
quotations.passage: To be sure, Trump has fulminated on Twitter against the judges who rebuffed him. But his tirades have earned him a reprimand––if a brief, vague one––from his own Supreme Court nominee.

quotations.author: Thomas De Quincey
quotations.passage: They fulminated the most hostile of all decrees.

quotations.author: David Brooks
quotations.passage: While they were the opposition, Democrats fulminated that the Republicans were so deep in the pockets of Big Pharma that they wouldn’t even let the government negotiate lower drug prices.

quotations.author: Thomas Pynchon
quotations.passage: the present owners couldn't afford the electric bills anymore, several amateur gaffers, sad to say, having already been fulminated trying to bootleg power in off the municipal lines.

quotations.author: Alistair Horne
quotations.passage: On 19 February a jubilant Bigeard announced that his 3rd R.P.C. had seized eighty-seven bombs, seventy kilos of explosive, 5,120 fulminate of mercury detonators, 309 electric detonators, etc.

fulminate.title: fulminate

etymologies: From Middle English fulsom, equivalent to full +‎ -some. The meaning has evolved from an original positive connotation "abundant" to a neutral "plump" to a negative "overfed". In modern usage, it can take on any of these inflections. See usage note.

The negative sense "offensive, gross; disgusting, sickening" developed secondarily after the 13th century and was influenced by Middle English foul (“foul”). In the 18th century, the word was sometimes even spelled foulsome.

definitions.text: Offensive to good taste, tactless, overzealous, excessive.
Excessively flattering (connoting insincerity).

examples: The fulsome thanks of the war-torn nation lifted our weary spirits.
definitions.text: Characterised or marked by fullness; abundant, copious.

examples: Her fulsome timbre resonated throughout the hall.
definitions.text: Fully developed; mature.

quotations.author: Jonathan Swift
quotations.passage: [T]he Weather exceeding hot, I entreated him to let me bathe in a River that was near. He consented, and I immediately stripped myself stark naked, and went down softly into the stream. It happened that a young Female Yahoo standing behind a Bank, saw the whole proceeding, and enflamed by Desire, as the Nag and I conjectured, came running with all speed, and leaped into the Water within five Yards of the Place where I bathed. [...] She embraced me after a most fulsome manner; [...]
quotations.work: Travels into Several Remote Nations of the World. [ Gulliver’s Travels ]

quotations.author: Walter Scott
quotations.passage: You will hear the advanced enfans perdus, as the French call them, and so they are indeed, namely, children of the fall, singing unclean and fulsome ballads of sin and harlotrie.

quotations.author: Mark Twain
quotations.passage: And by hideous contrast, a redundant orator was making a speech to another gathering not thirty steps away, in fulsome laudation of "our glorious British liberties!"
quotations.work: A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur’s Court

quotations.author: James Joyce
quotations.passage: He addressed me in several handwritings with fulsome compliments as a Venus in furs [...]

quotations.author: Cardiff City
quotations.passage: City overcame a spirited effort from Cardiff's Championship rivals Bristol City in a keenly contested Carabao Cup semi-final on Tuesday night, with manager Pep Guardiola fulsome in his praise for Lee Johnson's men over two legs.

quotations.author: David Turner
quotations.passage: These extra services before Christmas Day were in addition to fulsome train facilities on the day, with many companies running a Sunday service.

fulsome.title: fulsome

etymologies: From French funambule or its source, Latin funambulus, from funis (“rope”) + ambulare (“walk”).

definitions.text: A tightrope walker or a similar performer on a slack rope.

quotations.author: David Hakim
quotations.passage: A female funambulist, Maria Spelterini, on various occasions tightrope-walked across the Niagara Gorge with peach baskets on her feet, blindfolded, or manacled.

funambulist.title: funambulist

etymologies: From Middle French funerail, from Latin funereus +‎ -al.

definitions.text: Of or relating to a funeral.
Similar to or befitting the mood or elements of a funeral: slow; black colors; formal; dignified or solemn.

quotations.author: James Joyce
quotations.passage: From the belfries far and near the funereal deathbell tolled unceasingly while all around the gloomy precincts rolled the ominous warning of a hundred muffled drums punctuated by the hollow booming of pieces of ordnance.

quotations.author: George RaymondRichardMartin
quotations.passage: Seven were chosen to push the funereal boat to the water, in honor of the seven faces of god.

quotations.author: William Beckford
quotations.passage: A funereal gloom prevailed over the whole scene.
quotations.work: An Arabian Tale, from an Unpublished Manuscript

quotations.author: Jeffery Farnol
quotations.passage: "Sounds curst funereal, Zeb! O my poor nunky! Go fetch 'em, Sergeant, and let me see 'em—'twill distress and pain me I know but—go fetch 'em!"

quotations.author: H. P. Lovecraft
quotations.passage: There was something menacing and uncomfortable in the funereal stillness, in the muffled, subtle trickle of distant brooks, and in the crowding green peaks and black-wooded precipices that choked the narrow horizon.

quotations.author: Peter Carey
quotations.passage: It was like a room in which someone has died. They made love but it was somehow funereal and they looked into each other's eyes with sadness and nuzzled each other for comfort.

funereal.title: funereal

etymologies: From Latin fūniculus (“thinner cord”), diminutive from fūnis (“rope, cord”) + -culus. By surface analysis, funicul(us) +‎ -ar.

definitions.text: Of, pertaining to, resembling, or powered by a rope or cable.
Of or pertaining to the umbilical cord.
Having a fleshy covering of the seed formed from the funiculus, the attachment point of the seed.
Synonym of catenary.

A particular type of rail transit system which ascends a steep urban or mountain incline, having usually two cars sharing a single pair of tracks, with the cars linked by a moving cable and an arrangement of pulleys such that the descending car assists in the hoisting of the ascending car, i.e. the two cars serve as counterweights for each other.

quotations.author: Dr Joseph Brennan
quotations.passage: England's funiculars mostly hug the coast, and this is no coincidence. The development of the Victorian and Edwardian seaside resort played a central role in the uptake of funicular railways across England.

funicular.title: funicular

etymologies: Corruption of falbala; first attested in the late 1600s or early 1700s. Not related to fur.

definitions.text: A frill, flounce, or ruffle, as on clothing; a decorative piece of fabric, especially one gathered or pleated as into a ruffle, etc.
A small, showy ornamentation.
To adorn with a furbelow; to ornament.

quotations.author: Henry James
quotations.passage: Winterbourne stood looking after her; and as she moved away, drawing her muslin furbelows over the gravel, said to himself that she had the tournure of a princess.

quotations.author: Edith Wharton
quotations.passage: Within, among the bric-a-brac and furbelows, he found Miss Painter seated in a redundant purple armchair with the incongruous air of a horseman bestriding a heavy mount.

quotations.author: Frances Trollope
quotations.passage: I do not think that from the blissful time when I was sixteen, up to my present solemn five-and-thirty, I could ever have been tempted to look a second time at any miss under the chaperonship of such a dame as that feather and furbelow lady.

quotations.author: John George Wood
quotations.passage: All the other furbelows, and portions of this one[this Medusa] that lay below the expansion, floated as usual through the water, except that on some occasions an accessory power was obtained by pressing a portion of another furbelow to the side of the glass and making it adhere just like the portion that was exposed to the surface of the air.

quotations.author: Louisa May Alcott
quotations.passage: “Well, I don’t know that fifty is much for a dress, with all the furbelows and notions you have to have to finish it off these days.”

quotations.author: Lucy Maud Montgomery
quotations.passage: Those dresses are good, sensible, serviceable dresses, without any frills or furbelows about them, and they’re all you’ll get this summer.

quotations.author: E. J. H. Corner
quotations.passage: Each plant has several oarweed fronds on the top of a flat stem, well adapted to swaying in one direction but rigid in the other; along the rigid edges, where the water flows and eddies, develop the wavy furbelows.

quotations.author: Alexander Alderson
quotations.passage: The band played ceaselessly. Even when the other instruments were resting the pianist kept up his monotonous vamping, with a dreary furbelow for embellishment here and there, to which some few of the dancers continued to shuffle round the floor.

quotations.author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon
quotations.passage: Mrs. Palmer, and her furbelowed daughters-in-law, who will probably carry enough of the scarlet fever about them, to remind you unpleasantly of the officiousness which preserved the lives of three daughters, when two might have been parted with advantageously enough.
quotations.work: Lady Anne Granard; or, Keeping up Appearances.

furbelow.title: furbelow

etymologies: From Middle English *furtyve (implied in furtyvely (adverb)), from Middle French furtif, furtive (“furtive, stealthy”) (modern French furtif), from Latin fūrtīvus (“clandestine, furtive, secret; concealed, hidden; stolen”), from fūrtum (“theft; robbery”) (from fūr (“thief”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- (“to bear, carry”)) + -īvus (suffix forming adjectives).

definitions.text: Of a thing: done with evasive or guilty secrecy.
Of a thing: that has been acquired by theft; stolen; also taken stealthily.
Of a person or an animal: sly, stealthy.
Of a person, etc.: inclined to steal; pilfering, thieving.

quotations.author: William Wordsworth
quotations.passage: [T]ender cares and mild domestic Loves, / With furtive watch, pursue her [a swan] as she moves; […]
quotations.work: The Complete Poetical Works of William Wordsworth

quotations.author: Charles Dickens
quotations.passage: "Don't call me Solomon. Do you want to be the death of me?" asked the man, in a furtive, frightened way.

quotations.author: Charles Dickens
quotations.passage: So, Riderhood looking after him as he went, and he with his furtive hand laid upon the dagger as he passed it, and his eyes upon the boat, were much upon a par.

quotations.author: William Makepeace Thackeray
quotations.passage: The proprietor of the house cowered over a bed-candle and a furtive tea-pot in the back drawing-room.

quotations.author: Alice Kipling
quotations.passage: At the edge of my kingdom scurry / ⁠Creatures in feathers and furs— / Crows in a furtive hurry— / ⁠Hungry and cringing curs— […]
quotations.work: Hand in Hand: Verses by a Mother and Daughter

quotations.author: George Orwell
quotations.passage: Actually, as Winston well knew, it was only four years since Oceania had been at war with Eastasia and in alliance with Eurasia. But that was merely a piece of furtive knowledge which he happened to possess because his memory was not satisfactorily under control.

quotations.author: François Gayot de Pitaval
quotations.passage: […] The Defendant never vvas acknovvledged by the Sieur Harrouard’s Family, nor by that of his VVife. Thus, granting him to have been in Possession of his Son’s Estate, it vvould only be a furtive and clandestine, not a public and avovved Possession; and consequently such a Possession as is incapable of founding a just and legal Title.
quotations.work: A Select Collection of Singular and Interesting Histories.

quotations.author: Washington Irving
quotations.passage: I noticed the same singular, and as it were, furtive glance over the shoulder that had attracted my attention in the Cassino.

quotations.author: Matthew Prior
quotations.passage: Novv shine these Planets vvith substantial Rays? / Does innate Lustre gild their measur'd Days? / Or do they (as your Schemes, I think, have shovvn) / Dart furtive Beams, and Glory not their ovvn, / All Servants to that Source of Light, the Sun?

quotations.author: Edward Bulwer-Lytton
quotations.passage: All women have their foibles. Wise husbands must bear and forbear. Is that all? wherefore, then, is her aspect so furtive, wherefore on his a wild, vigilant sternness?
quotations.work: What will He Do with It?

quotations.author: John Alec Baker
quotations.passage: Gluttonous, hoarding jay; he should have hedge-hopped and lurched from tree to tree in his usual furtive manner.
quotations.work: The Peregrine, The Hill of Summer & Diaries: The Complete Works of J. A. Baker

furtive.title: furtive

etymologies: From French fusillade, from fusiller (“shoot with a firearm”), from fusil (“rifle, gun”).

definitions.text: The simultaneous firing of a number of firearms.
A rapid burst.
To fire, or attack with, a fusillade.

quotations.author: W. W. Jacobs
quotations.passage: But her husband was on his hands and knees groping wildly on the floor in search of the paw. If he could only find it before the thing outside got in. A perfect fusillade of knocks reverberated through the house, and he heard the scraping of a chair as his wife put it down in the passage against the door.

fusillade.title: fusillade

etymologies: The noun is derived from Middle English fustian (“type of fabric, probably made from cotton, flax, or wool; piece of fustian spread over a bed or mattress”) [and other forms], from Old French fustaine, fustaigne (modern French futaine), from Medieval Latin fūstāneum, from (pannus) fūstāneus or (tela) fūstānea, of disputed origin.

Sense 3 (“inflated, pompous, or pretentious speech or writing”) is possibly from the fact that the fabric was sometimes used to make cushion- and pillowcases, thus suggesting that the speech or writing is “padded” or “stuffed”; compare bombast. The relationship between sense 4 (“hot drink made of a mixture of alcoholic beverages with egg yolk, lemon, and spices”) and the fabric is unclear.
The adjective is from an attributive use of the noun.

definitions.text: Originally, a kind of coarse fabric made from cotton and flax; now, a kind of coarse twilled cotton, or cotton and linen, stuff with a short pile and often dyed a dull colour, which is chiefly prepared for menswear.
A class of fabric including corduroy and velveteen.
Inflated, pompous, or pretentious speech or writing; bombast; also , incoherent or unintelligible speech or writing; gibberish, nonsense.
Chiefly in rum fustian: a hot drink made of a mixture of alcoholic beverages (as beer, gin, and sherry or white wine) with egg yolk, lemon, and spices.
Made out of fustian (noun sense 1).
Of a person, or their speech or writing: using inflated, pompous, or pretentious language; bombastic; grandiloquent; also using incoherent or unintelligible language.
Imaginary; invented.
Useless; worthless.

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: VVWhere's the Cooke, is supper ready, the house trim'd, rushes strevv'd, cobvvebs svvept, the seruingmen in their nevv fustian, their vvhite stockings, and euery officer his vvedding garment on?
quotations.work: Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: For Gods sake thrust him down staires, I cannot indure such a fustian rascall.
quotations.work: The Second Part of Henrie the Fourth

quotations.author: Christopher Marlowe
quotations.passage: Wag[ner]. Vilaine, call me Maister Wagner, and let thy left eye be diametarily fixt vpon my right heele, with quasi vestigias nostras insistere [as if to follow in our footsteps]. / Clo[wn]: God forgiue me, he speakes Dutch fustian: / well, Ile folow him, Ile serue him, thats flat.
quotations.work: The Tragicall History of D. Faustus.

quotations.author: Ben Jonson
quotations.passage: Monsieur Orenge, yond' Gallants obserues vs; pr'y thee let's talke Fustian a little and gull 'hem: make 'hem beleeue vve are great Schollers.
quotations.work: The Comicall Satyre of Euery Man out of His Humor.

quotations.author: Ben Jonson
quotations.passage: [T]he Scene, Gargaphie: vvhich I doe vehemently suspect for some fustian countrie, but let that vanish.

quotations.author: John Dryden
quotations.passage: I am much deceiv'd if this be not abominable fustian, that is, thoughts and vvords ill sorted, and vvithout the least relation to each other: […]
quotations.work: The Spanish Fryar: Or, the Double Discovery.

quotations.author: Alexander Pope
quotations.passage: And he, vvhose Fustian’s so sublimely bad, / It is not Poetry, but Prose run mad: […]
quotations.work: An Epistle from Mr. Pope, to Dr. Arbuthnot

quotations.author: William Makepeace Thackeray
quotations.passage: He was soon at ease with his honest host, whose manners were quite simple and cordial, and who looked and seemed perfectly a gentleman, though he wore a plain fustian coat, and a waistcoat without a particle of lace.
quotations.work: The Virginians. A Tale of the Last Century

quotations.author: Thomas Hardy
quotations.passage: His clothes were of fustian, and his boots hobnailed, yet in his progress he showed not the mud-accustomed bearing of hobnailed and fustained peasantry.
quotations.work: Wessex Tales: Strange, Lively, and Commonplace

quotations.author: Thomas Hardy
quotations.passage: [S]he was conscious of a rough coffin passing her shoulder, borne by four men. It was open, and in it lay the body of a young man, wearing the smockfrock of a rustic, and fustian breeches.
quotations.work: Wessex Tales: Strange, Lively, and Commonplace

quotations.author: James Joyce
quotations.passage: His fustian shirt, sanguineflowered, trembles its Spanish tassels at his secrets.

quotations.author: John Florio
quotations.passage: Monélle, a roguish or fustian word, a word in pedlers French, signifying wenches, strumpets or whores.
quotations.work: A Worlde of Words, or Most Copious, and Exact Dictionarie in Italian and English

quotations.author: Robert Burton
quotations.passage: If hee can havvke & hunt, ride a horse, play at cards and dice, svvagger, drinke, svveare, take Tobacco vvith a grace, sing, dance, vveare his cloathes in fashion, court and please his mistris, talke bigge fustian, insult, scorne, contemne others and vse a litle mimicall and apish complement aboue the rest, he is a compleat, (Egregiam verò laudem) a vvell-qualified Gentleman, these are most of their imployments, this their greatest cõmendation.

quotations.author: James Edwin Thorold Rogers
quotations.passage: Fustian, of which I found only one entry before 1401, occurs frequently in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. It appears to have been a ribbed cloth. […] On one occasion (1443) it is described as 'white ribbed fustian.'
quotations.work: A History of Agriculture and Prices in England

quotations.author: Daniel Coit Gilman
quotations.passage: The different names given to fustian cloths depend upon their degree of fineness, and the manner in which they are woven and finished. […] In all fustians there is a warp and filling, or weft thread, independent of the additional filling-thread forming the pile; but in corduroys the pile thread is only 'thrown in' where the corded portions are and is absent in the narrow spaces between.

quotations.author: Tirthankar Roy
quotations.passage: The East India company was pursuing its own financial interests, but in doing so was also fostering the establishment of industries such as calico printing — an industry that would have not achieved the same degree of accomplishment if it had confined itself simply to the printing of European fustians (mixed cottons) and linens, both of which were more difficult to print on than cotton.
quotations.work: How India Clothed the World: The World of South Asian Textiles, 1500-1850

quotations.author: David Meredith Reese
quotations.passage: Fustian is a species of coarse twilled cotton, but may be considered as a general term which comprehends several varieties of cotton fabrics, as corduroy, jean, velveret, velveteen, thickset, thickset cord, and other stout cloths for men's wearing apparel; from their strength and cheapness, they are very serviceable to agricultural people. It is generally dyed of an olive, leaden, or other colours. […] Fustians are either plain or twilled.

quotations.author: fall
quotations.passage: Fustian originally referred to a large variety of textiles of linen-and-cotton blend; later it came to mean all-cotton textiles. Common varieties of the fancy fustians are corduroy, jean, pillow, thickset, velveret and velveteen.
quotations.work: Material History Bulletin = Bulletin d’histoire de la Culture Matérielle

quotations.author: Susan M. Ouellette
quotations.passage: Fustians, a large group of general-purpose fabrics were mainly woven with a tight heavy texture. Sometimes they were plainly woven, but fustians could also be fashioned with “tufts” creating fabric like corduroy or velveteen. Fustians were used for anything from draperies to dresses or upholstery to men’s waistcoats.
quotations.work: US Textile Production in Historical Perspective: A Case Study from Massachusetts

quotations.author: Steve Haywood
quotations.passage: In the nineteenth century fustian cutting was a major occupation right across the North West and thousands of people in the cotton towns were employed at it. Sometimes the work was done at tables but more often than not the cloth was stretched across rollers and they'd walk up and down all day, slicing through the threads of the weave row by row, using tiny blades fashioned from watch springs and honed until they were as sharp as razorblades. Cutting even a basic fustian, they could walk ten or eleven miles over the length of a shift. With more sophisticated fustians – fabrics like velveteen, for instance – you had to walk further, much further.
quotations.work: Narrowboat Dreams: A Journey North by England’s Waterways

quotations.author: Homer
quotations.passage: Nothing that belongs to Homer seems to have been more commonly mistaken than the just Pitch of his Style: Some of his Translators having svvell'd into Fustian in a proud Confidence of the Sublime; others sunk into Flatness in a cold and timorous Notion of Simplicity.

quotations.author: Joseph Addison
quotations.passage: Claudian in the description of his infant Titan descants on this glory about his head, but has run his description into most wretched fustian.
quotations.work: The Works of the Right Honourable Joseph Addison, Esq;

quotations.author: Horace Walpole
quotations.passage: Every preparative of pomp, attitude, and lofty language were called in to make him [John Stuart, 3rd Earl of Bute] worthy of himself. His admirers were in ecstasies; the few that dared to sneer at his theatric fustian, did not find it quite so ridiculous as they wished.
quotations.work: Memoirs of the Reign of King George the Third .

quotations.author: Benjamin Disraeli
quotations.passage: Sensible Englishmen, like Endymion and Trenchard, looked upon the whole exhibition as fustian, and received the revelations with a smile of frigid courtesy.

quotations.author: Ambroise Vollard
quotations.passage: What made [Édouard] Manet a veritable prophet in his day, was that he brought a simple formula to a period in which the official art was merely fustian and conventionality.
quotations.work: Paul Cézanne : His Life and Art

quotations.author: Rupert Christiansen
quotations.passage: Anything grandiose or historically based tends to sound flat and banal when it reaches English, partly because translators get stuck between contradictory imperatives: juggling fidelity to the original sense with what is vocally viable, they tend to resort to a genteel fustian which lacks either poetic resonance or demotic realism, adding to a sense of artificiality rather than enhancing credibility.

quotations.author: Richard Cook
quotations.passage: RUMFUSTIAN. The yolks of twelve eggs, one quart of strong beer, one bottle of white wine, half a pint of gin, a grated nutmeg, the juice from the peeling of a lemon, a small quantity of cinnamon, and sufficient sugar to sweeten it; […]

quotations.author: William Hone
quotations.passage: Rum Fustian is a "night-cap" made precisely in the same way as the preceding [egg-posset or egg-flip], with the yolks of twelve eggs, a quart of strong home-brewed beer, a bottle of white wine, half-a-pint of gin, a grated nutmeg, the juice from the peel of a lemon, a small quantity of cinnamon, and sugar sufficient to sweeten it.
quotations.work: The Year Book of Daily Recreation and Information

quotations.author: Robert F. Riddell
quotations.passage: Rum fustian [i]s prepared at Oxford as follows: whisk up to a froth the yolks of six eggs and add them to a pint of gin and a quart of strong beer; boil up a bottle of sherry in a sauce-pan, with a stick of cinnamon or nutmeg grated, a dozen large lumps of sugar, and the rind of a lemon peeled very thin; when the wine boils, it is poured upon the beer and gin and drank hot.
quotations.work: Indian Domestic Economy and Receipt Book;

quotations.author: Gabriel Harvey
quotations.passage: I was never so splenetique, when I was most dumpish, but I could smile at a frise jest, when the good man would be pleasurable, and laugh at fustion earnest, when the merry man would be surly.
quotations.work: Pierces Supererogation: Or A New Prayse of the Old Asse. A Preparative to Certaine Larger Discourses, Intituled Nashes S. Fame

quotations.author: Thomas Coryat
quotations.passage: For my clothes being but a threed-bare fustian case vvere so meane (my cloake onely excepted) that the Boores could not haue made an ordinary supper vvith the mony for vvch they should haue sold them; […]

quotations.author: Richard Steele
quotations.passage: About a fortnight since, as I was diverting myself with a pennyworth of walnuts at the Temple-gate, a lively young fellow in a fustian jacket shot by me, beckoned a coach, and told the coachman he wanted to go as far as Chelsea.

quotations.author: Tobias Smollett
quotations.passage: [F]or all my bit of a fustian frock, that cost me in all but forty shillings, I believe, betvveen you and me, knight, I have more dust in my fob, than all these povvdered sparks put together.

quotations.author: Edna O’Brien
quotations.passage: Her husband was trying to calm her down, assuage her, and in the end what she did was to put a handkerchief over her face and secure it with the brim of a fustian hat.

quotations.author: Benjamin Jonson
quotations.passage: Svb[tle]. VVhy, you must entertaine him. Fac[e]. VVhat'll you doe / VVith these the vvhile? Svb. VVhy, haue 'hem vp, and shew 'hem / Some Fustian Booke, or the Darke Glasse.

quotations.author: Henry Cockeram
quotations.passage: VVherein by the way let me pray thee to obserue that I haue also inserted […] euen of the fustian termes, vsed by too many vvho study rather to bee heard speake, than to vnderstand themselues.

quotations.author: Decimus Junius Juvenalis
quotations.passage: And why wou'dst thou these mightly Morsels chuse, / Of Words unchaw'd, and fit to choak the Muse? / Let Fustian Poets with their Stuff be gone, / And suck the Mists that hang o're Helicon; […]

quotations.author: Henry Hallam
quotations.passage: [Alexander] Pope, after censuring the haste, negligence, and fustian language of [George] Chapman, observes "that which is to be allowed him, and which very much contributed to cover his defects, is a free daring spirit that animates his translation, which is something like what one might imagine Homer himself would have written before he arrived at years of discretion."

quotations.author: John Skelton
quotations.passage: Hard to make ought of that is nakid nought; / This fustiane maistres and this giggisse gase, / Wonder is to wryte what wrenchis she wrowght, / To face out her foly with a midsomer mase; […]
quotations.work: The Poetical Works of John Skelton

fustian.title: fustian

etymologies: First attested in 1656; borrowed from Latin fūstīgātus, perfect passive participle of fūstīgō (“to cudgel to death”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from fūstis (“a cudgel”) + -igō.

definitions.text: To hit someone with a club.
To harshly criticize someone.

fustigate.title: fustigate

etymologies: From gad (“sharp point, spike; (dialectal) sharp-pointed rod for driving cattle, horses, etc., goad”) +‎ fly, in the sense of a fly which irritates cattle, etc., by biting them, similar to the prodding of a goad. Gad is derived from Middle English gad, gadde (“metal spike with a sharp point; stick with a sharp point for driving animals, goad; metal bar or rod, ingot; (by extension) lump of material; metal rod for measuring land; (by extension) unit of linear measure equal to about 10 to 16 feet”), borrowed from Old Norse gaddr (“spike; goad”), from Proto-Germanic *gazdaz (“spike; goad”), further etymology uncertain. Displaced native Old English bēaw.

Sense 2.1.1 (“person who upsets the status quo”) may allude to the Apology by the Greek philosopher Plato (428/427 or 424/423 – 348/347 B.C.E.), where he describes Socrates (c. 470 – 399 B.C.E.) acting as a goad to the Athenian political scene like a gadfly (Ancient Greek μῠ́ωψ (mŭ́ōps)) arousing a sluggish horse.

definitions.text: Any dipterous (“two-winged”) insect or fly of the family Oestridae (commonly known as a bot fly) or Tabanidae (horse fly), noted for irritating animals by buzzing about them, and biting them to suck their blood; a gadbee.
A person who upsets the status quo by posing novel or upsetting questions, or attempts to stimulate innovation by being an irritant.
Synonym of gadabout (“a person who restlessly moves from place to place, seeking amusement or the companionship of others”).

examples: He’s a regular gadfly and takes advantage of his friend’s generosity.
definitions.text: A person who takes without giving back; a bloodsucker.

quotations.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
quotations.passage: The nomads of Africa are constrained to wander by the attacks of the gadfly, which drives the cattle mad, and so compels the tribe to emigrate in the rainy season and drive off the cattle to the higher sandy regions.

quotations.author: Gabriel Harvey
quotations.passage: He that made that ryme in jest, little considered what a gad-fly may doe in earnest. It is small wisedome to contemne the smallest enemy; the gad-fly is a little creature, but some little creatures be stingers; […]
quotations.work: Pierces Supererogation: Or A New Prayse of the Old Asse. A Preparative to Certaine Larger Discourses, Intituled Nashes S. Fame

quotations.author: James Thomson
quotations.passage: Light fly his slumbers, if perchance a flight / Of angry gad-flies fasten on the herd; […]

quotations.author: Rafael Argullol
quotations.passage: Vengeful Hera transformed her [Io] into an animal (a beautiful cow), and imposed upon her the company of a gadfly to sting her continuously, thus forcing her to escape on an endless pilgrimage.
quotations.work: The End of the World as a Work of Art: A Western Story

quotations.author: Philip Massinger
quotations.passage: VVhat gad flye tickles so this Macrinus, / That vp-flinging thy tayle, he breakes thus from me.

quotations.author: Morris Kline
quotations.passage: There is a function for the gadfly who poses questions that many specialists would like to overlook. Polemics is healthy.
quotations.work: Why the Professor Can’t Teach: Mathematics and the Dilemma of University Education

quotations.author: Andrew Martin
quotations.passage: What was required now was the intervention of some men who were not gadflies. […] The logic of [Charles] Pearson's arguments was accepted, up to a point, by a consortium of businessmen. In August 1854, […] the consortium obtained royal assent for […] the Metropolitan Railway. […] In 1859, when it looked as though the Metropolitan Railway Company would be wound up with no line built, he [Pearson] wrote a pamphlet: A Twenty Minutes Letter to the Citizens of London in Favour of the Metropolitan Railway and City Station. Gadfly he may have been, but by this 'letter' he persuaded the Corporation of London to invest £200,000 in the line, a most unusual example of a public body investing in a Victorian railway.
quotations.work: Underground Overground: A Passenger’s History of the Tube

quotations.author: John Leland
quotations.passage: Dr. [Carl] Hart, 54, the first tenured African-American science professor at Columbia, is a gadfly among drug researchers and a rock star among advocates for decriminalizing drugs.

quotations.author: George Chapman
quotations.passage: VVhat VVinnie? VVife, I say? out of dores at this time! vvhere should I seeke the Gad-flye?

quotations.author: Thomas Middleton
quotations.passage: VVhere are those gad-flies going? to some Junket novv; […]

quotations.author: Samuel Richardson
quotations.passage: [Y]our Harriet may turn gadfly, and never be easy but vvhen she is forming parties, or giving vvay to them, that may make the home, that hitherto has been the chief scene of her pleasures, undelightful to her.
quotations.work: The History of Sir Charles Grandison.

gadfly.title: gadfly

etymologies: From Middle English gainsayen, ȝeinseggen (“to say against, say in opposition to”), equivalent to gain- +‎ say. Compare Old Danish gensige (“to speak against; gainsay”), Swedish gensaga (“a speaking against; protest”).

definitions.text: To say something in contradiction to.

quotations.author: Charles Dickens
quotations.passage: So she had, cried Scrooge. You’re right. I will not gainsay it, Spirit. God forbid!

quotations.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
quotations.passage: Know then that in the time of the Great Rebellion (the history of which by the learned Lord Clarendon I most earnestly commend to your attention) this Manor of Baskerville was held by Hugo of that name, nor can it be gainsaid that he was a most wild, profane, and godless man.
quotations.work: The Hound of the Baskervilles: Another Adventure of Sherlock Holmes

quotations.author: Socrates of Constantinople
quotations.passage: […] vve are able with playne demonstration to proue, and vvith reason to persvvade that in tymes past our fayth vvas alike, that then vve preached thinges correspondent vnto the forme of faith already published of vs, so that none in this behalfe can repyne or gaynesay vs.
quotations.work: The Avncient Ecclesiasticall Histories of the First Six Hundred Yeares after Christ, Wrytten in the Greeke Tongue by Three Learned Historiographers, Eusebius, Socrates, and Euagrius. [...]

quotations.author: Abel Upshur
quotations.passage: The supreme court, therefore, may assume jurisdiction over subjects and between parties, not allowed by the constitution, and there is no power in the federal government to gainsay it.
quotations.work: A Brief Enquiry into the Nature and Character of our Federal Government

quotations.author: Griffith acted
quotations.passage: And there was something childlike about Griffith, too, even in his Matlock days, as a deceptively sharp 'simple country lawyer,' a big-kid boyishness that did not mask his intelligence or gainsay his authority.

gainsay.title: gainsay

etymologies: From a specialised use of gate (“way, manner, behaviour, habit", properly "way, path, street, journey”), from Middle English gate (“way, path, road, street”), from Old Norse gata (“path, lane, alley, road”), from Proto-Germanic *gatwǭ (“passageway, street”). Doublet of gate.

examples: Carrying a heavy suitcase, he had a lopsided gait.
definitions.text: A manner of walking or stepping; a bearing or carriage while moving on legs.
One of the distinct patterns of locomotion exhibited by a horse, occurring either naturally or as a result of training.
To teach a specific gait to a horse.
A sheaf of corn.
A charge for pasturage.

pronunciations.accent: Wales, without the pane – pain merger

gait.title: gait

etymologies: From French galimafrée, from Old French calimafree (“stew of various kinds of meats”); further etymology uncertain, but possibly from a combination of Old French galer (“to have fun, to enjoy oneself”) and Old Northern French (Picard) mafrer (“to eat gluttonously”).

definitions.text: A hash of various kinds of meats; a ragout.
Any absurd medley; an elaborate mishmash.

quotations.author: Andrew Allen Harwood
quotations.passage: At length, having discussed in turn pilaus, keebaubs, ollas, and a legion of gallimaufrys not mentioned in the classic pages of Kitchener and Ude, the cook's brain became completely addled by the elaborate and conflicting directions bestowed upon him; […]

The name "googol" was invented by a child (Dr. Kasner's nine-year-old nephew) who was asked to think up a name for a very big number, namely, 1 with a hundred zeros after it. He was very certain that this number was not infinite, and therefore equally certain that it had to have a name. […] A googolplex is much bigger than a googol, much bigger than a googol times a googol. A googol times a googol would be 1 with 200 zeros, whereas a googolplex is one with a googol of zeros. You will get some idea of the size of this very large but finite number from the fact that there would not be enough room to write it, if you went to the farthest star, touring all the nebulae and putting down zeros every inch of the way.

etymologies: From Middle English gossomer, gosesomer, gossummer (attested since around 1300, and only in reference to webs or other light things), usually thought to derive from gos (“goose”) + somer (“summer”) and to have initially referred to a period of warm weather in late autumn when geese were eaten — compare Middle Scots goesomer, goe-summer (“summery weather in late autumn; St Martin's summer”) and dialectal English go-harvest, both later connected in folk-etymology to go — and to have been transferred to cobwebs because they were frequent then or because they were likened to goose-down. Skeat says that in Craven the webs were called summer-goose, and compares Scots and dialectal English use of summer-colt in reference to "exhalations seen rising from the ground in hot weather". Weekley notes that both the webs and the weather have fantastical names in most European languages: compare German Altweibersommer (“Indian summer; cobwebs, gossamer”, literally “old wives' summer”) and other terms listed there.

definitions.text: A fine film made up of cobwebs, seen floating in the air or caught on bushes, etc.

etymologies: Learned borrowing from Late Latin gravāmen (“physical inconvenience”) and Medieval Latin gravāmen (“grievance”), from Latin gravāre + -men (suffix forming neuter nouns of the third declension). quotations.passage: It's like saying that Dickens put in all this crude, comic stuff to please the groundlings. I don't think he did.
quotations.work: Invitation to Learning: English & American Novels

quotations.author: More money
quotations.passage: They serve to allow the thousands of groundlings who attend alongside the celebrities to talk, to swap ideas and generally to stick their fingers in the air to see which way the wind is blowing.

quotations.author: Robert Ignatius Letellier
quotations.passage: At the same time, as we gather from his Journal des Débats notice of Le Prophète, Berlioz was well aware of Meyerbeer's demagogic streak, his readiness to bemuse the groundling with loud commonplaces.
Still, the folio Ben looks to publish will be well beyond the purse of most scholars, let alone a groundling.

quotations.author: Norman Rush
quotations.passage: The point, to her, seemed to be to show that whatever was going on around him was subordinate to the great private productive secret-not-necessarily-related-to-anything-his-groundling-friends-were-talking-about trains of thought that Douglas was having.

quotations.author: Capel Lofft
quotations.passage: It is not the good workman that is wont to quarrel with his tools ; adminicular aids and clinging propensities are fit only for the groundling, the child who is unable to walk upright and must be fain to crawl and to creep on as he best may.

quotations.author: Wilbur Gleason Zeigler
quotations.passage: On Tuesday, April 17th, 1906, a business man of San Francisco ascended for the first time in five years to one of the upper stores of the highest sky-scraper in the Newpaper Angle. He was a groundling who had kept his ears as well as his feet to the earth.
quotations.work: The Story of the Great Disaster: San Francisco's 1906 Earthquake and Fire

quotations.author: Field Artillery Association
quotations.passage: The poor plodding groundling, helpless and impotent, is swooped upon at will, day and night, completely wiped out at the whim of the low- flying plane, which soars off leaving complete and utter destruction behind it!

quotations.author: Erin Bried
quotations.passage: He then enlisted in the air force and served as a groundling in North Africa, Sicily, and England.
quotations.work: How to Build a Fire: And Other Handy Things Your Grandfather Knew

quotations.author: Pat Cunningham
quotations.passage: Present at the Battle of Jutland, he had been recalled for the duration of this war and, being in the area, he had come to see how his little lad was faring in the sky. I was given permission to fall out and join him, gladly setting aside my groundling's bayonet.
quotations.work: The Fear in the Sky: Vivid Memories of Bomber Aircrew in World War Two

quotations.author: John Lambshead
quotations.passage: Simon noticed a groundling look intently at Walsingham's purse and nudge his mate.

quotations.author: Martha Wells
quotations.passage: One, a short groundling with dark leathery skin and long white hair, said, "It's not your house, Ventl. You, stranger, did you come here to trade?"
quotations.work: Stories of the Raksura: The Dead City & The Dark Earth Below

quotations.author: Markus Heitz
quotations.passage: It was obvious that the brown-haired groundling had been involved in some heavy hand-to-hand combat recently.
quotations.work: Dark Paths: The Legends of the Alfar

quotations.author: Athalya Brenner-Idan
quotations.passage: It is not good for the groundling to be alone I will make for it a help as its counterpart (2.18).

quotations.author: Margaret Hebblethwaite
quotations.passage: The two of them were naked, the groundling and his woman, they were not ashamed.
quotations.work: Opening the Scriptures: Faith Throughout the Year

quotations.author: Megan McKenna
quotations.passage: It isn't until three chapters later that this groundling receives a name—Adam; at that point, the groundling is no longer referred to as “it” in the text, but becomes “him.”

groundling.title: groundling

etymologies: Attested in the 1530s, as grows ("moorhen"), a plural used collectively. The origin of the noun is unknown; the following derivations have been suggested:
The verb is derived from the noun.

The origin of the verb is uncertain; it is possibly borrowed from Norman groucier, from Old French groucier, grousser (“to grumble, murmur”) [and other forms] (whence grutch (“to complain; to murmur”) and grouch). The further etymology is unknown, but it may be derived from Frankish *grōtijan (“to make cry, scold, rebuke”) or of onomatopoeic origin.
The noun is derived from the verb.

Uncertain; possibly from British dialectal groosh (“excellent, very good”) (Lothian (Scotland)), grosh (northeast Lancashire) and groshy (“having thriving vegetation; juicy and tender; of weather: good for vegetation, rainy”) (Lancashire, Yorkshire), grushie (“having thriving vegetation”) (Scotland); from Scots groosh (“excellent, very good”) (Lothian, obsolete), grush (obsolete), grushie, grushy (“growing healthily or lushly; excellent, very good”) (both archaic), from gross (“lacking refinement, coarse; fat; large”) + -ie (suffix meaning ‘rather, somewhat’).

definitions.text: Any of various game birds of the subfamily Tetraoninae which inhabit temperate and subarctic regions of the Northern Hemisphere; specifically, the red grouse (Lagopus scotica) native to heather moorland on the British Isles.
The flesh or meat of this bird eaten as food.
To hunt or shoot grouse.
To complain or grumble.
A cause for complaint; a grumble.

examples: I had a grouse day.
That food was grouse.
definitions.text: Excellent.

quotations.author: Ben Jonson
quotations.passage: Looke to 't, young growse: Ile lay it on, and sure; / Take 't off who's wull.
quotations.work: The Workes of Benjamin Jonson. The Second Volume.

quotations.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
quotations.passage: Grouse away!" he growled. "If grousin' made a man happy, you'd be the champion."

quotations.author: Kipling
quotations.passage: If you're cast for fatigue by a sergeant unkind, / Don't grouse like a woman, nor crack on, nor blind; / Be handy and civil, and then you will find / That it's beer for the young British soldier.

quotations.author: Owen Salusbury Brereton
quotations.passage: Among fowls for the table [of King Henry VIII] are crocards, winders, runners, grows, and peions, but neither Turky or Guiney-fowl.
quotations.work: Archaeologia: Or, Miscellaneous Tracts Relating to Antiquity

quotations.author: Rien Poortvliet
quotations.passage: The shy black grouse, “with an eye on every feather,” can only thrive in vast, absolutely undisturbed heath and moorlands. Therefore, unfortunately, there are not too many black grouse.
quotations.work: The Living Forest: A World of Animals

quotations.author: Kaltenbrunner: “All Everest parties around one table!

Otherwise, it is extremely quiet, and you have the view of the North Face. You won’t meet anyone at the Kangshung Face too.

quotations.author: Mudrooroo

quotations.author: Tim Winton
quotations.passage: They were the grousest ladies she′d ever met.

quotations.author: Stujo

grouse.title: grouse

etymologies: From Middle English gile, from Anglo-Norman gile, from Old French guile (“deception”), from Frankish *wīl (“ruse”), from Proto-Germanic *wīlą, from Proto-Indo-European *wey- (“to turn, bend”). Cognate via Proto-Germanic with wile.
Variant forms.

definitions.text: Astuteness often marked by a certain sense of cunning or artful deception.
Deceptiveness, deceit, fraud, duplicity, dishonesty.
To deceive, beguile, bewile.
A surname from French.

quotations.author: Edmund Spenser
quotations.passage: Who means no guile, be guiled soonest shall

quotations.author: Phil Dawkes
quotations.passage: It was a result that owed a lot to a moment of guile from Ramires but more to a display of guts from the Brazilian and his team-mates after Terry's needless dismissal eight minutes before half-time for driving a knee into the back of Alexis Sanchez off the ball.

quotations.author: Rory Houston
quotations.passage: Estonia were struggling to get to grips with the game while Ireland were showing a composure and guile that demonstrated their experience in play-off ties.
Jesus saw Nathanael coming to him, and saith of him, Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile!

quotations.author: William Reddington
quotations.passage: […] a curdly, yeasty head on a Guile of Beer.

quotations.author: Hester Thrale Piozzi
quotations.passage: Perkins told me Yesterday that his Guile of Beer had a Summer-head on't, like as one sees in the last Weeks of Brewing in a forward Spring:—The Phænomenon surprized him I find.

guile.title: guile

etymologies: From Middle English guise, gise, gyse, from Old French guisse, guise, vise (“guise, manner, way”), from Old Frankish *wīsa (“manner, way, fashion”), from Proto-Germanic *wīsǭ (“manner, way”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“to see, view, behold, perceive”). Cognate with Old High German wīsa (“way, manner”), Old English wīse (“way, manner”), Dutch wijze (“way, manner”). More at wise.

definitions.text: A customary way of speaking or acting; a fashion, a manner, a practice (often used formerly in such phrases as "at his own guise"; that is, in his own fashion, to suit himself.)
An external appearance in manner or dress; an appropriate indication or expression; a garb; a shape.

examples: Under the guise of patriotism
definitions.text: A misleading appearance; a cover, a cloak.
To dress.
To act as a guiser; to go dressed up in a parade etc.

examples: Sup guise? — What's up, guys?
definitions.text: Deliberate misspelling of guys.
A surname.

quotations.author: Russell Brand
quotations.passage: Ought we be concerned that our rights to protest are being continually eroded under the guise of enhancing our safety?

quotations.author: Phil McNulty

quotations.author: Vane

guise.title: guise

etymologies: From Latin gustātus, participle of gustō (“to taste”), +‎ -ory.

definitions.text: Of, or relating to, the sense of taste.

quotations.author: Bill Henry
quotations.passage: WHERE TO DINE—Well, Mary Ward, our courageous gustatory investigatress, has finally completed her rounds of the eateries and, with her last despairing effort, dashed off this report on the road houses: […]

quotations.author: Robert Audi
quotations.passage: I see the field, and this experience is the visual parallel of hearing a bird (an auditory experience), touching a glass (a tactual experience), smelling roses (an olfactory experience), and tasting mint (a gustatory experience).
quotations.work: Epistemology: A Contemporary Introduction to the Theory of Knowledge

quotations.author: Ken Belson
quotations.passage: The point, Goldstein discovered through a lot of long days hanging out in parking lots, is that tailgating — the gustatory madness, the multigenerational camaraderie, the decked-out vans — is as essential a part of football as the game itself.

gustatory.title: gustatory

etymologies: From Hindustani گیند خانہ (gendxānā) / गेंदख़ाना (gendxānā, “racquet court”), from گیند / गेंद (gend, “ball”) + خانہ / ख़ाना (xānā, “court”). Influenced by gymnastics and gymnasium.

definitions.text: A competition where riders and horses display a range of skills and aptitudes.
A place of public resort for athletic games, etc.
A meeting for such sports.
Synonym of motorkhana.
Any event, situation, etc., with a broad array of elements.

quotations.author: Winston Churchill
quotations.passage: In the afternoon the British held athletic sports, an impromptu military tournament, and a gymkhana, all of which caused much merriment and diversion, and the Boers profited by the cessation of the shell fire to shovel away at their trenches.

quotations.author: John Law
quotations.passage: These privileged gentlemen have a fine club on the Fateh Maidan, a suburb of Hyderabad city, and they enjoy sports and races at the local gymkhana, in fact, they have a very good time, if one may judge by their appearance.

quotations.author: John Wyndham
quotations.passage: There was argument, public, private, and bar-parlor, with heated championship of one term or another on near-scientific, quasi-etymological, and a number of other grounds, but gradually one term began to dominate this philological gymkhana.

gymkhana.title: gymkhana

etymologies: From Middle English habilement, from Old French habillement (“clothes”).

definitions.text: Clothes, especially clothing appropriate for someone's job, status, or to an occasion.
Equipment or furnishings characteristic of a place or being; trappings.

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: She / In th' habiliments of the goddess Isis / That day appeared, and oft before gave audience […]
quotations.work: Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies

quotations.author: Edmund Spenser
quotations.passage: Forth came that auncient Lord and aged Queene, / Arayd in antique robes downe to the ground, / And sad habiliments right well beseene; / A noble crew about them waited round / Of sage and sober Peres, all gravely gownd; / Whom farre before did march a goodly band / Of tall young men,° all hable armes to sownd, / But now they laurell braunches bore in hand; / Glad signe of victorie and peace in all their land.

quotations.author: Charles Dickens
quotations.passage: […] Mrs Crummles was then occupied in exchanging the habiliments of a melodramatic empress for the ordinary attire of matrons in the nineteenth century.
quotations.work: The Life and Adventures of Nicholas Nickleby

quotations.author: William Makepeace Thackeray
quotations.passage: Her maid having a taste in dressmaking—to which art she had been an apprentice at Paris, before she entered into Miss Blanche’s service there—was kept from morning till night altering and remodelling Miss Amory’s habiliments; and rose very early and went to bed very late, in obedience to the untiring caprices of her little taskmistress.

quotations.author: William Somerset Maugham
quotations.passage: Bananas with their great ragged leaves, like the tattered habiliments of an empress in adversity, grew close up to the house.

habiliment.title: habiliment

definitions.text: To make accustomed; to accustom; to familiarize.
To settle as an inhabitant.

quotations.author: Charlotte Brontë
quotations.passage: My first quarter at Lowood seemed an age; and not the golden age either; it comprised an irksome struggle with difficulties in habituating myself to new rules and unwonted tasks.

quotations.author: Jeremy Taylor
quotations.passage: [B]y often praying in such manner and in all circumstances, vve shall habituate our souls to prayer, by making it the business of many lesser portions of our time: and by thrusting in betvveen all our other imployments, it vvill make every thing relish of Religion, and by degrees turn all into its nature.
quotations.work: The Rule and Exercises of Holy Living.

quotations.author: Hannah More
quotations.passage: It seems so very important to ground young persons in the belief that they will not inevitably meet in this world with reward and success according to their merit, but to habituate them to expect even the most virtuous attempts to be often, though not always disappointed, that I am in danger of tautology on this point.
quotations.work: Strictures of the Modern System of Female Education

quotations.author: Nadine Gordimer
quotations.passage: […] quarrels in discotheques were settled by the final curse-word of guns. State violence under the old, past regime had habituated its victims to it. People had forgotten there was any other way.

quotations.author: William Temple
quotations.passage: After the Conquests made by Caesar upon Gaul, and the nearer Parts of Germany […] great Numbers of Germans and Gauls resorted to the Roman Armies and to the City it self, and habituated themselves there, as many Spaniards, Syrians, Graecians had done before upon the Conquest of those Countries.

habituate.title: habituate

etymologies: Borrowed from French habitué, past participle of habituer (“to frequent”), from Late Latin habituare (“to habituate”), from habitus.

examples: A month ago the new smoking ban turned thousands of bar-room habitués into reluctant exiles from their usual corner seat.
definitions.text: One who frequents a place.
A devotee.

quotations.author: Walter Besant
quotations.passage: At half-past nine on this Saturday evening, the parlour of the Salutation Inn, High Holborn, contained most of its customary visitors. […] In former days every tavern of repute kept such a room for its own select circle, a club, or society, of habitués, who met every evening, for a pipe and a cheerful glass.

quotations.author: Alan Rusbridger
quotations.passage: Indeed, many guests even became habitués in order to blaze a trail with reckless abandon seven days a week.

quotations.author: Ludovic Hunter-Tilney
