etymologies: Borrowed from French iconoclaste and its etymon Medieval Latin īconoclastēs, from Medieval Greek εἰκονοκλάστης (eikonoklástēs, literally “image breaker”). By surface analysis, icono- +‎ -clast.

definitions.text: One who destroys religious images or icons, especially an opponent of the Orthodox Church in the 8th and 9th centuries, or a Puritan during the European Reformation.
One who opposes orthodoxy and religion; one who adheres to the doctrine of iconoclasm.
One who attacks cherished beliefs; a maverick.

quotations.author: Eugene TeSelle
quotations.passage: In the days of the early Christian church, people who opposed the veneration (reverence) of images were called iconoclasts.

quotations.author: James Bennet
quotations.passage: After all, the fact that any discussion of the possibility is greeted with hysterical revulsion guarantees that only two types of people will take the "pro" side in public: fearless iconoclasts who do not care what anyone thinks of them; and racists.

quotations.author: Spencer Kornhaber
quotations.passage: Coming so soon after the death of David Bowie, it’s a moment to consider how deeply important iconoclasts are to the evolution of a culture. Do they change the world by trying to change it, or do they change the world through the radical act of simply being themselves?

quotations.author: George Johnson
quotations.passage: Relishing the role of iconoclast, he confounded the scientific establishment by dismissing the consensus about the perils of man-made climate change as “tribal group-thinking.”

iconoclast.title: iconoclast

etymologies: From idea + -ate (verb-forming suffix).
From idea + -ate (adjective-forming suffix).
From Late Latin ideatum. See idea.

definitions.text: To apprehend in thought so as to fix and hold in the mind; to memorize.
To generate an idea.
Produced by an idea.
The actual existence supposed to correspond with an idea; the correlate in real existence to the idea as a thought or existence.

quotations.author: Devika Rege
quotations.passage: Two thousand young men and women from across the country had gathered under canvas tents on a public ground for a weekend of ideating and networking.

ideate.title: ideate

etymologies: From Latin īdyllium, from Ancient Greek εἰδύλλιον (eidúllion), from diminutive of εἶδος (eîdos, “form, shape”).

definitions.text: Any poem or short written piece composed in the style of Theocritus's short pastoral poems, the Idylls.
An episode or series of events or circumstances of pastoral or rural simplicity, fit for an idyll; a carefree or lighthearted experience.
A composition, usually instrumental, of a pastoral or sentimental character, e.g. Siegfried Idyll by Richard Wagner.

quotations.author: Alan Rusbridger
quotations.passage: Its pages contain not just recipes but an idyll of prelapsarian plenty, passed down the generations by those who still connect with pagan forces: Saturnus and his groaning table, a Saturnalia from the Golden Age.

idyll.title: idyll

etymologies: From idyll + -ic.

definitions.text: Of or pertaining to idylls.
Extremely happy, peaceful, or picturesque.
An idyllic state or situation.

quotations.author: H. G. Wells
quotations.passage: My fellow-creatures, from whom I was thus separated, began to assume idyllic virtue and beauty in my memory.

quotations.author: August–September
quotations.passage: The rest of the road was as idyllic as the start.

I think I learned more from my family than they did from me in the brief idyllic time we spent together. None of them much more than a mile from home, they carried the aura of a close-knit community as a shield against against the unknown.

quotations.author: August–September
quotations.passage: He could retire to the idyllic with the knowledge that he had not been wanting when Romance called.

idyllic.title: idyllic

etymologies: Borrowed from French idée fixe (literally “fixed idea”).

definitions.text: An idea dominating the mind and maintained despite evidence to the contrary; , an obsession.
A recurring musical theme; a leitmotif.

quotations.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
quotations.passage: “There is the condition which the modern French psychologists have called the ‘idée fixe,’ which may be trifling in character, and accompanied by complete sanity in every other way. A man who had read deeply about Napoleon, or who had possibly received some hereditary family injury through the great war, might conceivably form such an ‘idée fixe’ and under its influence be capable of any fantastic outrage.”

quotations.author: Roy Porter
quotations.passage: The sage's solitary fantisizings about the heavens have turned monstrous, his yearnings for knowledge have swollen into idées fixes
quotations.work: Flesh in the Age of Reason

quotations.passage: a definite musical figure, called the 'idée fixe,' unifying the work throughout by its constant reappearance in various aspects and surroundings
quotations.work: Grove's Dictionary of Music and Musicians

idée_fixe.title: idée fixe

etymologies: Borrowed from Middle French ignoble, from Latin ignōbilis, from in- (“not”) + gnōbilis, later nōbilis (“noble”).

definitions.text: Not noble; plebeian; common.
Not honorable; base.
Not a true or "noble" falcon; said of certain hawks, such as the goshawk.
Of an element, dangerously reactive.
To make ignoble; to bring low.

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: I was not ignoble of descent.
quotations.work: Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: A base, ignoble mind, / That mounts no higher than a bird can soar.
quotations.work: Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies.

quotations.author: Thomas Gray
quotations.passage: far from the madding crowd's ignoble strife
quotations.work: Designs by Mr. R [ ichard ] Bentley, for Six Poems by Mr. T. Gray

ignoble.title: ignoble

etymologies: Borrowed from French ignominie, from Latin ignōminia, from ig- (“not”) + nomen (“name”) (prefix assimilated form of in-).

definitions.text: Great dishonor, shame, or humiliation.

quotations.author: Herman Melville
quotations.passage: But like Czar Peter content to toil in the shipyards of foreign cities, Queequeg disdained no seeming ignominy, if thereby he might happily gain the power of enlightening his untutored countrymen.

quotations.author: Norman Lindsay
quotations.passage: Bradly came out from hiding with a dyspeptic grunt, too depressed by ignominy to send a curse after the old woman.

quotations.author: Alan Rusbridger
quotations.passage: It was tribal, almost relentless and, in the case of the official England band, there was a degree of ignominy, too, for repeatedly playing a tune for which the words go “Fuck the IRA”, something that could lead to a full breakdown of their relationship with the FA.

quotations.author: Liz Robbins
quotations.passage: The lawyer who shot to ignominy last week with a racist rant at a Manhattan lunch spot apologized Tuesday on social media, where a video of his threat to call immigration agents on Spanish-speaking workers had first gone viral.

quotations.author: Russian diplomat in Switzerland says he resigns over Ukraine invasion
quotations.passage: "I studied to be a diplomat and have been a diplomat for twenty years," Bondarev wrote. "The (Russian foreign) ministry has become my home and family. But I simply cannot any longer share in this bloody, witless and absolutely needless ignominy."

ignominy.title: ignominy

etymologies: Borrowed from French illicite, from Latin illicitus, from in- (“not”) + licitus (“allowed, permitted”), from licet (“it is allowed”). By surface analysis, il- +‎ licit.

examples: The bigamous marriage, while illicit, was not invalid.
definitions.text: Not approved by law, but not invalid.
Breaking social norms.
Unlawful.
A banned or unlawful item.

quotations.author: Madeleine Albright
quotations.passage: Such migrants may violate our laws against illicit entry, but if that's all they do then they are trespassers, not criminals.
quotations.work: Memo to the President Elect: How We Can Restore America's Reputation and Leadership

quotations.author: Alan Clark
quotations.passage: I only can properly enjoy carol services if I am having an illicit affair with someone in the congregation.

quotations.author: Ian McDonald
quotations.passage: Ayşe Erkoç learned long ago that the secret of doing anything illicit in Istanbul is to do it in full public gaze in the clear light of day. No one ever questions the legitimacy of the blatant.

quotations.author: Shane Darke
quotations.passage: A large number of studies, however, have reported that it is rare for the user of 'hard' drugs not to have initiated cannabis use prior to the other illicits.
quotations.work: The Life of the Heroin User: Typical Beginnings, Trajectories and Outcomes

illicit.title: illicit

etymologies: Borrowed from Middle French illusorie (modern French illusoire), derived from Latin illūsōrius (“mocking, ironical”).

definitions.text: Resulting from an illusion; deceptive, imaginary, unreal.

quotations.author: Jadunath Sinha
quotations.passage: The invalidity of a cognition is the otherwiseness of its object, and is known by a sublating cognition. The illusory cognition of silver knows illusory silver, but does not know its otherwiseness.

quotations.author: Katharine Viner
quotations.passage: Yet for this new womanosphere, the response is not advancing policies like paid family leave or affordable childcare, but to return to an idealized, illusory past where being a wife and mother was viewed as a woman’s sole purpose.

illusory.title: illusory

etymologies: From Middle English imbiben, from Latin imbibō, from im- + bibō (“to drink”) (whence also beverage), from Proto-Italic *pibō, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₃-, whence also potable, potion.

definitions.text: To drink (used frequently of alcoholic beverages).

examples: to imbibe knowledge
definitions.text: To take in; absorb.
To steep; to cause to absorb liquid.

quotations.author: Mary Shelley
quotations.passage: “Every minute,” continued M. Krempe with warmth, “every instant that you have wasted on those books is utterly and entirely lost. You have burdened your memory with exploded systems, and useless names. Good God! in what desert land have you lived, where no one was kind enough to inform you that these fancies, which you have so greedily imbibed, are a thousand years old, and as musty as they are ancient? I little expected in this enlightened and scientific age to find a disciple of Albertus Magnus and Paracelsus. My dear Sir, you must begin your studies entirely anew.”

quotations.author: John A. Logan, Jr.
quotations.passage: Perhaps in the case of the vodka-drinking peasant it is this weekly parboil which saves his life and postpones the dreadful day when the constant imbibing of unlimited quantities of the deadly liquor must be paid for.

quotations.author: Justin O. Schmidt
quotations.passage: Without its sting, the common yellowjacket would be unable to steal ham from our sandwich or imbibe the sweet juice from our peach.

quotations.author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon
quotations.passage: To eradicate that error, already but too deeply imbibed, to subdue and triumph over human infirmity, was indeed difficult, but to Rosilia a derogation from virtue was still more so.

quotations.author: Marsha Keith Schuchard
quotations.passage: Like the late Dr Falk (d. 1782), Grabianka was a native of Podolia, where Sabbatian influences were strong among local Jews, and he imbibed many of their notions.

quotations.author: Katharine Murphy
quotations.passage: If you’ve been imbibing Craig’s Kelly’s Covid monologues over the summer and wondering why Scott Morrison lets one of his own MPs regularly contradict the official public health advice without rebuke, let me try to answer your question.

imbibe.title: imbibe

etymologies: From Middle English imbibicion, inbibicioun, from Middle French imbibicion. By surface analysis, imbibe +‎ -ition.

definitions.text: The act of imbibing.

quotations.author: Thomas Browne
quotations.passage: For beside the common way and road of reception by the root, there may be a refection and imbibition from without; For gentle showrs refresh plants, though they enter not their roots; […]
quotations.work: Hydriotaphia, Urne-buriall, Together with The Garden of Cyrus

quotations.author: Joseph Thomas James Hewlett
quotations.passage: He was bobbing it up and down just above the pommel of his saddle, being rather sleepy from the imbibition of a little too much of Mr. Tit Dowell’s strong beer.

imbibition.title: imbibition

etymologies: Borrowed from Latin imbricātus (“tiled”).

definitions.text: Alternative form of imbricated (“overlapping”).
To overlap in a regular pattern.
To undergo or cause to undergo imbrication.

quotations.author: George Francis Atkinson
quotations.passage: The pileus is sessile, or sometimes narrowed at the base into a short stem, the caps often numerous and crowded together in an overlapping or imbricate manner.
quotations.work: Studies of American Fungi. Mushrooms, Edible, Poisonous, etc.

imbricate.title: imbricate

etymologies: Borrowed from Italian imbroglio (“tangle, entanglement, muddle”) (im-, alternative form of in- (prefix forming verbs denoting derivation) + broglio (“confusion; intrigue, fraud, rigging, stuffing”); see also imbrogliare (“to tangle”)), cognate with and probably from an earlier form of French embrouiller (“to embroil, muddle”) (em- (“em-”), a form of en- (“en-”, prefix meaning ‘caused’) + brouiller (“to confuse, mix up”)). Doublet of embroil.

definitions.text: A complicated situation; an entanglement.

quotations.author: Thomas Gray
quotations.passage: Into the drawers and china pry, / Papers and books, a huge imbroglio! / Under a tea-cup he might lie, / Or creased, like dogs-ears, in a folio.
quotations.work: The Works of Thomas Gray; Vol. I Containing the Poems, with Critical Notes; a Life of the Author; and an Essay on His Poetry; by the Rev. John Mitford

quotations.author: Erica Jong
quotations.passage: Your trip here will never quite go as planned. […] There may be strikes, mixed-up reservations, maddening imbrogli of all sorts. But they will be charming imbrogli because the Italian people are charming, down to the whimsical tone of their language.
quotations.work: Tuscany and Umbria: The Collected Traveler

quotations.author: Judith Bendheim Guedalia
quotations.passage: He [Edward Michael Adler] was inducted into the imbroglio of the Vietnam War, which so many of his age group and middle class Orthodox Jewish upbringing easily avoided by staying in university or going into the clergy. He didn't.

quotations.author: Denis MacShane
quotations.passage: [David] Cameron's decision to hold a referendum alters the chemistry of politics. The casual way he offered a simple Yes–No referendum to Scotland in 2011 has led to a quasi-insoluble imbroglio over the future of the British Constitution.
quotations.work: Brexit: How Britain Will Leave Europe

imbroglio.title: imbroglio

etymologies: From Latin imbuō (“wet, moisten”). Compare imbibe.

definitions.text: To instill or inspire (someone) with a certain quality, feeling, or idea.

examples: The shirt was imbued with his scent.
definitions.text: To wet or stain an object completely with some physical quality.

examples: The entire text is imbued with the sense of melancholy and hopelessness.
definitions.text: In general, to act in a way which results in an object becoming completely permeated or impregnated by some quality.

quotations.author: Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley
quotations.passage: The patriarchal lives of my protectors caused these impressions to take a firm hold on my mind; perhaps, if my first introduction to humanity had been made by a young soldier, burning for glory and slaughter, I should have been imbued with different sensations.

quotations.author: An Essay about the Origin and Virtue of Gems
quotations.passage: I might leave the answering of one part of the objection to physicians and chymists, who teach, that the antimonial glass and cup imbue wine and other liquors with a strong emetic quality, without any sensible loss of weight.
quotations.work: THE WORKS OF THE HONOURABLE ROBERT BOYLE.

imbue.title: imbue

etymologies: From French immémorial. By surface analysis, im- +‎ memorial.

examples: The rocks had stood overlooking the valley since time immemorial.
definitions.text: That is beyond memory; ancient.

quotations.author: Benjamin Disraeli
quotations.passage: We will ride this morning to what we call the grove of Daphne. It is a real laurel grove. Some of the trees must be immemorial, and deserve to have been sacred, if once they were not so.

quotations.author: James Redfoord Bulwer
quotations.passage: ...the fact of the immemorial taking of the toll, though it would be rightful in its origin if the spot was in a port, and wrongful if it was not in a port, did not of itself afford sufficient ground for inferring that the spot was an antient port, or that such special services were rendered, either by express stipulation in some lost grant, or by immemorial usage, as would support such a grant or custom.
quotations.work: The Law Reports. Court of Common Pleas.

quotations.author: Herbert George Wells
quotations.passage: Now, I still think that for this box of matches to have escaped the wear of time for immemorial years was a strange, and for me, a most fortunate thing.

quotations.author: Theodore Dalrymple
quotations.passage: Were it not that the fields are vast in extent, those proclaiming themselves part of State Farm’s, the scene might be immemorial.
quotations.work: The Wilder Shores of Marx: Journeys in a Vanishing World

immemorial.title: immemorial

etymologies: The adjective is first attested in 1534, the verb in 1548; borrowed from Latin immolātus, perfect passive participle of immolō (“to sacrifice”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

definitions.text: To kill as a sacrifice by burning.
To kill, harm, or destroy by fire.
Immolated, sacrificed.

quotations.author: William Makepeace Thackeray
quotations.passage: She imparted these stories gradually to Miss Crawley; gave her the whole benefit of them; felt it to be her bounden duty as a Christian woman and mother of a family to do so; had not the smallest remorse or compunction for the victim whom her tongue was immolating; nay, very likely thought her act was quite meritorious, and plumed herself upon her resolute manner of performing it.

quotations.author: December
quotations.passage: Evidently some, or all, of the boars immolated themselves, for the train crew are reported to have picked up three dead boars and continued to Sézanne, the next stop, where they gave them to the local hospital cooks.

quotations.author: A.S. Byatt
quotations.passage: A secular style, a new beginning after the iconoclastic excesses under young Edward VI, when angels, Mothers and Children had flared and crackled in the streets, immolated to a logical absolute God who disliked images.

immolate.title: immolate

etymologies: From Middle English enmuren and Middle French emmurer, both from Old French enmurer, from Latin immūrō, from in- + mūrus (“wall”). Modern spelling is modelled after the Latin.

definitions.text: To cloister, confine, imprison or hole up: to lock someone up or seclude oneself behind walls.

examples: John's body was immured Thursday in the mausoleum.
definitions.text: To put or bury within a wall.
To wall in.
To trap or capture (an impurity); chiefly in the participial adjective immured and gerund or gerundial noun immuring.
A wall; an enclosure.

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: […] Troy, within whose strong emures […]
quotations.work: Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies

quotations.author: Emily Dickinson
quotations.passage: Immured in Heaven! What a Cell! / Let every bondage be, / Thou Sweetest of the Universe, / Like that which ravished thee!

quotations.author: Mary Meeke
quotations.passage: The gentlemen looked at each other for a solution of this strange event, each presuming an order had been obtained to again immure the unfortunate Clara.

quotations.author: John Stagg
quotations.passage: [I]n the reign of Henry the Second, a body happening, by chance, to be dug up near Glastonbury Abbey, without any symptoms of putrefaction or decay, the Welch, the descendants of the Ancient Britons, tenacious of the dignity and reputation of that illustrious hero [King Arthur], vainly supposed it could be no other than the body of their justly-boasted Pen-Dragon; and that he had been immured in that sepulchre by the spells of some powerful and implacable inchanter.
quotations.work: The Minstrel of the North: Or, Cumbrian Legends.

quotations.author: Rosina Bulwer Lytton
quotations.passage: In a happy moment for the Levy-Lawson-Levis, Lady Lytton was betrayed, seized, and immured. The Editor saw his chance, and made the Metropolis ring with the outrage. Levi was saved; so also was Lady Lytton.

quotations.author: Michael Bronski
quotations.passage: Mattes creates a perversely sympathetic character: one who is so immured and immersed in his own self-pity/-hatred that his only connection to life is to dominate and control those with whom he connects.

quotations.author: Robert Chambers
quotations.passage: The dreadful punishment of immuring persons, or burying them alive in the walls of convents, was undoubtedly sometimes resorted to by monastic communities.

immure.title: immure

etymologies: From Middle English immutable, from Latin immūtābilis (“unchangeable”); im- +‎ mutable.

examples: The government has enacted an immutable law.
definitions.text: Unable to be changed without exception.

examples: Constants are immutable.
definitions.text: Not able to be altered in the memory after its value is set initially.
Something that cannot be changed.

quotations.author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon
quotations.passage: Mutable as is our nature, it delights in the immutable: and we expect as much constancy as if all time, to say nothing of our own changeableness, had not shewn that ever "the fashion of this world passeth away."

quotations.author: Peter Kent
quotations.passage: In the trustless cryptocurrency world, you can still trust the cryptocurrency community and its mechanisms to ensure that the blockchain contains an accurate and immutable—unchangeable—record of cryptocurrency transactions.

immutable.title: immutable

etymologies: From Old French impassible.

definitions.text: Unable to feel emotion; impassive.
Incapable of suffering detriment or injury.
Unable to suffer, or feel pain.
Misspelling of impassable.

quotations.author: Reginald Heber
quotations.passage: [W]e say it is unreasonable, that this [the bread or host of the Eucharist] should be changed into flesh, […] into that body of Christ, which is in heaven; he remaining there, and being whole and impassible, and unfrangible, this, we say, is unreasonable and impossible: […]
quotations.work: The Whole Works of the Right Rev. Jeremy Taylor, D.D.

impassible.title: impassible

etymologies: From im- (prefix meaning ‘not’) +‎ passive (“which is, or is capable of being, acted on; (obsolete) which suffers, or may suffer, pain, death, etc.”, adjective).

definitions.text: Having, or revealing, no emotion.
Still or motionless.

quotations.author: Phil McNulty
quotations.passage: It was a victory that clearly meant so much to Van Gaal as the normally impassive manager raced from his seat in the technical area to celebrate Lingard's winner.

impassive.title: impassive

etymologies: Inherited from Middle English impacience, from Old French impacience (modern French impatience), from Latin impatientia. By surface analysis, im- +‎ patience.

definitions.text: The quality of being impatient; lacking patience; restlessness and intolerance of delays; anxiety and eagerness, especially to begin something.

impatience.title: impatience

etymologies: From im- +‎ pecunious, from Latin pecūniōsus, from pecūnia (“money”) + -ōsus (“full of”).

definitions.text: Lacking money.

quotations.author: William S. Gilbert
quotations.passage: When I, good friends, was called to the bar, / I'd an appetite fresh and hearty, / But I was, as many young barristers are, / An impecunious party.

quotations.author: Pelham Grenville Wodehouse
quotations.passage: [I]t would be a simple matter, sir, to find some impecunious author who would be glad to do the actual composition of the volume for a small fee.

quotations.author: September
quotations.passage: The Rhymney (51 route miles), once an impecunious hanger-on of the Taff Vale, had enjoyed its own route through Caerphilly into Cardiff since 1871, [...].

impecunious.title: impecunious

etymologies: Borrowed from Latin impediō (“to shackle”), from pēs (“foot”) (compare pedestrian). First attested use as a verb was in William Shakespeare's Macbeth, see quotations.

examples: impede someone's progress
definitions.text: To get in the way of; to hinder.

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: That I may powre my Spirits in thine Eare, / And chastise with the valour of my Tongue / All that impeides thee from the Golden Round, / Which Fate and Metaphysicall ayde doth seeme / To haue thee crown'd withall.
quotations.work: Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies

quotations.author: Robert Jordan
quotations.passage: “Everything had been ticking along like a fine clock, even with Bornhald impeding, until this new one appeared with his Gray Men. Ordeith scrubbed bony fingers through greasy hair. Why could not his dreams at least be his own?”

quotations.author: Lisa Bonos
quotations.passage: The human-machine imbalance made Sellers concerned that the modern thirst for AI-powered optimization was starting to impede human interaction.

impede.title: impede

etymologies: From Latin imperiōsus (“mighty, powerful”), from imperium (“command, authority, power”).

definitions.text: Domineering, arrogant, or overbearing.
Urgent; intensely compelling.
Imperial or regal.

quotations.author: Christopher Marlowe
quotations.passage: The frowning lookes of fiery Tamburlaine, / That with his terrour and imperious eies, / Commands the hearts of his associates, […]
quotations.work: Tamburlaine the Great. The First Part

quotations.author: Fyodor Dostoyevsky
quotations.passage: […] she glanced about her in an imperious, challenging sort of way, with looks and gestures that clearly were unstudied.

quotations.author: Stephen Crane
quotations.passage: She was quick, beautiful, imperious, while he was quiet, slow, and misty.

quotations.author: April
quotations.passage: I had travelled one morning down to Aylesbury, and had left my train, and was about to cross the footbridge, when I heard the imperious whistle of a "B1." I paused, and round the bend came the "Master Cutler" with its engine working absolutely flat out.

quotations.author: Salman Rushdie
quotations.passage: “Hey, sir? Sir, excuse me?” The blonde was calling out to him, in imperious tones that insisted on a reply.

quotations.author: Phil McNulty
quotations.passage: Saliba, meanwhile, has returned to Arsenal looking like the finished article after the 21-year-old France defender spent loan spells at Saint-Etienne, Nice and Marseille. He has been imperious since the opening game at Brentford, establishing a formidable partnership with Gabriel.

quotations.author: Katharine Viner
quotations.passage: Back in France, once the fourth republic yielded to the fifth, Gaullist rule proved imperious and sometimes blinkered – but effective.

quotations.author: David Wallace-Wells
quotations.passage: The conflict has been a military humiliation, the world’s most expensive and imperious fighting force held at bay by the disposable drones and cheap missiles of a much lesser power.

quotations.author: Ambrose Bierce
quotations.passage: Circumstances of an imperious nature, which it is unnecessary to relate here, had prevented him from taking service with that gallant army which had fought the disastrous campaigns ending with the fall of Corinth.
quotations.work: An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge

quotations.author: Harry E. Wedeck
quotations.passage: An old man to whom a few drops of phosphoric ether had been administered experienced repeated and imperious venereal wants.

quotations.author: Ephraim Judson
quotations.passage: All the terrors of Antichrist; his cruel ediets and anathemas that were thundered from his imperious throne, like storms of fire and brimstone […]
quotations.work: Ambassadors appointed by Christ to treat with mankind on the subject of reconciliation to God

imperious.title: imperious

etymologies: From Late Middle English imperturbable (“undisturbed; impossible to disturb”), borrowed from Late Latin imperturbābilis, from Latin im- (variant of in- (prefix meaning ‘not’)) + Late Latin perturbabilis (“perturbable”) (from Latin perturbō (“to confuse; to alarm, disturb, trouble, perturb”) + -bilis (suffix forming adjectives denoting a capacity or worth of being acted upon)). Perturbō is derived from per- (intensifying prefix) + turbō (“to agitate, disturb, unsettle, perturb; to upset”) (from turba (“disorder, disturbance, turmoil”) (possibly from Ancient Greek τῠ́ρβη (tŭ́rbē, “confusion, disorder, tumult”), either from Pre-Greek, or Proto-Indo-European *(s)twerH- (“to agitate, stir up; to urge on, propel”)) + -ō (suffix forming infinitives of regular first-conjugation verbs)). By surface analysis, im- (prefix meaning ‘not’) +‎ perturbable.

definitions.text: Not capable of being, or not easily, perturbed, excited, or upset; calm and collected, even under pressure.

quotations.author: Walter Scott
quotations.passage: [T]he good Dominie bore all his disasters with gravity and serenity equally imperturbable. "Prodi-gi-ous!" was the only ejaculation they ever extorted from the much-enduring man.

quotations.author: Walter Scott
quotations.passage: In the meanwhile, Sir Piercie Shafton sate still as a stone on the chair in which he had deposited himself, […] his eyes cast up to the ceiling as if he had meant to count every mesh of cobweb with which the arched roof was canopied, wearing at the same time a face of as solemn and imperturbable gravity, as if his existence had depended on the accuracy of his calculation.

quotations.author: Anthony Munday
quotations.passage: [T]o a vvise man there can happen no iniury or offence at all, to molest the felicity of his minde, vvhich (in the Stoicks opinion) ought to bee imperturbable, and his heart adamantine.
quotations.work: The Dumbe Divine Speaker, or: Dumbe Speaker of Diuinity.

quotations.author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon
quotations.passage: "We may keep it by us," replied the pawnbroker, "for months; there is no demand for such articles." "But," exclaimed she, eagerly, "I shall soon redeem it!" "So you all say," returned the man, with imperturbable coolness.
quotations.work: Ethel Churchill: Or, The Two Brides.

quotations.author: Geoffrey Freeman Allen
quotations.passage: This sort of thing is meat and drink to the born Controller—and Controllers are born with the right imperturbable temperament for the job; hence the fact that they are recruited from many different grades of operating staff, and some recruits don't stay the course.

imperturbable.title: imperturbable

etymologies: From Latin impervius (“that cannot be passed through”), from in- (“not”) + pervius (“letting things through”).

examples: The man was completely impervious to the deception we were trying.
definitions.text: Unaffected or unable to be affected by something.

examples: Although patchworked and sagging, the roof proved impervious to the weather.
definitions.text: Preventive of any penetration; impenetrable, impermeable, particularly of water.

examples: The old car seemed to be impervious to the wear and tear of age.
definitions.text: Immune to damage or effect.

quotations.author: Winston Churchill
quotations.passage: Although the Celebrity was almost impervious to sarcasm, he was now beginning to exhibit visible signs of uneasiness, the consciousness dawning upon him that his eccentricity was not receiving the ovation it merited.

quotations.author: The $300bn Google-Meta advertising duopoly is under attack
quotations.passage: For the past decade there were two more or less universally acknowledged truths about digital advertising. First, the rapidly growing industry was largely impervious to the business cycle.

quotations.author: Robin Leleux
quotations.passage: The white faience façade, the glazed Doultonware Carrera marble, was made locally. And being glazed, it was impervious to London's sooty atmosphere, enabling easier cleaning.

impervious.title: impervious

etymologies: From Middle English impetuous, from Old French impetueux, from Late Latin impetuōsus (“violent”), from Latin impetus (“attack, violence”).

definitions.text: Making arbitrary decisions, especially in an impulsive and forceful manner.
Characterized by sudden violence or vehemence.

quotations.author: John Milton
quotations.passage: […] and the Thunder, / Wing'd with red Lightning and impetuous rage, / Perhaps hath spent his shafts […]

quotations.author: Edmund Spenser
quotations.passage: For with such puissance and impetuous maine / Those Champions broke on them, that forst the fly, / Like scattered Sheepe, whenas the Shepherds swaine / A Lyon and a Tigre doth espye, / With greedy pace forth rushing from the forest nye.

quotations.author: Jane Austen
quotations.passage: […] and before breakfast was ready, they had gone through the subject again and again; with the same steady conviction and affectionate counsel on Elinor's side, the same impetuous feelings and varying opinions on Marianne's, as before.

quotations.author: Jane Austen
quotations.passage: "Oh! where, where is my uncle?" cried Elizabeth, darting from her seat as she finished the letter, in eagerness to follow him, with-out losing a moment of the time so precious; but as she reached the door, it was opened by a servant, and Mr. Darcy appeared. Her pale face and impetuous manner made him start […]

quotations.author: Walter Scott
quotations.passage: Rough and impetuous as a wild boar, where only earthly force was to be apprehended, he had all the characteristic terrors of a Saxon respecting fawns, forest-fiends, white women, and the whole of the superstitions which his ancestors had brought with them from the wilds of Germany.

quotations.author: William Makepeace Thackeray
quotations.passage: The shrewd kind confidant used gently to hint the sad fact to the impetuous hero of this piece. The impetuous hero knew this quite well.

quotations.author: Mark Twain
quotations.passage: When they were placed in position they thought it was time to begin,—and then did begin, too, and with a most impetuous energy, without waiting for anybody to give the word.

quotations.author: Mary Wollstonecraft Godwin
quotations.passage: After being two days the prey of impetuous, varying emotions, Maria began to reflect more calmly on her present situation, for she had actually been rendered incapable of sober reflection, by the discovery of the act of atrocity of which she was the victim.
quotations.work: Posthumous Works of the Author of A Vindication of the Rights of Woman.

quotations.author: Beethoven, Louis Van
quotations.passage: But it was natural, that the impetuous, restless young artist should incline more to excess of strength than of delicacy in his playing.

quotations.author: Alan Rusbridger
quotations.passage: The prime minister thought he could sagely steer his impetuous American friends away from actions they would later regret. It turns out they were just playing him for a patsy[.]

quotations.author: Jeffrey Goldberg
quotations.passage: How these developments might come about and what they will mean for humanity seems far more important to probe than Isaacson’s preferred focus on explaining Musk’s abusive, erratic, impetuous behavior.

quotations.author: Ann Radcliffe
quotations.passage: He stands, and views in the faint rays / Far, far below, the torrent's rising surge, / And listens to the wild impetuous roar

quotations.author: Peter Christen Asbj&oslash￵rnsen
quotations.passage: Having made a few vain attempts at engrossing my attention in my book, I was obliged to let myself be carried away by the impetuous torrent of the squire's eloquence.

impetuous.title: impetuous

etymologies: From Middle English implācāble (“immitigable, unappeasable”) from Old French implacable (“harsh, unrelenting; implacable”) (modern French implacable), from Latin implācābilis (“unappeasable, implacable; irreconcilable”), from im- (variant of in- (prefix meaning ‘not’)) + plācābilis (“placable; appeasing, moderating, pacifying, propitiating; acceptable”) (from plācō (“to assuage, pacify, placate; to appease; to reconcile”) + -bilis (suffix forming adjectives indicating a capacity or worth of being acted upon)).

definitions.text: Not able to be placated or appeased.
Impossible to prevent or stop; inexorable, unrelenting, unstoppable.
Adamant; immovable.

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: He is knight dubb'd with vnhatche'd Rapier, and on carpet consideration, but he is a diuell in priuate brall, soules and bodies hath he diuorc'd three, and his incensement at this moment is so implacable, that satisfaction can be none, but by pangs of death and sepulcher: Hob, nob, is his word: giu't or take't.
quotations.work: Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies

quotations.author: John Stagg
quotations.passage: [I]n the reign of Henry the Second, a body happening, by chance, to be dug up near Glastonbury Abbey, without any symptoms of putrefaction or decay, the Welch, the descendants of the Ancient Britons, tenacious of the dignity and reputation of that illustrious hero [King Arthur], vainly supposed it could be no other than the body of their justly-boasted Pen-Dragon; and that he had been immured in that sepulchre by the spells of some powerful and implacable inchanter.
quotations.work: The Minstrel of the North: Or, Cumbrian Legends.

quotations.author: James D. Hornfischer
quotations.passage: The battleships Washington and South Dakota pushed through the sea with an implacable ease.
quotations.work: Neptune’s Inferno: The U.S. Navy at Guadalcanal

quotations.author: John Bunyan
quotations.passage: Indeed Cain hated his Brother, because his own works were evil, and his Brothers righteous; and if thy Wife and Children have been offended with thee for this, they thereby shew themselves to be implacable to good; and thou hast delivered thy soul from their blood.
quotations.work: The Pilgrim’s Progress from This World, to That which is to Come

implacable.title: implacable

etymologies: First attested in the 15th century, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English implicaten (poorly attested), from implicat(e) (“wrapped, entwined; involved, connected (with)”, possibly also used as the past participle of implicaten) +‎ -en (verb-forming suffix), borrowed from Latin implicātus, perfect passive participle of implicō (“to entangle, involve”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from plicō (“to fold”). Doublet of imply and employ.

First attested in the first part of the 15th century, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English implicat(e) (“wrapped, entwined; incolved, connected (with)”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix), -ate (noun-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more.

examples: The evidence implicates involvement of top management in the scheme.
definitions.text: To show to be connected or involved in an unfavorable or criminal way.

examples: What did Nixon's visit to China implicate for Russia?
definitions.text: To imply, to have as a necessary consequence or accompaniment.
To imply without entailing; to have as an implicature.
To fold or twist together, intertwine, interlace, entangle, entwine.
The thing implied.
used in implicate order
Involved, intricate.

quotations.author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon
quotations.passage: But it is of no use talking now; the servants will soon be stirring, and it would be rather awkward to be found here." "For you, perhaps, madam," sneered Sir George. "Rather for yourself," replied she, with the greatest composure; "you might be implicated in the charge of murder."
quotations.work: Ethel Churchill: Or, The Two Brides.

quotations.author: Robert Jones Burdette
quotations.passage: I shall cancel, without further provocation, the next lecture engagement that is implicated with a peep o' day train.

quotations.author: A punch in the gut
quotations.passage: Mostly, the microbiome is beneficial. It helps with digestion and enables people to extract a lot more calories from their food than would otherwise be possible. Research over the past few years, however, has implicated it in diseases from atherosclerosis to asthma to autism.

implicate.title: implicate

etymologies: From Middle French implicite, from Latin implicitus, past participle of implico (“to infold, involve, entangle”); see implicate.

examples: Poets often leave behind an implicit message within their words.
definitions.text: Suggested indirectly, without being directly expressed; Implied.
Contained in the essential nature of something but not openly shown.
Having no reservations or doubts; unquestioning or unconditional; usually said of faith or trust.
entangled, twisted together.

quotations.author: Ronald Reagan
quotations.passage: The Bible and its teachings helped form the basis for the Founding Fathers' abiding belief in the inalienable rights of the individual, rights which they found implicit in the Bible's teachings of the inherent worth and dignity of each individual.

quotations.author: anonymous author
quotations.passage: He is not only a zealous advocate for pusilanimous and passive obedience, but for the most implicit faith in the dictatorial mandates of power.
quotations.work: Considerations on Behalf of the Colonists

quotations.author: Homer
quotations.passage: In his deep fleece […] I cling implicit.

implicit.title: implicit

etymologies: From im- + politic.

definitions.text: Not in accordance with good policy.

quotations.author: January
quotations.passage: On at least one such occasion, in L.N.E.R. days, I discovered later that what I had written was precisely what the authorities wanted to be said, though it would have been highly impolitic for my chief to have given me this information rather than the formal reproof that I received!

quotations.author: Diarmaid MacCulloch
quotations.passage: Even when it was impolitic to admire, let alone name, Evagrius, his descriptions of progress in the spiritual life could not be and were not ignored […] .

quotations.author: Ross Douthat
quotations.passage: And thereafter it became impolitic to say anything critical about the Harris sprint.

impolitic.title: impolitic

etymologies: From im- + ponderable.

definitions.text: Not ponderable; without sensible or appreciable weight; incapable of being weighed.
Difficult or impossible to comprehend or evaluate.

A substance or body, which is not ponderable, i.e., which not does not having a detectable amount of matter or measurable mass. An imponderable substance or body; specifically, in the plural, a name formerly applied to heat, light, electricity, and magnetism.
An imponderable question.
A factor that cannot be anticipated.

quotations.author: Christian Wolmar
quotations.passage: One key imponderable is the attitude of the companies that will no longer have a role in the business. It is worth noting here that several have already thrown the towel in or been gently pushed out, such as Stagecoach and National Express.

imponderable.title: imponderable

etymologies: First attested in 1477, in Middle english; from Latin importūnus +‎ -ate (adjective-forming suffix), modelled on Middle French importuné. By surface analysis, importune +‎ -ate (compare inopportune). The noun was substantivized from the adjective, see -ate (noun-forming suffix).
First attested in 1574; adapted borrowing of French importuner (“to bother, disturb”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

definitions.text: Persistent or pressing, often annoyingly so.
Given to importunate demands, greedily or thoughtlessly demanding.
An importuner.
To importune, or to obtain by importunity.

quotations.author: Henry James
quotations.passage: Nick was on the point of declaring again that he was a humbug, so vivid was his inner sense of what he thought of his factitious public utterances, which had the cursed property of creating dreadful responsibilities and importunate credulities for him.

quotations.author: William Butler Yeats
quotations.passage: Trembling in every limb I raise my loud im­portunate cry, / And in a sacred terror wait the Delian god’s reply.
quotations.work: Sophocles ’ King Oedipus : A Version of the Modern Stage

quotations.author: Elisabeth Celnart
quotations.passage: [...] if you reprimand or punish them, be assured every one will consider you importunate as well as ridiculous.
quotations.work: The Gentleman and Lady's Book of Politeness and Propriety of Deportment: Dedicated to the Youth of Both Sexes

quotations.author: John Pym
quotations.passage: This will put an Answer into the Kings mouth, against all importunates.
quotations.work: A Collection of Scarce and Valuable Tracts, on the Most Interesting and Entertaining Subjects

importunate.title: importunate

etymologies: From Middle French importuner and its etymon Medieval Latin importūnor (“to make oneself troublesome”), from Latin importūnus (“unfit, troublesome”), originally "having no harbor".
From Middle English importune, inportune, from Anglo-Norman and Middle French importun and its etymon Classical Latin importūnus.

definitions.text: To bother, irritate, trouble.
To harass with persistent requests.
To approach to offer one's services as a prostitute, or otherwise make improper proposals.
To import; to signify.
Grievous, severe, exacting.
Inopportune; unseasonable.
Troublesome; vexatious; persistent.
Synonym of importuner.

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: Gentlemen, importune me no farther, / For hovv I firmly am resolu'd you knovv: / That is, not to bestovv my yongest daughter, / Before I haue a husband for the elder: […]
quotations.work: Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: You were kneel'd to, & importun'd otherwise / By all of vs; […]
quotations.work: Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies

quotations.author: Edmund Spenser
quotations.passage: It importunes death.

quotations.author: Edmund Spenser
quotations.passage: And therewithall he fiercely at him flew, / And with importune outrage him assayld [...].

quotations.author: Edmund Spenser
quotations.passage: And their importune fates all satisfide.

quotations.author: Jonathan Swift
quotations.passage: [W]e have been obliged to hire Troops from several Princes of the Empire, whose Ministers and Residents here, have perpetually importuned the Court with unreasonable Demands, under which our late Ministers thought fit to be Passive.
quotations.work: The Conduct of the Allies, and of the Late Ministry, in Beginning and Carrying on the Present War

quotations.author: Jane Austen
quotations.passage: But I will no longer importune my young cousin.

quotations.author: Francis Bacon
quotations.passage: Of all other affections it [envy] is the most importune and continual.

quotations.author: Michel de Montaigne
quotations.passage: To deliberate, be it but in slight matters, doth importune me.

quotations.author: George Puttenham
quotations.passage: And yet in some Courts it is otherwise vsed, for in Spaine it is thought very vndecent for a Courtier to craue, supposing that it is the part of an importune: […]

quotations.author: Roger North
quotations.passage: Which shew that importunate People will affirm any Thing, to serve Turns, though never fo senseless; hoping some, that understand little, or are very willing, will give credit upon their Authority: And, if Justice must stay till such Importunes are satisfied, there’s a ne plus ultra of all Law.
quotations.work: Examen: or, An Enquiry into the Credit and Veracity of a Pretended Complete History;

quotations.author: Lady Hester Stanhope
quotations.passage: The Priests of the Holy Land sent me a letter he had written them about me thanking them for their civility to me, & desiring they wd. serve me in every thing &c, therefore these confounded importunes laid themselves at my feet, but his letter was admirable, nobody ever saw such a thing, his coats of Arms printed upon a paper as large as a gazette extraordinary and full as large as my hand open!!!
quotations.work: The Nun of Lebanon: The Love Affair of Lady Hester Stanhope and Michael Bruce : Their Newly Discovered Letters

importune.title: importune

etymologies: Learned borrowing from Latin imprecātiō (“calling down of curses”), from imprecor (“call down, invoke”).

definitions.text: The act of imprecating, or invoking evil upon someone; a prayer that a curse or calamity may befall someone.
A curse.

quotations.author: John Dryden
quotations.passage: Hear then this dreadful imprecation; hear it: / 'Tis lay'd on all; not any one exempt: […]

quotations.author: Charles Dickens
quotations.passage: Mr. Gamfield growled a fierce imprecation on the donkey generally, but more particularly on his eyes; and, running after him, bestowed a blow on his head.

quotations.author: Emily Brontë
quotations.passage: He drank the spirits and impatiently bade us go; terminating his command with a sequel of horrid imprecations too bad to repeat or remember.

quotations.author: Stephen Crane
quotations.passage: Her son turned to look at her as she reeled and swayed in the middle of the room, her fierce face convulsed with passion, her blotched arms raised high in imprecation. "May Gawd curse her forever," she shrieked.

quotations.author: Upton Sinclair
quotations.passage: All life had turned to rottenness and stench in them--love was a beastliness, joy was a snare, and God was an imprecation.

imprecation.title: imprecation

etymologies: From Late Middle English imprenable, impregnable (“impossible to capture, impregnable”), from Old French imprenable (modern French imprenable (“impregnable”)), from im- (a variant of in- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + prenable (“(military) of a building, position, etc.: takable”) (from prendre (“to take”) + -able (suffix meaning ‘creating an effect or influence’)). Prendre is derived from Latin prēndere, present active infinitive of prēndō, a variant of prehendō (“to catch, lay hold of; to grasp; to grab, snatch; to seize, take”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰed- (“to find; to hold; to seize, take”). The intrusive g in the English word was modelled after words like deign and reign.

From impregnate (verb) +‎ -able (suffix meaning ‘able or fit to be done’ forming adjectives). Impregnate is either derived from impregnate (“pregnant”, adjective), or from its etymon Medieval Latin or Late Latin impraegnātus (“made pregnant”), past participle of impraegnō (“to make pregnant”), from Latin im- (a variant of in- (prefix meaning ‘in, inside, within’)) + praegnāre (“pregnant”) (from praegnāns, a variant of praegnās (“pregnant”), from prae- (prefix meaning ‘before; in front’) + *gnāscor (archaic), nāscor (“to be born; to grow, spring forth; to arise, proceed”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁- (“to beget; to give birth; to produce”)).

definitions.text: Of a fortress or other fortified place: able to withstand all attacks; impenetrable, inconquerable, unvanquishable.
Too strong to be defeated or overcome; invincible.
Capable of being impregnated; impregnatable.

quotations.author: Herman Melville
quotations.passage: Unerringly impelling this dead, impregnable, uninjurable wall, and this most buoyant thing within; there swims behind it all a mass of tremendous life, only to be adequately estimated as piled wood is—by the cord; and all obedient to one volition, as the smallest insect.

quotations.author: Upton Sinclair
quotations.passage: Jurgis got up, wild with rage; but the door was shut and the great castle was dark and impregnable.

quotations.author: Robert South
quotations.passage: [A]s for the Friendship of the World; […] he may at last be no more able to get into the other's Heart, than he is to thrust his Hand into a Pillar of Brass. The Man's Affection, amidst all these Kindnesses done him, remaining wholly unconcerned, and impregnable; just like a Rock, which being plied continually by the Waves, still throws them back again into the Bosom of the Sea that sent them, but is not at all moved by any of them.
quotations.work: Twelve Sermons Preached upon Several Occasions.

quotations.author: Bolton
quotations.passage: And with Bolton suffering a wretched run of five straight home defeats – their worst run in 109 years – Chelsea fans would have been forgiven for expecting a comfortable win. But surely they did not anticipate the ease with which their team raced into an almost impregnable half-time lead.

quotations.author: November
quotations.passage: The reproductive strategies of troop members, especially those of impregnable females, are suggested to influence patterns of range use.

impregnable.title: impregnable

etymologies: From Latin imprimātur (“let it be printed”), third person singular present subjunctive passive form of imprimere (“to imprint”).

definitions.text: An official license to publish or print something, especially when censorship applies.
Any mark of official approval.

quotations.author: John Milton
quotations.passage: Sometimes 5 Imprimaturs are seen together dialogue-wise in the Piatza of one Title page, complementing and ducking each other with their shav'n reverences, whether the Author, who stands by in perplexity at the foot of his Epistle, shall to the Presse or to the spunge.
quotations.work: Areopagitica; a Speech of Mr. John Milton for the Liberty of Unlicenc’d Printing, to the Parlament of England

quotations.author: Elisabeth Achelis
quotations.passage: This ingenious plan expressed in a booklet by the Italian Roman Catholic priest had received three Nihil Obstats and two Imprimaturs from his bishop.

quotations.author: Richard Hall
quotations.passage: Children, the final imprimatur to family life, are being borrowed, adopted, created by artificial insemination.

quotations.author: Michael Billington
quotations.passage: Even with the imprimatur of Tynan and Hobson, the play was not an instant hit.

quotations.author: Jane Shaw
quotations.passage: The author suggests that Grace is hoping to meet at church a respectable marriage candidate who will have the imprimatur of her pastor and the church community.

imprimatur.title: imprimatur

etymologies: Unadapted borrowing from French impromptu.

examples: an impromptu speech

definitions.text: Improvised; without prior preparation, planning, or rehearsal.

examples: happened impromptu
was done impromptu
definitions.text: Extemporaneously; without prior preparation, planning, or rehearsal.
A short musical composition for an informal occasion often with the character of improvisation and usually to be played solo.
Any composition, musical or otherwise, that is created on the spot without preparation.
To compose offhand.

quotations.author: Rachel Trent
quotations.passage: The city of Placerville, California, also known as Hangtown, is losing the noose on its logo. […] After an impromptu citizens’ jury agreed to hang a man accused of a crime, the town became known as Hangtown. It took on the name Placerville in 1854.

quotations.author: Paul McCartney
quotations.passage: I can appreciate that Macca’s band plays faithful to the source material, never putting too obvious a personal spin on the music. It’s sometimes frustrating, especially when the solo part in “Get Back” is screaming for some impromptu finesse, but it’s mostly fair.

quotations.author: Christopher H. Gibbs
quotations.passage: The second impromptu is a dance-like Allegretto in A flat major, with a trio in D flat major employing arpeggiated textures.

impromptu.title: impromptu

etymologies: From the Latin improvidens, equivalent to in- +‎ provident.

definitions.text: failing to provide for the future; reckless
incautious; prone to rashness

quotations.author: Beatrix Potter
quotations.passage: When Benjamin Bunny grew up, he married his Cousin Flopsy. They had a large family, and they were very improvident and cheerful.
quotations.work: The Tale of The Flopsy Bunnies

improvident.title: improvident

etymologies: From Middle English impudent, originally meaning immodest, shameless, from Latin impudēns (“shameless”), ultimately from in- +‎ pudere (“to feel shame”).

examples: The impudent children would not stop talking in class.
definitions.text: Not showing due respect; bold-faced, impertinent.
Lacking modesty or shame; indelicate.

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: Sir Iohn, sir Iohn, I am well acquainted with your maner of wrenching the true cause,the false way. It is not a confident brow, nor the throng of wordes, that come with such (more then impudent) sawcines from you, can thrust me from a leuell consideration, […]

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: Dian. Good my Lord, / Aske him vpon his oath, if hee do’s thinke / He had not my virginity. / Kin. What saift thou to her? / Ber. She’s impudent my Lord, / And was a common gamester to the Campe. / Dia. He do’s me wrong my Lord: If I were so, / He might haue bought me at a common price.
quotations.work: Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies

quotations.author: Charles Dickens
quotations.passage: “Wickam,” retorted Mrs. Pipchin, coloring, “is a wicked, impudent, bold-faced hussy.”

quotations.author: Emma Jane Worboise
quotations.passage: And another asked me if I had come to get a Canadian sweetheart; and a third, one of the impudentest, most conceitedest fellows I ever did set eyes upon, nudged me, so that I spilled my coffee all over my second-best damask-silk apron—the one with bugle fringe, you know, Miss Capel—and says he, 'Is it a case of Barkis is willin'?'

So she caught him, and kissed him, and with an impudent face, said vnto him, I haue peace offerings with me: this day haue I paid my vowes. Therefore came I forth to meete thee, diligently to seeke thy face, and I haue found thee.
Wine and women will make men of vnderstanding to fall away, and he that cleaueth to harlots will become impudent.

impudent.title: impudent

etymologies: From Middle French impudicité, from Latin impudicus (“shameless, immodest”) + Middle French -ité. By surface analysis, im- +‎ pudic +‎ -ity.

definitions.text: Immodesty; shamelessness.

quotations.author: George Sale
quotations.passage: It must be observed that though a man is allowed by the Mohammedan, as by the Jewish law, to repudiate his wife even on the slightest disgust, yet the women are not allowed to separate themselves from their husbands, unless it be for ill usage, want of proper maintenance, neglect of conjugal duty, impotency, or some cause of equal import; but then she generally loses her dowry, which she does not, if divorced by her husband, unless she has been guilty of impudicity or notorious disobedience.

impudicity.title: impudicity

etymologies: Borrowed from Middle French impugner, from Latin impugnō, from im- + pugnō (“fight”), from pugnus (“fist”), as in English pugilism (“fighting with fists, boxing”).

definitions.text: To assault, attack.
To verbally assault, especially to argue against an opinion, motive, or action; to question the truth or validity of; cast doubt on.

Incarnato is derived from Ecclesiastical Latin and Late Latin incarnātus (“having been made incarnate”), the perfect passive participle of incarnō (“to become or make incarnate; to make into flesh”), from in- (suffix meaning ‘in, inside, within’) + Latin carō (“flesh, meat; body”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut off”)) + -ō (suffix forming regular first-conjugation verbs). By surface analysis, in- +‎ Latin carn- +‎ -ade +‎ -ine.
The noun and verb are derived from the adjective.

Adjective senses 2 and 3 (“of the blood-red colour of raw flesh; (figurative) bloodstained, bloody”) and noun sense 2 (“blood-red colour of raw flesh”) are due to William Shakespeare’s use of the word as a verb in Macbeth (c. 1606): see the quotation below.

incarnadine.title: incarnadine

etymologies: First attested in 1395, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English incarnat(e) (“(of God or Christ) embodied in human form or flesh, incarnate; provided with new tissues, healed; (with devel, in curses) bloody”), borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin incarnātus, perfect passive participle of incarnor (“to be made flesh, become incarnate”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from in- + Latin carō (“flesh”, carn- in its oblique stem) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). By surface analysis, in- +‎ Latin carn- +‎ -ate.
First attested in 1533; borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin incarnātus, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more.
From in- + carnate.

definitions.text: Embodied in flesh; given a bodily, especially a human, form; personified.
Flesh-colored; crimson.
To embody in flesh; to invest with a bodily, especially a human, form.
To gain full existence (bodily or otherwise).
To incarn; to become covered with flesh; to heal over.
To make carnal; to reduce the spiritual nature of.
To put into or represent in a concrete form, as an idea.
Not in the flesh; spiritual.

incarnate.title: incarnate

etymologies: The adjective is first attested in 1534, the verb circa 1631; borrowed from Latin incohātus (“begun, unfinished”), perfect passive participle of incohō (“to begin”), see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3). Cognate with Spanish incoar (“to initiate, commence, begin”).

definitions.text: Recently started but not fully formed yet; just begun; only elementary or immature.
Chaotic, disordered, confused; also, incoherent, rambling.
Of a crime, imposing criminal liability for an incompleted act.
A beginning, an immature start.
To begin or start (something).
To cause or bring about. In the field of criminology, to encourage, assist, conspire, aid and abet, incite, etc.
To make a start.

incommensurable.title: incommensurable

etymologies: Learned borrowing from French incommoder (“to bother, disconcert, incommode”), from Latin incommodāre, the present active infinitive of incommodō (“to inconvenience”), from in- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + commodō (“to accommodate, adapt; to bestow, provide; to hire, lend”) (from com- (a variant of con- (prefix indicating completeness or intensification)) + modō (the ablative or singular of modus (“manner, method, way; bound, limit; measure”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *med- (“to measure”))). The English word is analysable as in- (prefix meaning ‘not’) +‎ commode (“(archaic or obsolete) to provide (someone or something) with an appropriate, suitable, or necessary thing; to meet the requirements of (someone or something), suit; to repair (something)”).

The adjective is a learned borrowing from French incommode (“causing discomfort; inconvenient; troublesome; undesirable, unwanted, unwelcome”), from Latin incommodus (“inconvenient; disagreeable, troublesome; unfit, unsuitable, unseasonable”), from in- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + commodus (“becoming, suitable; comfortable, commodious; convenient; useful; opportune, timely; friendly, pleasant”) (from com- (a variant of con-) + modus): see further at etymology 1. The English word is analysable as in- (prefix meaning ‘not’) +‎ commode (“(obsolete) convenient, opportune; suitable”).
The noun is derived from the adjective.

definitions.text: To make (someone) uncomfortable; to discomfort, to disturb, to trouble.
To cause (someone or something) inconvenience; to hinder, to impede, to inconvenience, to obstruct.
Inapt; unsuitable.
Inconvenient; troublesome.
Something which causes inconvenience or trouble; a bother, an incommodity, an inconvenience.
