incondite.title: incondite

etymologies: From Latin incongruus, from in- (“not”) + congruus (“congruent”), equivalent to in- +‎ congruous.

definitions.text: Not similar or congruent; not matching or fitting in.

examples: 20 and 25 are incongruous with respect to 4.
definitions.text: Of two numbers, with respect to a third, such that their difference can not be divided by it without a remainder.

quotations.author: Charlotte Brontë
quotations.passage: [P]erhaps he thought me, with my basket of summer fruit, and my lack of the dignity age confers, an incongruous figure in such a scene.

quotations.author: Upton Sinclair
quotations.passage: Ona was blue-eyed and fair, while Jurgis had great black eyes with beetling brows, and thick black hair that curled in waves about his ears—in short, they were one of those incongruous and impossible married couples with which Mother Nature so often wills to confound all prophets.

quotations.author: Jack London
quotations.passage: Ardent suns had likewise tanned his face till it was swarthy as a Spaniard's. The yellow mustache appeared incongruous in the midst of such swarthiness.
A slightly incongruous note is struck by the National Westminster Bank beside the Vine [pub], a tiny dolls' house of a building, about the size of a garden shed, in herringbone-patterned brick.

quotations.author: Wayne Rooney
quotations.passage: For a few moments England toyed with the idea of making it a more difficult night than necessary. Scotland had scored a goal that seemed incongruous to the rest of their performance and, briefly, a fiercely partisan crowd sensed an improbable comeback.

incongruous.title: incongruous

etymologies: From Middle English incontinent, from Old French incontinent, from Latin incontinens, from in + continens.

definitions.text: Unable to contain or retain.
Plagued by incontinence; unable to retain natural discharges or evacuations, most commonly of urine or feces.
Lacking moral or sexual restraint, moderation or self-control, especially of sexual desire.

examples: an incontinent river of pure water
definitions.text: Unrestrained or unceasing.
Immediate; without delay.
Immediately, forthwith.
One who is unchaste.

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: He says he will return incontinent:
quotations.work: Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies

quotations.author: Ben Jonson
quotations.passage: O, old Incontinent, dost not thou shame

quotations.author: Thoughty2
quotations.passage: About 90% of all koalas have chlamydia... which makes them incontinent, so they spend all day pissing themselves.
quotations.work: Is This the Most Stupid Animal in the World?

quotations.passage: The male body, opened and bleeding, can assume the shameful attributes of the incontinent female body as both cause of and justification for its evident vulnerability and defeat.

quotations.author: Richard Grafton
quotations.passage: [Jesus] was borne in Bethlem a City of Juda: where incontinent by the glorification of the Angels, the agnition of the Shepeherds, the veneration of the wise men, the prophecy of holy Simeon, and the admiration of the Doctours, he was had in honour.
quotations.work: A Chronicle at Large and Meere History of the Affayres of Englande

quotations.author: Thomas Nashe
quotations.passage: "As how, my lambkin," blushing, she replide, / "Because I in this dancing schoole abide? / If that it be, that breede's this discontent, / We will remoue the camp incontinent: / For shelter onelie, sweete heart, came I hither, / And to auoide the troblous stormie weather; / But now the coaste is cleare, we will be gonne, / Since, but thy self, true louer I haue none."

incontinent.title: incontinent

etymologies: From in- + controvertible.

examples: incontrovertible evidence
Her statement that dogs are mammals is incontrovertible.
definitions.text: Not capable of being denied, challenged, or disputed; closed to questioning.

quotations.author: Leonard Hatch
quotations.passage: Just now he was wearing a suit of maple-syrup brown with faint but incontrovertible purple stripes.

quotations.author: November
quotations.passage: There is incontrovertible evidence that electrification of itself has great publicity value, but this would be greatly enhanced if the public knew in more detail how it would transform their services.

quotations.author: Coral Davenport
quotations.passage: All said that the incontrovertible evidence that climate change has already arrived—in the form of frighteningly extreme wildfires, drought, storms and floods afflicting every corner of the United States—has helped build political support.

incontrovertible.title: incontrovertible

etymologies: From Latin incorporeus +‎ -al. By surface analysis, in- +‎ corporeal.

definitions.text: Having no material form or physical substance.
Relating to an asset that does not have a material form; such as a patent.
Something that is incorporeal.

quotations.author: John Milton
quotations.passage: Thus incorporeal spirits to smaller forms / Reduced their shapes immense.

quotations.author: Richard Bentley
quotations.passage: Sense and perception must necessarily proceed from some incorporeal substance within us.
quotations.work: [ A Confutation of Atheism ] (please specify the sermon)

quotations.author: OwenFelltham
quotations.passage: The World is all vicissitude and conversion. Nor is it onely true in Materials and Substances; but even in Spirits, in Incorporeals; […]
quotations.work: Resolves or, Excogitations. A Second Centurie.

quotations.author: Thomas Taylor
quotations.passage: The divine nature of the celestial bodies cannot be seen through the telescope, and incorporeals are not to be viewed with a microscopic eye: […]
quotations.work: The Cratylus, Phædo, Parmenides and Timæus of Plato .

quotations.author: John H. Smyth
quotations.passage: Where the interest in a piece of land of one of six heirs to the deceased father’s estate was levied upon and it was claimed as a homestead, the Court said: “It is an incorporeal, and an incorporeal cannot be the object of the homestead act.”
quotations.work: The Law of Homestead and Exemptions

quotations.author: Gaius
quotations.passage: It is manifest that incorporeals are incapable of transfer by delivery. But urban praedial rights may be ceded in court, and rural ones may also be mancipated.
quotations.work: The Institutes of Gaius and Rules of Ulpian .

incorporeal.title: incorporeal

etymologies: From Middle English incorrigible, from Middle French incorrigible (1334), or directly from Latin incorrigibilis (“not to be corrected”), from in- (“not”) +‎ corrigere (“to correct”) +‎ -ibilis (“-able”), equivalent to in- +‎ corrigible. Recorded since 1340.

examples: The construction flaw is incorrigible; any attempt to amend it would cause a complete collapse.
definitions.text: Defective and impossible to materially correct or set aright.

examples: an incorrigible youth
definitions.text: Unmanageable; impervious to correction by punishment or pain.

examples: His dark soul was too incorrigible to repent, even at his execution.
definitions.text: Incurably depraved; not reformable.
Unchangeably established in a belief or habit.

examples: The statement "My knee hurts" is incorrigible.
definitions.text: Intrinsically incapable of being corrected; impossible to disprove, by its very nature.
Impossible to cure.

examples: The incorrigibles in the prison population are either lifers or habitual reoffenders.
definitions.text: An incorrigibly bad person.

quotations.author: Michael White
quotations.passage: Gordon Brown may have his grumpy, Granita moments, but as a strategist he is an incorrigible optimist.
It may appear as an epidemic, as a hereditary complaint, or as an obstinate and incorrigible disease again and again recurring.

incorrigible.title: incorrigible

etymologies: Borrowed from Latin incrēdulus (“unbelieving”).

definitions.text: Skeptical, disbelieving, or unable to believe.
Expressing or indicative of incredulity.
Difficult to believe; incredible.

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: Why euery thing adheres togither, that no dramme of a scruple, no scruple of a scruple, no obstacle, no incredulous or vnsafe circumstance […] .
quotations.work: Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies

quotations.author: Edgar Rice Burroughs
quotations.passage: Xodar listened in incredulous astonishment to my narration of the events which had transpired within the arena at the rites of Issus.

quotations.author: John le Carré
quotations.passage: In safe flats and dark restaurants, never the same one twice, we ate quiet meals, exchanged our goods and gazed upon each other with the incredulous contentment that passes between mountaineers when they are standing on the peak.

quotations.author: Reuters
quotations.passage: Reactions at Sun's campus, an hour's drive from San Francisco, ranged from the fearful to the incredulous.

quotations.author: Drachinifel
quotations.passage: Then came a report over the radio from one of St. Lo's pilots. He was reporting seeing ships, and they weren't American. Worse still, they were close. Incredulous, Admiral Sprague demanded confirmation, and, circling in closer, the pilot radioed back: "I can see pagoda masts. I see the biggest meatball flag on the biggest battleship I ever saw!"
quotations.work: The Battle of Samar - Odds? What are those?

quotations.author: David Brill
quotations.passage: Maybe David Ruben had some valid points about the ACLU on the national level from an historical perspective, although critcizing a non-gay organization for not loudly defending gay rights in 1952 seems a little incredulous.

incredulous.title: incredulous

etymologies: From Late Latin incubus, from Latin incubō (“nightmare, one who lies down on the sleeper”), from incubō (“to lie upon, to hatch”, from in- (“on”) +‎ cubō (“to lie down”)).

definitions.text: An evil spirit supposed to oppress people while asleep, especially to have sex with women as they sleep.
A feeling of oppression during sleep, sleep paralysis; night terrors, a nightmare.
Any oppressive thing or person; a burden.
One of various of parasitic insects, especially subfamily Aphidiinae.

quotations.author: March and April
quotations.passage: Ahead of us the lowering smoke-screen of Leeds and her gloomy satellites hung like an incubus over the land.

quotations.author: Colin Jones
quotations.passage: Notions of civic virtue were at that moment changing, in ways which would make of Louis's alleged vices an incubus on the back of the monarchy.

incubus.title: incubus

etymologies: Borrowed from Latin inculcātus, perfect passive participle of inculcō (“impress upon, force upon”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from in- (“in”) + calcō (“tread upon, trample”), from calx (“heel”). Participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English.

definitions.text: To teach by repeated instruction.
To induce understanding or a particular sentiment in a person or persons.
Inculcated.

quotations.author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
quotations.passage: Those impious Pigs, / Who, by frequent squeaks, have dared impugn / The settled Swellfoot system, or to make / Irreverent mockery of the genuflexions / Inculcated by the arch-priest, have been whipt / Into a loyal and an orthodox whine.
quotations.work: Oedipus Tyrannus; Or, Swellfoot The Tyrant: A Tragedy in Two Acts

quotations.author: Francis Bacon
quotations.passage: all preachers , especially such as be of good temper , and have wisdom with conscience , ought to inculcate and beat upon a peace , silence , and surseance
quotations.work: A Wise and Moderate Discourse, Concerning Church-Affaires

quotations.author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon
quotations.passage: she had a perfect Parisian accent, was musical—all French women sing—had a great deal of tournure, the value of which she was always inculcating on her pupils: "La Grace plus belle que la beauté," was invariably the quotation when putting on her shawl; and, it must be confessed, that never did five English girls put on shawls to such perfection.
quotations.work: Lady Anne Granard; or, Keeping up Appearances.

quotations.author: Aldous Huxley
quotations.passage: But wordless conditioning […] cannot inculcate the more complex courses of behaviour.

quotations.author: Clive Staples Lewis
quotations.passage: The right defense against false sentiments is to inculcate just sentiments.

quotations.author: S. H. Chua
quotations.passage: The institutional forces — school, psychiatry, police — that inculcate conformity and enforce heterosexuality in gay youth.

quotations.author: Steven Eke
quotations.passage: But there is also real opposition to Nato expansion - and even to Nato's continued existence after the Cold War. / This is a view shared by a very large part of Russia's military and foreign affairs establishment. / Educated and trained during the Soviet period, they are still inculcated with notions of super-power military might. / It has been painful for these people to see Nato's outer edge creep ever closer to what was once the frontier of the USSR.

quotations.author: Andrew Willet
quotations.passage: Wee had neede to haue the word of God often inculcate and beaten vpon vs.

inculcate.title: inculcate

etymologies: From Latin incumbentem + English -ent (suffix denoting the causing, doing, or promoting of an action). Incumbentem is the accusative singular of incumbēns (“reclining”), the present active participle of incumbō (“to lay upon, to lean or recline on; to fall upon, to press down on”), from in- (prefix meaning ‘against; into; on, upon’) + *cumbō (“to lie down, recline”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱewb-).

From Middle English incumbent, encumbent (“holder of an ecclesiastical benefice, dean, parson, etc.; cleric (?)”), from Medieval Latin incumbēns (“holder of a church position”) + Middle English -ent (suffix denoting one that causes, does, or promotes an action). Incumbēns is derived from Medieval Latin incumbō (“to obtain; to possess”), from Latin incumbō (“to lay upon, to lean or recline on; to fall upon, to press down on”): see etymology 1.

examples: the incumbent toe of a bird
definitions.text: Chiefly followed by on or upon: leaning, or lying, reclining, or resting, on something else.
Of an anther: lying on the inner side of the filament; also, of a cotyledon: having its back lying against the radicle.

examples: the incumbent toe of a bird
definitions.text: Of a body part such as a hair, spine, or wing: bent downwards or otherwise positioned so that it, or part of it, rests on or touches something else; specifically , of the hind toe of a bird: fully resting on a support.

examples: If the incumbent senator dies, he is replaced by a person appointed by the governor.
definitions.text: Being the current holder of an office or a title; specifically , of an ecclesiastical benefice.
Oppressive, pressuring.

examples: Proper behaviour is incumbent on all holders of positions of trust.
definitions.text: Followed by on or upon: imposed on one as an obligation, especially due to one's office or position.
Hanging or leaning over.
Putting much effort into an activity or some work.
Weighing on one's mind.
The current holder of an office or title; the holder of an ecclesiastical benefice.
A holder of a position as supplier to a market or market segment that allows the holder to earn above-normal profits.

quotations.author: John Milton
quotations.passage: Then with expanded wings he stears his flight / Aloft, incumbent on the dusky Air / That felt unusual weight, […]

quotations.author: Walter Scott
quotations.passage: [M]any a rock, / Hurled by primæval earthquake shock / From Benvenue's grey summit wild, / And here, in random ruin piled, / They frowned incumbent o'er the spot, / And formed the rugged sylvan grot.

quotations.author: Walter Scott
quotations.passage: [H]e foresaw not that he was losing for ever the opportunity of acquiring habits of firm and incumbent application, of gaining the art of controuling, directing, and concentrating the powers of his own mind for earnest investigation,—an art far more essential than even that learning which is the primary object of study.

quotations.author: George Eliot
quotations.passage: He has always remained friendly to me, though before his promotion, when he was an incumbent of this diocese, we had a little controversy about the Bible Society.

quotations.author: William Faulkner
quotations.passage: But if they had waited about the store to see what would happen when he arrived who until last night anyway must have still believed himself the incumbent, they were disappointed. […] A few days later they learned that the new smith was living in the house […]

quotations.author: Thomas Hobbes
quotations.passage: Ambition, and Covetousnesse are Passions also that are perpetually incumbent, and pressing; vvhereas Reason is not perpetually present, to resist them: and therefore vvhensoever the hope of impunity appears, their effects proceed.

quotations.author: George Berkeley
quotations.passage: But, as for solid, corporeal Substances, I desire you to shevv vvhere Moses makes any mention of them; and, if they shou'd be mentioned by him, or any other inspired VVriter, it vvou'd still be incumbent on you to shevv, those VVords vvere not taken in the vulgar Acceptation, or an unknovvn Quiddity, vvith an absolute Existence.
quotations.work: Three Dialogues between Hylas and Philonous.

quotations.author: Henry Wotton
quotations.passage: [I]f the great Doore, be Arched, vvith some braue Head, cut in fine Stone or Marble for the Key of the Arch, and tvvo Incumbent Figures gracefully leaning vpon it, tovvards one another, as if they meant to conferre; I should thinke this a sufficient entertainement, for the first Reception, of any Iudicious Sight, […]

quotations.author: Robert Boyle
quotations.passage: [U]pon the tops of high Mountains, the Air vvhich bears against the restagnant Quick-silver, is less press'd by the less ponderous incumbent Air; and consequently is not able totally to hinder the descent of so tall and heavy a Cylinder of Quick-silver, as at the bottom of such Mountains did but maintain an Æquilibrium vvith the incumbent Atmosphere.
quotations.work: New Experiments Physico-Mechanicall, Touching the Spring of the Air, and Its Effects

quotations.author: Joseph Addison
quotations.passage: Here, as ’tis said, the Rebel Giants lye, / And vvhen to move th’incumbent Load they try, / Ascending Vapours on the Day prevail, / The Sun looks sickly, and the Skie grovv pale.
quotations.work: Remarks on Several Parts of Italy, &c. in the Years 1701, 1702, 1703

quotations.author: Edward Bulwer-Lytton
quotations.passage: And, rising from his incumbent posture, he sought to force the end of the weed [a cigar] between the teeth of the dog.
quotations.work: “My Novel”; Or Varieties in English Life

quotations.author: Asa Gray
quotations.passage: [T]he anther either looks inwards or outwards. When it is turned inwards, or is fixed to that side of the filament which looks towards the pistil or centre of the flower, the anther is incumbent or intorse, as in Magnolia and the Water-Lily. When turned outwards, or fixed to the outer side of the filament, it is extorse, as in the Tulip-tree.
quotations.work: First Lessons in Botany and Vegetable Physiology

quotations.author: Thomas Fuller
quotations.passage: But whether parishes,—as usually understood for places bounded in regard of the profits from the people therein, payable only to a pastor incumbent there;—I say, whether such parishes were extant in this age, may well be questioned, as inconsistent with the community of ecclesiastic profits, which then seemed jointly enjoyed by the bishop and his clergy.

quotations.author: Dan Bilefsky
quotations.passage: Analysts said that, while China sought to wield political influence in Vancouver, whatever role it played was unlikely to have swung the vote. ¶ Kennedy Stewart, the incumbent mayor and Mr. [Ken] Sim's left-wing rival, agreed. "Chinese interference isn't the primary reason I lost," he said. "But it may have been a contributing factor." He received 29 percent of the vote to Mr. Sim's 51 percent.

quotations.author: Reuters
quotations.passage: Sunday's results confirmed that Uruguay had followed a global trend of incumbent parties losing vote share compared with the previous election, as the biggest year for elections in history comes to an end.

quotations.author: Edward Gibbon
quotations.passage: The North must again have been alarmed, and agitated, by the invasion of the Huns; and the nations vvho retreated before them, must have pressed vvith incumbent vveight on the confines of Germany.

quotations.author: Thomas Sprat
quotations.passage: Certainly all men truly Zelous, vvill most industriously endeavor to perform the first kind of good VVorks alvvaies; those, I mean, that are incumbent on all Christians.
quotations.work: A Sermon Preached before the King at White-hall December the 22. 1678

quotations.author: April–September
quotations.passage: He begged Mrs. Tope's pardon when she found it incumbent on her to correct him in every detail of his summary of the facts, but pleaded that he was merely a single buffer getting through life upon his means as idly as he could, and that so many people were so constantly making away with so many other people, as to render it difficult for a buffer of an easy temper to preserve the circumstances of the several cases unmixed in his mind.

quotations.author: Braden Dupuis
quotations.passage: When the fires finally come for Whistler, the evacuation process will be hectic, to put it lightly. It is incumbent upon all of us to ensure we're well prepared.

quotations.author: Andrew Zimmern
quotations.passage: While it's incumbent on Congress to act, Zimmern told guests on Monday night that everyone can play a part. He encouraged seeing hunger firsthand by volunteering at shelters and talking about it to keep the issue at the forefront as a matter of "moral urgency.".

quotations.author: Edward Young
quotations.passage: Hath the cleft Centre open'd vvide to Thee? / Death's inmost Chambers didst Thou ever see? / E'er knock at his tremendous Gate, and vvade / To the black Portal thro' th' incumbent Shade?

quotations.author: James Thomson
quotations.passage: [T]he spreading beech, that o'er the stream / Incumbent hung, […]

quotations.author: Robert Southey

quotations.author: The first presidential debate: Back in the centre
quotations.passage: Mr [Barack] Obama's problems were partly structural. An incumbent must defend the realities and compromises of government, while a challenger is freer to promise the earth, details to follow. Mr Obama's odd solution was to play both incumbent and challenger, jumping from a defence of his record to indignation at such ills as over-crowded classrooms and tax breaks for big oil companies.

quotations.author: Philip Haigh
quotations.passage: Just as interest grew under previous incumbent-but-one Grant Shapps, so interest could wane under new Transport Secretary Mark Harper.

quotations.author: David Remnick
quotations.passage: But the prospect of a Presidential election as a contest of the ancients is not a heartening one, and the anxieties it provokes cannot be dismissed as ageism. What are younger people, especially, to make of a political culture in which incumbents cling so tenaciously to their seats? The median age for senators is now around sixty-five. Mitt Romney, announcing his retirement, at the age of seventy-six, wasn't wrong to declare that it is time for a new generation of leaders to take the helm.

quotations.author: Schumpeter
quotations.passage: American capitalism is becoming like its European cousin: established firms with the scale and scope to deal with a growing thicket of regulations are doing well, but new companies are withering on the vine or selling themselves to incumbents.

incumbent.title: incumbent

definitions.text: Improper, immodest, or indecent.

indecorous.title: indecorous

etymologies: From in- + defeasible.

definitions.text: Not liable to being annulled or declared void.

indefeasible.title: indefeasible

etymologies: From Latin indēlēbilis (“indestructible”). By surface analysis, in- +‎ delible.

examples: This ink spot on the contract is indelible.
This stain on my shirt is indelible.
Written with indelible pen.

examples: That horrible story just might make an indelible impression on the memory.
definitions.text: Incapable of being canceled, lost, or forgotten.
Incapable of being annulled.

quotations.author: Patricia Cohen

indelible.title: indelible

etymologies: From indemn (“unhurt”) +‎ -ify (forming verbs)
From in- (“into”) + damnify (“to injure; to wrong”), assimilated to indemn and indemnify (“secure against loss; compensate, reimburse”).

definitions.text: To secure against loss or damage; to insure.
To compensate or reimburse someone for some expense or injury.
to hurt, to harm

indemnify.title: indemnify

etymologies: Borrowed from Late Latin indigenus (“native, born in a country”), from indi- (indu-), an old derivative of in (“in”), gen- the root of gignō (“give birth to”), and English -ous. examples: The Aboriginals were indigenous to Victoria before the World War.
The Ainu are the indigenous ethnic group of Japan's Hokkaido Island.
definitions.text: Native to a land, especially before colonization.

examples: The Ainu are the indigenous ethnic group of Japan's Hokkaido Island.
definitions.text: In particular, of or relating to a people (or their language or culture) that inhabited a region prior to the arrival of people of other cultures which became dominant (e.g., through colonialism), and which maintains a distinct culture.
Innate, inborn.

examples: That style of pottery is indigenous to that region.
definitions.text: Original to a geographical area.

quotations.work: Wild Apples: The History of the Apple Tree

quotations.passage: Horses, like camels, had once been indigenous to Latin America but had become extinct.
quotations.work: Open Veins of Latin America: Five Centuries of the Pillage of a Continent

quotations.author: Esra Özyürek

Utterly lacking or in need of something specified.
A person in need, or in poverty.

quotations.passage: At the end of the Falklands war two years earlier too, the Queen, whose second son, Andrew, had served as a helicopter pilot with the task force, was singularly untriumphalist and showed no inclination to follow her prime minister’s injunction to rejoice at victory.

quotations.author: Alan Rusbridger
quotations.passage: Southwark council, which took out the injunction against Matt, believes YouTube has become the "new playground" for gang members.

quotations.author: Katharine Viner
quotations.passage: The judges said Trump must issue new orders reflecting the permanent injunction within 10 days.

injunction.title: injunction

etymologies: The adjective is first attested in the 1420s, the verb in 1602; from Middle English innat(e) (“innate, inborn”), borrowed from Latin innātus (“inborn, innate”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), perfect active participle of innāscor (“to be born in, grow up in”), from in- (“in, at on”) + nāscor (“to be born”); see natal, native. The verb is derived from the adjective, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

definitions.text: Inborn; existing or having existed since birth.

examples: innate ideas
definitions.text: Originating in, or derived from, the constitution of the intellect, as opposed to acquired from experience.
Instinctive; coming from instinct.

examples: an innate anther
definitions.text: Joined by the base to the very tip of a filament.
To cause to exist; to call into being.

quotations.author: Charles Dickens
quotations.passage: As if she held the clue to something secret in his breast, of the nature of which he was hardly informed himself. As if she had an innate knowledge of one jarring and discordant string within him, and her very breath could sound it.

quotations.author: John Locke
quotations.passage: It would be sufficient to convince unprejudiced Readers of the falseness of this Supposition, if I should only shew (as I hope I shall in the following Parts of this Discourse) how Men barely by the Use of their natural Faculties, may attain to all the Knowledge that they have, without the help of any innate Impressions […]

quotations.author: Ben Jones
quotations.passage: Ironically, given France's innate reluctance to permit competition at home, the first breach in Renfe's monopoly came from SNCF offshoot Ouigo España in 2021.

quotations.author: Robert South
quotations.passage: There is an innate light in every man, discovering to him the first lines of duty, in the common notions of good and evil, which, by cultivation and improvement, may be advanced to higher and brighter discoveries.

quotations.author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon
quotations.passage: Perhaps, from an innate desire of justification, sorrow always exaggerates itself.

quotations.author: John Marston
quotations.passage: I never saw a foole leane : the chub-fac’d fop / Shines sleek with full cramm’d fat of happinesse, / VVhilst studious contemplation sucks the juice / From wisards cheekes : who making curious search / For Natures secrets, the first innating cause / Laughs them to scorne, as man doth busy Apes / VVhen they will zany men.
quotations.work: Tragedies and Comedies Collected into One Volume

quotations.author: Margaret Cavendish, Duchess of Newcastle-upon-Tyne
quotations.passage: […] but the innating matter works not upon the dull matter, as upon a new material, for the innate matter is mixt with the dull part of matter […]

quotations.author: Thomas Fuller
quotations.passage: Here you may behold how each County is innated with a particular Genius, inclining the Natives thereof to be dextrous, some in one profession, some in another […]
quotations.work: Anglorum Speculum, or The Worthies of England

innate.title: innate

etymologies: From Latin innocuus (“harmless”) (therefore, no gemination in + nocuous).

definitions.text: Harmless; producing no ill effect.
Inoffensive; unprovocative; unexceptionable.

quotations.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
quotations.passage: The shells fell for the most part innocuous; an eyewitness saw children at play beside the flaming houses; not a soul was injured.

quotations.author: Richard Chenevix Trench
quotations.passage: With its green cupola or tapering spire, / Which sunset touches with innocuous fire, / The little church appears, to sanctify / The precincts duly where men live and die— [...]
quotations.work: Sabbation; Honor Neale; and Other Poems

quotations.author: Bram Stoker
quotations.passage: Other things, too, there were, not less deadly though seemingly innocuous—dried fungi, the touch of which was death and whose poison was carried on in the air; also traps intended for birds, beast, fishes, reptiles, and insects; machines which could produce pain of any kind and degree, and the only mercy of which was the power of producing speedy death.
quotations.work: The Lair of the White Worm

quotations.author: David Foster Wallace
quotations.passage: The effects of any one instance of TV absorbing and pablumizing cultural tokens seems innocuous enough.
quotations.work: A Supposedly Fun Thing I’ll Never Do Again: Essays and Arguments

quotations.author: Wales
quotations.passage: As the half closed [Gareth] Bale and [Joe] Ledley both went close with good efforts, but [Craig] Bellamy picked up a yellow card for an innocuous challenge that also rules the new Liverpool man out of the trip to Wembley.

quotations.author: Gilbert Parker
quotations.passage: Ruth Devlin announced that the song must wait, though it appeared to be innocuous and child-like in its sentiments.

quotations.author: P. G. Wodehouse
quotations.passage: He sat down, and lighted a cigarette, casting about the while for an innocuous topic of conversation.

innocuous.title: innocuous

etymologies: From the Latin innuendō (“by nodding”), ablative singular form of innuendum (“a nodding”), gerund of innuō (“to give a nod”).

examples: She made a devious innuendo about her opponent, who was embarrassed.
definitions.text: A derogatory hint or reference to, or (often sexual) insinuation about, a person or thing.
A remark that is suggestive of something sexual without stating it explicitly.
A rhetorical device with an omitted but obvious conclusion, made to increase the force of an argument.
Part of a pleading in cases of libel and slander, pointing out what and who was meant by the libellous matter or description.
To interpret (something libellous or slanderous) in terms of what was implied.

quotations.author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon
quotations.passage: At dinner, a dish of stewed eels made Mr. Higgs a little pensive, and he remarked, "that the fair sex slipped through your fingers just like eels." This innuendo was, however, all that disturbed the enjoyment of the day, whose hilarity, as the newspapers say of a public dinner, was prolonged to a late hour.

quotations.author: Roger Moody
quotations.passage: From the start then, the prosecutor David Tudor-Price relied on innuendo to carry his case. […] his whole presentation was based on shoring-up the stereotypes.

quotations.author: Richard Fausset
quotations.passage: “The attacks and allegations from Candace [Owens] are either lies or they are innuendos thrown around with a total reckless disregard for the truth,” Mr. [Blake] Neff said.

quotations.author: Bunmi Sofola
quotations.passage: We were both quite good friends and apart from the playful innuendos about having an affair together we never really did anything.
quotations.work: Yours Sincerely: Selected Writings of Bunmi Sofola

quotations.author: Anna Banks
quotations.passage: Later in this phone call, Frank asks Libby on a date, and she accepts the invitation. [...] A similar road toward flirtatious innuendo seems to be at work in the following example. / FIELD NOTE / Fred: Who's that beautiful girl in that great sports car?! / Shirley: ((lightheartedly)) Shut up and get in the car! / Fred: You mean I get to ride with the beautiful girl? / […] Of course, flirtations may be touched off by more marked sexual innuendo. / FIELD NOTE / ((co-workers are working late, finishing a project)) / Velma: You know how it is when you're close but can't stop. / Sid: ((starts to give Velma a shoulder rub)) / Velma makes a comment with a possible sexual meaning, and Sid responds by initiating body contact (in a public place) to show that he hears (and follows up on) the sexual double entendre.
quotations.work: Fiction and Social Research: By Ice Or Fire

quotations.author: Paulina Palmer
quotations.passage: Donoghue represents the closet in Stir-Fry as a performance space of playful innuendo and verbal wit, while Hensher describes it in Kitchen Venom as an existential site to which the subject retreats in a paranoid attempt to avoid cultural and social definition.
quotations.work: The Queer Uncanny: New Perspectives on the Gothic

quotations.author: Jane K. Cowan
quotations.passage: This is kalaburi, a joking banter that includes stories, jokes, wordplays (puns and double entendres, which are often sexual), and playful innuendo.
quotations.work: Dance and the Body Politic in Northern Greece

quotations.author: Frank Towers Cooper
quotations.passage: A statement that a person's presence at a certain club may be "irksome," may be innuendoed that the person is of such bad character as not to be a fit associate with honourable men.
quotations.work: A Handbook of the Law of Defamation and Verbal Injury

innuendo.title: innuendo

etymologies: From Middle English inordinat, from Latin inōrdinātus (“not arranged, disordered, irregular”), from in- + ordinatus, past participle of ōrdināre (“to arrange, order”).

definitions.text: Excessive; unreasonable or inappropriate in magnitude.

quotations.passage: Mortifie therefore your members which are vpon the earth: fornication, vncleannesse, inordinate affection, euill concupiscence, and couetousnesse, which is idolatrie:

inordinate.title: inordinate

etymologies: Borrowed into late Middle English from Late Latin īnscrūtābilis, from in- (“not”) + scrūtō (“to examine”), corresponding to in- +‎ scrutable

examples: His inscrutable theories would years later become the foundation of a whole new science.
definitions.text: Difficult or impossible to comprehend, fathom, or interpret.
One who or that which is inscrutable; a person, etc. that cannot be comprehended.

quotations.author: Herman Melville
quotations.passage: The pale, inscrutable determinateness, and flinchless intrepidity of Pierre, now began to domineer upon them; for any social unusualness or greatness is sometimes most impressive in the retrospect.

quotations.author: Joseph Conrad
quotations.passage: It was unconscious, this smile was, though just after he had said something it got intensified for an instant. It came at the end of his speeches like a seal applied on the words to make the meaning of the commonest phrase appear absolutely inscrutable.

quotations.author: Robert Carlock
quotations.passage: She called my vanity license plate inscrutable! 'ICU81MI'? Hilarious!

quotations.author: Michael Snyder
quotations.passage: The writer Juan Rulfo, whose 1955 novel, “Pedro Páramo,” still stands as the central monument of modern Mexican literature, grew up in Jalisco and vividly depicted its arid, sun-blasted landscapes in his writing, while the architect Luis Barragán, who moved from Guadalajara to Mexico City in the 1930s, carried with him an appreciation for his home state’s cloisters, haciendas and humble country buildings, which he translated in his own work as austere, inscrutable volumes of stucco.
quotations.work: T: The New York Times Style Magazine

inscrutable.title: inscrutable

etymologies: Learned borrowing from Latin īnsēnsātus. By surface analysis, in- + sensate.
From the substantivation of the above adjective. See -ate (noun-forming suffix).
From Latin īnsēnsātus, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

definitions.text: Having no sensation or consciousness; unconscious; inanimate.
Senseless; foolish; irrational; thoughtless.
Unfeeling, heartless, cruel, insensitive.
Not responsive to sensory stimuli; unfeeling.
One who is insensate.
To render insensate; to deprive of sensation or consciousness.

quotations.author: Lord Byron
quotations.passage: Since thus divided — equal must it be / If the deep barrier be of earth, or sea; / It may be both — but one day end it must / In the dark union of insensate dust.

quotations.author: Walter Scott
quotations.passage: […] the sot, the gambler, the bully, the jockey, the insensate fool, were a thousand times preferable to Rashleigh;—[…]

quotations.author: Charles Dickens
quotations.passage: Stupidly dozing, or communing with her incapable self about nothing, she sat for a little while with her hands at her ears. . . . Finally, she laid her insensate grasp upon the bottle that had swift and certain death in it, and, before his eyes, pulled out the cork with her teeth.

quotations.author: Anne Brontë
quotations.passage: I was cold-hearted, hard, insensate.

quotations.author: Thomas Hardy
quotations.passage: Here, at any rate, hostility did not assume that slow and sickening form. It was a cosmic agency, active, lashing, eager for conquest: determination; not an insensate standing in the way.

quotations.author: Joseph Conrad
quotations.passage: […] the romping girl teased her . . . and was always trying to pick insensate quarrels with her about some "fellow" or other.

quotations.author: Edna St. Vincent Millay
quotations.passage: If I might be / Insensate matter / With sensate me / Sitting within, / Harking and prying, / I might begin / To dicker with dying.

quotations.author: Louis Joseph Vance
quotations.passage: But in his insensate passion for revenge upon one who had all but murdered him, he had forgotten all else but the moment's specious opportunity.

quotations.author: Frank Norris
quotations.passage: That insensate, bestial determination, iron-hearted, iron-strong, had beaten down opposition, had carried its point.

quotations.author: Frank L. Packard
quotations.passage: […] the most cold-blooded, callous murders and robberies, the work, on the face of it, of a well-organized band of thugs, brutal, insensate, little better than fiends.

quotations.author: Edward B. Schlesinger
quotations.passage: If the ophthalmic branch is cut the patient must be told about the hazards of having an insensate cornea.

quotations.author: Jeff G. van Baal
quotations.passage: The presence of severe pain with a deep plantar foot infection in a diabetic patient is often the first alarming symptom, especially in a patient with a previously insensate foot.

quotations.author: Minerva
quotations.passage: The innocuous trauma of high pressure jets and bubble massage to the insensate breast and back areas had caused the bruising seen in the picture.

quotations.author: James Oliver Curwood
quotations.passage: And this thought, blinding them to all else, insensating them to all emotions but that of vengeance, was thought of Josephine.

quotations.author: Shony A. Braun
quotations.passage: The train moved on again, keeping us prisoners in a stench-filled car, starving, suffocating, insensated.

insensate.title: insensate

etymologies: From French insipide, from Latin īnsipidus (“tasteless”), from in- (“not”) + sapidus (“savory”). In some senses, perhaps influenced by insipient (“unwise, foolish, stupid”).

examples: The diners were disappointed with the plain, insipid soup they were served.
definitions.text: Unappetizingly flavorless.

examples: The textbook had a most insipid presentation of the controversy.
definitions.text: Flat; lacking character or definition.

quotations.author: William Makepeace Thackeray
quotations.passage: If the secret history of books could be written, and the author’s private thoughts and meanings noted down alongside of his story, how many insipid volumes would become interesting, and dull tales excite the reader!

quotations.author: Christian Wolmar
quotations.passage: There was no limit on drinks, and the guy next to me tucked away a few G and Ts. I confined myself to a pleasant Brewdog Ale and a glass of slightly insipid wine.

quotations.author: The Roast
quotations.passage: “Look at this festive assembly. All of us, gathered here together, chuckling at jokes and silliness.” [laughter] “And jackanapery.” [rim shots] “I guess there's only one thing left to say. What is this shit?” [rim shot] [laughter] “[laughs] Very good.” “You call yourselves vampires? Bah. This entire evening has been nothing but a pageant of insipid nonsense.” “[laughing] Yes.” “Worshipping at the altar of your own mediocre frivolity. A jester's hollow dance. And who is laughing?” “Yeah! [whoops] [grunts]” “Vampires are supposed to have blood orgies and slaughter circles. Gah! You have all gone soft. You even invited humans to this asinine affair.”
quotations.work: What We Do in the Shadows

insipid.title: insipid

etymologies: From French insouciant, from in- (“not”, prefix) + souciant (“worrying”), 1828.

examples: an insouciant gesture
definitions.text: Casually unconcerned; carefree, indifferent, nonchalant.

quotations.author: Theresa Lewis
quotations.passage: "I am quite serious in saying that your loss must and would be felt; but I verily believe," added she, after a moment's hesitation, "that you are so insouciant yourself, that you cannot believe that every body else is not equally indifferent."
quotations.work: Dacre: A Novel. [...] In Three Volumes

quotations.author: William Somerset Maugham
quotations.passage: It was there [Cadiz, Spain] that on Sunday I had seen the populace disport itself, and it was full of life then, gay and insouciant.
quotations.work: The Land of the Blessed Virgin: Sketches and Impressions in Andalusia

quotations.author: Lucy Maud Montgomery
quotations.passage: When we left the Marr house, he [Peter] had boldly said to Felicity, "May I see you home?" And Felicity, much to our amazement, had taken his arm and marched off with him. […] As for me, I was consumed by a secret and burning desire to ask the Story Girl if I might see her home; but I could not screw my courage to the sticking point. How I envied Peter his easy, insouciant manner!

quotations.author: Richard Schickel
quotations.passage: […] [Jack] Nicholson turned to an assistant, bummed a cigarette, flashed one of his wolfish, insouciant grins and said, "We all have our little secrets, Seany."

quotations.author: Jo Ellison
quotations.passage: As a fashion editor, I pay obsessive attention to my appearance. Even when I pretend to look insouciant, each look has been painfully considered. The right earrings, coordinating shoes, the careful symmetry of a well-balanced look — these are things that please me. The gym has crushed my sartorial ambitions.

insouciant.title: insouciant

etymologies: Formed from Late Latin inspissātus (“thickened, having been made thick or thicker”), the perfect passive participle of inspissāre (“to thicken”).

definitions.text: To thicken a fluid, in the sense of making it more viscous, especially by boiling, evaporation, or condensation; to condense.
Of a fluid: to become more viscous.

quotations.author: Ronald M. Atlas
quotations.passage: Inspissate at 85°C (moist heat) for 45 min.

quotations.author: George Bacon Wood
quotations.passage: Instead of allowing the juice after the incision to inspissate on the capsule, he collected it immediately, and dried it by artificial heat.
quotations.work: The dispensatory of the United States of America

inspissate.title: inspissate

etymologies: Probably from Middle French insubstantiel, from Latin insubstantiālis, from in- + substantiālis. By surface analysis, in- +‎ substantial.

examples: The bridge was insubstantial and would not safely carry a car.
definitions.text: Lacking substance; not real or strong.

quotations.author: Christopher Paolini
quotations.passage: By manipulating the flow of magic, Eragon quickly descended from the Ra'zac's lair—which the insubstantial wall of stone once again hid—to the ledge.

insubstantial.title: insubstantial

etymologies: Learned borrowing from Latin īnsulāris (“of or belonging to an island”), from īnsula (“an island”), of uncertain origin.

definitions.text: Of, being, pertaining to, situated on, or resembling an island or islands.
Separate or isolated from the surroundings; having little regard for others' opinions or prejudices; provincial.
Having an inward-looking, standoffish, or withdrawn manner.
Relating to the insula in the brain.
Relating to insulin.

(often with a capital letter) Relating to the varieties of a language or languages spoken chiefly on islands. Insular Latin, Latin as it was spoken in Britain and Ireland. Insular Celtic, the Celtic languages of Britain, Ireland and also Brittany, as opposed to those spoken in mainland Europe other than Brittany. Insular Scandinavian, relating to the Icelandic and Faroese languages as opposed to the ones spoken in Sweden, Denmark and Norway.
An islander.

quotations.author: Herman Melville
quotations.passage: There now is your insular city of the Manhattoes, belted round by wharves as Indian isles by coral reefs—commerce surrounds it with her surf.

quotations.author: George Berkeley
quotations.passage: these insulars in general live in a gross saline air , and their vessels being less elastic are consequently less able to subdue and cast off what their bodies as sponges draw in
quotations.work: Siris, a chain of philosophical reflections and inquiries, concerning the virtues of tar-water

quotations.author: Washington Irving
quotations.passage: At the time of the arrival of the Tonquin he had about forty schooners, of from twenty to thirty tons burthen, and one old American ship. With these he held undisputed sway over his insular domains, and carried on intercourse with the chiefs or governors whom he had placed in command of the several islands.
quotations.work: Astoria, or Anecdotes of an Enterprise beyond the Rocky Mountains.

quotations.author: Jack London
quotations.passage: During the four years since his puppyhood he had lived the life of a sated aristocrat; he had a fine pride in himself, was even a trifle egotistical, as country gentlemen sometimes become because of their insular situation.

quotations.author: Owen Shows
quotations.passage: Making Sense of the Sixties used the typical Americanocentric documentary style that avoided a world or historical context for events […] Other countries were mentioned only insofar as they disturbed the insular course of events in the United States.

quotations.author: Edward Morgan Forster
quotations.passage: Harriet was fretful and insular. Miss Abbott was pleasant, and insisted on praising everything: her only regret was that she had no pretty clothes with her.

insular.title: insular

etymologies: From Latin insuperabilis.

definitions.text: Impossible to achieve or overcome or be negotiated.
Overwhelming or insurmountable.

quotations.author: September
quotations.passage: Regular services for passengers and goods were maintained for almost 50 years, but the speed limit of 16 m.p.h., imposed by the Board of Trade, proved an insuperable handicap after the introduction of competitive motor bus services.

quotations.author: James Lambert
quotations.passage: While Indian English may not have a uniform standard form throughout the country, this in itself is not an insuperable obstacle for lexicography.

quotations.author: Ronald Mann
quotations.passage: The basic problem before the court on Wednesday is that there is a Supreme Court case pretty closely on point – United States v. Bestfoods – in which the justices rejected the government’s argument that the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act was such an important statute that it should create an exception to traditional state-law doctrines that require a high (indeed, all but insuperable) bar for actions seeking to ignore corporate identities and, in the common phrase, “pierce the corporate veil.”

quotations.author: Christian Wolmar
quotations.passage: Underground stations were also slated for closure, and there were plans for massive ring roads to cater for the ever-growing numbers of people commuting into town by car. […] However, it soon dawned on politicians that this was unsustainable. Much of London would have had to be demolished to make way for the ring roads, and parking was becoming an insuperable difficulty.

quotations.author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon
quotations.passage: For the first time I steadily reviewed the obstacles—and to consider them was at once to see they were insuperable.

insuperable.title: insuperable

etymologies: Borrowed from Middle French intangible, from Medieval Latin intangibilis, from Late Latin tangibilis, from Latin tango.

definitions.text: Incapable of being perceived by the senses; incorporeal.

examples: an intangible quality of serenity in the music
definitions.text: Difficult to define or describe clearly, but nonetheless perceived.
Anything intangible.
Incorporeal property that is saleable though not material, such as bank deposits, stocks, bonds, and promissory notes.

quotations.author: Aaron Cohen
quotations.passage: Diaghilev's love for Nijinsky was as deep and as sincere and reliant as a bond could be, it being based on all those intangibles of love that cannot be enumerated.

intangible.title: intangible

etymologies: Borrowed from Latin integumentum (“a covering”).

definitions.text: A shell or other outer protective layer.
An outer protective covering such as the feathers or skin of an animal, a rind or shell.
The outer layer of an ovule, which develops into the seed coat.

quotations.author: James George Frazer
quotations.passage: The power of turning into an animal has this serious disadvantage that it lays you open to the chance of being wounded or even slain in your animal skin before you have the chance to put it off and scramble back into your human integument.

quotations.author: China Miéville
quotations.passage: […] if we're moved by the book's condemnation of a world wounded by exploitation, where the drive for profit hobbles the mass of humanity, bolsters vast integuments of oppression and repression, […]
quotations.work: A Spectre, Haunting: On the Communist Manifesto

quotations.author: Jack Vance
quotations.passage: Sarsem became a naked young epicene in an integument of lavender scales with puffs of purple hair like pom-poms growing down his back.

quotations.author: David Herbert Lawrence
quotations.passage: Her active living was suspended, but underneath, in the darkness, something was coming to pass. If only she could break through the last integuments!

integument.title: integument

definitions.text: Planned.
Made tense; stretched out; extended; forcible; violent.
Fiancé or fiancée.
simple past and past participle of intend

quotations.author: Edmund Spenser
quotations.passage: The same advauncing high above his head, / With sharpe intended sting so rude him smott

quotations.author: Joseph Conrad
quotations.passage: His mother had died lately, watched over, as I was told, by his Intended.

quotations.author: Joseph Conrad
quotations.passage: His purpose was to discover how long these guests intended to stay.

quotations.author: Cynthia Lowenthal
quotations.passage: That the monsters exceed the boundaries of scale produces much stageplay for the male suitors. For instance, when they must approach their "intendeds," the suitors slowly and with great trepidation approach, quickly speak, and scurry away like the frightened bunnies they are; when they must make actual contact, Fetherfool runs up and down a ladder to salute the Giant.
quotations.work: Performing Identities on the Restoration Stage

etymologies: From Middle English entrediten, from Old French entredire (“forbid”), from Latin interdīcō (“prohibit, forbid”), from inter- (“between”) + dīcō (“say”), from Proto-Indo-European *deyḱ-.

definitions.text: A papal decree prohibiting the administration of the sacraments from a political entity under the power of a single person (e.g., a king or an oligarchy with similar powers). Extreme unction/Anointing of the Sick is excepted.
An injunction.
To exclude (someone or somewhere) from participation in church services; to place under a religious interdict.
To forbid (an action or thing) by formal or legal sanction.
To forbid (someone) from doing something.
To impede (an enemy); to interrupt or destroy (enemy communications, supply lines etc).

quotations.author: John Milton
quotations.passage: Charged not to touch the interdicted tree.

quotations.author: April
quotations.passage: The Fife County Council, and other objectors, were successful in July [1950] in obtaining an interim interdict against this decision, but the Court of Session withdrew the interdict in January, and it was then stated that a civil court had no jurisdiction in the matter. […] Mr. Waller adds that when the railway was authorised in 1897, one of the clauses of the Act authorising the transfer of the line to the North British Railway provided that that company should work it in perpetuity, and it was this clause that caused the interim interdict to be granted.

quotations.author: David Clough
quotations.passage: In May [1995], the court issued an interdict preventing the service withdrawal, pending consultation on the closure to passenger traffic of three short stretches of railway around Glasgow and its hinterland that were only used by the Fort William Sleeper - and for which BR had failed to invoke standard closure procedures.

quotations.author: John Ayliffe
quotations.passage: An archbishop [may not only] excommunicate and interdict his suffragans, but his Vicar-General may also do the same.
quotations.work: Parergon Juris Canonici Anglicani: Or, A Commentary, by Way of Supplement to the Canons and Constitutions of the Church of England.

quotations.author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon
quotations.passage: Do not look so alarmed, Madame; every possible precaution has been taken to prevent infection. I have given the strictest orders to interdict any communication between her attendants and those devoted to your service.

quotations.author: James McPherson
quotations.passage: Grant did not cease his efforts to interdict Lee's supply lines and break through the defenses.

interdict.title: interdict

etymologies: The verb is derived from Late Middle English interlarden (“to mix fat into (something)”), borrowed from Old French entrelarder (modern French entrelarder (“(cooking) to put pieces of bacon into meat, interlard; (figurative) to furnish by interspersing, adorn something all over (e.g., a text, with verses, metaphors, etc.)”)), from entre- (prefix meaning ‘in between, between’) (from Latin inter-, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁entér (“between”)) + larder (“to smear with lard or fat, to lard”) (from lard (“bacon fat, lard”) + -er (a variant of -ier (suffix forming verbs))). Lard is from Latin lārdum, lāridum (“bacon fat, lard”); further etymology uncertain, probably borrowed from or related to Ancient Greek λᾱρῑνός (lārīnós, “fat, fatted”, adjective), possibly from λᾱρός (lārós, “delicious; sweet”) (possibly from Proto-Indo-European *leh₂w- (“to gain; to seize; benefit, prize”)) + -ινός (-inós) (a variant of -ῐνος (-ĭnos, suffix forming adjectives)). By surface analysis, inter- (prefix meaning ‘between’) +‎ lard (verb).
The noun is derived from Late Middle English interlarde (“abdominal fat”), from interlarden (verb) (see above).

definitions.text: To embellish or vary (something) by interspersing or mixing another thing with it; also, to intersperse or mix (something) into another thing to embellish or vary it; to interweave, to mingle.
To naturally intersperse (an animal's flesh or muscle) with layers of fat.
Followed by with: to coat the inside of a thing with (a substance).
Followed by with: to place layers or portions of a thing into (something); also, to place layers or portions of (something) into a thing; to interpolate, to interpose.
The abdominal fat of an animal.

quotations.author: Henry Fielding
quotations.passage: She then launched forth a Volley of dreadful Oaths, interlarded vvith some Language, not proper to be repeated here, […]

quotations.author: Walter Scott
quotations.passage: [T]he high-flown and ornate compliments with which the gallant knight of the sixteenth century interlarded his conversation, were as much the offspring of egotism and self-conceit, as the jargon of the coxcombs of our own days.

quotations.author: John Foxe
quotations.passage: And here is a knacke of Simons art, to enterlard a tale of vntruth, with some parcell of truth now and then among, that somethings being found true, may win credit to the rest which is vtterly false.
quotations.work: The Second Volume of the Ecclesiasticall Historie, Containing the Acts and Monuments of Martyrs

quotations.author: John Tillotson
quotations.passage: The great sin of Svvearing, […] doth many times surprise men unavvares into Perjury; And hovv can it be othervvise, vvhen men use to interlard all their careless talk vvith Oaths, but that they must often be Perjur'd?
quotations.work: The Works of the Most Reverend Dr. John Tillotson, Late Lord Archbishop of Canterbury

quotations.author: William Congreve
quotations.passage: But lying is a Figure in Speech, that interlards the greatest part of my Conversation.

quotations.author: John Philips
quotations.passage: They interlard their native Drinks vvith choice / Of strongest Brandy, yet scarce vvith these Aids / Enabl'd to prevent the suddain Rot / Of freezing Nose, and quick-decaying Feet.

quotations.author: Alexander Geddes
quotations.passage: Either, then, the sacred books of his nation were different from the sacred books of our present Hebrew Bible; or Josephus made no scruple of interlarding them with apocryphal stories.
quotations.work: Critical Remarks on the Hebrew Scriptures: Corresponding with a New Translation of the Bible

quotations.author: George Frederick Ruxton
quotations.passage: Here, over fiery "monaghahela," Jean Batiste, […] hobnobs with a stalwart leather-clad "boy," just returned from trapping on the waters of Grand River, on the western side the mountains, who interlards his mountain jargon with Spanish words picked up in Taos and California.

quotations.author: Mary Elizabeth Braddon
quotations.passage: [T]he names of places and horses and slangy technicalities of the turf, had interlarded the poor girl's brain-sick babble; […]

quotations.author: Gustav Heinrich Theodor Eimer
quotations.passage: The German student appears only too often to think that he must present his subject in the most difficult phraseology, excessively interlarded with strange words, as if he purposely would permit a glance into the treasures of his science and his knowledge only to an extremely narrow circle.

quotations.author: August
quotations.passage: The author has provided considerable information interlarded with some interesting quotations from contemporary accounts, but his booklet would have been much improved if the material had been arranged with more care.

quotations.author: Michael Drayton
quotations.passage: The lustie Salmon then, from Neptunes vvatry Realme, / VVhen as his season serues, stemming my tydefull Streame, / […] / VVhole graine doth rise in flakes, vvith fatnesse interlarded, / Of many a liquorish lip, that highly is regarded.
quotations.work: The Second Part, or A Continuance of Poly-Olbion from the Eighteenth Song.

quotations.author: Antonio de Guevara
quotations.passage: Flesshe ought not to be so leane, that hit abhorre: nor so fatte that it cloye the stomacke: but mene and enterlarded, to the ende that hit be sauourye.
quotations.work: The Golden Boke of Marcus Aurelius Emperour and Eloquent Oratour

quotations.author: Peter Martyr d’Anghiera
quotations.passage: But they [serpents] lose theyr taste, excepte they bee prepared after a certeyne fasshion: as doo peacockes and phesauntes except they bee interlarded beefore they bee rosted.
quotations.work: The Decades of the Newe Worlde or West India

quotations.author: William Lithgow
quotations.passage: [T]hey haue no barrels; but great Iarres made of earth, vvherein their VVine is put. And these Iarres are all inclosed vvithin the ground saue onely their mouthes, vvhich stand alvvayes open like to a Source or Cisterne; vvhose insides are all interlarded vvith pitch to preserue the earthen vessells vnbroke a sunder, in regard of the forcible VVine; yet making the taste thereof vnpleasant to liquorous lips; […]
quotations.work: The Totall Discourse, of the Rare Aduentures, and Painefull Peregrinations of Long Nineteene Yeares Trauyles, from Scotland, to the Most Famous Kingdomes in Europe, Asia, and Affrica.

quotations.author: Pliny the Elder
quotations.passage: Thus having raunged the most famous artificers distinctly according to their severall ages, I vvill run over them againe; as many I mean as excell the rest: and yet hovvsoever I make hast, I vvill not overpasse the multitude of others, but interlard (as it vvere) and disperse them among, as occasion shall be offered.
quotations.work: The Historie of the World. Commonly Called, The Naturall Historie of C. Plinius Secundus.

quotations.author: William Lithgow
quotations.passage: [T]here are in the City [Fez, Morocco] […] more than foure hundred and threescore Mosques; fifty vvhereof are vvell benefited and superbiously decored vvithin and vvithout, vvith glorious and extraordinary vvorkmanship, […] the vvalles and pillars being of grey Marble, interlarded vvith vvhite Alabaster, […]
quotations.work: The Totall Discourse, of the Rare Aduentures, and Painefull Peregrinations of Long Nineteene Yeares Trauyles, from Scotland, to the Most Famous Kingdomes in Europe, Asia, and Affrica.

quotations.author: Thomas Bartholin
quotations.passage: [I]n Mankind, this Membrane [the placental cotyledon] cleavs immediately to the vvomb, […] being framed of an innumerable company of Branches, of Veins, and Arteries, among vvhich blood out of the Vessels seems to be shed and interlarded.

quotations.author: The .LXII. Psalme
quotations.passage: My soule shal be satisfyed as it wer with interlarde and fatnes, and my mouth shall prayse thee with lippes full of ioye.
quotations.work: The Primer in Englysh after Salysburie Vse

interlard.title: interlard

etymologies: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin interlocūtor, from the agent noun counterpart (via the suffix -tor) of Latin interloquor (“speak between, issue an interlocutory decree”), from inter- + loquor (“speak”).
From French interlocutoire, from Latin interlocūtōrium.

definitions.text: A person who takes part in dialogue or conversation: a locutive partner.
A man in the middle of the line in a minstrel show who questions the endmen and acts as leader.
An interlocutory judgement or sentence.
A decree of a court.

quotations.author: Calvin Thomas
quotations.passage: Explanations which continually remind one's interlocutor of one's ignorance are a great damper upon the easy flow of talk.

quotations.author: Howard LaFranchi
quotations.passage: In the run-up to his return to the White House next Monday, Mr. Trump has rattled the world, and America’s neighborhood in particular, with a list of objectives – buying Greenland, seizing the Panama Canal, making Canada the 51st state – that treat friendly nations as weak interlocutors and impediments to be subdued.

quotations.author: Maureen Costonis
quotations.passage: The "interlocutor" greeted the audience and engaged in comical repartee with the "end men," named Tambo and Bones.

quotations.author: The Judicial System of Scotland
quotations.passage: A decree of the English Court of Chancery is not entitled to more respect in Scotland than a decree (interlocutor) of the Scottish Court of Session in England.

interlocutor.title: interlocutor

etymologies: From Middle English interminable, from Middle French interminable and its etymon Late Latin interminābilis. By surface analysis, in- +‎ terminable.

definitions.text: Existing or occurring without interruption or end; ceaseless, unending.
A repeating decimal.

quotations.author: William Makepeace Thackeray
quotations.passage: After supper Sir Pitt Crawley began to smoke his pipe; and when it became quite dark, he lighted the rushlight in the tin candlestick, and producing from an interminable pocket a huge mass of papers, began reading them, and putting them in order.

quotations.author: Joseph Conrad
quotations.passage: The sea-reach of the Thames stretched before us like the beginning of an interminable waterway.

quotations.author: Edgar Rice Burroughs
quotations.passage: It was now a beautiful, moonlit night. The air was crisp and invigorating. Behind them lay the interminable vista of the desert, dotted here and there with an occasional oasis.

quotations.author: Joseph Van Ness
quotations.passage: Life's interminable succession of stages.

interminable.title: interminable

etymologies: Borrowed from Latin internecīnus (“deadly”), from internecium (“a massacre, bloodbath; an eradication”) + -īnus. In Latin, the sememe 'between' was here not expressed by the prefix, it instead either had a somewhat emphatic meaning or meant "down, under", comparable to its use in other Latin terms related to death: see interficiō and intereō. The English current sense is thus a reanalysis of the Latin through English inter-.

examples: Internecine strife in Gaza claimed its most senior victim yesterday when militants assassinated one of the most hated security chiefs there.
definitions.text: Mutually destructive; most often applied to warfare.

examples: The Mongol people were plagued by internecine conflict until Genghis Khan unified them by focusing their aggression outwards on other peoples.
definitions.text: Characterized by struggle within a group, usually applied to an ethnic or familial relationship.

quotations.author: Mark Twain
quotations.passage: During the year of my engagement — 1869 — while I was out on the lecture platform, the daily letter that came for me generally brought me news from the front — by which expression I refer to the internecine war that was always going on in a friendly way between these two orthographists about the spelling of words.

quotations.author: Game Of Thrones
quotations.passage: Having survived “The Long Night,” Daenerys will now be turning her attention back to the problem that originally vexed her: Cersei Lannister. It will be interesting to see how the show tries to raise the stakes of an internecine squabble between competing monarchs when compared to an existential threat to humanity’s very existence, but this series has always excelled when it goes deep on the machinations of political chicanery.

internecine.title: internecine

etymologies: From Latin interpolātus, perfect passive participle of interpolō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Compare French interpoler.

examples: in verse 74, the second line is clearly interpolated, probably by some unknown medieval scribe
When interpolating an explanatory gloss, please enclose it in square brackets to make clear that it is interpolated.
definitions.text: To introduce (something) between other things; especially to insert (possibly spurious) words into a text.
To estimate the value of a function between two tabulated points.
During the course of processing some data, and in response to a directive in that data, to fetch data from a different source and process it in-line along with the original data.

quotations.author: Joseph F. Ossanna
quotations.passage: A macro is invoked in the same way as a request; a control line beginning .xx will interpolate the contents of macro xx.

interpolate.title: interpolate

etymologies: Learned borrowing from Latin interrēgnum, from inter- (prefix meaning ‘between’) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁entér (“between”)) + rēgnum (“reign; royal power”) (nominalized from the neuter of *rēgnus, from rēx (“king; ruler”, oblique stem rēg-) + -nus (suffix forming adjectives), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵ- (“to righten; to straighten”)).
The plural form interregna is a learned borrowing from Latin interrēgna.

examples: The Sasanian Interregnum of 628–632
definitions.text: A period of time between the end of one monarch's reign and the accession of their successor.
A break in continuity; a gap, an intermission.
A period of time between when a minister or pastor leaves a church and when a new one is installed.

A period of time between the end of one political leader's term and the start of the term of their successor; a period of time during which normal executive leadership is interrupted or suspended, and a polity is either left without leadership or has only a temporary one.
A temporary exercise of authority or rule during a period of time when there is no monarch or political leader.
Ellipsis of British Interregnum, the period of 1649–1660 when a republican state ruled Britain; the monarchy was then restored.

quotations.author: Edward Bellamy
quotations.passage: It was not till the kings had been shorn of power and the interregnum of sham democracy had set in, leaving no virile force in the state or the world to resist the money power, that the opportunity for a world-wide plutocratic despotism arrived.

quotations.author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon
quotations.passage: Is it not Pelham who wonders what becomes of servants when they are not wanted;—whether, like the tones of an instrument, they exist but when called for? About servants we will not decide; but that some such interregnum certainly occurs in female existence on rising from table, no one can doubt who ever noted the sound of the dining and the silence of the drawing-room.

quotations.author: William Gilmore Simms
quotations.passage: This was in that strange pause of the storm which is its most remarkable feature in the South—that singular interregnum of the winds, when, after giving repeated notice of their most terrific action, they seem almost to forget their purpose, and for a few moments appear to slumber in their inactivity.

quotations.author: May and June
quotations.passage: Between the end of the Fowler régime in 1931 and the advent of Stanier in 1932, there was a short interregnum during which Ernest Lemon was in charge, with Ernest Beames as his principal aide-de-camp.

quotations.author: Nick Hornby
quotations.passage: All I know is that you could, if you wanted to, find the answers to all sorts of difficult questions buried in that terrible war-torn interregnum between the first pubic hair and the first soiled Durex.

quotations.author: Linda Feldmann
quotations.passage: Another element leading to the quick-out-of-the-gate second Trump term took place during the four-year interregnum of President Joe Biden.

quotations.author: Peter Thiel
quotations.passage: Darker questions still emerge in these dusky final weeks of our interregnum.

quotations.author: Peter Bradshaw
quotations.passage: Plus, of course, the film is set at the start of the Trump interregnum of 2020-24, when it seemed as if the Capitol riots were the ultimate wake-up call and moderation had returned.

interregnum.title: interregnum

etymologies: From late Middle English interstice, from Old French interstice or directly from Latin interstitium (“a space between, gap, interval”), ultimately from intersistere (“to stand in between, to stop in the middle”), from inter- +‎ sistere (“to stand, to stop”).

definitions.text: A small opening or space between objects, especially adjacent objects or objects set closely together, such as between cords in a rope, components of a multiconductor electrical cable or atoms in a crystal.
A fragment of space.
An interval of time required by the Roman Catholic Church between the attainment of different degrees of an order.
A small interval of time free to be spent on activities other than one's primary goal.

quotations.author: Simon Jenkins
quotations.passage: Relics of the British empire now mostly survive in the interstices of the global economy. They are the major winners from the fiscal haemorrhage that has resulted from financial globalisation.

interstice.title: interstice

etymologies: From Latin intestīnum, neuter of intestīnus (“internal”), as Etymology 2, below.
From Latin intestīnus (“internal”), from intus (“within”).

definitions.text: The alimentary canal of an animal through which food passes after having passed all stomachs.
One of certain subdivisions of this part of the alimentary canal, such as the small or large intestine in human beings.
Domestic; taking place within a given country or region.
Internal.
Depending upon the internal constitution of a body or entity; subjective.
Shut up; enclosed.

quotations.author: John Milton
quotations.passage: Hoping here to end / Intestine war in heaven, the arch foe subdued.

quotations.author: Samuel Johnson
quotations.passage: [W]riters should cease from intestine hostilities; and, instead of sacrificing each other to malice and contempt, endeavour to avert persecution from the meanest of their fraternity.

quotations.author: Michel de Montaigne
quotations.passage: When you have alleaged all the reasons you can, and beleeved all to disavow and reject her, she produceth, contrarie to your discourses, so intestine inclination, that you have small hold against her.

quotations.author: David Hume
quotations.passage: a perpetual intestine struggle […] between authority and liberty

quotations.author: Ralph Hamor
quotations.passage: It being true that now after fiue yeeres intestine warre with the reuengefull implacable Indians, a firme peace (not againe easily to be broken) hath bin lately concluded […].
quotations.work: A True Discourse of the Present State of Virginia

quotations.author: Edward Gibbon
quotations.passage: Yet the success of Trajan, however transient, was rapid and specious. The degenerate Parthians, broken by intestine discord, fled before his arms.
quotations.work: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire

quotations.author: Biographical Memoir of Rear-Admiral John Willett Payne
quotations.passage: […] surrounded by an enemy rendered desperate from the calamities of intestine war.

quotations.author: August
quotations.passage: The subdivisions of the tribe have elders over them, to whose authority they frequently pay much more deference than to that of their Chan: they are appointed by popular election, and where distinguished by birth or affluence are called beys, elders, tarchans, or batuers; but if their conduct be such as to displease their constituents, they are deposed, and their office transferred to some other party—the natural consequence of these changes is intestine confusion and anarchy, and open defiance of the authority of the Chan and his council.

quotations.author: Henry Box Brown
quotations.passage: Now will any sensible person assert that five millions of Southerners, allowing all her white population to be in favor of Slavery, with an intestine foe, ready to spring upon her, as soon as the last chance of freedom presents itself, will be in danger of fighting twelve millions of free Northerners, who can call to their aid all these, and numerous other allies.
quotations.work: Narrative of H. B. Brown who escaped from slavery enclosed in a box

quotations.author: George Norman Clark
quotations.passage: In the speech attributed to him in More's History of King Richard the Third: Buckingham argues that war is never so mischievous as when it is intestine.

quotations.author: Benjamin Straumann
quotations.passage: If you wish this state to be immortal, if you wish your empire to be eternal, if you with your glory to continue everlasting, then it is our own passions, it is the turbulence and desire of revolution engendered among our own citizens, it is intestine evil, it is domestic plots that must be guarded against.

quotations.author: Ralph Cudworth
quotations.passage: Every thing labours under an intestine necessity.
quotations.work: The True Intellectual System of the Universe: The First Part; wherein All the Reason and Philosophy of Atheism is Confuted; and Its Impossibility Demonstrated

quotations.author: Emanuel Swedenborg
quotations.passage: There dwells in the hearts of all who are deeply sunk in hypocrisy, an intestine hatred against all who are truly spiritual;

quotations.author: William Cowper
quotations.passage: No thunders shook with deep intestine sound The blooming groves that girdled her around.
quotations.work: Poems by William Cowper, of the Inner Temple, Esq.

quotations.author: William Cowper
quotations.passage: Where now the vital energy that moved, While summer was, the pure and subtle lymph Through the imperceptible meandering veins Of leaf and flower? It sleeps; and the icy touch Of unprolific winter has impress'd A cold stagnation on the intestine tide.

quotations.author: Jackie DiSalvo
quotations.passage: (see title)
quotations.work: Milton and the Idea of Woman

quotations.author: Rebecca Brackmann
quotations.passage: Lambarde's metaphor seems to be slipping here, as he admits that the worst enemies are 'intestine', within the walls, so to speak, or even within the 'body' of the nation.
quotations.work: The Elizabethan Invention of Anglo-Saxon England

intestine.title: intestine
