quotations.author: Thomas Adams
quotations.passage: England.. hath now suppled, lithed and stretched their throats.

quotations.author: Daniel Rogers
quotations.passage: Give me also faith, Lord,.. to lithe, to form, and to accommodate my spirit and members.
quotations.work: Naaman the Syrian: His Disease and Cure

quotations.author: Lewis Grassic Gibbon
quotations.passage: So Cospatric got him the Pict folk to build a strong castle there in the lithe of the hills, with the Grampians dark and bleak behind it, and he had the Den drained and he married a Pict lady and got on her bairns and he lived there till he died.

quotations.author: Joseph Wright
quotations.passage: lithe widely used as a verb in nEng Sc and Ir, as a noun only in Cu

quotations.author: C.T. Onions
quotations.passage: to render lithe or thick, to thicken (broth, etc.)

quotations.author: Clive Upton
quotations.passage: lithe vt to THICKEN gravy V7.7 la:ð Y, laɪð Y Nt L, laɪð La Nt L
quotations.work: Survey of English Dialects: The Dictionary and Grammar

lithe.title: lithe

etymologies: From Middle English litigious, from Latin lītigiōsus. Compare Middle French litigieux.

definitions.text: Of or relating to litigation.
Inclined to engage in lawsuits.
Argumentative or combative.

quotations.author: Jonathan Swift
quotations.passage: This vvould of Necessity, breed an infinite Number of Brangles and litigious Suits in the Spiritual Courts, and put the vvretched Pastor at perpetual Variance vvith his vvhole Parish.
quotations.work: Considerations upon Two Bills Sent Down from the R [ ight ] H [ onourable ] the H [ ouse ] of L [ ords ] to the H [ onoura ] ble H [ ouse ] of C [ ommons of Ireland ] Relating to the Clergy of I [ relan ] d

quotations.author: James Bennet
quotations.passage: Tearing a page out of Monsanto's own playbook, the Public Patent Foundation (PUBPAT), an advocacy group whose mandate is to represent the public's interest in the patent system, filed suit (PDF) on behalf of 60 organic farmers, small farm organizations, and seed businesses this week against the litigious agrichemical and genetically modified (GM) seed giant.

litigious.title: litigious

etymologies: From Late Latin littoralis, from litoris (genitive of litus). The doubled 't' is a late medieval addition, and the more classical litoral is also sometimes found. Cognate to French littoral, Spanish litoral, Portuguese litoral, and more distantly to English lido (“outdoor pool”), via Italian lido (“beach, shore”).

definitions.text: Of or relating to the shore, especially the seashore.
A shore, coastline, or coast.
The zone of a coast between high tide and low tide levels.

quotations.author: H. N. Moseley
quotations.passage: The deep-sea fauna has probably been formed almost entirely from the littoral, not in the remotest antiquity, but only after food derived from the débris of the littoral and terrestrial faunas and floras became abundant.

quotations.author: Sir Charles Eliot
quotations.passage: […] these Chams belonged to the Malay-Polynesian group and their distribution along the littoral suggests that they were invaders from the sea […]

quotations.author: January and February
quotations.passage: The railway running along the littoral from Brighton westward to Portsmouth forms an important section of the L.B.S.C.R. (Central) secion of the Southern Railway.

quotations.author: Ambrose Pratt
quotations.passage: More than sixty per centum of the population of Australia is settled in the States along whose littoral the Lyrebird ranges[.]

quotations.author: May
quotations.passage: Just beyond the locomotive depot is the junction of the Anecho line, which curves sharply eastwards. It runs for the whole way along the flat, sandy littoral among coconut plantations, usually a mile or so inland.

quotations.author: Harold Bindloss
quotations.passage: The night was considerably clearer than anybody on board her desired when the schooner Ventura headed for the land. It rose in places, black and sharp against the velvety indigo, over her dipping bow, though most of the low littoral was wrapped in obscurity.

quotations.author: Edwin Black
quotations.passage: Buried within the Mediterranean littoral are some seventy to ninety million tons of slag from ancient smelting, about a third of it concentrated in Iberia. This ceaseless industrial fueling caused the deforestation of an estimated fifty to seventy million acres of woodlands.

littoral.title: littoral

etymologies: From Middle English livid, livide, from Old French livide, from Latin līvidus (“bluish, livid; envious”), from līveō (“be of a bluish color or livid; envy”), from Proto-Italic *sliwēō, from Proto-Indo-European *sliwo-, suffixed form of *(s)leh₃y- (“bluish”). See also Old English slā (“sloe”), Welsh lliw (“splendor, color”), Old Irish li, Lithuanian slyvas (“plum”), and Russian and Old Church Slavonic слива (sliva, “plum”).

definitions.text: Having a dark, bluish appearance.
Pale, pallid.
So angry that one turns pale; very angry; furious; liverish.

quotations.author: Charles Dickens
quotations.passage: Suppose it should not be done enough! Suppose it should break in turning out! Suppose somebody should have got over the wall of the back-yard, and stolen it, while they were merry with the goose—a supposition at which the two young Cratchits became livid! All sorts of horrors were supposed.
quotations.work: A Christmas Carol. In Prose. Being a Ghost Story of Christmas

quotations.author: Antoine? Deidier
quotations.passage: Jean Raynaud, cook, aged about twenty years, of a melancholy temperament, had his whole body covered with a purple livid colour, and a bubo under his left axilla; […] His lungs were covered with little livid spots, soft and pliant, without any hardness in their substance. The liver was larger and harder than ordinary, and was also full of livid purple spots; […]
quotations.work: The Philosophical Transactions (from the year 1720 to the year 1732) Abridged, and Disposed under General Heads

quotations.author: John Ruskin
quotations.passage: In [J. M. W.] Turner's distinctive work, colour is scarcely acknowledged unless under influences of sunshine. The sunshine is his treasure; his lividest gloom contains it; his greyest twilight regrets it, and remembers.
quotations.work: Proserpina: Studies of Wayside Flowers, while the Air was yet Pure among the Alps and in the Scotland and England which my Father Knew; Ariadne Florentina: Six Lectures on Wood and Metal Engraving given before the University of Oxford, in Michaelmas Term, 1872, with Appendix; The Opening of the Crystal Palace: Considered in some of its Relations to the Prospects of Art

quotations.author: Marie Corelli
quotations.passage: When all the surroundings were thus rendered as brilliant as possible, so that the corpse looked more livid and ghastly by comparison, I seated myself once more, and prepared to read the last message of the dead.
quotations.work: The Sorrows of Satan, or, The Strange Experience of one Geoffrey Tempest, Millionaire: A Romance

quotations.author: M. Barnard Eldershaw
quotations.passage: The house seemed unfamiliar in the dark stormy light; the red and purple glass of the front door made livid bruises on the linoleum; the green chenille curtain was like a veil of seaweed.

quotations.author: John Shirley
quotations.passage: Ulcers having had their beginning during a Disease, or before it, growing livid, pale or dry, plainly indicate the proximity of Death, their livid or pale colour being not only the sign of Cholerick, or Atrabiliary humours causing them, but also manifesting an extinction of the natural heat.
quotations.work: A Short Compendium of Chirurgery: Containing its Grounds & Principles. More Particularly Treating of Imposthumes, Wounds, Ulcers, Fractures & Dislocatons. Also a Discourse of the Generation and Birth of Man, very Necessary to be Understood by all Midwives and Child-bearing Women. With the Several Methods of Curing the French Pox: The Cure of Baldness, Inflammation of the Eyes, and Toothach [ sic ] : And an Account of Blood-letting, Cup-setting, and Blooding with Leeches

quotations.author: John Claudius Loudon
quotations.passage: 15939 Cap somew[hat] umbon[ate] smooth livid pale, Lamel[læ] annexed flesh-colored, Stipes sold smooth somew[hat] bulbous. [Describing a species of fungus.]
quotations.work: An Encyclopædia of Plants; Comprising the Description, Specific Character, Culture, History, Application in the Arts, and every other Desirable Particular Respecting all the Plants Indigenous, Cultivated in, or Introduced to Britain [...]

quotations.author: Francesco Verso
quotations.passage: I'm livid; a deathly pale light floods my face and I emanate a different smell. Charlie doesn't stop to analyse these subtle changes.

quotations.author: Tiffany Thayer
quotations.passage: Livider and livider Serjianni grew as the Princess let him have it. When she stopped, he growled. "Your Highness knows him better than I do," and he stalked off up the stairs.
quotations.work: Tiffany Thayer's Mona Lisa; I. The Prince of Taranto: A Fiction in Three Volumes

quotations.author: Richard Carpenter
quotations.passage: “Gave us a jolly good run. Viewed him across Gamley Heath, drew Meddington Big Wood, and then we lost him. Daddy was livid.”

livid.title: livid

etymologies: From Middle English lōth (“loath; averse, hateful”), from Old English lāð, lāþ (“evil; loathsome”), or Old Norse leið, leiðr (“uncomfortable; tired”) from Proto-Germanic *laiþaz (“loath; hostile; sad, sorry”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂leyt- (“to do something abhorrent or hateful”).

The word is cognate with Danish led (“disgusting, loathsome; nasty”), Dutch leed (“sad; (Belgium) angry”), French laid (“ugly; morally corrupt”), Catalan lleig (“ugly”), Icelandic leiður (“annoyed, vexed; sad; (archaic or poetic) annoying, wearisome”), Italian laido (“filthy, foul; obscene”), Old Frisian leed, Old High German leid (Middle High German leit, modern German leid (“uncomfortable”), Leid (“grief, sorrow, woe; affliction, suffering; harm, injury; wrong”)), Old Saxon lêð, lēth (“evil person or thing”), Swedish led (“bored; tired; (archaic) disgusting, loathsome; evil”).

examples: I was loath to return to the office without the Henderson file.
definitions.text: Averse, disinclined; reluctant, unwilling. Always followed by a verbal phrase.
Angry, hostile.
Loathsome, unpleasant.
Obsolete spelling of loathe.

quotations.author: Walter Scott
quotations.passage: "And thereupon I pledge thee," said the young nobleman, "which on any other argument I were loth to do—thinking of Ned as somewhat the cut of a villain."

quotations.author: John Bunyan
quotations.passage: Then said Faint-heart, Deliver thy Purse; but he making no haste to do it (for he was loth to lose his Money,) Mistrust ran up to him, and thrusting his hand into his Pocket, pull'd out thence a bag of Silver.
quotations.work: The Pilgrim’s Progress from This World, to That which is to Come

quotations.author: Eliza Haywood
quotations.passage: Frankville, whose only Fault was rashness, grew almost wild at the Recital of so unexpected a Misfortune, he knew not for a good while what to believe, loath he was to suspect the Count, but loather to suspect Camilla, yet flew into extremities of Rage against both, by turns: […]
quotations.work: Love in Excess: Or, The Fatal Enquiry. A Novel. The Third and Last Part

quotations.author: John Blaikie
quotations.passage: Of all the people in the world our countrymen are the loathest to give away their money without some reasonable quid pro quo; […]
quotations.work: The Old Times and the New

quotations.author: Arthur Sullivan
quotations.passage: If I to wed the girl am loth / A breach 'twill surely be—
quotations.work: Trial by Jury. A Novel and Original Dramatic Cantata

quotations.author: Dante Gabriel Rossetti
quotations.passage: Ah! dear one, I've been old so long, / It seems that age is loth to part, / Though days and years have never a song, / And, oh! have they still the art / That warmed the pulses of heart to heart?

quotations.author: Alberto Santos-Dumont
quotations.passage: When the dawn comes, red and gold and purple one is almost loath to seek the cheery, busy earth again, altho the novelty of landing in who knows what part of Europe affords still another unique pleasure. For many the greatest charm of spherical ballooning lies here.

quotations.author: Jack London
quotations.passage: The frizzle-headed man-eaters were loath to leave their fleshpots so long as the harvest of human carcases was plentiful. Sometimes, when the harvest was too plentiful, they imposed on the missionaries by letting the word slip out that on such a day there would be a killing and a barbecue.

quotations.author: February
quotations.passage: But capital was proving difficult to raise; rumours were in the air that the G.W.R. and L.S.W.R. were about to patch up their quarrel, and the people of Southampton, who twelve months earlier had staged a torch-light procession to celebrate the passing of the D.N.S.R. Act, were increasingly loath to part with their cash.

quotations.author: George Whetstone
quotations.passage: To Scriptures read they must their leasure frame, / Then loath they will both lust and wanton love; […]

quotations.author: Andrew Gray
quotations.passage: […] O Hypocrites! ye hope for Enjoyment of Christ, but be perswaded of it, Christ shall eternally loath you, and ye shall eternally loath Christ: […]
quotations.work: Great and Precious Promises: or, Some Sermons Concerning the Promises, and the Right Application thereof.

loath.title: loath

etymologies: Learned borrowing from Latin locus. Doublet of lieu.

examples: The cafeteria was the locus of activity.
definitions.text: A place or locality, especially a centre of activity or the scene of a crime.

examples: A circle is the locus of points from which the distance to the center is a given value, the radius.
definitions.text: The set of all points whose coordinates satisfy a given equation or condition.
A fixed position on a string of DNA or RNA, especially a chromosome, that may be occupied by one or more genes.
A passage in writing, especially in a collection of ancient sacred writings arranged according to a theme.

locus.title: locus

etymologies: Borrowed from Latin locūtiō, locūtiōnem (“speech”), from loquor (“speak”). Compare the French cognate locution.

examples: The television show host is widely recognized for his all-too-common locutions.
definitions.text: A phrase or expression peculiar to or characteristic of a given person or group of people.
The use of a word or phrase in an unusual or specialized way.

examples: informal locutions
definitions.text: Style of discourse or usage, or any particular utterance in such style.
A supernatural revelation where a religious figure, statue or icon speaks, usually to a saint.

quotations.author: David Foster Wallace
quotations.passage: Another way fathers impact sons is that sons, once their voices have changed in puberty, invariably answer the telephone with the same locutions and intonations of their fathers.

quotations.author: Judith Jarvis Thomson
quotations.passage: So it cannot be supposed that promisings differ from other word-givings in that a word-giver makes a promise only if he or she uses the locution "I promise".

locution.title: locution

etymologies: From Latin logomachia, from Ancient Greek λογομαχία (logomakhía).

definitions.text: Dispute over the meaning of words
A conflict waged only as a battle of words

quotations.author: Gilbert Keith Chesterton
quotations.passage: He was left over the coffee with Brayne, the hoary Yankee who believed in all religions, and Valentin, the grizzled Frenchman who believed in none. They could argue with each other, but neither could appeal to him. After a time this “progressive” logomachy had reached a crisis of tedium; Lord Galloway got up also and sought the drawing-room.

logomachy.title: logomachy

etymologies: From logo- (prefix meaning ‘word; speech’) +‎ -rrhea (suffix meaning ‘flowing’), probably modelled after verbal diarrhea. logo- is derived from Ancient Greek λόγος (lógos, “word; speech; utterance”) (from λέγω (légō, “to say, speak; to arrange; to gather”), from Proto-Indo-European *leǵ- (“to collect, gather”)), while -rrhea is from ῥοία (rhoía, “a flow, flux”) (from ῥέω (rhéō, “to flow”), from Proto-Indo-European *srew- (“to flow”)).

definitions.text: Excessive talkativeness.
Excessive use of words in writing; prolixity.
Excessive and often uncontrollable speaking due to a mental disorder.

quotations.author: Literary Degeneration
quotations.passage: These "Symbolists" are characterised by unbounded vanity and self-sufficiency; they are highly emotional; their thinking is hazy and disconnected. They suffer from "Logorrhea" or "sickly talkativeness," and are unable to perform any work which requires concentration and persistency.

quotations.author: James Monaco
quotations.passage: [Jacques] Rivette, bluntly, suffers from a good case of logorrhea. Even if he had none of these rationales, he would still make long films. In interviews he speaks in endless, ebullient sentences that surround their subjects like spider's webs and sometimes suffocate them.
quotations.work: The New Wave: Truffaut, Godard, Chabrol, Rohmer, Rivette

quotations.author: István Anhalt
quotations.passage: The baritone is angry, but still controlled: he does not indulge in compulsive over-rapid spurts of logorrhoeas but keeps to a 'chopped, short, hard, very pointed' staccato-like delivery, excited, but well articulated through interruptions of differing lengths.
quotations.work: Alternative Voices: Essays on Contemporary Vocal and Choral Composition

quotations.author: David Caute
quotations.passage: His purchase of a Dictaphone no doubt encouraged his natural loquacity, his ingrained prolixity (which he himself logorrhoea).
quotations.work: Isaac & Isaiah: The Covert Punishment of a Cold War Heretic

quotations.author: April
quotations.passage: The writer should endeavor to have his observations first of all, exact, then apposite, and finally as brief as the nature of the case will admit. [...] Logorrhea and irrelevancy are the bane of a society.
quotations.work: The Toledo Medical and Surgical Journal

quotations.author: Arthur Stringer
quotations.passage: So when I settled down that day I wrote feverishly and I wrote joyously. I wrote until my fingers were cramped and my head was empty. I surrendered to a blithe logorrhea that left me contentedly limp and lax and in need of an hour or two of open air.

quotations.author: Svetlana Boym
quotations.passage: The early period of glasnost' encouraged a variety of graphomania and logorrhea—from numerous letters to the newspapers to memoirs, "true stories," opinions, and revelations of wide political range.
quotations.work: Common Places: Mythologies of Everyday Life in Russia

quotations.author: Fred R. Ankersmit
quotations.passage: What must be said may sometimes be difficult to say and may require lots and lots of language—hence [Jacques] Derrida's endless logorrheas—but Derrida never raises his hands to Heaven in despair because his reading experience would exceed what he wishes to say.

quotations.author: Geoffrey Parker
quotations.passage: In many cases Philip [II of Spain] lapsed into a logorrhoea that not only revealed the thought processes that underlay his decisions but also shared details on his personal life – when and where he ate and slept; what he had just read; which trees and flowers he wanted to plant in his gardens (and where); how problems with his eyes, his legs or his wrist, or a cold or a headache, had made him fall behind with his paperwork.
quotations.work: Imprudent King: A New Life of Philip II

quotations.author: Darko Suvin
quotations.passage: Thus, from the 70s on, all the wondrous legal forms of 'self-management negotiations' (dogovaranja) proved inefficient within toothless 'indicative planning' and a profit-bent capitalist market. It spawned unbelievable logorrheas, for example in the norms occasioned by the 1972–80 laws about the new 'delegate system' of elections [...].
quotations.work: Splendour, Misery, and Possibilities: An X-ray of Socialist Yugoslavia

quotations.author: Thomas Laycock
quotations.passage: But, then, these persons have not only a copia verborum as to knowledge, but a volubility sometimes amounting to a logorrhœa in expressing what they know—although that may not be much.

quotations.author: Clarence Bynold Farrar
quotations.passage: When the patient was admitted to this hospital five years ago, the symptoms of excitement in the wide sense, violence, aggressiveness, destructiveness, logorrhœa, were in the foreground as they had been during the previous attacks.

quotations.author: Mahin Hassibi; Harry Breuer
quotations.passage: In agreement with the general consensus of writers on the subject, they affirmed that logorrhea (a loss of control over the flow of speech and subsequent flood of verbiage often seen in adult Wernicke's aphasics) is not characteristic of aphasic children.
quotations.work: Disordered Thinking and Communication in Children

quotations.author: Basant K. Puri
quotations.passage: The quantity of speech may be increased in mania and anxiety but reduced in dementia, schizophrenia and depression. [...] In logorrhoea, also called volubility, the speech is fluent and rambling, with the use of many words.

logorrhea.title: logorrhea

etymologies: Unknown. Compare lollypaloozer and lallapalootza, which are attested earlier with similar meaning. Compare also 19th century slang la-la something unusually good.

definitions.text: An outstanding, extreme, or outrageous example of its kind.

quotations.author: George Taubeneck
quotations.passage: When the show-down came, the other players informed him he had lost. One man had turned up a 2-4-6-8-9 of varied suits. ¶ "That," they all exclaimed, "is a Lollapalooza. It beats anything—even a Royal Flush."
quotations.work: The Marshal's Baton: The Specialty Sales Manager

quotations.author: Jim Travers
quotations.passage: Far from the grand events that were once considered – speaking to Parliament or a more modest version of the lollapalooza that brought millions into Chicago streets – this six-hour hi-how-are-you redefines low key.

lollapalooza.title: lollapalooza

etymologies: From Late Latin longanimitās, from longanimis, translating Ancient Greek μακροθυμία (makrothumía).

definitions.text: Patience or tolerance in the face of adversity; forbearance, long-suffering.

quotations.author: Thomas Browne
quotations.passage: It had overcome the patience of Job, as it did the meekness of Moses, and would surely have mastered any, but the longanimity, and lasting sufferance of God [...].

longanimity.title: longanimity

etymologies: Borrowed from French longueur (literally “length”).

definitions.text: A lengthy passage in a dramatic or literary work, especially a dull or tedious one; a period of boredom.

quotations.author: Adam Gopnik
quotations.passage: Most of the reasons given for its disappearance make sense: people are happier, busier; the work done by the anti-Freudian skeptics has finally taken hold of the popular imagination, so that people have no time for analytic longueurs and no patience with its mystifications.

quotations.author: Colin Jones
quotations.passage: He cultivated the aura, if not quite of the Anti-Christ, at least of an Anti-Sun King, discountenancing his uncle and shocking the dévots by preferring the intimacy and informality of a clique of drinking companions to the formal longueurs of the courtly round […] .

quotations.author: Michiko Kakutani
quotations.passage: [T]he reader can’t help feeling that a few judicious nips and tucks might have dispersed the longueurs that waft around the third quarter of the book.

quotations.author: Katharine Viner
quotations.passage: Claire Fontaine (who are actually a duo) have queered the phrase, lending its pungency and ambiguity to a biennale that I wish were nearly so succinct. There are longueurs. There are detours and incomprehensible delays.

longueur.title: longueur

etymologies: From Latin loquāx, loquācis (“talkative”) +‎ -ous or from loquacity +‎ -ous, ultimately from Latin loquor +‎ -acious.

definitions.text: Talkative; chatty.

quotations.author: James Fenimore Cooper
quotations.passage: On the other hand, Hetty was moody and silent. She was never loquacious, or if she occasionally became communicative, it was under the influence of some temporary excitement that served to arouse her unsophisticated mind; but, for hours at a time, in the course of this all-important day, she seemed to have absolutely lost the use of her tongue.

quotations.author: February
quotations.passage: " […] and as Mr. H., with his long purse and his willingness to receive hints, is no bad card in the game, he has been brought up to Abbotsford for a week; his taciturnity has long ago fled, and he is one of the most loquacious Borderers going. […] "

loquacious.title: loquacious

etymologies: Named after Lothario, a character in the play The Fair Penitent, a reference to a seducer of the same name in the metastory of the Quixote called The Impertinent Curious Man.

definitions.text: A man whose chief interest is seducing, usually women.

quotations.author: Herman Melville
quotations.passage: High times, indeed, if unprincipled young rakes like him are to be permitted to invade the sanctity of domestic bliss; though do what the Bashaw will, he cannot keep the most notorious Lothario out of his bed; for alas! all fish bed in common.

quotations.author: Rudyard Kipling
quotations.passage: He warned her 'gainst seductive youths in scarlet clad and gold, / As much as 'gainst the blandishments paternal of the old; / But kept his gravest warnings for (hereby my ditty hangs) / That snowy-haired Lothario Lieutenant-General Bangs.

quotations.author: Katharine Viner
quotations.passage: So much of the plot structure rested on Chandler being the second string: the maladroit loser to Joey’s lothario, the joker skating beneath Ross’s romantic gravity.

lothario.title: Lothario

etymologies: Borrowed from French louche.

definitions.text: Of questionable taste or morality; decadent.
Not reputable or decent.
Unconventional and slightly disreputable in an attractive manner; raffish, rakish.
A dubious or disreputable person or thing

examples: Certain anise-flavored drinks have developed a mystique based on the exotic appearance of louching.
definitions.text: To make (an alcoholic beverage, e.g. absinthe or ouzo) cloudy by mixing it with water, due to the presence of anethole. This is known as the ouzo effect.

quotations.author: William Makepeace Thackeray
quotations.passage: My uncle knows something about that fellow—Clavering knows something about him. There’s something louche regarding him.

quotations.author: Henry James
quotations.passage: The aunt will refuse; she will think the whole proceeding very louche!

quotations.author: The other half lives: The transatlantic appeal of the British ruling classes
quotations.passage: Upstairs Downstairs hosts the Kennedys and Wallis Simpson (these days, in British culture, the archetypal louche American).

quotations.author: Ignatiy Vishnevetsky
quotations.passage: Ever since X-Men: First Class set the series' clock back a few decades and installed Michael Fassbender's moody Magneto and James McAvoy's louche Charles Xavier as replacements for Ian McKellen and Patrick Stewart's chess-playing pappies, the big-screen X-Men's central conflict—Xavier's Booker T. Washington-esque School For Gifted Youngsters vs. a rogue's gallery of evil mutants, crew cuts, and politicos—has gotten a lot murkier.

quotations.author: Guy Trebay
quotations.passage: Anyone inside the business can also tell you that without Carine Roitfeld's louche sexy styling Tom Ford's Gucci might easily have come off looking like a high-end Club Monaco.

quotations.author: Barbara Cleverly
quotations.passage: 'That's right,' Joe smiled. 'Loafing about on the Mall with the louche of the town. And, speaking of the louche of the town, don't we have an appointment to interview one or two of them this morning?'

quotations.author: Tom Treece
quotations.passage: I'm outraged this louche has since fathered two children with another woman and that after all this questionable, nefarious behavior, Greer continues to see no conflict of interest in him being Terd's guardian.

quotations.author: Bill Cain
quotations.passage: "Rooster, you say? He seems to always appear at unusual times and locations. He strikes me as something of a legerdemain. Let's hope he is no louche when it comes to his role in all of this.

quotations.author: Paul Owens
quotations.passage: In distillation, the first few liters of absinthe to come out of the still are called the head; the last few liters are the tail. The head and tail don't have enough alcohol to keep the oils in suspension, so the absinthe comes out of the still louched.
quotations.work: The Little Green Book of Absinthe: An Essential Companion with Lore, Trivia, and Classic and Contemporary Cocktails

quotations.author: Heather E. Hutsell
quotations.passage: I found a little corner to stand in and pretended to sip my own louched absinthe.

quotations.author: Jason Sizemore
quotations.passage: Ah, Mr. Sizemore, the green fairy is best prepared carefully and slowly to appreciate its full potential. Simply fill the fountain with iced water, place your glass of absinthe below the spigot with a single sugar cube placed over a slotted spoon and adjust the tap to your desired flow. The cold water will gradually dissolve the sugar and mix with the absinthe in a process known as louching.
quotations.work: For Exposure: The Life and Times of a Small Press Publisher

louche.title: louche

etymologies: Learned borrowing from Latin lūbricus (“slippery”). Doublet of lubricious.

definitions.text: Slimy to the touch.

quotations.author: Sophocles

quotations.work: The Poetical Works of Percy Bysshe Shelley.

lubricous.title: lubricous

etymologies: From Middle English lūcre, lucor, lucour, lucur (“gain in money, profit; money; wages; illicit gain; advantage, benefit”), from Old French lucre or Latin lucrum (“advantage, profit; love of gain, avarice”), from Proto-Indo-European *leh₂w- (“gain, profit”) + *-tlom (variant of *-trom (suffix forming nouns denoting tools or instruments)).

definitions.text: Money, riches, or wealth, especially when seen as having a corrupting effect or causing greed, or obtained in an underhanded manner.

quotations.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
quotations.passage: […] [I]t's only fair that you should pocket the lucre. I've had my share already.

A Bishop then must be blamelesse, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behauiour, giuen to hospitalitie, apt to teach; / Not giuen to wine, no striker, not greedy of filthy lucre, but patient, not a brawler, not couetous; […]

quotations.author: John Bunyan
quotations.passage: By-ends and Silver-Demas both agree; / One calls, the other runs, that he may be / A sharer in his lucre; so these two / Take up in this World, and no further go.
quotations.work: The Pilgrim’s Progress from This World, to That which is to Come

quotations.author: William Cobbett
quotations.passage: When a man bargains for the price of maintaining such or such principles, or of endeavouring to make out such or such a case, without believing in the soundness of the principles or the truth of the case; such a man, whether he touch the cash (or paper-money) before or after the performance of his work, and whether he work with his tongue or his pen, may, I think be fairly charged with seeking after "base lucre;" for he, in such case, manifestly sells not only the use of his talents, but his sincerity into the bargain, and drives a traffic as nearly allied to soul-selling as any thing in this world can be; […]

lucre.title: lucre

etymologies: From the Latin lūcubrātiō (“nighttime study”), from lūcubrō (“work by artificial light”), from lūx (“light”). Compare luculent.

definitions.text: Intense and prolonged study or meditation; especially, late at night.
The product of such study; often, writings.

quotations.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne

quotations.author: Edward Gibbon

quotations.author: Carl Schurz

lucubration.title: lucubration

etymologies: From Latin lūculentus, from lūx (“light”).

definitions.text: Shining, brilliant.
Of language, speeches etc: lucid, brilliantly clear.

quotations.author: Robert Burton

definitions.text: Marked by lavishness and richness; sumptuous.

quotations.author: Anthony Burgess

lucullan.title: Lucullan

etymologies: From French ludique, from Latin ludo (“to play”).

definitions.text: Playful.

Of or pertaining to playfully fictitious or affected use of language, such as an exaggerated accent for respectfully comic effect or cutesy diction.

quotations.author: Jean-Louis Cazaux

ludic.title: ludic

quotations.author: Thomas Hardy

quotations.author: Joseph Conrad

quotations.author: John le Carré

lugubrious.title: lugubrious

etymologies: From Late Middle English lūminārī, lūminārīe (“lamp; source of spiritual light, example of holiness; glory”), borrowed from Old French luminarie (“lamp, lights, lighting; candles; brightness, illumination”), variant of luminaire (“light fixture”) (modern French luminaire), from Medieval Latin lūminārium, from lūmināre (“that which gives light; light; lamp; body giving light, especially a heavenly body”), from lūmen (“light; brightness”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“bright; to shine”)) + -āris (suffix forming adjectives indicating a relationship or a pertaining to). definitions.text: One who is an inspiration to others; one who has achieved success in one's chosen field; a leading light.
A body that gives light; especially, one of the heavenly bodies.
An artificial light; an illumination.

quotations.author: Thomas Carlyle

quotations.author: Nahal Toosi

quotations.author: John Wilford

quotations.author: David Williamson

But, when every intervening object is removed, and the Christian placed in the light of his countenance, all imperfection flies away.

luminary.title: luminary

From lump + -en (verbal suffix).

malaise.title: malaise

etymologies: From the name of Mrs. Malaprop, a character in the play The Rivals (1775) by Richard Brinsley Sheridan +‎ -ism. As dramatic characters in English comic plays of this time often had allusive names, it is likely that Sheridan fashioned the name from malapropos (“inappropriate; inappropriately”), from French mal à propos. Mrs. Malaprop is a classic example of a familiar comedic character archetype who unintentionally substitutes inappropriate but like-sounding words that take on a ludicrous meaning when used incorrectly.

examples: The script employed malapropism to great effect.
definitions.text: The blundering use of an absurdly inappropriate word or expression in place of a similar-sounding one.

examples: The translator matched every malapropism in the original with one from his own language.
The humor comes from all the malapropisms.
definitions.text: An instance of such use.
Rare form of malapropism.

Later adjective and noun uses may have been directly derived from Latin mercuriālis (adjective), whence Middle English mercurial (“under the astrological influence of the planet Mercury”).

definitions.text: The branch of philosophy which studies fundamental principles intended to describe or explain all that is, and which are not themselves explained by anything more fundamental; the study of first principles; the study of being insofar as it is being (Latin: ens in quantum ens).

In his Pensées, Pascal mentioned some first principles recognized within his metaphysics: space, time, motion, and number.
definitions.text: The view or theory of a particular philosopher or school of thinkers concerning the first principles which describe or explain all that is.

In the same way, “dish” started as the physical plate a meal is served on, before people started using it to represent the meal itself.

quotations.passage: There was an earthy smell, as of some dry miasma, which came through the fouler air.

quotations.author: May
quotations.passage: In 1883, the contract came up for renewal, the L.N.W.R. received it, and the City of Dublin Steam Packet Company was set aside. But there was a certain miasma of secrecy about the affair, so that many, especially in Ireland, looked for information and insisted on getting it.

quotations.author: Geoffrey Morrison
quotations.passage: It was into this lossy compression miasma that aptX was born.

miasma.title: miasma

etymologies: From French microcosme, from Latin microcosmus, from Ancient Greek μικρός (mikrós, “small”) + κόσμος (kósmos, “universe, order”), equivalent to micro- +‎ -cosm.

definitions.text: Human nature or the human body as representative of the wider universe; man considered as a miniature counterpart of divine or universal nature.
The human body; a person.
A smaller system which is seen as representative of a larger one.
A small natural ecosystem; an artificial ecosystem set up as an experimental model.

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: If you see this in the Map of my Microcosme, followes it that I am knowne well enough too?
quotations.work: Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies

quotations.author: Herbert Weir Smyth
quotations.passage: With a few actors at his disposition he created a microcosm of life.

quotations.author: April
quotations.passage: That short journey to Brighton was like a microcosm of the railway universe, embracing as it did a tunnel, a viaduct, two junctions, and two termini! Unfortunately, the route was far from direct.

quotations.author: Barry McIntyre
quotations.passage: ‘In a sense, the problems experienced at Bristol are like a microcosm of what is happening in the NHS - experienced surgeons battling against difficult circumstances, with inadequate resources and in a culture where the finding of scapegoats appears to be put before the finding of solutions.’

quotations.author: Phil Dawkes
quotations.passage: Steve Bruce's side have swung from highs to lows in what has been at best a wildly inconsistent start to the season. They experienced a microcosm of this within the opening 45 minutes at the Stadium of Light.

quotations.author: Li Huang
quotations.passage: It should come as no surprise to see promotional material and bulletin boards in the department’s languages, though English is also present in the signage of this microcosm of the institution.
quotations.work: Journal of Multilingual and Multicultural Development

quotations.author: Richard Wilcock
quotations.passage: The wider North West and Central Region is itself a microcosm of the industry's complexity. Covering the approaches to London Euston, stretching through Birmingham and the West Midlands, and reaching Manchester, Liverpool and beyond, it is a patchwork of overlapping markets, political geographies, and infrastructure types.

microcosm.title: microcosm

etymologies: From French mine (“appearance”) (whence also Danish mine and German Miene), perhaps from Breton min (“face of an animal”), or from Latin minio (“to redden”).

definitions.text: Demeanor; facial expression or attitude, especially one which is intended by its bearer.
A specific facial expression.
A group of related languages spoken by the Yao people.

quotations.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
quotations.passage: [T]aking the air with an infinite sadness of mien, like some disconsolate prisoner, Utterson saw Dr. Jekyll.
quotations.work: Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde

quotations.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
quotations.passage: Gentlest Guardians marked serene / His early hope, his liberal mien; […]

quotations.author: Joseph Turnley
quotations.passage: Beauty, like all divine gifts, is everywhere to be seen by the eye of the faithful admirer of nature; and, like all spirits, she is scarcely to be described by words. Her countenance and mien, her path, her hue and carriage, often surpass expression, and soothe the enthusiast into reverie and silence.

quotations.author: Stephen Foster
quotations.passage: Jenny's coming o'er the green, / Fairer form was never seen, / Winning is her gentle mien; / Why do I love her so?

quotations.author: Siobhan Roberts
quotations.passage: Although still young at heart and head, he looks more and more like his old friend Archimedes, increasingly bearded and increasingly grey, with an otherworldly mien – a look that should earn him a spot in the online quiz featuring portraits of frumpy old men under the rubric “Prof or Hobo?”

quotations.author: Claudia La Rocco
quotations.passage: It’s hard to say which is worse: the press-on smiles favored by many a ballet dancer, or the stony “I’m going to pretend this isn’t happening to me” miens often found in contemporary troupes like White Road.

mien.title: mien

etymologies: Borrowed from French milieu (“physical or social environment; group of people with a common point of view”), from Middle French milieu, meilleu, mileu, from Old French milliu, meillieu, mileu (“middle”), from mi- (prefix meaning ‘half’) (from Latin medius (“half; middle”)) + lieu, leu (“place”) (from Latin locus (“place; spot (specific location)”)).

definitions.text: An environment or setting; a medium; environs
A social environment or setting.
A group of people with a common point of view; a social class or group.

quotations.author: Tom O’Regan
quotations.passage: Australian cinema is a messy affair. It is a messiness not only in our ways of knowing, reading, consuming and producing films and the larger film-making milieu of which they are a part, but also a messiness among the films themselves […]

quotations.author: Kathleen L. Mosier
quotations.passage: In the electronic milieu, accuracy is accomplished by the technology, and the appropriate strategy for judgment is likely to entail ensuring coherence within and across electronic and naturalistic components of the ecology.
quotations.work: The Oxford Handbook of Cognitive Engineering

quotations.author: Brendan Ryan
quotations.passage: The library as solely a physical space will not survive in the digital milieu. Services should be directed towards user needs and desires in the current academic climate.
quotations.work: Optimizing Academic Library Services in the Digital Milieu: Digital Devices and Their Emerging Trends

quotations.author: Danna Nolan Fewell
quotations.passage: The question is, then, what is the relationship of biblical narrative to its literary milieu? […] One must simultaneously biblical narrative in light of its clear historical connections to its literary milieu, while carefully analyzing the profound differences separating it from its milieu as well.
quotations.work: The Oxford Handbook of Biblical Narrative

quotations.author: Percy Hughes
quotations.passage: The distinction between the constituents in, and the conditions of, the integral life-career of person is well brought out in contrasting the attitudes of attention which persons normally develop with the milieux or social media which serve as the theater for their exercise. […] The assertive attitude of challenge finds its milieux in the domains of sport, art, exercise, industry, etc., to which the conception of gestalt may well be extended.
quotations.work: The Center, Function and Structure of Psychology

quotations.author: William Arbuckle Reid
quotations.passage: Confronted by the multiplicity of the milieus that could influence curriculum activity, we need some way of deciding not only what kinds of milieus should claim our attention, but also what kinds of knowledge about them we should attend to.
quotations.work: The Pursuit of Curriculum: Schooling and the Public Interest

quotations.author: James T. Dillon
quotations.passage: The unmistakable directness and violence of Jesus' action shows it to have been undertaken and executed precisely as if the milieu were indeed not there to be counted. Here again is the character of action taken in the very face of the milieu without taking any notice of it. In any event, the one certainty is that the Roman milieu, so entirely ignored by his teaching, here came conclusively to touch upon it, putting Jesus to an end.
quotations.work: Jesus as a Teacher: A Multidisciplinary Case Study

quotations.author: Sami Zubaida
quotations.passage: Certain milieus are described as cosmopolitan. Typically these are artistic, intellectual and bohemian milieus, but also the world of international business and high finance, and some mafias and underworlds.
quotations.work: Cosmopolitanism, Identity and Authenticity in the Middle East

quotations.author: John Neal Stewart
quotations.passage: The vast majority of our intensive child and adolescent treatment milieus operate within an adult-centric model, wherein staff play the central role in developing, instilling and enforcing the culture; a model that places virtually all power and authority in the hands of the supervising adults.
quotations.work: Attachment-Based Milieus for Healing Child and Adolescent Developmental Trauma: A Relational Approach for Use in Settings from Inpatient Psychiatry to Special Education Classrooms

quotations.author: Li Huang
quotations.passage: [F]rom the perspective of traditional linguistic landscapes thought, such an overwhelmingly English landscape would normally be considered to exert a negative effect on the vitality and feelings of worth of other languages within this specific multilingual milieu.
quotations.work: Journal of Multilingual and Multicultural Development

quotations.author: Debra Jacobs
quotations.passage: I suppose that’s not surprising, given the spiritual milieu in which I grew up. My mother gasped in sorrow at any news of a bombing in Israel and appropriately “oy veyed” when a Jew was accused of a crime, but she couldn’t tell you what the Shabbat blessing meant.

quotations.author: Iris Murdoch
quotations.passage: It's not easy to find someone whom one has mislaid for years in London, particularly if she belongs to the sort of milieu that Anna belonged to, but clearly the first thing to do is look in the telephone book.

milieu.title: milieu

etymologies: First attested in 1598; borrowed from Latin mīlitātus, perfect passive participle from mīlitō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Semantically from its cognate, French militer.

examples: to militate in favor of a particular result
Trade sanctions militate against international cooperation.
definitions.text: To give force or effect toward; to influence.
To serve as a soldier or participate in warfare.

quotations.author: January and February
quotations.passage: The 8-ft. singles were pre-eminently express engines, and were not satisfactory on secondary duties where frequent stops were called for, which militated against their being retained in service.

quotations.author: Harry E. Wedeck
quotations.passage: It has been at least an academic tradition, if no more, that mathematical studies militate against amatory inclinations.

quotations.author: Bernard E. Harcourt
quotations.passage: There are no missing values for burglary victimization in the data, whereas there are ten missing values for robbery―and as many for physical assault. This fact would militate in favor of using burglary as the independent variable.

quotations.author: James Lambert
quotations.passage: There are a number of theoretical concerns which might seem to militate against the successful creation of a dictionary of Indian English.

quotations.author: Nathanael Brent
quotations.passage: This..moues many Italian Caualiers to militate in the warres of Holland.

militate.title: militate

etymologies: From Middle English milksop, mylk sop, mylke soppe, equivalent to milk +‎ sop.

definitions.text: A piece of bread sopped in milk.
A dish consisting of bread pieces in a bowl, sprinkled with sugar and covered in hot milk.
An easily frightened, ineffectual, or weak person.

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: And vvho doth lead them but a paltrey fellovv,? / Long kept in Brittaine at our mothers cost, / A milkesopt, one that neuer in his life / Felt so much colde as ouer shooes in snovv: […]
quotations.work: The Tragedy of King Richard the Third.

quotations.author: William Makepeace Thackeray
quotations.passage: “That milksop of a creature pretend to be worthy of such a woman as Mrs. Pendennis,” broke out the Doctor: “where will impudence stop next!”

milksop.title: milksop

etymologies: French, meaning "thousand flowers".

definitions.text: A background of many small flowers and plants, popular in tapestry of the Middle Ages in Europe.

millefleur.title: millefleur

etymologies: Named after Caspar Milquetoast, a character from the comic strip The Timid Soul, created by American cartoonist Harold Tucker Webster (1885–1952) and first published in 1924; the character was named after the American dish milk toast (“a food consisting of toasted bread in warm milk”), from milque (pseudo-Gallicism derived from English milk) +‎ toast.

definitions.text: Meek, timid; lacking character or effectiveness.
A person of meek or timid disposition; a person who lacks character or effectiveness.

quotations.author: Donald William Nicholson
quotations.passage: The truth is that we are cursed with a "milquetoast" Government operating under "milquetoast" policies. Fear has become a national policy.
quotations.work: Congressional Record: Proceedings and Debates of the 82d Congress, First Session: Appendix

quotations.author: Edward Christie Banfield
quotations.passage: If Bach had any guts, he wouldn't take that. He's too much of a Milquetoast guy.

quotations.author: William G. Lycan
quotations.passage: I should have listened to my mother when she told me to stay out of journalism because of idiot milquetoast jerk reporters like you!

quotations.author: Barry Gifford
quotations.passage: [Al] Lettieri turns [Sally] Struthers on and she strokes his big gun and waves it (and her big tits) in his face and flaunts her partiality for the tough thug Lettieri over her milquetoast husband.
quotations.work: Out of the Past: Adventures in Film Noir

quotations.author: John Rosemond
quotations.passage: Like that well-meaning mom, parents employ Milquetoast speech whenever they whine, complain, plead, entreat, entice, bribe, and explain themselves persuasively.
quotations.work: Parenting by the Book: Biblical Wisdom for Raising Your Child

quotations.author: Gerard DeGroot
quotations.passage: Ricky [Nelson] was the perfect commodity: an artist who did not upset milktoast America. He was Elvis [Presley] without grease, without swinging hips.
quotations.work: The 60s Unplugged: A Kaleidoscopic History of a Disorderly Decade

quotations.author: Christopher Kelly
quotations.passage: And if Dick Leonard didn't appreciate Patrick's incisive criticism—if it inspired a streak of vindictiveness in his usually milquetoast boss and Dick ended up making his assistant's life miserable?

quotations.author: Isabelle Huppert
quotations.passage: Moreover, "Eva" boasts little style beyond what its biggest star is able to bring to the table. Viewers hoping for more of the milquetoast elegance that [Benoît] Jacquot previously brought to the likes of "Farewell, My Queen" and "Diary of a Chambermaid" will be disappointed.

quotations.author: The twenty-second Psalm
quotations.passage: We know that theology must be common to all believers, but again we also know that some enjoy only milquetoast (german milchspeise[2]), while others can eat solid food, and that one and the same truth is apprehended in different ways, for it is not possible to accommodate all these ways to the grasp of all, while not depriving them of the truth itself.
quotations.work: Dr. Martin Luther’s Complete Writings (english translation)

quotations.author: Fulton Oursler
quotations.passage: The Milquetoasts of this world seldom wake up in time to get tough effectively, Mr. [Harold Tucker] Webster fears. [...] Webster considers him a worthy citizen—of the kind that had better begin to show a little more spunk before it is too late.

quotations.author: Muriel Larson
quotations.passage: The Milquetoasts of this world are the victims of the steamrollers. I used to be numbered among the Milquetoasts and was periodically used or flattened! I came to realize, however, that even though Christians are to be humble and cooperative, they also are accountable to God to use their time wisely, to do what He wants them to do, and to stand up for what is right and biblical.

quotations.author: Richard M. Fried
quotations.passage: That scientists favored international control of the atom made conservatives even more mistrustful. J[ohn] Parnell Thomas rued the surrender of control to such "a group of milktoasts."
quotations.work: Nightmare in Red: The McCarthy Era in Perspective

quotations.author: Frank Manchel
quotations.passage: Of the thirteen films he [Douglas Fairbanks] made independently, the most noteworthy was WILD AND WOOLLY (1917), a melodramatic story about an Eastern milquetoast who becomes a frontier hero.

quotations.author: Louis Baldwin
quotations.passage: [Clare Boothe Luce] was no woman to be married to a milquetoast, and Henry R[obinson] Luce, cofounder and colorful, forceful honcho of the nascent Time empire, was anything but that.
quotations.work: Women of Strength: Biographies of 106 who have Excelled in Traditional Male Fields, A.D. 61 to the Present

quotations.author: Elizabeth A. Ford
quotations.passage: Initially, our heroine hooks up with some milktoast of a guy with lots of money and little personality. Then he comes along—a man she can't push over, a man her wealth and social position can't influence.
quotations.work: The Makeover in Movies: Before and After in Hollywood Films, 1941–2002

quotations.author: Vanessa Friedman
quotations.passage: When the verdict comes down, the transformation of the wunderkind founder of Theranos from black-clad genius to besuited milquetoast will be an integral part of the story.

milquetoast.title: milquetoast

etymologies: From Latin mīmēticus or its etymon Ancient Greek μῑμητικός (mīmētikós, “imitative”). By surface analysis, mime +‎ -etic.

definitions.text: Exhibiting mimesis.
Imitative.
Something mimetic or imitative.
A type of mnemonic in the form of a picture. (Can we add an example for this sense?)

examples: caloric restriction mimetic
exercise mimetic
serotonin mimetic
definitions.text: A substance with similar pharmacological effects as another substance or as a lifestyle intervention such as diet or exercise.

quotations.author: Herbert Weir Smyth
quotations.passage: No enthusiasm recalled by mimetic art could hold poise with the intensity of the actual exultation of the Athenians on that day when they saw the Persian fleet hacked to pieces in the narrow strait.

quotations.author: Katharine Viner
quotations.passage: This is a planned city, built wholesale from scratch, and coloured with a mimetic sense of humour. Lusail has a replica Place Vendôme. Lusail has a fake Beverly Hills (still under construction).

mimetic.title: mimetic

etymologies: Borrowed from Middle French minatoire, from Late Latin minātōrius. Compare menace.

definitions.text: Threatening, menacing.

quotations.author: Henry James
quotations.passage: […] her father quietly addressed a few words, by letter, to George Flack. This communication was not of a minatory order; it expressed on the contrary the loose sociability which was the essence of Mr. Dosson's nature.

quotations.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
quotations.passage: Number 3, Lauriston Gardens wore an ill-omened and minatory look.

quotations.author: Thomas Carlyle
quotations.passage: […] the Place de Grève, with its thirty thousand Regulars, its whole irregular Saint-Antoine and Saint-Marceau, is one minatory mass of clear or rusty steel; […]

quotations.author: P. D. James
quotations.passage: She shook hands firmly with Dalgliesh and gave him a minatory glance as if welcoming a new patient from whom she expected trouble.

quotations.author: Edward Gorey
quotations.passage: In the cottage next to the post office Alma Crumble broke her wrist stirring batter, at which the Bug declared in a minatory tone that ‘That was enough of that.’
quotations.work: The Haunted Tea-Cosy: A Dispirited and Distasteful Diversion for Christmas

minatory.title: minatory

etymologies: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

definitions.text: plural of minutia

minutiae.title: minutiae

etymologies: From Middle English merth, myrthe, murhthe, from Old English myrgþ (“mirth, joy”), from Proto-West Germanic *murgiþu (“briefness, brevity”); equivalent to merry +‎ -th (abstract nominal suffix). Cognate with Middle Dutch merchte (“pleasure, joy, delight”).

definitions.text: The emotion usually following humor and accompanied by laughter.
That which causes merriment.

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: But sorrow that is couch'd in seeming gladness / Is like that mirth fate turns to sudden sadness.
quotations.work: Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies

quotations.author: Jane Austen
quotations.passage: To this speech Bingley made no answer; but his sisters gave it their hearty assent, and indulged their mirth for some time at the expense of their dear friend's vulgar relations.

quotations.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
quotations.passage: And he began to laugh again, and that so heartily, that, though I did not see the joke as he did, I was again obliged to join him in his mirth.

quotations.author: James Joyce
quotations.passage: Phantasmal mirth, folded away: muskperfumed.

quotations.author: Constance Garnett
quotations.passage: All these acquaintances he observed with difficulty concealing their mirth at something; the same mirth that he had perceived in the lawyer's eyes, and just now in the eyes of this groom.

quotations.author: William Babington Maxwell
quotations.passage: She was a fat, round little woman, richly apparelled in velvet and lace, […] ; and the way she laughed, cackling like a hen, the way she talked to the waiters and the maid, […]—all these unexpected phenomena impelled one to hysterical mirth, and made one class her with such immortally ludicrous types as Ally Sloper, the Widow Twankey, or Miss Moucher.

quotations.author: Willa Cather
quotations.passage: Their eyes met and they began to laugh. They laughed as children do when they cannot contain themselves, and can not explain the cause of their mirth to grown people, but share it perfectly together.

mirth.title: mirth

etymologies: From Ancient Greek from μισέω (miséō, “I hate”) and ἄνθρωπος (ánthrōpos, “man; human”); compare miser.

definitions.text: One who has a negative view of the entire human race.
Someone who distrusts or avoids other people.

quotations.author: Jonathan Swift
quotations.passage: Alas, poor Dean! his only scope / Was to be held a misanthrope.
quotations.work: On the Death of Jonathan Swift

quotations.author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon
quotations.passage: I cannot love evergreens—they are the misanthropes of nature. To them the spring brings no promise, the autumn no decline; they are cut off from the sweetest of all ties with their kind—sympathy.

misanthrope.title: misanthrope

etymologies: From mis- + begotten.

definitions.text: Born out of wedlock; illegitimate.
Ill-conceived.
Bad; worthless.
past participle of misbeget
One born illegitimately (i.e., out of wedlock); a bastard.
A person born into infelicitous circumstances.

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: But as the Deuill would haue it, three mis-be-gotten Knaues, in Kendall Greene, came at my Back, […]
quotations.work: Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies

quotations.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
quotations.passage: “Foolish woman!” responded the physician, half coldly, half soothingly. “What should ail me to harm this misbegotten and miserable babe? The medicine is potent for good, and were it my child—yea, mine own, as well as thine! I could do no better for it.”

quotations.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
quotations.passage: Rather, as there was something abnormal and misbegotten in the very essence of the creature that now faced me—something seizing, surprising and revolting—this fresh disparity seemed but to fit in with and to rëinforce it; […]
quotations.work: Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde

quotations.author: Scott Tobias
quotations.passage: Many of the strangest, most misbegotten studio films of the last 20 years have been comedies, perhaps because middle-aged executives have no comprehension of what the younger generation finds funny.

quotations.author: Norman Lindsay
quotations.passage: "Do they not sneakingly bestow on me their crass inability to do anything with their own misbegotten progeny, a subterfuge which I scornfully fub off on text-books?"

quotations.author: Elizabeth Wurtzel
quotations.passage: There was the guy I spent a misbegotten night with who said he'd call me and never did but came to the party anyway, and I felt primed for a confrontation.
quotations.work: Prozac Nation : Young and Depressed in America

quotations.author: Christopher Paolini
quotations.passage: He chose then to push away his misbegotten regret and to concentrate instead on his relief: relief that he was free of the grim demands of his self-imposed quest and that his only remaining obligations were those born of his current position.

quotations.author: Philippa Foot
quotations.passage: By preserving the incapable and “misbegotten”, and by insisting that they be the object of compassionate attention, it would cause even the strong to be infected with gloom and nihilism.
quotations.work: Nietzsche: A Collection of Critical Essays

misbegotten.title: misbegotten

etymologies: Borrowed from French miscellanées, from Latin mīscellānea, from miscellus (“mixed”), from misceō (“to mix”).

definitions.text: An assortment of miscellaneous items.

examples: a monthly miscellany of literature
definitions.text: A collection of writings on various subjects or topics; an anthology.
The condition of being miscellaneous, of being a hodgepodge.

quotations.author: Louis H. Sullivan
quotations.passage: All of these critics and theorists agree, however, positively, unequivocally, in this, […] that miscellany is abhorrent to their sense; that the sixteen-story building must not consist of sixteen separate, distinct, and unrelated buildings piled one upon the other until the top of the pile is reached.

miscellany.title: miscellany

etymologies: From Middle English miscible, from Late Latin miscibilis (“that can be mixed”), from Latin miscēre (“to mix”).

definitions.text: Able to be mixed together in all proportions.

miscible.title: miscible

etymologies: From Middle English myscreaunt, miscreaunt, from Old French mescreant (1080) "mis-believer", present participle of mescreire "to misbelieve" (modern mécroire). Cognate with French mécréant.

definitions.text: Lacking in conscience or moral principles; unscrupulous.
Holding an incorrect religious belief.

examples: The teacher sent the miscreants to see the school principal.
definitions.text: One who has behaved badly, or illegally.
One not restrained by moral principles; an unscrupulous villain.
One who holds a false religious belief; a misbeliever.

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: Thou art a Traitor, and a Miscreant; / Too good to be so, and too bad to liue, / Since the more faire and christall is the skie, / The vglier seeme the cloudes that in it flye:
quotations.work: Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies: Published According to the True Originall Copies

quotations.author: Edmund Spenser
quotations.passage: Arise thou cursed Miscreaunt, / That hast with knightlesse guile and trecherous train / Faire knighthood fowly shamed

quotations.author: Christopher Marlowe
quotations.passage: Now wil the Christian miscreants be glad, / Ringing with ioy their superstitious belles: / And making bonfires for my ouerthrow. / But ere I die those foule Idolaters / Shall make me bonfires with their filthy bones, […]
quotations.work: Tamburlaine the Great. The First Part

quotations.author: Cindy Patton
quotations.passage: How do we get fair treatment when confronting miscreant workers sometimes means no care at all?

quotations.author: Joseph Addison
quotations.passage: A meagre Catchpole hurries me to fail; No Miscreant, so remorseless, ever tore / Thy Journals, Fog, or knock'd at Franklin's door
quotations.work: A Riddle of Dean Swift's verfified

quotations.author: Thomas De Quincey
quotations.passage: Before thine eyes, thou mild and blessed one, said he, half aloud, are these miscreants daring to hold their market, and trafficking in their hellish drugs

miscreant.title: miscreant

etymologies: The noun is derived from Late Middle English misnoumer (“(law) mistaken identification of a person; plea based on such misidentification”), from Anglo-Norman mesnomer, a noun use of Anglo-Norman mesnomer, mesnommer, and Old French mesnomer, mesnommer (“to name incorrectly”), from mes- (prefix meaning ‘badly, wrongly’) + nomer, nommer (“to name”) (from Latin nōmināre, the present active infinitive of nōminō (“to name”), from nōmen (“name”) (from Proto-Indo-European *h₁nómn̥ (“name”)) + -ō (suffix forming regular first-conjugation verbs)).
The verb is derived from the noun.

definitions.text: A mistake in the naming of a person or place; a misidentification.
An incorrect use of a term, especially one which is misleading; a misname.

examples: The name Chinese checkers is a misnomer since the game has nothing to do with China.
The word blackboard as applied to green or brown chalkboards is a misnomer but is not incorrect, as the broad sense of the word is idiomatic.
definitions.text: A term which is misleading, even if firmly established, technically correct, or both.

examples: It’s a misnomer that all doctors have bad handwriting.
definitions.text: Something which is asserted not to be true; a mistaken belief, a falsehood, a myth.
To use an incorrect, and especially misleading, name for (someone or something); to misidentify, to misname.

quotations.author: Illinois. Appellate Court
quotations.passage: […] plaintiff's misstyling himself as corporation in initial complaint constituted case of misnomer.

quotations.author: Katharine Viner
quotations.passage: Rewilding […] is also a misnomer, for whether by getting rid of tens of thousands of sheep in Patagonia or introducing a living species as a surrogate for an extinct one – Sayaguesa cattle in place of aurochs in Croatia’s Velebit Mountains, for instance – rewilding requires more human intervention than its name suggests.

misnomer.title: misnomer

etymologies: From Ancient Greek μισογυνία (misogunía) and μισογύνης (misogúnēs, “woman hater”), from μισέω (miséō, “I hate”) + γυνή (gunḗ, “woman”). By surface analysis, miso- +‎ -gyny.

definitions.text: Hatred of, contempt for, or prejudice against women.

quotations.author: Joanne Marie Greer
quotations.passage: Although she argues against a simplistic conflation of types of prejudice, she suggests that misogyny is typically present in both narcissistic and obsessive forms of anti-Semitic prejudice.

Contempt.

Serving as a missile; intended to be thrown.

etymologies: From Middle English mitigaten (“to relieve pain, soothe; (swelling) to abate; (hemorrhoids) to relieve; (the mind) to placate, appease; to end, check; to stop, cease”), from mitigat(e) (“mitigated, alleviated, relived”, also used as the past participle of mitigaten) +‎ -en (verb-forming suffix), borrowed from Latin mītigātus, the perfect passive participle of mītigō (“to make soft, ripe; to tame, pacify”), from mītis (“gentle, mild, ripe”) + -igō (“to do, make”), of uncertain origin, but perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *meh₁y- (“mild, soft”).
From Middle English mitigat(e) (“mitigated”, also used as the past participle of mitigaten and of mitigate in Early Modern English), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more.

definitions.text: To reduce, lessen, or decrease and thereby to make less severe or easier to bear.
To downplay.

Mitigated, alleviated.

quotations.author: Greg Morse

mitigate.title: mitigate

etymologies: Borrowed from Late Latin mnemonicus or its etymon Ancient Greek μνημονῐκός (mnēmonĭkós, “pertaining to memory or remembrance, memorial”) + English -ic (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives). Mνημονῐκός (Mnēmonĭkós) is derived from μνήμων (mnḗmōn, “mindful, remembering”) + -ῐκός (-ĭkós, suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives); while μνήμων (mnḗmōn) is from μνάομαι (mnáomai, “to be mindful, remember”) (from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to mind; to think”)) + -μων (-mōn, suffix forming adjectives and agent nouns).

Noun sense 1 (“something used to help in remembering a thing”) is borrowed from Latin mnēmonicum (“something used to help in remembering a thing”), from Ancient Greek μνημονικόν (mnēmonikón, “something used to help in remembering a thing”), a noun use of the neuter form of μνημονῐκός (mnēmonĭkós, adjective): see etymology 1. Noun sense 3 (“synonym of mnemonics”) is borrowed from Late Latin mnemonica, a noun use of the feminine form of mnemonicus: see etymology 1.

definitions.text: Especially of a series of ideas, letters, words, etc.: intended to help in remembering.
Of or relating to mnemonics (“the study of techniques for remembering anything more easily”).
Of or relating to memory.
Something (especially a series of ideas, letters, words, etc.) used to help in remembering a thing; a memory aid.
The human-readable, textual form of an assembly language instruction, not including operands.
Synonym of mnemonics (“the study of techniques for remembering anything more easily”).

quotations.author: Alex Kimbell

mnemonic.title: mnemonic

etymologies: From Middle English modicum, from Latin modicum (“a little, a small amount”), a noun use of the neuter form of modicus (“moderate; restrained, temperate; reasonable”) + -cum (suffix forming neuter nouns). Modicus is derived from modus (“a measure; a bound, limit”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *med- (“to measure”)) + -icus (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives).
The plural form modica is derived from Latin modica.

examples: Unable to garner even a modicum of support for his plan, he conceded to follow the others.
The constitutional requirement <for copyright protection> necessitates independent creation plus a modicum of creativity.
definitions.text: A modest, small, or trifling amount.

Certain modica of pudding and praise are from time to time gladly exchanged for the fascination of his presence, which exchange once effected, the bargain is finished, and each party goes off his several way.

quotations.author: August

quotations.author: Christian Wolmar

modicum.title: modicum

A surname from Irish.
An English surname transferred from the given name.

quotations.author: Theodore Roethke

moor.title: moor

etymologies: From Dutch moeras (“marsh, swamp”), an alteration (with influence from Dutch moer (“moor”)) of a direct descendant of Middle Dutch marasch (“marsh”). The Middle Dutch word is a borrowing from Old French mareis, from Proto-West Germanic *marisk. Doublet of marish and marsh, and linked in part to moor. Compare quagmire.

definitions.text: A tract of soft, wet ground; a marsh; a fen.
Anything that entraps or makes progress difficult.

quotations.author: John Ruskin
quotations.passage: Seven miles to the north of Venice, the banks of sand, which near the city rise little above low-water mark, attain by degrees a higher level, and knit themselves at last into fields of salt morass, raised here and there into shapeless mounds, and intercepted by narrow creeks of sea.

quotations.author: Ian Johnson
quotations.passage: The gay man must fully understand the reasons why he is as he is, and face the mass of unconscious shit put there by our society. This is the great morass between the philosophy and the actualization.

quotations.author: Thomas Pynchon
quotations.passage: I wrote to Sacramento about that historical marker, and they've been kicking it around their bureaucratic morass for months.

morass.title: morass

etymologies: From Latin mordax (“given to biting, corrosive”) (from mordere (“to bite, sting”)) + -ious.

definitions.text: Biting, causing a physical bite or sting; corrosive
Sharp or caustic in style or tone.
Sharp in intent, sarcastic.
Prone to biting, aggressive (of an animal etc.).

quotations.author: Ernest Bramah

quotations.author: Samuel Klinefelter Hoshour
quotations.passage: Not gyved with connubial relations, I entered upon my migration entirely isolated, with the exception of a canine quadruped whose mordacious, latrant, lusorious, and venatic qualities, are without parity.

mordacious.title: mordacious

etymologies: From French mordant, from Latin mordeō. Doublet of mordent.

definitions.text: Having or showing a sharp or critical quality.
Serving to fix a dye to a fiber.
Any substance used to facilitate the fixing of a dye to a fibre; usually a metallic compound which reacts with the dye using chelation.
Any corrosive substance used in etching.
A glutinous size used as a ground for gilding, to make the gold leaf adhere.

examples: Mordant these goods for dyeing.
definitions.text: To subject to the action of, or imbue with, a mordant.

quotations.author: L.F. Salzman
quotations.passage: In dyeing two mediums are required, the colouring matter and the mordant which fixes the dye in the wool.

mordant.title: mordant

etymologies: From New Latin morganāticus, from the Medieval Latin phrase mātrimōnium ad morganāticum, from Proto-Germanic *murgnagebō (“morning gift”) (whence Old English morgenġiefu).

definitions.text: Designating a marriage (or the wife involved) between a man of higher rank and a woman of lower rank, often having various legal repercussions (typically that such a wife has no claim on the husband's possessions or title). It was not an aspect of English law, but was common in other royal houses, especially in Germany.

quotations.author: James Joyce

quotations.author: Assassination of the Austrian royal heir and wife
quotations.passage: Francis Ferdinand's marriage was a morganatic alliance, and in consequence of a declaration which he made when contracting it, his children do not inherit his rights to the Austrian crown.

quotations.author: Rebecca West
quotations.passage: Because of her noble birth, she bitterly resented her position as a morganatic wife.

quotations.author: Colin Jones
quotations.passage: Louis's association with the pious widow, Madame de Maintenon (with whom he contracted a morganatic marriage in 1684) had led to a new tone of piety, even prudery, at court.

quotations.author: Alan Rusbridger
quotations.passage: This will not be a morganatic marriage—one where titles are not passed to any children—the prince and Mrs Parker Bowles being beyond the usual age of procreation and so unlikely to have new heirs to complicate matters.

quotations.author: Marsha Keith Schuchard

morganatic.title: morganatic

etymologies: From Latin moribundus (“dying”).

definitions.text: Approaching death; about to die; dying; expiring.
Almost obsolete; nearing an end.
A person who is near to dying.

quotations.author: Joseph Conrad

moribund.title: moribund

etymologies: From French morose, from Latin mōrōsus (“particular, scrupulous, fastidious, self-willed, wayward, capricious, fretful, peevish”), from mōs (“way, custom, habit, self-will”). See moral.

definitions.text: Sullen, gloomy; showing a brooding ill humour.

quotations.author: Robert Michael Ballantyne
quotations.passage: If there is any boy or man who loves to be melancholy and morose, and who cannot enter with kindly sympathy into the regions of fun, let me seriously advise him to shut my book and put it away. It is not meant for him.
quotations.work: The Coral Island: A Tale of the Pacific Ocean

quotations.author: 10's

morose.title: morose

etymologies: From French morphème. Ultimately from Ancient Greek μορφή (morphḗ, “shape, form”). By surface analysis, morph +‎ -eme.

definitions.text: The smallest linguistic unit within a word that can carry a meaning. It may be a letter, a syllable, or otherwise.

quotations.author: Thomas Pyles
quotations.passage: Just as a regiment is ultimately made up of soldiers, so the sentence is of morphemes—they are its ultimate constituents.

quotations.author: Peter Matthews
quotations.passage: There is therefore a natural tendency in both American and European structural linguistics to insist that the word should be syntactically decomposed. For writers such as Hockett (1958), or for that matter the early Chomsky (1957), the indivisible unit of grammar was the morpheme, and the relationship of morpheme to morpheme within the word […] was to be handled no differently from that of word to word in any larger structure.

morpheme.title: morpheme

etymologies: Unadapted borrowing from French mot juste.

definitions.text: The perfectly appropriate word or phrase for the situation.

quotations.author: David Streitfeld
quotations.passage: Wattpad is not the sort of site where writers talk about suffering for their art or spend hours searching for the mot juste.

mot_juste.title: mot juste

etymologies: From French motif (1848), with the meaning of "main idea or theme". Doublet of motive.

examples: See how the artist repeats the scroll motif throughout the work?
definitions.text: A recurring or dominant element; an artistic theme.
A short melodic or lyrical passage that is repeated in several parts of a work.
A decorative figure that is repeated in a design or pattern.
A decorative appliqué design or figure, as of lace or velvet, used in trimming.
The physical object or objects repeated at each point of a lattice. Usually atoms or molecules.
A basic element of a move in terms of why the piece moves and how it supports the fulfilment of a stipulation.
In a nucleotide or aminoacid sequence, pattern that is widespread and has, or is conjectured to have, a biological significance.

motif.title: motif

etymologies: From motile + -ity.

definitions.text: The state of being motile (moving).
The degree to which something is motile.

motility.title: motility

etymologies: 1670-80. Probably back-formation from motley.

definitions.text: To mark with blotches of different color, or shades of color, as if stained; to spot; to maculate.
A distinguishing blotch of colour.

examples: The most common symptom is a mild mottle on the youngest leaves of infected plants.
definitions.text: A mottled or spotted pattern.
Any of several species of genus Logania of butterflies, found from Burma to the Philippines and New Guinea.

quotations.author: F.J. Thwaites

mottle.title: mottle

One who sells by deception; a con artist.
Any boastful, false pretender.
An acrobat.
To act as a mountebank.
To cheat by boasting and false pretenses.

mountebank.title: mountebank

etymologies: The noun is borrowed from Massachusett mugquomp, mummugquomp (“war leader”).
