quotations.author: Anna Katharine Green
quotations.passage: But when I had crossed the threshold, I was astonished at the paucity of facts to be gleaned from the inmates themselves.

quotations.author: October
quotations.passage: For sheer paucity of railway facilities, probably the record in Great Britain is held by the Scottish county of Nairn, which has about eight miles of railway and two stations—Nairn and Auldearn.

quotations.author: January
quotations.passage: This paucity of trains helps to explain why electrification is not planned between Paris and Belfort.

quotations.author: Po Bronson
quotations.passage: Your tax refund might be late, owing to a paucity of number crunchers.

quotations.author: Christian Wolmar
quotations.passage: I have always argued that despite my opposition to rail privatisation, I should be grateful that John Major won the 1992 election on a platform to sell off the railways, as otherwise my column would have disappeared given the paucity of things to write about.

quotations.author: Gene Stratton-Porter
quotations.passage: Here is where the paucity of our language is made manifest.

quotations.author: Saul Bellow
quotations.passage: Genteel America was handicapped by meagerness of soul, thinness of temper, paucity of talent.

quotations.author: James Lambert
quotations.passage: There are also texts that present more lengthy lists, of between ten and thirty examples, and in doing so include some less common terms. But, on the whole, there is at present a paucity of information about these terms.

paucity.title: paucity

etymologies: From Spanish pecadillo, diminutive form of pecado (“sin”), from Latin peccatum (“sin, error, fault”), from peccō (“to sin, offend”).

definitions.text: A small flaw or sin.
A petty offense.

quotations.author: Douglas Coupland
quotations.passage: We tolerate Irene and Phil’s mild racist quirks and planet-destroying peccadilloes (“I could never own any car smaller than my Cutlass Supreme”) because their existence acts as a tranquilizer in an otherwise slightly-out-of-control world.
quotations.work: Generation X: Tales for an Accelerated Culture

quotations.author: Gail Collins
quotations.passage: The sex scandal issue isn’t really central, since Americans have a long record of voting for the candidates they think can deliver, regardless of private peccadilloes.

quotations.author: Robert Dean Frisbee
quotations.passage: When he comes to the prayer, he sometimes does me the honor of personally recommending me to the Lord, advising him that I am a worthy man and begging him to condone my occasional peccadillos.

quotations.author: John O’Connell
quotations.passage: No sexual peccadillo is left unremarked upon.

peccadillo.title: peccadillo

etymologies: The adjective is borrowed from Middle French peccant (“unhealthy”) (modern French peccant), and from its etymon Late Latin peccantis, the genitive singular of peccāns (“offending; sinning, transgressing”, adjective), from Latin peccāns (“wrongdoer”), a noun use of the active present participle of peccō (“to offend; to sin, transgress”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ped- (“to fall; to stumble; to step; to walk”).

As regards adjective sense 3 (“diseased, unhealthy”) as used in peccant humours, compare Middle French l'umeur peccante, humeurs peccantes, Old French humeurs pechantes, and Late Latin humores peccantes.
The noun is derived from the adjective.

definitions.text: Of a person, etc.: that commits or has committed an offence or a sin; blameworthy, culpable, offending, sinful, sinning.
Of an action or thing: causing offence or sin; offensive, sinful.
Especially of humours of the body: diseased, unhealthy; also, causing disease.
Offending a norm, a rule, etc.; defective, faulty, wrong.
An offender; also, a sinner.

quotations.author: John Milton
quotations.passage: But let us call to Synod all the Blest / Through Heav'ns wide bounds; from them I will not hide / My judgments, how with Mankind I proceed, / As how with peccant Angels late they saw; / And in thir state, though firm, stood more confirmd.

quotations.author: Jonathan Swift
quotations.passage: It is allowed, that Senates and great Councils are often troubled with redundant, ebullient, and other peccant Humours, with many Diseases of the Head and more of the Heart; with strong Convulsions, with grievous Contractions of the Nerves and Sinews in both Hands, but especially the Right; with Spleen, Flatus, Vertigos and Deliriums; with Scrophulous Tumors full of fœtid purulent Matter; with sower frothy Ructations, with Canine Appetites and Crudeness of Digestion, besides many others needless to mention.
quotations.work: Travels into Several Remote Nations of the World. [ Gulliver’s Travels ]

quotations.author: Lord Byron
quotations.passage: I am truly sorry that I cannot accompany you in your ride this morning, owing to a violent pain in my face, arising from a wart to which I by medical advice applied a caustic. Whether I put too much, I do not know, but the consequence is, that not only I have been put to some pain, but the peccant part and its immediate environ are as black as if the printer's devil had marked me for an author.
quotations.work: Letters and Journals of Lord Byron: With Notices of His Life

quotations.author: Henry James
quotations.passage: [O]ne feels that no community can really be as purged of peccant humours as the typical American has for the most part found itself foredoomed to look.

quotations.author: Henry James
quotations.passage: Olive rested her eyes for some moments upon Mrs. Luna, without speaking. Then she said: 'Your veil is not put on straight, Adeline.' / 'I look like a monster—that, evidently, is what you mean!' Adeline exclaimed, going to the mirror to rearrange the peccant tissue.

quotations.author: Francis Bacon
quotations.passage: Thus haue I described and opened as by a kinde of dissection, those peccant humors (the principall of them) vvhich hath not onely giuen impediment to the proficence of Learning, but haue giuen also occasion, to the traducement thereof: […]
quotations.work: The Twoo Bookes of Francis Bacon. Of the Proficience and Aduancement of Learning, Diuine and Humane

quotations.author: Edmund Burke
quotations.passage: It is far from impossible to reconcide, […] the sacredness of as hereditary principle of succession in our government, vvith a povver of change in its application in cases of extreme emergency. Even in that extremity (if vve take the measure of our rights by our exercise of them at the Revolution) the change is to be confined to the peccant part only; to the part vvhich produced the necessary deviation; and even then it is to be effected vvithout a decomposition of the vvhole civil and political mass, for the purpose of originating a nevv civil order out of the first elements of society.
quotations.work: Reflections on the Revolution in France, and on the Proceedings in Certain Societies in London Relative to that Event.

quotations.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
quotations.passage: And we have a certain instinct, that where is great amount of life, though gross and peccant, it has its own checks and purifications, and will be found at last in harmony with moral laws.

quotations.author: Thomas Carlyle
quotations.passage: Syndic Gutzmar and the peccant Officials being summoned out to Strehlen, it had been asked of them, "Do you know this Letter?" Upon which they fell on their knees, "Ach Ihro Majestät [Oh Your Majesty]!" unable to deny their handwriting; […]
quotations.work: History of Friedrich II. of Prussia, Called Frederick the Great

quotations.author: Robert South
quotations.passage: [T]hat a peccant Creature should disapprove, and repent of every Violation of, and Declination from the Rules of just and honest, this, right Reason discoursing upon the Stock of its ovvn Principles, could not but infer.
quotations.work: Twelve Sermons Preached upon Several Occasions.

quotations.author: George Meredith
quotations.passage: [He] was bereaving his houses of the matronly government, deprived of which they were all of them likely soon to be at sixes and sevens with disorderly lacqueys, peccant maids, and cooks in hysterics.

quotations.author: Lytton Strachey
quotations.passage: [T]he fact that the peccant doctor [Sir James Clark, 1st Baronet] continued in the Queen's service made the Hastings family irreconcilable and produced an unpleasant impression of unrepentant error upon the public mind.

quotations.author: William Prynne
quotations.passage: [O]ur ovvne Statutes […] precisely prohibit the satyricall depraving, traducing, or derogation of the Common Prayer-Booke, and of the Sacrament of the Lords Supper in any Enterludes, Playes or Rimes, (in vvhich kinde Playes had been formerly peccant) under severe penalties.
quotations.work: Histrio-mastix. The Players Scourge, or, Actors Tragædie

quotations.author: Robert South
quotations.passage: [T]he VVorld is novv so peccant upon this Account, that I am afraid Instances vvould be mistaken for Invectives.
quotations.work: Twelve Sermons Preached upon Several Occasions.

quotations.author: John Ayliffe
quotations.passage: Nor is the Party cited bound to appear, if the Citation be evidently peccant in point of Form or Matter.
quotations.work: Parergon Juris Canonici Anglicani: Or, A Commentary, by Way of Supplement to the Canons and Constitutions of the Church of England.

quotations.author: Richard Whitlock
quotations.passage: Yet this conceitednesse and Itch of being taken for a Counsellour, maketh more Reprovers, than Peccants in the vvorld.
quotations.work: Ζωοτομία [ Zōotomía ], or, Observations on the Present Manners of the English

peccant.title: peccant

etymologies: From Latin pecūlātus, past participle of pecūlor (“defraud, embezzle”).

definitions.text: To embezzle.

peculate.title: peculate

etymologies: From Latin pecūniārius, from pecūnia (“money”), itself from pecū (“cattle”) and thus related to fee.

examples: He chose the degree for pecuniary reasons, but had no real interest in it.
definitions.text: Of, or relating to, money; monetary, financial.

quotations.author: Bertrand Russell
quotations.passage: The views of philosophers, with few exceptions, have coincided with the pecuniary interests of their class.

quotations.author: Anthony Trollope
quotations.passage: Perhaps the reader will suppose after this that the doctor had some pecuniary interest of his own in arranging the squire's loans; or, at any rate, he will think that the squire must have thought so.

pecuniary.title: pecuniary

etymologies: From Middle English pedagoge, from Middle French pedagogue, from Latin paedagōgus, from Ancient Greek παιδαγωγός (paidagōgós), from παῖς (paîs, “child”) + ἀγωγός (agōgós, “guide”) (from ἄγω (ágō, “lead”)). By surface analysis, ped- (“child”) +‎ -agogue.

definitions.text: A teacher or instructor of children; one whose occupation is to teach the young.
A pedant; one who by teaching has become overly formal or pedantic in his or her ways; one who has the manner of a teacher.
A slave who led the master's children to school, and had the charge of them generally.
To teach.

quotations.author: Henry Fielding
quotations.passage: Jones chid the pedagogue for his interruption, and then the stranger proceeded.
quotations.work: The History of Tom Jones, a Foundling

quotations.author: HarryBlank
quotations.passage: "No, that won't work." Reynders sighed, not in frustration — she was an excellent pedagogue, and never got frustrated while instructing — but in mental exhaustion. This project was testing the limits of what she could handle, in her state, though that was nothing compared to the number it was doing on Udo's head. "But it doesn't need to work. ATCP doesn't ossify, that's why it's armageddon-proof. We'd never be able to make this function if we were using standard protocols."

quotations.author: Oliver Goldsmith
quotations.passage: And novv I have gone thus far, perhaps you vvill think me some pedagogue, vvilling, by a vvell-timed puff, to encrease the reputation of his ovvn school; but such is not the case.
quotations.work: The Bee, a Select Collection of Essays, on the Most Interesting and Entertaining Subjects

pedagogue.title: pedagogue

etymologies: From Middle French pedant, pedante, from Italian pedante (“a teacher, schoolmaster, pedant”), associated with unrelated Italian pedagogo (“teacher, pedagogue”). Compare French pédant.

definitions.text: A person who makes an excessive or tedious show of their knowledge, especially regarding rules of vocabulary and grammar.
A person who is overly concerned with formal rules and trivial points of learning.
A teacher or schoolmaster.
Pedantic.
To be or act as a pedant.

quotations.author: Michel de Montaigne
quotations.passage: I have in my youth oftentimes beene vexed to see a Pedant [tr. pedante] brought in, in most of Italian comedies, for a vice or sport-maker, and the nicke-name of Magister to be of no better signification amongst us.

quotations.author: Abraham Woodhead
quotations.passage: […] as any occasion of going behond[sic – meaning beyond] the sea with sombody, or pedanting in some Gentlemans house, &c., for clergy-employment I will accept of none.

quotations.author: spring
quotations.passage: Tediously he pedanted, hedging around concerning the Perfect State, eventually coming out into the open with his own private Perfect State plan.

quotations.author: Mark Barrowcliffe
quotations.passage: ‘Most people in this country aren’t Christian, the standard package should not be Christian,’ Gerrard pedanted.

quotations.author: Mark Dahl
quotations.passage: Jim’s mother pestered him daily for a month to come home for a talk. At first he rejected the offer, knowing what to expect, dear old dad would dance around the room pedanting about some shit that didn’t make sense anyway.
quotations.work: Covenant Betrayed: Revelations of the Sixties, the Best of Time; the Worst of Time

quotations.author: Ira Nayman
quotations.passage: “Okay,” she said to the investigators, “how can I help you?” / “You, uhh, wouldn’t happen to have seven bodies lying around, would you?” Bao Bai-Leung, feeling a little ridiculous, asked. “Maybe in…your closet?” / “As I under stand human Anna to my,”[sic] Blarcch Beletchian pedanted at them, “there is not enough room for bodies to lie in a small space like a closet. Unless they were midgets like this person, or their limbs were detachable, or the closet was a gateway to eleven-dimensional space, or –” / “Oh, great!” TOM put in. “We got a literalist, here!”
quotations.work: The Multiverse is a Nice Place to Visit, But I Wouldn’t Want to Live There

quotations.author: Katharine Viner
quotations.passage: So, why do pedants pedant? We don’t really know, but some tangential studies infer it’s to do with a mixture of personality, status-signalling and group identification.

quotations.author: Alex Beeton
quotations.passage: When one Oxford fellow was ejected in 1648 he immediately wrote to his royalist patron seeking employment ‘going behond [sic] the sea with sombody, or pedanting in some Gentlemans house’.128 Whether he succeeded or not is not known, but others certainly ended up ‘pedanting’.
quotations.work: ‘Not Infected with the Venime of the Times’: The Rump Parliament and Places of Learning, 1649-53

pedant.title: pedant

etymologies: Borrowed from French pédéraste, from Ancient Greek παιδεραστής (paiderastḗs, “lover of boys”), from παῖς (paîs, “boy”) and ἐραστής (erastḗs, “lover”).

definitions.text: A man who is engaged in an erotic relationship with an adolescent boy; a practitioner of pederasty.

pederast.title: pederast

etymologies: From Latin pedester (oblique stem pedestri-) + English -an.

examples: pedestrian crossing
pedestrian zone
definitions.text: Of or intended for those who are walking.

examples: His manner of dress was pedestrian but tidy.
a pedestrian life
definitions.text: Ordinary, dull; everyday; unexceptional.

examples: The choreographer prefers pedestrian movements.
definitions.text: Pertaining to ordinary, everyday movements incorporated in postmodern dance.
A walker; one who walks or goes on foot, especially as opposed to one who uses a vehicle.
An expert or professional walker or runner; one who performs feats of walking or running.

quotations.author: Alan Marshall
quotations.passage: The piezoelectric pedestrian tubeways depicted for Shanghai 2121 will provide all-weather pedestrian transportation citywide.
quotations.work: Ecotopia 2121: A Vision for Our Future Green Utopia in 100 Cities

quotations.author: Phil McNulty
quotations.passage: England were hugely impressive in the first half in particular, when their supporters inside this magnificent bowl at Stade Velodrome roared their approval as Russia were pressed into submission and made to look pedestrian.

quotations.author: Paradox Interactive
quotations.passage: Their prose is pedestrian, their ideas weak. Hail them.

quotations.author: Ralph Davol
quotations.passage: […] how the troops came marching out for evening exercise under Captain Preston; how pedestrians and street urchins taunted them, shouting "Lobsters," "Bloody-backs," and flinging snow-balls, turnips, […]
quotations.work: Two Men of Taunton: In the Course of Human Events, 1731-1829

pedestrian.title: pedestrian

etymologies: From Late Latin peiōrātus (“worsened”, past participle of peiōrāre (“worsen”), from Latin peior (“worse”)) +‎ -ive. Compare French péjoratif (“depreciative, disparaging”). By surface analysis, pejorate +‎ -ive.

definitions.text: Disparaging, belittling or derogatory.
A disparaging, belittling, or derogatory word or expression.

quotations.author: Nathan Taylor Pemberton
quotations.passage: These days, on platforms like X, slopulism is a pejorative label often applied to posts by politicians and pundits alike, anyone who shares out lowest-common-denominator ideas designed to appeal to loyal political bases.

quotations.author: Edgar Momplaisir
quotations.passage: “Get away from me, freak.” “Actually, my designation is Logic-y. I take issue with the pejorative when I am simply a product of your self-inflicted bifurcation.”

pejorative.title: pejorative

etymologies: From Latin pelagicus (and possibly pelagus); from Ancient Greek πελαγικός (pelagikós), from πέλαγος (pélagos, “sea”). By surface analysis, -pelag +‎ -ic.

definitions.text: Living in the open sea rather than in coastal or inland waters.
Of or pertaining to oceans.
Any organism that lives in the open sea rather than in coastal or inland waters.

quotations.author: Richard Ellis
quotations.passage: Besides, seeing a shark in an aquarium tank is not the same as seeing a shark in the wild, in its natural, pelagic habitat.

quotations.author: Shuang-Lin Dong
quotations.passage: The main fish species in freshwater ponds in China are silver carp, bighead carp, grass carp, common carp, crucian carp, black carp (Mylopharyngodon piceus), mud carp (Cirrhinus molitorella), etc. According to their live habitat, they can be divided relatively into pelagic and benthic fish.

quotations.author: David Farrier
quotations.passage: Drifting idly around a broad oceanic arc, the bottle collides softly with tens of thousands of pelagic plastics all colonized by hard-shelled organisms, including barnacles, coralline algae, foraminifera and bivalve molluscs.

quotations.author: Percy Algernon Taverner
quotations.passage: The Albatrosses are true pelagics and seldom come to land except to nest.

pelagic.title: pelagic

etymologies: From Late Middle English pelf, pelfe (“stolen goods, booty, spoil; forfeited property; money, riches; property; valuable object”), possibly from Anglo-Norman pelf (a variant of pelfre (“booty, loot”)) and Old French peufre (“frippery; rubbish”); further etymology uncertain, possibly a metathesis of Old French felpe, ferpe, frepe (“a rag”). The English word is perhaps related to Late Latin pelfa, pelfra, pelfrum (“forfeited or stolen goods”), Middle French peuffe and French peufe, peuffe (“old clothes; rubbish”) (Normandy), and pilfer.

definitions.text: Money, riches; gain, especially when dishonestly acquired; lucre, mammon.
Rubbish, trash; specifically refuse from plants.
Dust; fluff.
A contemptible or useless person.

quotations.author: John Dryden
quotations.passage: During his Office, Treason vvas no Crime. / The Sons of Belial had a Glorious Time: / For Shimei, though not prodigal of pelf, / Yet lov'd his vvicked Neighbour as himself.

quotations.author: Robert Burton
quotations.passage: For what greater folly can there be, or madnesse, then to […] keepe backe from his wife and children, neither letting them, nor other friends use or enjoy that which is theirs by right, and which they much need perhaps; like a hog, or dog in the manger, he doth onely keep it, because it shall doe no body else good, hurting himselfe and others; and for a little momentary pelfe, damne his owne soule.

quotations.author: Robert Burton
quotations.passage: Now for women, in stead of laborious studies, they have curious, needleworkes, Cut-workes, spinning, bone-lace, and many prettie devises of their owne making, to adorne their houses, […] Which to her guests she shews, with all her pelfe, / Thus far my maides, but this I did my self.

quotations.author: Thomas Dekker
quotations.passage: Raph. Sirra Hammon Hammon, dost thou thinke a shooe-maker is so base, to be a bawd to his own wife for cõmodity! take thy gold, choake with it: were I not lame, I would make thee eate thy words. / Firke. A shoomaker sell his flesh and blood, oh indignitie! / Hodg. Sirra, take up your pelfe, and be packing.
quotations.work: The Dramatic Works of Thomas Dekker

quotations.author: Bholanauth Chunder
quotations.passage: The inscriptions on the walls are homilies from the Koran—actual 'sermons in stones'. The inlaid characters in diamond, and other precious stones, have been all abstracted away by the pelf-loving Jaut and Mahratta—leaving the walls defaced with the hollow marks of the chisel.
quotations.work: The Travels of a Hindoo to Various Parts of Bengal and Upper India.

quotations.author: Frederick Tatham
quotations.passage: But, sighing after his fancies and visionary pursuits, he rebelled and fled fifty miles away for refuge from the lace caps and powdered wigs of his priggish sitters, and resumed his quaint dreams and immeasurable phantasies, never more to forsake them for pelf and portraiture.

quotations.author: Dale Wimbrow
quotations.passage: When you get what you want in your struggle for pelf, and the world makes you King for a day, / Then go to the mirror and look at yourself, and see what that guy has to say.

quotations.author: Nicholas von Hoffman
quotations.passage: Some of the rich classmates were keeping their pelf to themselves.

quotations.author: Ford S. Worthy
quotations.passage: In advertising, show business, and journalism, people work themselves to the nub for glitz and glory more than for pelf.

quotations.author: Harriet P. Gross
quotations.passage: She writes about those she might have known first-hand: teenage girls cowering in bunkers … friends making promises they can never keep … rich folk fattened on wartime pelf, poor folk surviving by wit alone.

quotations.author: Nick Cohen
quotations.passage: Every wised-up wit who mistakes knowingness for knowledge proclaims that Peter Mandelson is a gutless fixer; a master manipulator who will twist and dodge around the clock to keep the privileges of power and pelf. […] If only the idle stereotype were true.

quotations.author: Alex Preston
quotations.passage: Houellebecq seems to be saying that French society, in the form of its politicians, its journalists, its academics and not least its novelists, will get exactly what it deserves – a state run by those who believe in something bigger and grander than the pelf and perquisites of their elevated positions.

pelf.title: pelf

etymologies: The adjective is a learned borrowing from Latin pellūcidus, perlucidus (“transparent, pellucid; very bright; very understandable”), from per- (prefix meaning ‘through; throughout; completely, thoroughly’) + lūcidus (“clear; full of light, bright, shining; (figuratively) easily understood, clear, lucid”) (from lūceō (“to shine; to become visible, show through; (figuratively) to be apparent, conspicuous, or evident”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“bright; to see; to shine”)) + -idus (suffix meaning ‘tending to’ forming adjectives)).
The noun is derived from the adjective.

definitions.text: Allowing the passage of light; translucent or transparent.
Easily understood; clear.
Of music or some other sound: not discordant or harsh; clear and pure-sounding.
Of a person, their mind, etc.: able to think and understand clearly; not confused; clear, sharp.
Easily recognized or seen through; apparent, obvious.
Something which allows the passage of light; a translucent or transparent object.

quotations.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
quotations.passage: The thick vegetation met overhead, interlacing into a natural pergola, and through this tunnel of verdure in a golden twilight flowed the green, pellucid river, beautiful in itself, but marvelous from the strange tints thrown by the vivid light from above filtered and tempered in its fall.

quotations.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
quotations.passage: Most of the pool was quite shallow, but under the cliff where the beach was hollowed out it was four or five feet deep. It was to this part that a swimmer would naturally go, for it formed a beautiful pellucid green pool as clear as crystal.
quotations.work: The Case Book of Sherlock Holmes

quotations.author: John Locke
quotations.passage: Blood to the naked Eye appears all red; but by a good Microscope, vvherein its lesser parts appear, shevvs only some fevv Globules of Red, svvimming in a pellucid Liquor; and hovv these Globules vvould appear, if Glasses could be found, that yet could magnifie them 1000, or 10000 times more, is uncertain.

quotations.author: Isaac Newton
quotations.passage: This Crystal is a pellucid fissile Stone, clear as VVater or Crystal of the Rock, and vvithout Colour; enduring a red Heat vvithout losing its transparency, and in a very strong Heat calcining vvithout Fusion.
quotations.work: Opticks: Or, A Treatise of the Reflections, Refractions, Inflections and Colours of Light.

quotations.author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon
quotations.passage: As a stream, clear and bright, becomes foul with weeds, and stagnates by its distant meanderings from its pure and pellucid source,—so the active imagination, the capacious intellect of Douglas, those high and valuable endowments, had, by an undue use of them, been perverted.

quotations.author: Robert Michael Ballantyne
quotations.passage: The sea was shining like a sheet of glass, […] and the bright sea-weeds and the brilliant corals shone in the depths of that pellucid water, as we rowed over it, like rare and precious gems.
quotations.work: The Coral Island: A Tale of the Pacific Ocean

quotations.author: Christina Rossetti
quotations.passage: You cannot think what figs / My teeth have met in, / What melons icy-cold / Piled on a dish of gold / Too huge for me to hold, / What peaches with a velvet nap, / Pellucid grapes without one seed: […]

quotations.author: Fritz Lanham
quotations.passage: Written in spare, pellucid prose, the book reads like a close-to-the-bone memoir.

quotations.author: Judith Butler
quotations.passage: [Y]ou never receive me apart from the grammar that establishes my availability to you. If I treat that grammar as pellucid, then I fail to call attention precisely to that sphere of language that establishes and disestablishes intelligibility, and that would be precisely to thwart my own project as I have described it to you here.
quotations.work: Gender Trouble: Feminism and the Subversion of Identity

quotations.author: Henry Robinson Luce
quotations.passage: Opera star [Giorgio] Tozzi sings with the richness of burnished bronze and [Sharon] Daniels complements him with her pellucid soprano.

quotations.author: Johann Jacob Hainlin
quotations.passage: A Pellucid is not seen, but percieved[sic] by the privation of Colour. So vve see not Air in Air, VVater in VVater, Glass in Glass, and every Pellucid in an equal Pellucid; and because vve knovv they are not coloured, vve count them to be diaphanous, viz. that may be seen, or shone thorough.
quotations.work: Synopsis Mathematica Universalis: Or, A Brief System of Mathematics

quotations.author: Herman Boerhaave
quotations.passage: The true Astroites, vvhich in the sun-shine throvvs out a brisk light radiating from one certain point, belongs to the class of Pellucids.
quotations.work: Elements of Chemistry. Being the Annual Lectures of Hermann Boerhaave, M.D.

pellucid.title: pellucid

etymologies: Unadapted borrowing from French penchant, present participle of pencher (“to tilt, to lean”), from Middle French, from Old French pengier (“to tilt, be out of line”), from Vulgar Latin *pendicāre, a derivative of Latin pendere (“to hang”).

examples: He has a penchant for fine wine.
definitions.text: A taste, liking, or inclination for (something).
A card game resembling bezique.
In the game of penchant, any queen and jack of different suits held at the same time.

quotations.author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon
quotations.passage: Marie even then began the course which, in after-years, secured her so vast an influence in the court,—alternately taking up and laying down her claim to the youthful monarch's penchant; administering to his amusement, and ready to encourage his passing fancies.

quotations.author: October
quotations.passage: THE LONDON & NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY. By O. S. Nock. Ian Allan. 30s. / [...] One scarcely imagined, for example, that the great steel works at Crewe owed its existence to Sir Richard Moon's penchant for the principle of "Do it yourself", a principle born of a methodical, economical and far-seeing mind.

quotations.author: Stephen Roberts
quotations.passage: Just like Marple, there's a plaque at the London terminus [Paddington] commemorating a fictional character - a polite, friendly little bear from darkest Peru who has a penchant for marmalade sarnies.

penchant.title: penchant

etymologies: From Middle English pensif, pensyfe, pencyve, from Old French pensif (“thoughtful”), from penser (“to think”) (from Latin pēnsō) + -if (English -ive).

examples: He sat in pensive silence, weighing his options carefully.
definitions.text: Engaged in, involving, or reflecting deep or serious thought.

examples: The author’s tone grows pensive in the final chapters.
definitions.text: Having the appearance of deep, often melancholic, thinking.
Looking thoughtful, especially from sadness.

quotations.author: David Hume
quotations.passage: Abstruse thought and profound researches I prohibit, and will severely punish, by the pensive melancholy which they introduce
quotations.work: Enquiries concerning the human understanding and concerning the principles of moral.

quotations.author: Miguel de Cervantes
quotations.passage: [T]he donkey, pensive, with bowed head, twitching his ears from time to time, thinking the tempest of stones had not yet ended and was still falling around his head […] .

quotations.author: J.G. Ballard
quotations.passage: Through the deep grass the faces of the three children glowed like pensive moons.

pensive.title: pensive

etymologies: From Latin paenultimus (“penultimate”) +‎ -ate (adjective-forming suffix), from paene (“almost”) +‎ ultimus (“last”). Equivalent to pene- +‎ ultimate. Compare French pénultième.
From a substantivation of the above adjective. Equivalent to Latin paenultimus +‎ -ate (noun-forming suffix).

definitions.text: Next to last, second to last; immediately preceding the end of a sequence, list, etc.
Of or pertaining to a penult.
Relating to or denoting an element of a related collection of curves that is arbitrarily close to a degenerate form.
pre-eminent, ultimate, best; par excellence, top-quality
The penultimate day of a month.
The penultimate syllable of a word or metrical line.
The penultimate element of a collection of curves.
The penultimate (next to lowest) card in a suit.

quotations.author: Robert Plot
quotations.passage: […] they [the sounds of an echo] next strike the ultimate secondary object, then the penultimate and antepenultimate; […]
quotations.work: The natural history of Oxford-shire: Being an Essay Toward the Natural History of England

quotations.author: Samuel Butler
quotations.passage: But it should frequently happen that offspring should resemble its penultimate rather than its latest phase, and should thus be more like a grand-parent than a parent.

quotations.author: Jack London
quotations.passage: “Your clothes don't weigh more'n seven pounds. And seven from—hum—say one hundred an' twenty-three—one hundred an' sixteen is your stripped weight.” / But at the penultimate word, Mary cried out with sharp reproof: / “Why, Billy Roberts, people don't talk about such things.”

quotations.author: Ethan Marshall
quotations.passage: Ultimately, I reach the most penultimate existential questions: “What is the meaning of this? Is there any?”
Our Lutheran concern for the ultimates (the Gospel) has allowed us to neglect some of the penultimates (bodily healing), failing to stress the total implications of that ultimate Gospel.
quotations.work: Minutes of the Adjourned Meeting of 22nd Biennial Convention of the United Lutheran Church in America

quotations.author: E. Chambers
quotations.passage: Antepenultimate is that before the Penultimate, or the last but two.

quotations.author: Arthur Campbell-Walker
quotations.passage: Penultimate, the. — Beginning with the lowest card but one of the suit you lead originally, if it contains more than four cards.

penultimate.title: penultimate

etymologies: From Medieval Latin pēnūriōsus. See penury from Latin penuria (“want”), related to paene (“scarcely”), c. 1400. Compare French pénurie.

examples: The old man died a penurious wretch; eighty-thousand dollars in the mattress and as many holes in the roof.
definitions.text: Miserly; excessively cheap.

examples: The penurious stew would have been more accurately labelled broth.
definitions.text: Not bountiful; thin; scant.

examples: The poor penurious horde, naught in the cooking pot and naught in the belly.
definitions.text: Impoverished; wanting for money.

quotations.author: October
quotations.passage: As the Swindon, Marlborough & Andover, conceived in 1872 and opened between the first two places in 1881 and to Andover and the L.S.W.R. in 1883, it was one of many small, ambitious and penurious Victorian lines, deeply concerned in the skulduggery characteristic of inter-railway dealings of that age and vexed by the G.W.R.

penurious.title: penurious

etymologies: Borrowed from Latin per contra.

definitions.text: in contrast, on the contrary

quotations.author: Matthew Prior
quotations.passage: Lord Oxford has been a twelvemonth in Herefordshire, as far from us, literally, though not geographically, as if he had been with you in Ireland. He has writ no more to us, than if we were still ministers of state. But, in the balance of account, per contra, I have lord Harley at London; and have either lived with him at Wimple, or upon him here, ever since his father left us.

quotations.author: John Laird
quotations.passage: […] Per contra, Hobbes, who was no tyrannophobe, declared instead that political citizens were as a God to one another, while non-political men were to one another as arrant wolves (II, h).

per_contra.title: per contra

etymologies: Borrowed from Latin perambulō, perambulātus. Equivalent to per- +‎ ambulate.

definitions.text: To walk around, roam, or stroll.
To inspect (an area) on foot.

quotations.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
quotations.passage: The officials, in their gowns of grey, with a white St. Andrew’s cross on back and breast, and a white cloth carried before them on a staff, perambulated the city, adding the terror of man’s justice to the fear of God’s visitation.

quotations.author: William Booth
quotations.passage: Take, for instance, one of the most wretched classes of the community, the poor fellows who perambulate the streets as Sandwich Men. These are farmed out by certain firms.
quotations.work: In Darkest England and the Way Out

quotations.author: Jack London
quotations.passage: They dragged themselves from the swamp singly, and in twos and threes, more dead than alive, mere perambulating skeletons, until at last there were thirty of us.

perambulate.title: perambulate

etymologies: From Middle English parchaunce, from Old French par cheance (“by chance”).

examples: You wouldn't, perchance, have a bottle opener on you, would you?
definitions.text: Perhaps.

quotations.author: John Donne
quotations.passage: Perchance he for whom this bell tolls may be so ill, as that he knows not it tolls for him […]
quotations.work: Deuotions upon Emergent Occasions, and Seuerall Steps in My Sicknes

quotations.author: Alfred Tennyson
quotations.passage: “Yet pull not down my palace towers, that are / So lightly, beautifully built: / Perchance I may return with others there / When I have purged my guilt.”

quotations.author: Robert Browning
quotations.passage: A great black bird, Apollyon's bosom-friend, / Sailed past, nor beat his wide wing dragon-penned / That brushed my cap—perchance the guide I sought.
quotations.work: “Childe Roland to the Dark Tower Came”

perchance.title: perchance

etymologies: From Middle English perdurable, from Old French pardurable, from Medieval Latin perdūrābilis, from Latin perdurāre (“to endure”), from per- (“throughout”) + durare (“to last”).

definitions.text: Very durable; long-lasting.

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: O perdurable shame! Let's stab our selues.
quotations.work: Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies

quotations.author: John Skelton
quotations.passage: In Paradyce, that place of pleasure perdurable / The progeny of parrottis, were fayre and fauorable

quotations.author: Philip James Bailey
quotations.passage: Ere now marmoreal floods had spread their couch / Of perdurable snow, or granite wrought / Its skyward impulse from earth's hearth of fire / Up to insanest heights.

quotations.author: Max Beerbohm
quotations.passage: The Duke had given her already a horde of fine gifts; but these, he had said, were nothing—trash in comparison with the gift that was to ensure for her a perdurable felicity.
quotations.work: Zuleika Dobson, or, An Oxford Love Story

quotations.author: Ezra Pound
quotations.passage: There is one quality which unites all great and perdurable writers, you don't NEED schools and colleges to keep 'em alive.

quotations.author: Mastroianni
quotations.passage: Together, our studies show that the perception of moral decline is pervasive, perdurable, unfounded and easily produced.

perdurable.title: perdurable

etymologies: From Latin peregrinari (“to live or travel abroad”). See also peregrine and pilgrim.
From Latin peregrinatus (“having travelled abroad”), past participle of peregrinari.

definitions.text: To travel from place to place, or from one country to another, especially on foot; hence, to sojourn in foreign countries.
To travel through a specific place.
Peregrine; having travelled; exotic, foreign.

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: His humour is loftie, his discourse peremptorie: his tongue fyled, his eye ambitious, his gate maiesticall and his general behauiour vaine, rediculous, & thrasonicall. He is too picked, too spruce, too affected, to od, as it were, too peregrinat as I may call it.
quotations.work: A Pleasant Conceited Comedie Called, Loues Labors Lost.

quotations.author: James Fenimore Cooper
quotations.passage: You know the inveterate peregrinating habits of the club, and can judge, from your own besetting propensity to change your residence monthly, how difficult it might prove to resist the temptation of traversing a soil that is still virgin, so far as the perambulating feet of the members of our fraternity are concerned.
quotations.work: Notions of the Americans: Picked Up by a Travelling Bachelor. In Two Volumes

quotations.author: Edward Bulwer-Lytton
quotations.passage: Imagine this figure, grotesque, peregrinate, and to the eye of a peasant certainly diabolical, then perch it on the stile in the midst of those green English fields, and in sight of that primitive English village; there let it sit straddling, its long legs dangling down, a short German pipe emitting clouds from one corner of those sardonic lips, its dark eyes glaring through the spectacles full upon the Parson, yet askant upon Lenny Fairfield. Lenny Fairfield looked exceedingly frightened.
quotations.work: “My Novel”; Or Varieties in English Life

peregrinate.title: peregrinate

etymologies: From Middle English peregrin, borrowed from Old French peregrin, from Latin peregrīnus (“foreign”). Doublet of pilgrim.

examples: The Romani are perpetually peregrine people.
definitions.text: Wandering, travelling, migratory.
Not native to a region or country; foreign; alien.
Lacking essential debility.
Extrinsic or from without; exotic.
With "tone" Referring to the tonus peregrinus or 'wandering tone' in ecclesiastical chant and mode theory.
The peregrine falcon.
A foreigner; a person resident in a country other than his or her own.
A male given name from Latin; and of mostly British usage.

quotations.author: Francis Bacon
quotations.passage: peregrine and preternatural heat
quotations.work: Sylua Syluarum: Or A Naturall Historie. In Ten Centuries.

quotations.author: Mervyn Peake
quotations.passage: As soon as she had smiled her face altered again, and the petulant expression peregrine to her features took control.

peregrine.title: peregrine

etymologies: From Anglo-Norman peremptorie, parentorie et al. (Modern French péremptoire), and its source, Latin peremptōrius (“deadly; precluding debate, decisive”), from perimō (“destroy, thwart”), from per- (“thorough”) + emō (“to obtain, buy”).

definitions.text: Precluding debate or expostulation; not admitting of question or appeal.

examples: As this trial has now been postponed multiple times, there will be an adjournment to April 24, peremptory on the parties.
definitions.text: Of a date or deadline, absolutely requiring compliance or attendance; brooking no further delay; proceeding whether a party attends or not; final.
Positive in opinion or judgment; absolutely certain, overconfident, unwilling to hear any debate or argument (especially in a pejorative sense); dogmatic.
Firmly determined, resolute; obstinate, stubborn.
Accepting no refusal or disagreement; imperious, dictatorial.
A challenge to the admission of a juror, without the challenger needing to show good cause.

quotations.author: Oscar Wilde
quotations.passage: Upon the other hand, there are a great many people who, having no private property of their own, and being always on the brink of sheer starvation, are compelled to do the work of beasts of burden, to do work that is quite uncongenial to them, and to which they are forced by the peremptory, unreasonable, degrading Tyranny of want.
quotations.work: The Soul of Man Under Socialism

quotations.author: Francis Scott Fitzgerald
quotations.passage: […] less surprising than that he had been depressed by a book. Something was making him nibble at the edge of stale ideas as if his sturdy physical egotism no longer nourished his peremptory heart.

quotations.author: Francis Bacon
quotations.passage: there is no reason but if any of the outlawries be indeed without error, but it should be a peremptory plea to the person in a writ of error, as well as in any other action.

quotations.author: Andrew Marr
quotations.passage: He marched under a placard reading "End Bossiness Now" but decided it was a little too peremptory, not quite British, so changed the slogan on subsequent badges, to "End Bossiness Soon."

quotations.author: Anthony Howard
quotations.passage: Though today (surveying that yellowing document) I shudder at the peremptory tone of the instructions I gave, Alastair - in that same volume in which I get chastised for my coverage of the Macmillan rally - was generous enough to remark that my memorandum became 'an office classic'.

peremptory.title: peremptory

etymologies: The adjective is borrowed from Latin perennis (“lasting through the whole year or for several years, perennial; continual, everlasting, perpetual”) + English -al (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives). Perennis is derived from per- (“completive or intensifying prefix with the sense of doing something all the way through or entirely”) + annus (“year; season, time”) (possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂et- (“to go”)). By surface analysis, per- +‎ -ennial.
The noun is derived from the adjective.

examples: a perennial stream
definitions.text: Lasting or remaining active throughout the year, for multiple years, or all the time.

examples: His artwork has a perennial beauty.
definitions.text: Continuing without cessation or intermission for several years, or for an undetermined or infinite period; never-ending or never failing; perpetual, unceasing.

examples: a perennial candidate in elections
Change is a perennial theme in politics.
definitions.text: Appearing or recurring again and again; recurrent.
Appearing again each year; annual.
Of a plant: active throughout the year, or having a life cycle of more than two growing seasons.
A plant that is active throughout the year, or has a life cycle of more than two growing seasons.
A thing that lasts forever.
A person or thing (such as a problem) that appears or returns regularly.

quotations.author: Samuel Johnson
quotations.passage: Good humour may be defined a habit of being pleased, a constant and perennial softness of manner, easiness of approach, and suavity of disposition; […]

quotations.author: Charles Dickens
quotations.passage: She has a large gold eye-glass, has Lady Tippins, to survey the proceedings with. If she had one in each eye, it might keep that other drooping lid up, and look more uniform. But perennial youth is in her artificial flowers, and her list of lovers is full.

quotations.author: Herman Melville
quotations.passage: That desert's age the gorge may prove, / Piercing profound the mountain bare; / Yet hardly churned out in the groove / By a perennial wear and tear / Of floods; nay, dry it shows within; / But twice a year the waters flow, / Nor then in tide, but dribbling thin: […]
quotations.work: Clarel: A Poem and Pilgrimage in the Holy Land.

quotations.author: Edmund Burke
quotations.passage: The perennial existence of bodies corporate and their fortunes, are things particularly suited to a man who has long views; who meditates designs that require time in fashioning; and which propose duration when they are accomplished.
quotations.work: Reflections on the Revolution in France, and on the Proceedings in Certain Societies in London Relative to that Event.

quotations.author: Henry David Thoreau
quotations.passage: It [the pond] is a clear and deep green well, half a mile long and a mile and three quarters in circumference, and contains about sixty-one and a half acres; a perennial spring in the midst of pine and oak woods, without any visible inlet or outlet except by the clouds and evaporation.
quotations.work: Walden; or, Life in the Woods

quotations.author: Thomas Carlyle
quotations.passage: Has Ireland been governed in a 'wise and loving' manner? A government and guidance of white European men which has issued in perennial hunger of potatoes to the third man extant,—ought to drop a veil over its fact, and walk out of court under conduct of proper officers; saying no word; expecting now of a surety sentence either to change or die.

quotations.author: John Evelyn
quotations.passage: [W]hat is most admirable is the vast enclosure, and variety of ground, in ye large garden, containing vineyards, cornefields, meadows, groves (whereof one is of perennial greens), and walkes of vast lengthes, so accurately kept and cultivated, that nothing can be more agreeable.
quotations.work: Memoirs, Illustrative of the Life and Writings of John Evelyn

quotations.author: William Derham
quotations.passage: And there is such a thing as Subterraneous Heat, […] [a]s is manifest from the smoking of perennial Fountains in frosty VVeather, and VVater dravvn out of Pumps and open VVells.
quotations.work: Physico-Theology: Or, A Demonstration of the Being and Attributes of God, from His Works of Creation.

quotations.author: Chinle Miller
quotations.passage: These offshore Sonoman mountains likely formed an orogenic (mountainous) barrier to moisture inland, resulting in a mountain-shadow onshore desert punctuated by regional annual and large basin perennial streams draining into a forearc saline sea.
quotations.work: In Mesozoic Lands: The Mesozoic Geology of Arches and Canyonlands National Parks

quotations.author: Leonard Welsted
quotations.passage: There, on perennial Adamant design'd, / The various Fortunes of your Race you'll find: […]

quotations.author: John Boyle O’Reilly
quotations.passage: Her name was Liberty! Earth lay before her, / And throbbed unconscious fealty and truth; / Morning and night men hastened to adore her, / And from her eyes Peace drew perennial youth.

quotations.author: Free-lance
quotations.passage: Ludgate Hill is not Moirosi’s Mountain, but, after all, is only a gentle ascent of about half an inch in the foot, over a length of about two hundred yards, up which unshod omnibus horses would trot with a full load in any weather. Yet there it must remain, a chief thoroughfare in the heart of London, a perennial cause of complaint, and of fear, disgust, and injury to man and horse.
quotations.work: Horses and Roads: Or How to Keep a Horse Sound on His Legs

quotations.author: Annie Besant
quotations.passage: Of all the questions which, throughout the centuries, have escaped from the lips of man, there is none which has been asked with such persistence, none which has possessed interest more perennial, than "Whence do I come? Whither shall I go?" Man's origin, man's hereafter, have ever been of intensest interest to man.

quotations.author: Robert Fiske Griggs
quotations.passage: One would have supposed from the appearance of the country at the end of the first season after the eruption that practically all plants except the trees and bushes had been destroyed, and that revegetation must be due to new seedlings started on the ash. Such, however, is not the case. Excavation of the root systems of the new plants shows that they are old perennials which have come through the ash from the old soil.

quotations.author: Sterling Whitaker
quotations.passage: Some of the stars on our list are perennials who fill huge venues year after year after year, but there's also a returning superstar on our list of the hottest summer tours of 2019.

perennial.title: perennial

etymologies: From Late Latin perfervidus, from Latin per- + fervidus. By surface analysis, per- +‎ fervid; compare pellucid.

definitions.text: Extremely, excessively, or feverishly passionate; zealous.

quotations.author: Philip George Chadwick
quotations.passage: Manders — perfervid — 'hell'-ing excitedly (was there no one left on earth to convert but me?), quoting over a century from Marx and Nietzsche to Lenin, Lloyd George, and Eden, and on to Vessant and Mundaine and himself...

quotations.author: Lawrence Durrell
quotations.passage: In this case he saw himself sitting beside the breathing slender figure of Pia like someone in an old engraving – a beastly old Rembrandt exhaling the perfervid gloom of Protestantism and a diet of turnips.

quotations.author: Nick Cave
quotations.passage: Ah threw mahself down the porch steps and fell to mah knees in the middle of the yard, wringing mah hands and beating at the sky and wailing and reeling in the red dust and petitioning the almighty with perfervid prayer.
quotations.work: And the Ass Saw the Angel

quotations.author: Joseph O'Conner
quotations.passage: A clown, Grantley Dixon, a perfervid parrot, with his militant slogans and second-hand attitudes: like all coffee-house radicals a screaming snob at heart.

quotations.author: Ross Douthat
quotations.passage: Once again we’re debating the programming choices of prominent podcasters: In March the instigating event was Joe Rogan giving a platform to Ian Carroll, a propagator of perfervid critiques of Israel; this time it’s Tucker Carlson giving a platform to Nick Fuentes, the Hitler-admiring leader of the so-called groyper right.

perfervid.title: perfervid

etymologies: From Latin perfidiōsus (“treacherous”), from perfidia. By surface analysis, perfidy +‎ -ous.

definitions.text: Of, pertaining to, or representing perfidy; disloyal to what should command one's fidelity or allegiance.

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: TRINCULO (speaking about Caliban): By this light, a most perfidious and drunken / monster: when his god's asleep, he'll rob his bottle.
quotations.work: Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies

quotations.author: Edward Forster
quotations.passage: Ali Baba not only remained with his perfidious guest, who sought his life in return for his hospitaliy, until Morgiana had served the supper, but he conversed with him on various subjects, which he thought might amuse him, and did not leave him till he had finished the repast he had provided.

quotations.author: Oliver Goldsmith
quotations.passage: The perfidious Ricimer soon became dissatisfied with Anthe'mius, and raised the standard of revolt.

quotations.author: Andrew Lang
quotations.passage: [S]he knew Huntly for the ambitious traitor he was, a man peculiarly perfidious and self-seeking.

quotations.author: Art: The Velocipede of Modernism
quotations.passage: When the Nazis branded Feininger a "degenerate artist" in 1937, he left 54 paintings for safekeeping with a Bauhaus friend named Hermann Klumpp. After the war, and for the rest of Feininger's life, the perfidious Klumpp refused to give them back.

quotations.author: John Dugdale
quotations.passage: Enraged, the 2010 Nobel literature laureate thundered that he was “flabbergasted to learn that this kind of gossip can find its way into a respectable publication such as the Book Review” - a “slanderous and perfidious” instance of the convergence of posh and pop that his book inveighs against.

perfidious.title: perfidious

etymologies: From Middle French perfidie, from Latin perfidia from perfidus (“faithless, treacherous, false”), from fides (“faith”); related to, for example, English fidelity.

definitions.text: A state or act of violating faith or allegiance; violation of a promise or vow, or of trust.
An illegitimate act of deception, such as using symbols like the Red Cross or white flag in a false claim of surrender to gain proximity to an enemy for purposes of attack.
A state or act of deceit.

quotations.author: Lassa Oppenheim with Ronald Francis Roxburgh
quotations.passage: Stratagems must be carefully distinguished strategy from perfidy, since the former are allowed, whereas the latter is prohibited.

quotations.author: Leslie C. Green
quotations.passage: Abuse of a protective emblem amounts to perfidy and constitutes a war crime under the customary law of armed conflict.
quotations.work: The contemporary law of armed conflict

quotations.author: Sidney Axinn
quotations.passage: Ruses of war are legitimate so long as they do not involve treachery or perfidy on the part of the belligerent resorting to them.

quotations.author: James Bennet
quotations.passage: Cyberattacks almost inevitably involve an element of deception, such as tricking a user to click on a malicious link. So, to what extent could cyberattacks count as perfidy and therefore be illegal given international humanitarian law?

quotations.author: Barbara Wertheim Tuchman
quotations.passage: Germans could not get over the perfidy of it. It was unbelievable that the English, having degenerated to the stage where suffragettes heckled the Prime Minister and defied the police, were going to fight.

quotations.author: Honda becomes chain letter victim
quotations.passage: Honda Motor Co. is the latest victim of e-mail perfidy, which started when a phony chain letter promised that the automaker would give away free cars.

quotations.author: McCain expected to make amends on Letterman show
quotations.passage: Letterman roared about the perfidy of lying politicos.

perfidy.title: perfidy

etymologies: From Middle English par force, from Anglo-Norman, from Old French par force (“by force”).

definitions.text: By constraint of circumstances; of necessity; as a matter of course.
By force.
To force; to compel.

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: If she denie, Lord Hastings goe with him, / And from her iealous Armes pluck him perforce.
quotations.work: Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: For you, most wicked sir, whom to call brother / Would even infect my mouth, I do forgive / Thy rankest fault; all of them; and require / My dukedom of thee, which, perforce, I know / Thou must restore.
quotations.work: Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies

quotations.author: Jane Austen
quotations.passage: Mr. Wickham's happiness and her own were perforce delayed a little longer, and Mr. Collins's proposal accepted with as good a grace as she could..

quotations.author: James Joyce
quotations.passage: So, bevelling around by Mullett's and the Signal House which they shortly reached, they proceeded perforce in the direction of Amiens street railway terminus

quotations.author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
quotations.passage: "Keep fast thy hold, for by such stairs as these," / The Master said, panting as one fatigued, / "Must we perforce depart from so much evil."

quotations.author: July
quotations.passage: Accordingly work perforce had to be begun. The first sod was cut at Anley, near Settle, in November, 1869, […]

quotations.author: John Wyndham
quotations.passage: It was by no means pleasant to realize that there was an unknown number of menaces up there over your head, quietly circling and circling until someone should arrange for them to drop - and that there was nothing to be done about them. Still, life has to go on - and novelty is a wonderfully short-lived thing. One became used to the idea perforce.

quotations.author: Alejandro Portes
quotations.passage: Adult immigrants must perforce learn some English, and their children are likely to become English monolinguals.

quotations.author: European Court of Human Rights
quotations.passage: The central issue in this case is whether the procedures followed respected the applicants’ family life or constituted an interference with the exercise of the right to respect for family life which could not be justified as necessary in a democratic society. […] It is true that Article 8 contains no explicit procedural requirements, but this is not conclusive of the matter. The relevant considerations to be weighed by a local authority in reaching decisions on children in its care must perforce include the views and interests of the natural parents.

perforce.title: perforce

etymologies: From Late Latin perfunctōrius (“careless, negligent”), from the past participial stem of perfungor, perfunct- (“perform, carry through”), from per- + fungor.

examples: a perfunctory kiss
definitions.text: Done only or merely to conform to a minimal standard or to fulfill a protocol or presumptive duty.

examples: He did a perfunctory job cleaning his dad's car, finishing quickly but leaving a few spots still dirty.
definitions.text: Performed in a careless or indifferent manner as a thing of rote.

quotations.author: Edgar Rice Burroughs
quotations.passage: I caught the gist of what he was saying--which in effect was that he had found and captured this Galu, that she was his and that he defied anyone to question his right of possession. It appeared to me, as I afterward learned was the fact, that I was witnessing the most primitive of marriage ceremonies. The assembled members of the tribe looked on and listened in a sort of dull and perfunctory apathy, for the speaker was by far the mightiest of the clan.

quotations.author: Saul Bellow
quotations.passage: He then poured some wine for me to taste, and harassed me with perfunctory courtesies that had to be acknowledged.

quotations.author: Ali Barthwell
quotations.passage: The second section of the episode charged from Winterfell to Highgarden and Oldtown in a way that felt perfunctory. I found myself asking, “We’re just getting to Winterfell?”

quotations.author: Luke Broadwater
quotations.passage: Even as former administration officials and Democratic leaders called on the president to tell his supporters to “go home,” Mr. Trump for hours did little to discourage them from storming the building. Instead, he issued two perfunctory tweets in which he asked them merely to remain “peaceful.”

quotations.author: Peter Bowbrick
quotations.passage: Alternatively it may mean that a perfunctory search is enough to ensure that a purchase is acceptable, so less search is carried out.
quotations.work: The Economics of Quality, Grades, and Brands

perfunctory.title: perfunctory

etymologies: From French périgée via Latin perigeum, perigaeum, ultimately from Ancient Greek περί (perí, “near”) + γῆ (gê, “Earth”).

definitions.text: The point, in an orbit about the Earth, that is closest to the Earth: the periapsis of an Earth orbiter.
The point, in an orbit about any planet, that is closest to the planet: the periapsis of any satellite.
The point, in any trajectory of an object in space, where it is closest to the Earth.

quotations.author: Natalie Angier
quotations.passage: As the moon wheels around Earth every 28 days and shows us a progressively greater and then stingier slice of its sun-lightened face, the distance between the moon and Earth changes, too. At the nearest point along its egg-shaped orbit, its perigee, the moon may be 26,000 miles closer to us than it is at its far point.

quotations.author: John H. Rogers
quotations.passage: Conjunctions of I and II [Io and Europa] occur when they are near perigee and apogee respectively; conjunctions of II and III [Europa and Ganymede] occur when II [Europa] is near perigee.

quotations.author: Serge Brunier
quotations.passage: The resolution of the images obtained by this American probe [Messenger] will depend on its altitude [above Mercury] at any one time: about ten meters at perigee (200km altitude), but only one 1 km at apogee (15000km).

quotations.author: Ruth Walker
quotations.passage: [Nereid’s] apogee—farthest point from Neptune—is five times the distance of its perigee—its closest point.

perigee.title: perigee

etymologies: From French péripatétique, from Latin peripatēticus, from Ancient Greek περιπατητικός (peripatētikós, “given to walking around”), from περιπατέω (peripatéō, “to walk around”), from περί (perí, “around”) (English peri-)+ πατέω (patéō, “to walk”).

definitions.text: Tending to walk about.
Constantly travelling.
One who walks about; a pedestrian; an itinerant.
A disciple of Aristotle.
Of or pertaining to the philosophy or methods of Aristotle, or to his followers.

quotations.author: Elizabeth Day
quotations.passage: After peripatetic upbringing that took her from America to Portugal, Switzerland, Belgium and England, [Mary-Kay] Wilmers read French and Russian at Oxford.

quotations.author: James Howell
quotations.passage: The true peripatetic school.

quotations.author: Harry E. Wedeck
quotations.passage: Demetreius of Phalerum, a peripatetic philosopher of the fourth century B.C., wrote an amatory treatise entitled Eroticus - no longer, however, extant.

quotations.author: Albert Upton
quotations.passage: He who would think clearly must think like a peripatetic even if he is unwilling to walk like one.
quotations.work: Design for Thinking: A First Book in Semantics

peripatetic.title: peripatetic

etymologies: From Late Latin peripetia, and its source Ancient Greek περιπέτεια (peripéteia), from περιπίπτω (peripíptō, “to change suddenly”), from περί (perí, “round, around, about”) + the stem of πίπτω (píptō, “to fall”).

definitions.text: A sudden reversal of fortune as a plot point in Classical tragedy.
Any sudden change in circumstances; a crisis.
A turning point in psychosocial development.

quotations.author: Herbert Weir Smyth
quotations.passage: If we recoil with the consternation of surprise at such a conclusion, it is no defense to invoke as parallel the peripeteia by which Euripides in his Ion leads us to expect one ending yet effects another.

quotations.author: John Fowles
quotations.passage: Once more I was a man in a myth, incapable of understanding it, but somehow aware that understanding it meant it must continue, however sinister its peripeteia.

quotations.author: Alistair Horne
quotations.passage: They were to bestride the Algerian scene like demigods until the tragic peripeteia of 1961 […]

quotations.author: Elizabeth Abel
quotations.passage: The visual moment whose consequences Freud began to ponder in the essay on the phallic stage has evolved into a peripeteia: "Some day or other it happens that the child whose own penis is such a proud possession obtains a sight of the genital parts of a little girl; he must then become convinced of the absence of a penis in a creature so like himeself. With this, however, the loss of his own penis becomes imaginable, and the threat of castration achieves its delayed effect."
quotations.work: Virginia Woolf and the Fictions of Psychoanalysis

peripeteia.title: peripeteia

etymologies: From peripher(y) + -al.

definitions.text: On the periphery or boundary.
Beside the point.
Unimportant.
Auxiliary.
Related to or located in the peripheral nervous system.
A peripheral device.
Peripheral vision.

quotations.author: Isolation and analysis of the gene encoding peripheral myelin protein zero
quotations.passage: We have isolated the gene encoding the Schwann cell glycoprotein P0, the major structural protein of the peripheral myelin sheath.

quotations.author: Human Connection
quotations.passage: Check your peripheral's manual for the information you'll need.
quotations.work: Making MS-DOS & PC-DOS work for you

quotations.author: Ziff-Davis Publishing Company
quotations.passage: Check your peripheral's owners' manual to see at what speed your peripheral transmits or receives information, and then record this on the DIP Switch Information chart in the column at the left.

quotations.author: Steve Birchall
quotations.passage: Turn on the Mac, and check your peripheral. Since you've already installed your device driver, it should be available where you need it....

quotations.author: Eric Jerome Dicke
quotations.passage: We hailed a cab. The moment we got in, she stared at me with how-can-a-man-be-so-cruel eyes. I felt her glare, saw some of its fiery glow in my peripheral. The heat made me glance her way.

quotations.author: Maynard James Keenan
quotations.passage: Peripheral on the package / Don't care to settle in / Time to feed the monster / I don't need another friend / Comfort is a mystery / Crawling out of my own skin / Just give me what I came for / Then I'm out the door again

quotations.author: Kim Louise
quotations.passage: He would hear the coach's admonition, "Always check your peripheral," after the ringing stopped in his ears. But before then, his eyes were fixed on the ball and a possible interception, not the receiver angling toward him.

quotations.author: Saye Z. B. Zonen
quotations.passage: As I sat by the window and read, I caught sight of the mailman in my peripheral.

peripheral.title: peripheral

etymologies: From Ancient Greek περίφρασις (períphrasis).

definitions.text: The use of a longer expression instead of a shorter one with a similar meaning, for example "I am going to" instead of "I will".

examples: Language learners sometimes use periphrases like "did go" where a native speaker would use "went".
Native speakers use periphrases like "did not go" where a language learner might use "went not".
definitions.text: Expressing a grammatical meaning (such as a tense) using a syntactic construction rather than morphological marking.
The substitution of a descriptive word or phrase for a proper name (a type of circumlocution).
The use of a proper name as a shorthand to stand for qualities associated with it.

quotations.author: Larret Langley
quotations.passage: Periphrasis a single thought expands, / And uses many words for what but few demands.
quotations.work: A Manual of the Figures of Rhetoric

quotations.author: F. D. Morice
quotations.passage: The "glen," or the "brake of the lion," is Pindar's favourite periphrasis for Nemea.

periphrasis.title: periphrasis

etymologies: From Middle English permeable, permiable, from Latin permeābilis.

examples: permeable strata
Rainwater sinks through permeable rock to form an underground reservoir.
definitions.text: Able to be permeated; absorbing or allowing the passage of fluids.

examples: permeable borders
permeable boundaries
definitions.text: Allowing the passage of persons, information, or other things, especially when such passage occurs despite hopes or expectations otherwise.

quotations.passage: One hundred thirty-one small, highly permeable masonry wall specimens built of concrete blocks or of bricks were treated with cement-water paints or with other waterproofings.
quotations.work: Publications of the National Bureau of Standards

permeable.title: permeable

examples: water permeates sand
definitions.text: To pass through the pores or interstices of; to penetrate and pass through without causing rupture or displacement; applied especially to fluids which pass through substances of loose texture

examples: Bright sunshine permeates the room on a sunny day.
definitions.text: To enter and spread through; to pervade.

examples: (Can we add an example for this sense?)
definitions.text: A watery by-product of milk production.

examples: (Can we add an example for this sense?)
definitions.text: Liquid that has passed through a filtration system.

quotations.author: O. Henry
quotations.passage: In the fulness of time there was an eruption of the merry-makers to the sidewalk. The uninvited guests enveloped and permeated them, and upon the night air rose joyous cries, congratulations, laughter and unclassified noises born of McGary's oblations to the hymeneal scene.

quotations.author: William Shackleton
quotations.passage: The old smell of dead whale permeates everything. It is a strange and curious place.

quotations.author: May and June
quotations.passage: Also, much depended on an exceptional esprit de corps which permeated the whole staff, and achieved miracles of promptitude in such details as engine-changing and the marshalling of trains.

quotations.author: Kaori Enjoji
quotations.passage: The do-or-die mentality gambaru permeates Japanese society, where the pursuit of a goal can carry more significance than the outcome.

permeate.title: permeate

etymologies: From Middle English, from Old French pernicios, from Latin perniciōsus (“destructive”), from perniciēs (“destruction”), from per (“through”) + nex (“slaughter, death”).
Analyzable as pernīx ("swift") + -ious.

examples: pernicious influence
pernicious effects
They warned of the pernicious effects of misinformation.
The weed has a pernicious influence on local crops.
definitions.text: Causing much harm in a subtle way.
Causing death or injury; deadly.
Insidiously villainous: intending to cause harm, especially in a subtle way.
swift; celeritous.

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: Ang. Belieue me on mine Honor, / My words expresse my purpose. / Isa. Ha? Little honor, to be much beleeu'd, / And most pernitious purpose: Seeming, seeming. / I will proclaime thee Angelo, looke for't.
quotations.work: Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies

quotations.author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon
quotations.passage: […] her health also having suffered by the change, she immediately, when told of Douglas's projected departure from India, felt the strongest desire to accompany him; and to which Colonel Melbourne the more readily consented, having with reluctance yielded to her request of quitting England, willing as he had been to sacrifice the enjoyment of her society rather than that she should submit to the disadvantages attendant upon a residence in a clime usually found so pernicious to the female constitution.

quotations.author: Emma Goldman
quotations.passage: Puritanism no longer employs the thumbscrew and lash; but it still has a most pernicious hold on the minds and feelings of the American people.

quotations.author: Jacob Kastrenakes
quotations.passage: In January, the company laid off a third of its staff and renounced ads as a pernicious influence on the world, without mentioning that Google and Facebook are so good at ads there’s hardly room for anyone else to compete.

quotations.author: Toni Bentley
quotations.passage: A man has always been a woman’s best excuse to avoid her destiny; that a man is her destiny is one of patriarchy’s most pernicious tenets. What a scam.
quotations.work: The New York Times Book Review

pernicious.title: pernicious

etymologies: First attested in 1603; borrowed from Latin perōrātus, perfect passive participle of perōrō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). By surface analysis, per- +‎ orate.

definitions.text: To speak or declaim at great length, especially in a pompous or grandiloquent manner; to harangue.
To make a peroration; to make a formal recapitulation at the end of a speech.

perorate.title: perorate

From Middle French parpain, see etymology of French parpaing.

A vertical joint (usually mortar) between bricks or blocks in a horizontal course.

quotations.author: William Shakespeare

quotations.work: Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies

perpend.title: perpend

definitions.text: Any monetary or other incidental benefit beyond salary.

examples: After the wonderful service that evening he didn’t hesitate in laying a substantial perquisite on the table.
definitions.text: A gratuity.

examples: Private jets and motor yachts are perquisites of the rich.
definitions.text: A privilege or possession held or claimed exclusively by a certain person, group or class.

quotations.author: David L. Lieber
quotations.passage: The tithe properly belongs to the Lord who, in turn, assigns it to the Levites as payments for their sanctuary labors. Thus levitical and priestly perquisites are gifts from God.

quotations.author: Thomas S. Kuhn
quotations.passage: Why is progress a perquisite reserved almost exclusively for the activities we call science?

perquisite.title: perquisite

etymologies: From French persiflage, from persifler (“to quiz, tease, mock”), from per- + siffler (“to whistle”), from Latin sībilō (“whistle”).

examples: After the third strike he returned to the bench to face the inevitable persiflage from his teammates.

examples: Polite dinner calls for persiflage rather than in-depth possibly offensive discussion.
definitions.text: Frivolous, lighthearted discussion of a topic.

quotations.author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon
quotations.passage: No one can deny Lady Charlotte Bury's assertion, that no well-regulated young female will ever indulge in a species of amusement so improper as flirtation; but it must be admitted, that having a pleasant partner is preferable to not dancing, and that a little persiflage, a little raillery, a little flattery, go far to make a partner pleasant.

persiflage.title: persiflage

Suggested to be from Etruscan 𐌘𐌄𐌓𐌔𐌖 (φersu, “mask; masked individual; actor”), which could be a loan from Ancient Greek πρόσωπον (prósōpon, “face; appearance; mask used in ancient theatre to denote a character or, more generally, a social role”). Doublet of person and parson.

An imaginary person representing a particular type of client or customer, considered when designing products and services that will appeal to them.

quotations.author: Ben Cost

Wokefishermen can be thought of like catfishers — those who use fake online personas to defraud victims — but only for sex instead of money.

quotations.author: Ira Kaufman

persona.title: persona

definitions.text: Of acute discernment; having keen insight; mentally perceptive.
Able to physically see clearly; quick-sighted; sharp-sighted.

quotations.author: David K. Jose
quotations.passage: As a gay prisoner my incarceration has given me a perspicacious view of our judicial system.

perspicacious.title: perspicacious

etymologies: From pertinace +‎ -ious, from Old French pertinace, from Latin pertinax, from per- (“very”) + tenax (“tenacious”).

definitions.text: Holding tenaciously to an opinion or purpose.
Stubbornly resolute or tenacious.

quotations.author: William Makepeace Thackeray
quotations.passage: When that divine took his leave, not a little discomfited and amazed at the pertinacious obstinacy of the women, Laura repeated her embraces and arguments with tenfold fervour to Helen, who felt that there was a great deal of cogency in most of the latter.

quotations.author: Henry James
quotations.passage: He would really have to make up his mind to care for his wife or not to care for her. What would Lady Vandeleur say to one alternative, and what would little Joscelind say to the other? That is what it was to have a pertinacious father and to be an accommodating son.

quotations.author: Henry Rider Haggard
quotations.passage: For, whether they were attracted by the lantern, or by the unaccustomed smell of a white man for which they had been waiting for the last thousand years or so, I know not; but certainly we were presently attacked by tens of thousands of the most bloodthirsty, pertinacious, and huge mosquitoes that I ever saw or read of.

pertinacious.title: pertinacious

To read completely.
To look over casually; to skim.
To go from place to place; to wander.
An examination or perusal; an instance of perusing.

quotations.author: Charlotte Brontë
quotations.passage: Sitting on a low stool, a few yards from her arm-chair, I examined her figure; I perused her features.

quotations.author: William Petty
quotations.passage: This survey may be made by perusing al Books and taking notice of all Mechanicall Inventions.

quotations.author: Tobias Smollett
quotations.passage: And let not the incredulous reader pretend to doubt the truth of this phenomenon, until he shall have first perused the ingenious Peter Kolben’s Natural History of the Cape of Good Hope, where the inhabitants commonly use to strike fire with the shin-bones of lions which have been killed in that part of Africk.

quotations.author: Henry Rider Haggard

quotations.author: William L. Shirer

quotations.author: Doug Stanton

quotations.author: Al Lovejoy

quotations.author: Katharine Viner

quotations.author: Robert Ruark
quotations.passage: I loved to straggle off in the mornings […] , just perusing around for firewood.

quotations.author: Dave Robson
quotations.passage: A peruse of the website looked promising […]

peruse.title: peruse

examples: The medication had a pervasive effect on the patient's health.

pervasive.title: pervasive
