quotations.author: George Colman
quotations.passage: In the evening I shall hope for the honour of your Lordship's company to take a dish of tea there, or a sullabub warm from the cow.

quotations.author: Elizabeth Raffald
quotations.passage: Whip Syllabubs. Take a Pint of thin Cream, rub a Lump of Loaf Sugar on the Out-side of a Lemon, and sweeten it to your Taste, then put in the Juice of a Lemon, and a Glass of Madeira Wine, or French Brandy, mill it to a Froth with a Chocolate Mill, and take it off as it rises, and lay it upon a Hair Sieve, then fill one half of your Posset Glasses, a little more than half full with White Wine, and the other half of your Glasses a little more than half full of Red Wine, then lay on your Froth as high as you can, but observe that it is well drained on your Sieve, or it will mix with your Wine, and spoil your Syllabubs.

quotations.author: Hannah Glasse
quotations.passage: To Make a Syllabub under the Cow. Put a bottle of either red or white wine, ale, or cyder, into a china bowl, sweeten it with sugar, and grate in some nutmeg; then hold it under the cow, and milk into it till it has a fine froth at the top; strew over it a handful of currants, clean washed and picked, and plumped before the fire. You may make this syllabub at home, by having new milk made as warm as from the cow, and pouring it out of a tea pot, or any other vessel with a spout, holding your hand very high.
quotations.work: The Complete Confectioner; or, Housekeeper's Guide: To a Simple and Speedy Method of Understanding the Whole Art of Confectionary; [...]

quotations.author: Maria Eliza Ketelby Rundell
quotations.passage: London Syllabub. Put a pint and a half of port or white wine into a bowl, nutmeg grated, and a good deal of sugar, then milk into it near two quarts of milk, frothed up. If the wine be not rather sharp, it will require more for this quantity of milk. In Devonshire clouted cream is put on the top, and pounded cinnamon and sugar.
quotations.work: A New System of Domestic Cookery; Formed upon Principles of Economy: and Adapted to the Use of Private Families

quotations.author: Thomas Hughes
quotations.passage: [A]s small boys, we pelt one another and the village school-girls and our nursemaids and young lady cousins with they hay, till, hot and weary, we retire to tea or syllabub beneath the shade of some great oak or elm standing up like a monarch out of the fair pasture; […]

quotations.author: Una
quotations.passage: [H]is kind mother, when she fancied the croquet was flagging, thought of a sillabub—and lo! in walked a meek looking cow, adorned with flowers, and furnished the party with a most fragrant and most refreshing draught.

quotations.author: Hannah Glasse
quotations.passage: To make Everlasting Syllabubs. Take three pints of the thickest and sweetest cream you can get, a pint of rhenish, half a pint of sack, three lemons, near a pound of double refined sugar, beat and sift your sugar, and put it to the cream; grate off the yellow rind of three lemons, put that in, and squeeze the juice of the three lemons into your wine; put that to the cream, beat all together with a whisk just half an hour, then take it up all together with a spoon, and fill your glasses.
quotations.work: The Complete Confectioner; or, Housekeeper's Guide: To a Simple and Speedy Method of Understanding the Whole Art of Confectionary; [...]

quotations.author: Maria Eliza Ketelby Rundell
quotations.passage: Everlasting, or Solid, Syllabubs. Mix a quart of thick raw cream, one pound of refined sugar, a pint and a half of fine raisin wine, in a deep pan; put to it the grated peel and the juice of three lemons. Beat, or whisk it one way, half an hour; then put it on a sieve with a bit of muslin laid smooth in the shallow end till next day. Put it in glasses. It will keep good, in a cool place, ten days.
quotations.work: A New System of Domestic Cookery;

quotations.author: Agatha Christie
quotations.passage: Mushroom soup. Curried chicken and rice. Syllabubs. A savoury of chicken livers and bacon.

quotations.author: Rowland Hill
quotations.passage: I like Paul's plain style best. Better to feed the appetite of the hungry, than to tickle the fancies of the whimsical. This breed of preachers are apt soon to preach themselves out of breath, and come to nothing. May you and I never be the retailers of such whipt-syllabub divinity—better keep a cook's-shop to satisfy the craving appetite, than a confectioner's-shop to regale the depraved appetite of the dainty. Good brown-bread preaching is the best after all.

definitions.text: A relationship of mutual benefit, especially among different species.

examples: Bees and flowers display symbiosis. The bees get nectar and the flowers get pollinated.

definitions.text: A figure of speech that uses the name of a part of something to represent the whole, or the whole to represent a part, or a specific kind or instance to represent the general category, or the general category to represent a specific kind or instance, or the constituent material to represent the thing made from it.

A taxonomic genus within the family Achilidae – certain planthoppers.

etymologies: Partly from Late Latin syntaxis and partly from its etymon, Ancient Greek σύνταξις (súntaxis), from σύν (sún, “together”) + τάξις (táxis, “arrangement”), from τάσσω (tássō, “to arrange”). Doublet of syntaxis.

The formal rules of formulating the statements of a computer language.
The study of the structure of phrases, sentences, and language.

quotations.author: Andrew Radford
quotations.passage: The incorporation of a rule of V MOVEMENT into our description of English Syntax turns out to have fundamental theoretical implications for our overall Theory of Grammar: it means that we are no longer able to posit that the syntactic structure of a sentence can be described in terms of a single Phrase-marker representing its S-structure. For, the postulation of a rule of V-MOVEMENT means that we must recognise at least two different levels of structure in our Theory of Grammar — namely, a level of D-structure (formerly known as ‘Deep Structureʼ) which serves as input to the rule, and a separate level of S-structure which is formed by application of the rule.

The combination of thesis and antithesis.

quotations.author: Andrew Marvell
quotations.passage: But in the mean time […] it looks all so like subterfuge and inveagling; it is so nauseating and teadious a task, that no man thinks he ovvs the Author so much service as to find out the reason of his ovvn Categoricalness for him.
quotations.work: The Rehearsal Transpros’d: Or, Animadversions upon a Late Book, Entituled, A Preface, Shewing what Grounds there are of Fears and Jealousies of Popery

quotations.author: William Cowper
quotations.passage: John Gilpin's spouse said to her dear, / Though wedded we have been / These twice ten tedious years, yet we / No holiday have seen.

tedious.title: tedious

etymologies: Learned borrowing from Latin temerārius (“accidental, casual, rash, reckless”), from temerē (“by chance, at random, rashly”).

definitions.text: Characterized by temerity; recklessly daring or bold.

quotations.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
quotations.passage: To look back upon the past year, and see how little we have striven and to what small purpose; and how often we have been cowardly and hung back, or temerarious and rushed unwisely in; and how every day and all day long we have transgressed the law of kindness;—it may seem a paradox, but in the bitterness of these discoveries, a certain consolation resides.
quotations.work: Across the Plains: With Other Memories and Essays

quotations.author: Thomas More
quotations.passage: […] he furthwith by thinstinct of yͤ spirite of god, in repꝛoche of all such temerarious bold & blind iudgement, geuē vpon a mā whose inward mind and sodain change they cannot see, shoꝛtly proued thē al deceiued, […]
quotations.work: The Workes of Sir Thomas More Knyght

quotations.author: John Buchan
quotations.passage: It was a very bright, hot winter's day, and try as I might, I could not bring myself to think of any danger. I believe that in this way most temerarious deeds are done; the doer has become insensible to danger, and his imagination is clouded with some engrossing purpose.

quotations.author: Edgar Rice Burroughs
quotations.passage: With a vicious lunge the elephant swerved to the right to dispose of this temerarious foeman who dared intervene between himself and his intended victim; but he had not reckoned on the lightning quickness that could galvanize those steel muscles into action so marvelously swift as to baffle even a keener eyesight than Tantor’s.

quotations.author: David Herbert Lawrence
quotations.passage: Primarily and supremely man is always the pioneer of life, adventuring onward into the unknown, alone with his own temerarious, dauntless soul.

temerarious.title: temerarious

etymologies: From Middle English temerite, temeryte, from Old French temerité, from Latin temeritās (“chance, accident, rashness”), from temere (“by chance, casually, rashly”). By surface analysis, temer(arious) +‎ -ity.

definitions.text: Reckless boldness; foolish bravery.
An act or case of reckless boldness.
Effrontery; impudence.

quotations.author: Charles Dickens
quotations.passage: One day when he knew old Lobbs was out, Nathaniel Pipkin had the temerity to kiss his hand to Maria Lobbs.
quotations.work: The Posthumous Papers of the Pickwick Club

quotations.author: Thomas Hardy
quotations.passage: Elizabeth trotted through the open door in the dusk, but becoming alarmed at her own temerity, she went quickly out again by another which stood open in the lofty wall of the back court.
quotations.work: The Mayor of Casterbridge: The Life and Death of a Man of Character.

quotations.author: Edith Wharton
quotations.passage: Draper, dear lad, had the illusion of an "intellectual sympathy" between them.... Draper's temerities would always be of that kind.

quotations.author: Firishta
quotations.passage: Jewan Sadit, who stood before the prince, observing his youthful temerity, threw himself between him and danger, and with a nervous arm, wielding a sharp sabre, of the hard tempered steel of Damisk, rushing upon the tyger, he struck him across the forehead.
quotations.work: Tales translated from the Persian of Inatulla of Delhi

quotations.author: Herbert George Wells
quotations.passage: Terror seized me, a horror of my temerity.

quotations.author: Edgar Rice Burroughs
quotations.passage: I am surprised that you, sir, a man of letters yourself, should have the temerity so to interrupt the progress of science.

quotations.author: James Fennimore Cooper
quotations.passage: He had very nearly been guilty of the temerity of arrogating to himself another title in the presence of those he most respected.

quotations.author: Woody Allen
quotations.passage: That's jejune? You have the temerity to say that I'm talking to you out of jejunosity? I am one of the most june people in all of the Russias!

temerity.title: temerity

etymologies: From Old French tempeste (French tempête), from Latin tempestas (“storm”), from tempus (“time, weather”). Displaced native Old English hrīþ.

definitions.text: A storm, especially one with severe winds.
Any violent tumult or commotion.
A fashionable social gathering; a drum.
To storm.
To disturb, as by a tempest.
A surname transferred from the nickname.

quotations.author: John Milton
quotations.passage: . . . the seal / And bended dolphins play; part huge of bulk, / Wallowing unwieldy, enormous in their gait, / Tempest the ocean.

quotations.author: Alexander Pope
quotations.passage: For a Tempest. Take Eurus, Zephyr, Auster and Boreas, and cast them together in one Verse. Add to these of Rain, Lightning, and of Thunder (the loudest you can) quantum sufficit. Mix your Clouds and Billows well together till they foam, and thicken your Description here and there with a Quicksand. Brew your Tempest well in your Head, before you set it a blowing.

quotations.author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
quotations.passage: Oh! dark lowered the clouds on that horrible eve, / And the moon dimly gleamed through the tempested air.

quotations.author: Herman Melville
quotations.passage: As every sailor knows, a spicy gale in the tropic latitudes of the Pacific is far different from a tempest in the howling North Atlantic.
quotations.work: Omoo: A Narrative of Adventures in the South Seas;

quotations.author: Mostyn John Armstrong
quotations.passage: BEAT on, proud billows; Boreas blow; / Swell, curled waves, high as Jove's roof; / Your incivility doth show, / That innocence is tempest proof; / Though surly Nereus frown, my thoughts are calm; / Then strike, Affliction, for thy wounds are balm. [Attributed to Roger L'Estrange (1616–1704).]
quotations.work: History and Antiquities of the County of Norfolk. Volume IX. Containing the Hundreds of Smithdon, Taverham, Tunstead, Walsham, and Wayland

quotations.author: James Yoxall
quotations.passage: The desert storm was riding in its strength; the travellers lay beneath the mastery of the fell simoom. […] Roaring, leaping, pouncing, the tempest raged about the wanderers, drowning and blotting out their forms with sandy spume.

quotations.author: Tobias Smollett
quotations.passage: Comforted with these reflections, the tempest of his soul subsided

quotations.author: Ambrose Bierce
quotations.passage: They awaited the word "forward"—awaited, too, with beating hearts and set teeth the gusts of lead and iron that were to smite them at their first movement in obedience to that word. The word was not given; the tempest did not break out.

tempest.title: tempest

etymologies: From Middle English temporal, temporel (“transitory, worldly, material, of secular society”), from Old French temporel or Latin temporālis (“of time (in grammar), temporary, relating to time as opposed to eternity”), from tempus (“time, period, opportunity”) +‎ -ālis.
From Middle English, from Middle French timporal, temporal, from Late Latin temporālis, from tempora (“the temples of the head”) +‎ -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix). Doublet of temporalis.

examples: temporal power, temporal courts
The Right Honourable the Lords Spiritual and Temporal of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland in Parliament assembled
definitions.text: Of or relating to the material world, as opposed to sacred or clerical.
Lasting for a short time only.
Of or relating to time as distinguished from space.
Of or relating to the sequence of time or to a particular time.
Relating to or denoting time or tense.
Anything temporal or secular; a temporality.
Of or situated in the temples of the head or the sides of the skull behind the orbits.
Ellipsis of temporal bone.
Any of a reptile's scales on the side of the head between the parietal and supralabial scales, and behind the postocular scales.

quotations.author: John Dryden
quotations.passage: for God's people love always to be dealing as well in temporals as spirituals

quotations.author: September and October
quotations.passage: The [papal] train was in use until 1871, when the Pope [Pius IX] lost his temporal power.

quotations.author: Thomas Penn
quotations.passage: Not long before, he had ruefully acknowledged in a letter to his pious mother that most of his appointments to the bench of bishops had been motivated by distinctly temporal impulses.
quotations.work: Winter King: The Dawn of Tudor England

quotations.passage: The things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.

quotations.author: James Russell Lowell
quotations.passage: He assigns supremacy to the pope in spirituals, and to the emperor in temporals.

temporal.title: temporal

etymologies: From Middle French temporiser (“to wait one's time, temporize”) + English -ize (suffix forming verbs). Temporiser is derived from Medieval Latin temporizāre, from Latin temporāre (“to delay, put off”) + -izāre (suffix forming the present active infinitive of verbs). Temporāre is derived from tempor-, the inflected stem of tempus (“age, time, period; season of the year; due, opportune, or proper time”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *temp-, *ten- (“to extend, stretch (in the sense of a stretch of time)”), or *temh₁- (“to cut (in the sense of a section of time)”)) + -āre. Compare temporalize.

definitions.text: To deliberately act evasively or prolong a discussion in order to gain time or postpone a decision, sometimes so that a compromise can be reached or simply to make a conversation more temperate; to stall for time.
To discuss, to negotiate; to reach a compromise.
To apply a temporary piece of dental work that will later be removed.
To comply with the occasion or time; to humour, or yield to, current circumstances or opinion; also, to trim (“fluctuate between parties, so as to appear to favour each”).
To delay, especially until a more favourable time; to procrastinate.
To take temporary measures or actions to manage a situation without providing a definitive or permanent solution.

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: The Dolphin is too wilfull opposite, / And will not temporize with my intreaties: / He flatly saies, heell not lay downe his Armes.
quotations.work: Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: Pedro. Nay, if Cupid haue not spent all his quiuer in Venice, thou wilt quake for this shortly. / Bened[ick]. I looke for an earthquake too then. / Pedro. Well, you will temporize with the howres, [...]

quotations.author: Henry Fielding
quotations.passage: How do you expect to rise in the Church, if you can't temporize, and give into the Opinion of your Superiors?

quotations.author: Walter Scott
quotations.passage: I ought to have temporized with this singular being, learned the motives of its interference, and availed myself of its succor, [...]

quotations.author: Francis Bacon
quotations.passage: The Earle of Lincolne [John de la Pole, 1st Earl of Lincoln] deceiued of his hopes of the Countries concourse vnto him (in which case he would haue temporized) and seeing the businesse past Retraict, resolued to make on where the King [Henry VII of England] was, and to giue him Battaile; [...]
quotations.work: The Historie of the Raigne of King Henry the Seventh

quotations.author: Robert Burton
quotations.passage: Happy he, in that he is freed from the tumults of the world, hee seekes no honours, gapes after no preferment, flatters not, envies not, temporizeth not, but liues priuately, and well contented with his estate, [...]
This is especially true when we're faced with temporizing a patient who will ultimately receive veneer restorations.

quotations.author: Samuel Daniel
quotations.passage: Yet seeking at the first to temporize, / She tries if that some short imprisonment / would calme their heat; when that would not suffize, / Then to exile him shee must needes consent: [...]
quotations.work: The First Fowre Bookes of the Ciuile Wars between the Two Houses of Lancaster and Yorke

quotations.author: Elizabeth Cary, Viscountess Falkland
quotations.passage: Though that her heart were fired, and swollen with anger, she temporiseth so, 'twas undiscovered: [...]
quotations.work: The History of the Life, Reign, and Death of Edward II, King of England, and Lord of Ireland

quotations.author: Thomas Babington Macaulay
quotations.passage: [William] Penn, therefore, exhorted the fellows not to rely on the goodness of their cause, but to submit, or at least to temporise.
quotations.work: The History of England from the Accession of James II

temporize.title: temporize

etymologies: From tendency +‎ -ious, after German tendenziös.

examples: That he was a supporter of the cause was clear, because his reports from the front were tendentious.
definitions.text: Having a tendency, written or spoken, with a partisan, biased or prejudiced purpose, especially a controversial one; implicitly or explicitly slanted; biased.

quotations.author: Karen Tumulty
quotations.passage: President-elect Donald Trump abruptly abandoned some of his most tendentious campaign promises Tuesday, saying he does not plan to prosecute Hillary Clinton for her use of a private email system or the dealings of her family foundation, has an “open mind” about a climate-change accord from which he vowed to withdraw the United States and is no longer certain that torturing terrorism suspects is a good idea.

quotations.author: Anthony Lambert
quotations.passage: It is a canard trotted out by lazy or tendentious journalists that nationalised British Railways lacked entrepreneurial flair.

tendentious.title: tendentious

etymologies: From Middle English tenebrose, from Anglo-Norman tenebrous (earlier tenebrus), from Latin tenebrōsus, itself from tenebrae (“darkness, shadows”).

definitions.text: Dark and gloomy; obscure.

quotations.author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
quotations.passage: Over their heads the towering and tenebrous boughs of the cypress / Met in a dusky arch, […]

quotations.author: Elizabeth Jane Bellamy
quotations.passage: […] and it is inevitable that her murdered spirit become a denizen of Jerusalem's tenebrous woods.
quotations.work: Translations of Power: Narcissism and the Unconscious in Epic History

quotations.author: Georges Duby
quotations.passage: White was more delicate, more feminine, more beautiful. Dark was more robust, more masculine, more tenebrous.
quotations.work: A History of Women in the West: Renaissance and Enlightenment Paradoxes

quotations.author: Kazuo Ishiguro
quotations.passage: Although Ishiguro’s novels are arguably more overtly concerned with emo- tional and psychological matters than with historical ones, it is certainly no accident that he sets all of his novels, as Margaret Atwood maintains, “against tenebrous historical backdrops.”

tenebrous.title: tenebrous

audio.accent: Standard Southern British, General American, Canada

etymologies: Borrowed from Latin tenet (“he, she, or it holds”), from teneō (“hold; have”). Compare obsolete tenent. See tenable.

definitions.text: An opinion, belief, or principle that is held as absolute truth by someone or especially an organization.

pronunciations.accent: Standard Southern British, General American, Canada
Standard Southern British, General American, Canada
Standard Southern British, General American, Canada

quotations.author: Enlightenment Therapy
quotations.passage: The Buddhist concept of tanha, for example — roughly translated as “blind demandingness” — encapsulates many tenets of R.E.B.T. and points the way toward emotional equanimity: stop asking more of the universe than it can possibly deliver.

quotations.author: Katharine Viner
quotations.passage: Opposition to climate science has become not just the badge of honour for far-right politicians like Ukip’s Paul Nuttall. It has become the central tenet of their appeal to unreason.

tenet.title: tenet

etymologies: From Medieval Latin tentātīvus (“trying, testing”), from tentō, past participle tentātus (“to try, test”); see tent, tempt.

definitions.text: A trial; an experiment; an attempt.
A schedule for an event or a programme.
Of or pertaining to a trial or trials; essaying; experimental.

examples: He gave a tentative answer, unsure of the final outcome.
We have a tentative plan for the weekend, but nothing is confirmed yet.
definitions.text: Uncertain; subject to future change.

examples: Her tentative steps showed her nervousness as she entered the room.
definitions.text: Restrained; polite; feeling one's way, not using full force.

quotations.author: Manohla Dargis
quotations.passage: Meanwhile, a bunch of hungry directors with digital cameras, time on their hands and not much money are making free-form studies about tentative hookups and long conversations among actual, overeducated, undermotivated young folks.

quotations.author: Rachel Hagan
quotations.passage: Hegseth's reference to the report being "low confidence" suggest it is tentative and its findings may change as more detail emerges.

tentative.title: tentative

etymologies: Irregularly formed from Latin tenuis (“thin, slight”) +‎ -ous. Compare tenuious.

examples: The aether was thought to be of tenuous strands.
Far from being amicable, the numbers seemed to turn their backs on each other, and I couldn't find a pair with even the most tenuous connection.
definitions.text: Thin in substance or consistency.

examples: His argument was not convincing in the debate, considering how tenuous it was.
definitions.text: Insubstantial.
Precarious, dependent upon unreliable things.

quotations.author: M. Lindsey Kaplan
quotations.passage: Paulina's repeated, almost anxious iteration of the lawfulness of her actions serves as a reminder of women's tenuous stance before the law in early modern English society.

quotations.author: September
quotations.passage: Is this connected to "pro-gay" Governor Weld's contract with some in the community—gay rights in exchange for keeping sex out of the picture? Those willing to make this 'bargain with the devil' depend for their tenuous status on keeping the rest of us in line, moralizing about the need to behave "beyond reproach," clarifying to the straight public that there are good gays and bad ones.

tenuous.title: tenuous

etymologies: Borrowed from Latin tergiversātus, perfect active participle of tergiversor (“to evade, to avoid, to turn one's back on”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from tergum (“back, hind”) +‎ versor (“to turn”). Compare French tergiverser.

definitions.text: To evade, to equivocate using subterfuge; to obfuscate in a deliberate manner.
To change sides or affiliation; to apostatize.
To flee by turning one's back.

quotations.author: Philip McCutchan
quotations.passage: The officials soon concluded that the easiest way to remain on good terms with the court was to elude responsibility, to tergiversate, to prevent results.

quotations.author: Colin Morris
quotations.passage: Henry had hesitated before authorising the spoliation; he would soon tergiversate on other matters of doctrine but this act was irreversible.
quotations.work: Pilgrimage: The English Experience from Becket to Bunyan

tergiversate.title: tergiversate

etymologies: The noun is derived from Termagant (“fictitious deity with a violent temperament represented as being worshipped by Muslims or other non-Christians”), from Middle English Termagaunt (“fictitious deity represented as being worshipped by Muslims; any pagan god”), from Anglo-Norman Tervagant, Tervagaunt, Tervagan, and Old French Tervagant, Tervagan (possibly with the addition of Anglo-Norman -aunt, Old French -ant (suffix forming present participles of verbs, some of which were used as nouns); modern French Tervagant (historical)); further etymology uncertain, one common suggestion being that it is from Latin ter (“three times, thrice”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes (“three”)) + vagāns (“rambling, wandering”) (the present active participle of vagor (“to ramble, roam, wander”), from vagus (“rambling, roaming, wandering”) (possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *Hwogos) + -or (inflected form of -ō (suffix forming regular first-conjugation verbs)). Medieval French chansons de geste named Termagant as one of three deities supposedly worshipped by Muslims, the others being Apollin and Mahound, and the name may allude to the wandering of the moon (the crescent moon being a common symbol of Islam) in the form of the mythological goddesses Selene in heaven, Diana on earth, and Proserpina in the underworld.
The reason for the shift in meaning from the fictitious deity to a brawling and turbulent person is unclear.
The adjective is derived from the noun.

definitions.text: A brawling, boisterous, and turbulent person or thing.
A censorious, nagging, and quarrelsome woman; a scold, a shrew.
Having the temperament of a termagant (noun sense 1); bad-tempered, brawling, boisterous, turbulent.
Of a woman, her behaviour, etc.: censorious, nagging, and quarrelsome; scolding, shrewish.
A fictitious deity with a violent temperament who featured in medieval mystery plays, represented as being worshipped by Muslims or other non-Christians.

quotations.author: John Dryden
quotations.passage: [F]earing his Father should knovv of it, and his VVife, vvho is a Termagant Lady: but vvhen he finds the Coast is clear, and his late ruffling knovvn to none but you, he vvill be drunk vvith joy.
quotations.work: Sr Martin Mar-all, or The Feign’d Innocence: A Comedy.

quotations.author: John Dryden
quotations.passage: But this Lady is so Termagant an Empress! and he so submissive, so tame, so led a Keeper, and as proud of his Slavery, as a French man: I am confident he dares not find her false, for fear of a quarrel vvith her; […]
quotations.work: The Kind Keeper; or, Mr. Limberham: A Comedy

quotations.author: Jonathan Swift
quotations.passage: […] I do not find hovv his E[xcellenc]y can be justly censured for favouring none but High-Church, High-flyers, Termagants, Laudists, Sacheverellians, Tip-top-gallon-men, Jacobites, Tantivyes, Anti-Hannoverians, Friends to Popery and the Pretender, and to Arbitrary Povver, […]
quotations.work: A Vindication of His Excellency the Lord C [ artere ] t, from the Charge of Favouring None but Tories, High-Churchmen and Jacobites.

quotations.author: Walter Scott
quotations.passage: [T]wo raw lads from a certain great manufacturing town […] were in the act of seeking for the speediest exit from the gardens; rather choosing to resign their share of the dinner, than to abide the farther consequences that might follow from the displeasure of his Highland Termagaunt.

quotations.author: William Makepeace Thackeray
quotations.passage: Yonder is Sarah Marlborough's palace, just as it stood when that termagant occupied it.
quotations.work: The Four Georges: Sketches of Manners, Morals, Court, and Town Life

quotations.author: Plato
quotations.passage: The name of Xanthippe, the wife of Socrates, has become proverbial for a termagant.

quotations.author: Thomas Babington Macaulay
quotations.passage: No person who had a natural interest in the Princess [Anne, Queen of Great Britain] could observe without uneasiness the strange infatuation which made her the slave of an imperious and reckless termagant [Sarah Churchill, Duchess of Marlborough].
quotations.work: The History of England from the Accession of James the Second

quotations.author: Bernard Mac Laverty
quotations.passage: 'Mrs Kane has been filling us in on some background information on Owen.' The woman nodded, drumming her nicotined fingers. 'And I have been assuring her that the boys who arrive here thimbleriggers and termagants are the least of our worries. But we do not send them out that way. Do we, Brother?'

quotations.author: Samuel Butler
quotations.passage: They [authors] would not suffer the stout'st Dame, / To swear by Hercules his Name, / Make feeble Ladies, in their Works, / To fight like Termagants and Turks; […]
quotations.work: Hudibras. The First and Second Parts.

quotations.author: John Gay
quotations.passage: This Girl is so excessively ill-bred, and such an arrant Termagant, that I cou'd as soon fall in love vvith a Tigress. She hath a handsom Face, 'tis true, but in her Temper she is a very Fury.

quotations.author: Émile Gaboriau
quotations.passage: [T]he Widow Chupin […] poured forth a torrent of invective upon Gevrol and his agents, accusing them of persecuting her family […] At first the General tried to impose silence upon the terrible termagant; but he soon discovered that he was powerless; besides all his subordinates were laughing.

quotations.author: Robertson Davies
quotations.passage: Easier divorce, equal pay for equal work as between men and women, no discrimination between the sexes in employment—these were her causes, and in promoting them she was no comic-strip feminist termagant, but reasonable, logical, and untiring.

quotations.author: Thomas Nashe
quotations.passage: [R]idiculous senseles sentences, finicall, flaunting phrases, and termagant inkhorne tearmes throughout his booke, […]
quotations.work: Haue with You to Saffron-Walden. Or, Gabriell Harveys Hunt is Up.

quotations.author: Richard Brome
quotations.passage: O Cupid vvhat a Termagant tyrant art thou / Over poore subjects of sixteene! There is not one / Among a hundred of those ticklish Trifles / But is more taken vvith a Toy at sixteene / Then six and tvventy: […]

quotations.author: Danton Remoto
quotations.passage: What if I stayed on at the University of Nottingham in Malaysia as the Head of School of English? The remuneration was not something to be sneeze at, but I had to remain cheerful and composed even in the face of a hostile dean, spoiled students and termagant parents.

quotations.author: Isaac Bickerstaff
quotations.passage: He answered Phillis a little abruptly at supper the same evening, upon which she threw his periwig into the fire. 'Well,' said he 'thou art a brave termagant jade: do you know, hussy, that fair wig cost forty guineas?'

quotations.author: John Arbuthnot
quotations.passage: The Eldest vvas a termagant, imperious, prodigal, levvd, profligate VVench, as ever breath'd; she used to Rantipole about the House, pinch the Children, kick the Servants, and torture the Cats and the Dogs; […]
quotations.work: John Bull in His Senses: Being the Second Part of Law is a Bottomless-Pit.

quotations.author: Frances Sheridan
quotations.passage: But the eldest daughter vvas alvvays her darling, vvho I understand is pretty much of her mother's ovvn cast; and makes a very termagant vvife to a very turbulent husband.

quotations.author: Jedediah Cleishbotham
quotations.passage: "That's as muckle as till say, Bark, Bawtie, and be dune wi't!—I tell ye," raising her termagant voice, "I want my bairn! is na that braid Scots?"
quotations.work: Tales of My Landlord, Second Series

quotations.author: William Seymour Tyler
quotations.passage: [Lamprocles] is introduced in Xen[ophon] Mem[orabilia] ii. 2, holding a conversation with his father [Socrates] touching his filial duty to his termagant mother [Xanthippe].

quotations.author: Anthony Burgess
quotations.passage: These bishops with their termagant wives throw the book at us and say believe because I demand belief and by God I will burn or hang and quarter you if you do not.

termagant.title: termagant

etymologies: Learned borrowing from Latin terminus (“boundary, limit”). Doublet of term, Terminus, and termon.

examples: The river reached its terminus at the wide delta near the sea.
definitions.text: The end or final point of something.
The end point of a transportation system, or the town or city in which it is located.

examples: A bronz statue marked the terminus of the king's dominion.
definitions.text: A boundary or border, or a post or stone marking such a boundary.
The god of boundaries and landmarks, focus of the important Roman festival of Terminalia.

quotations.author: H.G. Wells
quotations.passage: My brother supposes they must have filled outside London, for at that time the furious terror of the people had rendered the central termini impossible.

quotations.author: June
quotations.passage: The arrangement for certain long-distance trains to call at suburban stations (saving passengers the trouble of journeying to the termini), which proved popular last year, is being extended.

quotations.author: China
quotations.passage: Wuhan is the terminus for cruises to the Yanzi[sic – meaning Yangtze] River gorges.

quotations.author: Paul Bigland
quotations.passage: Thirty-five years ago, many journeys around London meant having to pass through the centre of the capital. That's no longer the case, which takes real pressure off the city's termini as well as underground routes such as the Circle Line.

terminus.title: terminus

etymologies: From Terpsichore (“the Muse of dance in Greek mythology”).

definitions.text: Of or relating to dancing.
A person who dances, especially professionally.

quotations.author: Charles Dickens
quotations.passage: This was such an entirely new view of the Terpsichorean art as socially practised, that Mrs Lammle looked at her young friend in some astonishment

quotations.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

etymologies: From Middle English thing, from Old English þing, from Proto-West Germanic *þing, from Proto-Germanic *þingą.

Cognate with Saterland Frisian Ding (“thing”), West Frisian ting, ding (“thing”), Dutch ding (“thing”), German Low German Ding (“thing”), German Ding (“thing”), Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, Norwegian Nynorsk, and Swedish ting (“thing”), Faroese ting (“parliament, assembly”), Icelandic þing (“congress, assembly”), Scots hing (“thing”).

The word originally meant "assembly", then came to mean a specific issue discussed at such an assembly, and ultimately came to mean most broadly "an object". Compare Latin rēs, also meaning "legal matter", and same transition from Latin causa (“legal matter”) to "thing" in Romance languages. Modern use to refer to a Germanic assembly is likely influenced by cognates (from the same Proto-Germanic root) like Old Norse þing (“thing”), Danish ting, Swedish ting, and Old High German ding with this meaning.

etymologies: From French travesti (“disguised, burlesqued”), past participle of travestir (“to disguise”), borrowed from Italian travestire (“to dress up, disguise”), from tra- (“across”) +‎ vestire (“to dress”), from Latin vestiō (“to clothe, dress”), from Proto-Italic *westis (“clothing”), from Proto-Indo-European *wéstis (“dressing”) from verbal root *wes- (“to dress, clothe”); cognate to English wear. To make a travesty of; to parody.

quotations.author: Christopher Kimball

trepidation.title: trepidation

etymologies: From Middle English trīcen, trice, trise (“to pull or push; to snatch away; to steal”), from Middle Dutch trīsen (“to hoist”) (modern Dutch trijsen) or Middle Low German trissen (“to trice the spritsail”); further etymology uncertain. The word is cognate with Danish trisse, tridse (“to haul with a pulley”), Low German trissen, tryssen, drisen, drysen (“to wind up, trice”), German trissen, triezen (“to annoy or torment”).

From Middle English trīce, trise, in the phrase at a trīce (“with a single, quick motion; at once”, literally “with a pull or jerk”), later also in the phrases in a trice, on a trice, and with a trice. The word is ultimately from Middle English trīcen: see etymology 1 above.

From Middle English trīce, tryys, tryyst, from Middle Dutch trīse, trijs (modern Dutch trijs (“hoisting-block, pulley, windlass”)) or Middle Low German trīsse, trītse (“hoisting-rope, tackle”); probably related to the verb trice (see etymology 1 above), and perhaps to Old English tryndel (“roller, wheel”) (see further at trend, trindle). The English word is cognate with Danish tridse, trisse (“pulley”), Low German trissel (“dizziness; whirling”), German trieze (“crane; pulley”), Norwegian triss (“pulley”), Swedish trissa (“pulley, truckle”).

definitions.text: To pull, to pull out or away, to pull sharply.
To drag or haul, especially with a rope; specifically to haul or hoist and tie up by means of a rope.
Now only in the phrase in a trice: a very short time; the blink of an eye, an instant, a moment.
A pulley, a windlass (“form of winch for lifting heavy weights, comprising a cable or rope wound around a cylinder”).
A surname.

quotations.author: William Shakespeare

quotations.author: Arthur Hamilton Clark

quotations.passage: Blair brought out the febrile intensity of Stanhope, wiring himself into his ever more circumscribed troglodyte world, speculating moodily on the worm that went down when it thought it was coming up. Robert Philp thought Blair's ...

etymologies: From Latin tropus, from Ancient Greek τρόπος (trópos, “a manner, style, turn, way; a trope or figure of speech; a mode in music; a mode or mood in logic”), related to τροπή (tropḗ, “solstice; trope; turn”) and τρέπειν (trépein, “to turn”); compare turn of phrase. The verb is derived from the noun.

definitions.text: Something recurring across a genre or type of art or literature; a motif.
An addition (of dialogue, song, music, etc.) to a standard element of the liturgy, serving as an embellishment.
A figure of speech in which words or phrases are used with a nonliteral or figurative meaning, such as a metaphor.
A tangent space meeting a quartic surface in a conic.
The reciprocal of a node on a surface.
A short cadence at the end of the melody in some early music.
A pair of complementary hexachords in twelve-tone technique.
A cantillation pattern, or one of the marks that represents it.
Any of the ten arguments used in skepticism to refute dogmatism.
A particular instance of a property (such as the specific redness of a rose), as contrasted with a universal.
To use, or embellish something with, a trope.
To represent something figuratively or metaphorically, especially as a literary motif.
To turn into, coin, or create a new trope.
To analyse a work in terms of its literary tropes.
To think or write in terms of tropes.

quotations.author: Jonathan Swift

quotations.author: Francis Bacon

This grew speedily to an excess; for men began to hunt more after words than matter; and more after the choiceness of the phrase, and the round and clean composition of the sentence, and the sweet falling of the clauses, and the varying and illustration of their works with tropes and figures, than after the weight of matter, worth of subject, soundness of argument, life of invention, or depth of judgment.

quotations.passage: It is likewise witty, for […] a trope familiar to this author, you have here a comparison of—a woman's chastity to a piece of porcelain,—her honour to a gaudy robe,—her prayers to a fantastical disguise,—her heart to a trinket; and all these together to her lap-dog, and that founded on one lucky circumstance (a malicious critic would perhaps discern or imagine more) by which these things, how unlike soever in other respects, may be compared, the impression they make on the mind of a fine lady.

quotations.author: Ronald William Henry Turnbull Hudson
quotations.passage: Hence the section must be a conic passing through six nodes, that is, the plane touches the surface all along a conic, and is therefore a trope. quotations.author: Arthur Cayley
quotations.passage: I take account of conical and biplanar nodes, or, as I call them, cnicnodes, and binodes; of pinch-points on the nodal curve; and of close-points and off-points on the cuspidal curve: viz. I assume that there are / C, cnicnodes, / B, binodes, / j, pinch-points, / χ, close points, / θ, off-points, / deferring for the present the explanation of these singularities. The same letters, accented, refer to the reciprocal singularities. Or using "trope" as the reciprocal term to node, these will be / C′, cnictropes, / B′, bitropes, / j′, pinch-planes, / χ′, close-planes, / θ′, off-planes; / but these present themselves, not in the equations above referred to, but in the reciprocal equations.

quotations.author: John G. Johnstone
quotations.passage: If the antiphon comes to an end with the “Praeparatio” trope, a musical difficulty is presented by the trope’s cadence. Although the antiphon is in the E-plagal mode and the first three trope elements cadence on E, this trope cadences on G, a rare cadence tone in this mode.

quotations.author: George Perle
quotations.passage: The eighty six-note segments were originally tabulated by Hauer and are the basis of his twelve-tone system. Each of the remaining seventy-two hexachords must be paired with a dissimilar hexachord in order to form a trope.

quotations.author: Steven M. Brown
quotations.passage: The Torah was chanted in a loud and strong voice so that all could hear. This cantillation of the Torah—trope—is shown by musical notation which serves grammatical and exegetical functions, ta'amay hamikra or ta'amay n'ginah. They put down in a final form an oral tradition that had been maintained for centuries. The Ashkenazim today have six systems of cantillation, each reflective of the texts and time of chanting. For example, on Tishah B'av the tunes are sad and doleful; on Purim the trope resembles a speedy narrative; the readings of Yamim Nora'im are quite majestic, and so on.

quotations.author: Sara E. Karesh

quotations.author: Tanja Staehler
quotations.passage: For [Georg Wilhelm Friedrich] Hegel, ancient skepticism preserved the essence of the skeptical principle, and the tropes express this principle. In the earlier ten tropes, there is, according to Hegel, a lack of abstraction that becomes obvious in the fact that their diversity could be grasped under more general points of view. […] Sextus [Empiricus] explains that the first four tropes are based on the judging subject; these deal with the differences among animals, the differences among human beings, the differences that distinguish the various senses, and, finally, circumstantial differences.
quotations.work: Hegel’s History of Philosophy: New Interpretations

quotations.author: Brian Garrett
quotations.passage: Trope theory, though a minority view today, has been popular at various times throughout the history of philosophy, especially among medieval philosophers. Trope theory holds that properties and relations are themselves (unrepeatable) particulars. (Tropes are also called 'abstract particulars' – 'abstract' in the sense of fine, partial and diffuse, not in the sense of outside space and time.) Thus the redness of a particular billiard ball is a trope, located where the ball is and nowhere else. A different but exactly resembling billiard ball has a numerically different but exactly resembling redness trope. There is no colour property common to, or instantiated in, both balls (similarly all other properties and relations).
quotations.work: What is this Thing Called Metaphysics?

quotations.author: James Midgley Clark
quotations.passage: The motive for troping the introit was twofold. Firstly there was the desire to add colour, mystical fervour, to the restrained, matter-of-fact Roman rite. This part of the ritual lent itself very readily to embellishment and expansion.

quotations.author: Deborah Baker Wyrick
quotations.passage: By acting in loco parentis, the written word performs its own usurpations of generating authority and generated meanings. Therefore, after the brothers demolish the authority of the word as written, they ar able to substitute alternative authorities: the word as spoken, the word as added, the word as troped, the word as altered, the word as hidden.
quotations.work: Jonathan Swift and the Vested Word

trope.title: trope

etymologies: From Old Occitan trobar (“to find”) via Old French troubadour. Piecewise doublet of trouveur.

definitions.text: An itinerant composer and performer of songs in medieval Europe; a jongleur or travelling minstrel.

quotations.author: Alan Cowell
quotations.passage: Sitting in the courtroom ..., their laptops and tablets propped before them, power cables snaking through convoluted adapters, the Twitterati have sight of witnesses at all times – the troubadours, or perhaps the tricoteuses, of the digital revolution.

quotations.author: Hybrid Creatures
quotations.passage: “"Not a human, not yet a vampire," to paraphrase one of your contemporary musical troubadours.”
quotations.work: What We Do in the Shadows

troubadour.title: troubadour

etymologies: The adjective and noun are derived from Middle English truant, truand, truaund (“(adjective) idle; tending to vagrancy (uncertain; may be a use of the noun); (noun) beggar; mendicant friar; vagrant, wanderer; worthless person, rogue, scoundrel; one who is absent without leave, truant; one who shirks duties”), from Old French truant, truand (“(adjective) beggarly; roguish; (noun) a beggar, vagabond; a rogue”) (modern French truand), probably of Celtic origin, possibly from Gaulish *trugan, or from Breton truan (“wretched”), from Proto-Celtic *taratrom, from Proto-Indo-European *térh₁-tro-m, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *terh₁- (“to drill, pierce; to rub; to turn”).
Inherited from Middle English truaunten (“to obtain alms fraudulently; to behave like a rogue or scoundrel; to neglect a duty; to be idle or lazy”), and then partly:

definitions.text: Shirking or wandering from business or duty; straying; hence, idle; loitering.

examples: He didn’t graduate because he was chronically truant and didn’t have enough attendances to meet the requirement.
definitions.text: Of a student: absent from school without permission.
Having no real substance; unimportant, vain, worthless.
An idle or lazy person; an idler.
A student who is absent from school without permission; hence , a person who shirks or wanders from business or duty.
Synonym of sturdy beggar (“a person who was fit and able to work, but lived as a beggar or vagrant instead”); hence, a worthless person; a rogue, a scoundrel.

examples: The number of schoolchildren known to have truanted from this school has been unusually high.
definitions.text: Also used with the impersonal pronoun it : to shirk or wander from business or duty; of a student: to be absent from school without permission; to play truant.
To idle away or waste (time).

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: Ham[let]. And vvhat in faith make you from VVittenberg? / Hora[tio]. A truant disposition good my Lord.
quotations.work: The Tragicall Historie of Hamlet, Prince of Denmarke

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: For my part I may speake it to my shame, / I haue a truant beene to Chiualrie, […]
quotations.work: The History of Henrie the Fourth;

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: [S]ince I pluckt Geese, plaide Trevvant, and vvhipt Top, I knevv not vvhat 'tvvas to be beaten, till lately.
quotations.work: Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: […] I knovve you are no truant, / But vvhat is your affaire in Elsonoure?
quotations.work: The Tragicall Historie of Hamlet, Prince of Denmarke

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: Hang him truant, theres no true drop of bloud in him to be truly toucht vvith loue, if he be sadde, he vvantes money.

quotations.author: William Shakespeare
quotations.passage: VVhat simple thiefe brags of his ovvne attaine? / 'Tis double vvrong, to truant vvith your bed, / And let her read it in thy lookes at boord: […]
quotations.work: Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies

quotations.author: John Milton
quotations.passage: [W]ee are not to imitate them; nor to distrust God in the removal of that Truant help to our Devotion, vvhich by him never vvas appointed.

quotations.author: John Milton
quotations.passage: By this means they lost their time, and truanted in the fundamentall grounds of saving knovvledge, […]
quotations.work: Of Prelatical Episcopacy, and Whither It may be Deduc’d from the Apostolical Times by Vertue of Those Testimonies which are Alledg’d to that Purpose in Some Late Treatises

quotations.author: William Wordsworth
quotations.passage: Me, lured by hope its sorrows to remove, / A heart that could not much itself approve / O'er Gallia's wastes of corn dejected led, / Her road elms rustling high above my head, / Or through her truant pathways' native charms, / By secret villages and lonely farms, […]
quotations.work: The Complete Poetical Works of William Wordsworth

quotations.author: William Makepeace Thackeray
quotations.passage: Indeed, calamity is welcome to women if they think it will bring truant affection home again: and if you have reduced your mistress to a crust, depend upon it that she won't repine, and only take a very little bit of it for herself, provided you will eat the remainder in her company.

quotations.author: Emerson Hough
quotations.passage: Serene, smiling, enigmatic, she faced him with no fear whatever showing in her dark eyes. […] She put back a truant curl from her forehead where it had sought egress to the world, and looked him full in the face now, drawing a deep breath which caused the round of her bosom to lift the lace at her throat.
quotations.work: The Purchase Price: Or The Cause of Compromise

quotations.author: Virgil
quotations.passage: But vvhere thou seest a single Sheep remain / In shades aloof, or couch'd upon the Plain; / Or listlesly to crop the tender Grass; / Or late to lag behind, vvith truant pace; / Revenge the Crime; and take the Traytor's head, / E're in the faultless Flock the dire Contagion spread.
quotations.work: The Works of Virgil: Containing His Pastorals, Georgics, and Æneis.

quotations.author: John Trumbull
quotations.passage: In elder days, in Saturn's prime, / Ere baldness seized the head of Time, / While truant Jove, in infant pride, / Play'd barefoot on Olympus' side, / Each thing on earth had power to chatter, / And spoke the mother tongue of nature.
quotations.work: The Poetical Works of John Trumbull

quotations.author: William Cowper
quotations.passage: [I] have loved the rural vvalk / O'er hills, through valleys, and by rivers brink, / E'er since a truant boy I pass'd my bounds / T'enjoy a ramble on the banks of Thames.

quotations.author: Erasmus Darwin
quotations.passage: Dovvn the steep slopes He led vvith modest skill / The vvilling pathvvay, and the truant rill, […]
quotations.work: The Botanic Garden; a Poem, in Two Parts.

quotations.author: Washington Irving
quotations.passage: […] I fell desperately in love with a little daughter of the squire's about twelve years of age. This freak of fancy made me more truant from my studies than ever.

quotations.author: Virgil
quotations.passage: You loiter, vvhile the Spoils are born avvay: / Our Ships are laden vvith the Trojan Store, / And you like Truants come too late ashore.
quotations.work: The Works of Virgil: Containing His Pastorals, Georgics, and Æneis.

quotations.author: Oliver Goldsmith
quotations.passage: The village master taught his little school; / A man severe he vvas, and stern to vievv, / I knevv him vvell, and every truant knevv; […]

quotations.author: John Lyly
quotations.passage: VVhat made the Gods so often to trevvant from Heauen & mych [much] héere on earth, but beautie?

quotations.author: Thomas Fuller
quotations.passage: If in a dark businesse vve perceive God to guide us by the lantern of his providence, it is good to follovv the light close, lest vve lose it by our lagging behind. He [Eliezer] vvill not truant it novv in the afternoon, but vvith convenient speed returns to Abraham, vvho onely vvas vvorthy of such a Servant, vvho onely vvas vvorthy of such a Master.

quotations.author: John Garretson
quotations.passage: Thou Truantest much, and art very idle, which are most pernicious things.
quotations.work: English Exercises for School-boys to Translate into Latin.

quotations.author: Samuel Richardson
quotations.passage: Her good angel is gone a journey: Is truanting at least.
quotations.work: Clarissa. Or, The History of a Young Lady

quotations.author: John Ford
quotations.passage: I dare not be the Author / Of trevvanting the time then, neither vvill I.

truant.title: truant

etymologies: From Middle English trokel, trocle, trookyl, from Anglo-Norman trocle, from Medieval Latin trochlea (“a block, sheaf containing one or more pulleys”); or from a diminutive of truck (“wheel”), formed with -le, equivalent to truck +‎ -le.

From a back formation of truckle bed (a bed on which a pupil slept, because it was rolled on casters into a lower position under the master's larger bed), from Middle English trookylbed. Compare also trundle bed. Assisted by false association with Middle English *trukelen, truken, trokien, trukien, from Old English trucian (“to fail, diminish”), Low German truggeln (“to flatter, fawn”), see truck.(Can this(+) etymology be sourced?)

definitions.text: A small wheel; a caster or pulley.
A small wheel of cheese.
Ellipsis of truckle bed.
To roll or move upon truckles, or casters; to trundle.
To sleep in a truckle bed.
To act in a submissive manner; to fawn, submit to a superior. [with to]

quotations.author: Louisa May Alcott
quotations.passage: "Why in the world should you spend your money, worry your family, and turn the house upside down for a parcel of girls who don't care a sixpence for you? I thought you had too much pride and sense to truckle to any mortal woman just because she wears French boots and rides in a coupe," said Jo, who, being called from the tragic climax of her novel, was not in the best mood for social enterprises. "I don't truckle, and I hate being patronized as much as you do!" returned Amy indignantly, for the two still jangled when such questions arose.

quotations.author: William Graham Sumner
quotations.passage: There is no doubt […] that truckling to popularity is the worst political vice.

quotations.author: John Norris
quotations.passage: Religion it self is forced to truckle to worldly policy.
quotations.work: A Collection of Miscellanies, consisting of Poems, Essays, Discourses and Letters

truckle.title: truckle

etymologies: First attested circa 1540, from Middle French, from Latin truculentus (“fierce, savage”), from trux (“fierce, wild”).

examples: The truculent soldiers gave us a steely-eyed stare.
definitions.text: Cruel or savage.
Defiant or uncompromising.
Eager or quick to argue, fight or start a conflict.
Violent; rude; scathing; savage; harsh.
Destructive; deadly.

quotations.author: Charles Dickens
quotations.passage: She really was a most charming girl, and might have passed for a captive fairy, whom that truculent Ogre, Old Barley, had pressed into his service.

quotations.author: Charlotte Brontë
quotations.passage: In her turn, Helen Burns asked me to explain, and I proceeded forthwith to pour out, in my own way, the tale of my sufferings and resentments. Bitter and truculent when excited, I spoke as I felt, without reserve or softening.

quotations.author: James Joyce
quotations.passage: His face was very truculent, grey and massive, with black cavernous nostrils and circled by a scanty white fur.

quotations.author: Edgar Rice Burroughs
quotations.passage: Rokoff assumed a truculent air, attempting by bravado to show how little he feared Tarzan’s threats.

quotations.author: David Magarshack
quotations.passage: She might pity herself, but he must not pity her. She did not want any quarrel; she blamed him for wanting one, but she could not help assuming a truculent attitude.

quotations.author: Edgar Rice Burroughs
quotations.passage: If he came too close to a she with a young baby, the former would bare her great fighting fangs and growl ominously, and occasionally a truculent young bull would snarl a warning if Tarzan approached while the former was eating.

quotations.author: Joel Feinberg
quotations.passage: It is an important source of the value of moral rights then that — speaking very generally — they dispose people with opposed interests to be reasonable rather than arrogant and truculent.

quotations.author: SEAL Team Six
quotations.passage: These bitches is getting truculent.

quotations.author: John Morley
quotations.passage: Voltaire is never either gross or truculent.

quotations.author: Herbert George Wells
quotations.passage: […] or again, the first whispering of love, dainty and witty and tender, to the girl he served a few days ago with sateen, or a gallant rescue of generalised beauty in distress from truculent insult or ravening dog.
quotations.work: The Wheels of Chance: A Holiday Adventure

quotations.author: Rafael Sabatini
quotations.passage: Cahusac appeared to be having it all his own way, and he raised his harsh, querulous voice so that all might hear his truculent denunciation.

quotations.author: Gideon Harvey
quotations.passage: More or less truculent Plagues.
quotations.work: A Discourse of the Plague … with several waies for purifying the air in houses, streets

truculent.title: truculent

etymologies: From true + -ism.

definitions.text: A self-evident or obvious truth.
A banality or cliché.

quotations.author: October
quotations.passage: It is a truism that the site of stations is conditioned by history and geography, but Dover Marine especially owes its fascinating and unusual layout to these two factors.

quotations.author: Philip Bump
quotations.passage: It is a truism that the people who attend a rally for President Trump more than two years before he’s on the ballot again are generally strong supporters of President Trump.

quotations.author: Jeffrey Goldberg
quotations.passage: The phrase If something exists, there is porn of it used to be a clever internet meme; now it’s a truism.

quotations.author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon
quotations.passage: After a little decent sorrow had been put forth for the late "severe affliction," joined with some weariful truisms about resignation to the will of Providence, the rest of the epistle was filled up with reproofs about her ladyship's extraordinary and improper conduct in setting off without his consent!
quotations.work: Ethel Churchill: Or, The Two Brides.

quotations.author: Richard Klasco
quotations.passage: A medical “truism” holds that nose hair filters the air we breathe and therefore protects us from infection by airborne viruses, bacteria and other pathogens. But, as is often the case with truisms, its history may be more venerable than verified.

truism.title: truism

etymologies: From Middle English tryst, trist, from Old French triste, tristre (“waiting place, appointed station in hunting”), probably from a North Germanic source such as Old Norse treysta (“to make safe, secure”), from traust (“confidence, trust, security, help, shelter, safe abode”), from Proto-Germanic *traustą (“trust, shelter”), from Proto-Indo-European *deru-, *dreu-, *drū- (“to be firm, be solid”). Doublet of trust, see there for more.

definitions.text: A prearranged meeting or assignation, now especially between lovers to meet at a specific place and time.
A mutual agreement, a covenant.
A market fair, especially a recurring one held on a schedule, where livestock sales took place.
To make a tryst; to agree to meet at a place.
To arrange or appoint (a meeting time etc.).
To keep a tryst, to meet at an agreed place and time.

quotations.author: Alfred Tennyson
quotations.passage: And Vivien, like the tenderest-hearted maid / That ever bided tryst at village stile, / Made answer, either eyelid wet with tears: […]

quotations.author: Henry Miller
quotations.passage: A silence supreme and altogether European. Shutters drawn, shops barred. A red glow here and there to mark a tryst.

quotations.author: Richard Dawkins
quotations.passage: But, for the most part, we shall mark our progress to the dawn of life by the measure of those 40 natural milestones, the trysts that enrich our pilgrimage.
quotations.work: The Ancestor's Tale: A Pilgrimage to the Dawn of Life

quotations.author: John Buchan
quotations.passage: He said he was jealous, and craved something to ease his care. 'It's but a small thing I ask,' says he, 'but it will make me a happy man, and nothing ever shall come atween us. Tryst wi' me for Beltane's E'en on the Sker sands, at the green link o' the burn where the sands begin, on the ebb o' the tide when midnight is by, but afore cockcrow. For,' said he, 'that was our forbears' tryst for true lovers, and wherefore no for you and me?'

tryst.title: tryst

etymologies: From Latin tumēscēns (“swelling, bloating”).

definitions.text: Swollen or distended with fluid, as of erectile tissue.
Inflated or overblown.

quotations.author: Arlene Croce
quotations.passage: I think that in Gloria MacMillan uses this tumescent language for a comparatively modest purpose — to show how it was between men and women in the war — and the language inflates and perverts his meaning unconscionably.

tumescent.title: tumescent

etymologies: Borrowed from Latin tumidus (“swollen”).

definitions.text: Swollen, enlarged, bulging.
Cancerous, unhealthy.
Pompous, bombastic.

quotations.author: Thomas Carlyle
quotations.passage: Tumid blustering, with more or less of sincerity, which need not be entirely sincere, yet the sincerer the better, is like to go far.

tumid.title: tumid

examples: turbid water
turbid wine
definitions.text: Having the lees or sediment disturbed; not clear.
Smoky or misty.
Unclear; confused; obscure.

quotations.passage: On the 6th October, the 18th day of her illness, she presented the following phenomena: — pulse small and quick — urine yellow and turbid.

quotations.author: Edward Bulwer-Lytton
quotations.passage: He seeks in vain to occupy his days with rural pursuits; he to whom the excitements of a metropolis, with all its corruption and its vices, were the sole sources of the turbid stream that he called "pleasure!"

quotations.author: Jukka A. Räty
quotations.passage: This makes the estimation of the refractive index of the turbid liquid quite problematic.

quotations.author: Jeff Sparrow
quotations.passage: The resulting impression filled with turbid mash liquor, which was hand-pumped through a tube into a separate kettle.
quotations.work: Wild Brews: Beer Beyond the Influence of Brewer's Yeast

quotations.author: Marten Scheffer
quotations.passage: In the turbid state, the development of submerged vegetation is prevented by low underwater light levels.

quotations.author: Joseph Priestley
quotations.passage: Towards the last I increased the heat, and by that means produced a very turbid air, of which I collected a prodigious quantity.

quotations.author: Agnes Christina Laut
quotations.passage: Involuntarily, he stepped behind some alder brush off the trail. Another flutter of wind thinning the turbid mist.

quotations.author: Thad Godish
quotations.passage: The turbid air over major cities is often described as a dust dome.

quotations.author: Adrian Mackenzie
quotations.passage: Motion, to take a good example, is originally a turbid sensation, of which the native shape is perhaps best preserved in the phenomenon of vertigo.

quotations.author: Julia James
quotations.passage: Those turbid emotions swirled inside him again—part frustration, part anxiety.

quotations.author: Cecilia Muratori
quotations.passage: In the aforementioned paragraph 406 of the Encyclopedia, magnetic ecstasy is described as a confused and turbid experience because its content does not present itself in rational form: for this reason the state of the somnambulist should not be considered as a possible path to cognition (Erkenntnis).

turbid.title: turbid

etymologies: From Latin turgidus (“swollen, inflated”), from turgeō (“to swell”).

examples: I have a turgid limb.
definitions.text: Distended beyond the natural state by some internal agent, especially fluid, or expansive force.
Of a river, inundated with excess water as from a flood; swollen.
Overly complex and difficult to understand; grandiloquent; bombastic.

quotations.author: Harold McGee
quotations.passage: A vegetable that is fully moist and firm will seem both crisp and more tender than the same vegetable limp from water loss. When we bite down on a vegetable turgid with water, the already-stressed cell walls readily break and the cells burst open; in a limp vegetable, chewing compresses the walls together, and we have to exert much more pressure to break through them.
quotations.work: On Food and Cooking: The Science and Lore of the Kitchen

quotations.author: Christopher Paolini
quotations.passage: The Jiet River lay before them, as thick and turgid as a gorged snake, its crosshatched surface reflecting the same ghastly hue that pervaded the Burning Plains.

quotations.author: William Zinsser
quotations.passage: These were all basic tenets, but the principals wrote them down as if they had never heard them before—and maybe they hadn’t, or at least not for many years. Perhaps that’s why bureaucratic prose becomes so turgid, whatever the bureaucracy.

quotations.author: David Foster Wallace
quotations.passage: Sounding rather suspiciously like Professor H. Bloom’s turgid studies of artistic influenza […]

quotations.author: David Foster Wallace
quotations.passage: Published TV-scholarship sure reflects this mood. And the numbingly dull quality to most “literary” television analyses is due less to the turgid abstraction scholars employ to make television seem an OK object of aesthetic inquiry […]
